title: When you watch the acclaimed TV drama Time, remember this: I’ve seen inside our prisons and they are just as bleak | Alex South | The Guardian
description: The show depicts prisons as places characterised by violence and isolation, with no focus on rehabilitation. It’s depressingly accurate, says former prison officer Alex South
Author: Alex South
Headline: The show depicts prisons as places characterised by violence and isolation, with no focus on rehabilitation. It’s depressingly accurate, says former prison officer Alex South
Content: ‘Beautiful and ugly and exact, all at once.’ The cast of the latest series of Time.Photograph: BBC/BBC Studios/Peter MarleyView image in fullscreen‘Beautiful and ugly and exact, all at once.’ The cast of the latest series of Time.Photograph: BBC/BBC Studios/Peter MarleyOpinionPrisons and probationWhen you watch the acclaimed TV drama Time, remember this: I’ve seen inside our prisons and they are just as bleakAlex SouthThe show depicts prisons as places characterised by violence and isolation, with no focus on rehabilitation. It’s depressingly accurateAlex South is a former prison officer and the author of the memoirBehind These DoorsSun 18 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 12.37 EDTShareThenew series of Timeis not an easy watch. The opening seconds of Jimmy McGovern’s prison drama show a normal woman on a normal bus, as it drives up a normal road. But to the right of that road is a huge concrete wall, topped with barbed wire and CCTV cameras.The wall is only partly visible, just as prisons themselves tend to occupy a space towards the very edges of our thoughts. They exist, but not as part of normal life. But McGovern’s drama shows just how permeable that wall is.The show’s fictional young offender institution, HMYOI Alderwick, is a place that boils with anger. As new arrivals enter the prison, an officer tells them: “Keep going, ignore the noise.” As if you ever could. The sound of prisoners shouting and kicking their cell doors is an assault on the ears. Those scenes are louder than any headline, of which there are plenty these days; overcrowding, escapes from custody, thelatest early-release scheme. What McGovern does is crank the volume so loud it’s impossible to block out.The reality is that prisons are closer to us than they might seem. The Sentencing Act 2026 allows prisoners serving standard determinate sentences to be released after serving only a third of their sentence in custody. The early-release scheme is intended to help relieve the prison capacity crisis, but as therecent recall ratedemonstrates, this solution is temporary.Many of the boys in Time would not be eligible for early release. Murder, manslaughter and rape are among the stated exemptions. But the value of time in prison is not only determined by its length, but by how it is spent. Just as David Tennant’s character bemoans the lack of training or education for young men in custody, so do prison staff across the country. They know what is blindingly obvious: angry people don’t come out of prison less angry if they’ve been banged up for 23 hours a day.Life inside Alderwick demonstrates the futility of keeping people locked up for hours on end, isolated from one another and with nothing to do. The culture of “keep-aparts” is firmly entrenched in many English prisons, particularly those housing young adults. “Keep aparts” are as they sound; groups of prisoners who are quite literally kept apart, often due to gang issues or postcode wars. Prisoners known to have conflict with others end up with a long list of “keep-aparts” on their file. They must associate separately from their “keep aparts” – they cannot attend the gym, education or visits with anyone on that list. This results in staggered regimes that are increasingly complex to manage. Rather than everyone having three or four hours out a day, each group only has one hour.Short-term, this works. But in the long-term, this stifling conflict-management tactic only exacerbates division and violence.View image in fullscreenDavid Tennant and Louis McCartney in Time.Photograph: BBC/BBC Studios/Peter MarleyIn Time, an officer suggests a solution to this issue – perhaps all new entrants could be told that, from now on, they would have to associate with everyone living in their unit. No more “keep aparts”. The governor’s response is: “We’ll park that one for now.” But that’s the problem. We are parking it and never coming back. We are releasing people from prison but not addressing the issues that put them there in the first place. Letting people out early was inevitable; prisons are full. But when80% of all offending in England and Wales is reoffending, it suggests only a small minority come out changed for the better.Most institutions are depressingly similar to Alderwick: no education, no libraries, with prisoners barely allowed any time out of their cells at all. A report this year onchildren in custodyfound that, at almost every establishment in the youth custody estate, prisoners were locked behind their doors for as long as 19 hours a day. The overstretched,understaffed systemdoes not allow for integration, socialisation, healthy forms of argument and discussion, or opportunities for conflict resolution. If it did, perhaps early release might not feel like such a bad thing.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBeing banished to a place characterised by violence and being locked up may seem an appropriate punishment for criminals. But on release day, the only ones being punished are us. Because those angry boys who fight and kick and slash, the ones with the baby faces and sprinkling of acne, are the same boys who grow into men behind that imposing wall. They are the same boys who board that normal bus on that normal road, right next to you and I.This series of Time is beautiful and ugly and exact, all at once. The least realistic bit is the surplus of toilet roll in one boy’s cell. There’s never enough toilet roll inside. But the major flaw of the show is that it only lasts three episodes. Because the boys represented in those fictionalised prisons are still banged up in the real ones, while the rest of us ignore the noise.Alex South is a former prison officer and the author of the memoirBehind These DoorsExplore more on these topicsPrisons and probationOpinionUK criminal justiceTelevisionDavid TennantDramacommentShareReuse this content

title: The problem with telling people the world is ending | Climate crisis | The Guardian
description: In the face of terrible crises, it can feel right to shock people into action. But what if that has the opposite effect?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: In the face of terrible crises, it can feel right to shock people into action. But what if that has the opposite effect?
Content: Illustration: Elia BarbieriView image in fullscreenIllustration: Elia BarbieriThe big ideaClimate crisisThe problem with telling people the world is endingIn the face of terrible crises, it can feel right to shock people into action. But what if that has the opposite effect?Jay Van BavelSun 18 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 07.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThese days, it’s easy to succumb to hopelessness. Whether you’re thinking about the climate crisis, the prospect of AI apocalypse, war or political turmoil, the list of challenges facing humanity can seem insurmountable.It certainly feels unprecedented, and much of it may be. The sense of impending doom, on the other hand, is nothing new. And what we have learned from the past is that doomerism can lead to paralysis. If everyone freezes, then nothing changes – but if we want to have a chance of mitigating some of the threats I’ve mentioned then action is what’s required.In 1947,The Bulletin of the Atomic Scientistscreated an infamous magazine cover with a “Doomsday Clock”. The hands move closer to midnight whenever events push humanity a little closer to catastrophe. They move back when we make the world a little safer. The original setting was seven minutes to midnight, and the hands are now a mere 85 seconds away.The Doomsday Clock was a particularly memorable form of crisis communication. The idea was to wake people from their day-to-day routines and help them realise the grave risks facing us. As such, it stands in a long tradition of debate about how to inform, warn and inspire members of the public to take action.On one end of the spectrum are the doomers. These are often activists and whistleblowers who feel a genuine sense of dread about imminent disaster, and want to inspire the same alarm in others. Recently, former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxonmade headlinesby arguing that frontier AI models pose an existential risk to humanity.At the other end are critics who tend to dismiss these calls as either overblown or self-serving. These folks argue that hyperbolic claims either lead to needless panic or distract from more important issues.I find myself in a third camp of people who harbour sincere concerns about the problems facing humanity, but worry that feelings of dread will immobilise people. Inaction is a sensible response if you are led to believe that we are past the point of no return, or that the scope of the problem is so immense that anything you do won’t make a difference.The problem with doomerism isn’t necessarily that the risks are exaggerated, but that it may create a self-fulfilling prophecy – by engendering helplessness, rather than galvanising people.This aspect of human psychology has been well known for many years by experts on persuasion. When people hear messages designed toappeal to our fears, theycanbe moved to take action. But this only tends to work as a one-off, and only then when the messages convey a sense of efficacy – a belief that it’s still possible to make a difference. By contrast, if people are inundated with scary and overwhelming stories about the climate or AI, they tune out. Like the boy who cried wolf, those bearing these messages can quickly find themselves ignored.A big problem for us now, then, is that the modern information ecosystem tends to reinforce negativity. For decades, a core principle in the news business has been “if it bleeds, it leads”. This came from an understanding among journalists that humans are drawn to bad news. This principle now dominates what you see online.My colleagues and I looked at traffic to news stories onUpworthy.com. This was a website that became famous for conducting A/B tests of headlines to see which one drove clicks, and then using the most popular headline.We analysed 22,743 of these mini-experimentsand found that each additional negative word in a headline increased clicks by 2.3%. Psychologists call this the negativity bias: bad is more attention-grabbing than good.So how does consuming these stories affect our behaviour? We tested the impact of negative messaging around climate in amassive studywith 59,440 participants in 63 countries. We had climate experts create 11 different messages to determine exactly which of them changed beliefs and mobilised people to take real action.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markIf we want to motivate people in the face of dire threats, we must give them a reason to hopeThe messages included emphasising scientific consensus (for example, noting that “99% of expert climate scientists” agree on the facts), social norms (stating that a majority of people in each nation was concerned), consequences for one’s region (emphasising the increased frequency and severity of wildfires and floods) or the effects of climate change on future generations (asking participants to imagine writing a letter about their actions regarding the climate crisis that would be read by people decades from now).We also included a text loaded with doom and gloom that told participants: “If your anxiety about climate change is dominated by fears of starving polar bears, glaciers melting and sea levels rising, you are barely scratching the surface of what terrors are possible, even within the lifetime of a young adult today. And yet the swelling seas – and the cities they will drown – have so dominated the picture of climate change/global warming that they have blinded us to other threats, many much closer at hand and much more catastrophic …”This terrifying passage was the one that proved most effective at getting people to spread it on the internet or social media. But like other fear appeals, it failed in inspiring real action: it was the single worst message for getting people to make the time and effort to mitigate climate effects – by planting trees, for example. It also failed to increase belief in the climate emergency or support for climate policies.This absolutely doesn’t mean we should avoid sharing the facts about the climate crisis. The message that emphasised the overwhelming scientific consensus noted that the “Earth is warming and climate change is happening” due to human activity. It was more effective than negativity on every outcome we measured, except for sharing on the internet. It conveyed the facts in a sober manner, with the backing of 99% of climate scientists.What this shows is that, instead of making people feel inept and miserable, we need to take the exact opposite approach. Scientific consensus isn’t the only powerfully motivating message. My PhD student Danielle Goldwert has found that telling people about the potentialemotional benefitsof climate action – such as increased hope and connection – makes them significantly more likely to take action, be it political participation, advocacy, donating money to climate causes or changing their lifestyle.If we want to motivate people in the face of dire threats, we must give them a reason to hope. Without that, we are destined to doomscroll while the world burns.Jay Van Bavel is a professor of psychology and neural science at New York University.Further readingNot the End of the Worldby Hannah Ritchie (Vintage, £18.99Hope in the Darkby Rebecca Solnit (Canongate, £10.99)The Future We Chooseby Christiana Figueres and Tom Rivett-Carnac (Vintage, £12.99)Explore more on these topicsClimate crisisThe big ideafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: I saw rioting, looting, above all, anger. If French leaders think more violence will solve this, they’re mistaken  | Oliver Haynes | The Guardian
description: It’s a perfect storm of protesters with heartfelt grievances and others set on conflict. The key here is the sense of betrayal that united them on the streets, says journalist Oliver Haynes
Author: Oliver Haynes
Headline: It’s a perfect storm of protesters with heartfelt grievances and others set on conflict. The key here is the sense of betrayal that united them on the streets, says journalist Oliver Haynes
Content: Clashes between protesters and the French police at Place de la République in Paris, 17 October 2026.Photograph: Abitbol Shana/ABACA/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenClashes between protesters and the French police at Place de la République in Paris, 17 October 2026.Photograph: Abitbol Shana/ABACA/ShutterstockOpinionFranceI saw rioting, looting, above all, anger. If French leaders think more violence will solve this, they’re mistakenOliver HaynesIt’s a perfect storm of protesters with heartfelt grievances and others set on conflict. The key here is the sense of betrayal that united them on the streetsSun 18 Oct 2026 11.06 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 11.58 EDTShareThe first thing I learned on the streets ofParisthis weekend is that there is no arguing with teargas. I arrived at Place de la République just after 1pm yesterday. The mood was festive until police started firing volleys of teargas into the square from Rue du Faubourg-du-Temple.I didn’t see the inciting incident – if there even was one – and tried walking into the cloud of CS gas hanging in the air. It was impossible. The gas clings to your nose and burns your eyes, and you quickly start struggling to breathe. I retreated towards the Boulevard de Magenta, blinking furiously to stop the stinging.This approach to the crowd had been adopted by the authorities early in the day, causing chaos across the city and setting the tone for what would follow. A friend had to return to her home with her elderly parents because police had fired teargas “at random” at a crowd of young people in Strasbourg-Saint-Denis in the 10th arrondissement.I headed back up the Boulevard de Magenta. There I met protesters including a student at the Sorbonne, who had come to “support the highschoolers first and foremost, and to demand more money in public schools, from primary schools to universities”. Another major factor that he said had motivated him to come out on to the street “was the repression faced by highschoolers, who are under 18”, such asan incident in Lens, where a police grenade blew a 15-year-old’s hand to bits.Other protesters I spoke to came from various sections of society: young, old, white and from ethnic minority backgrounds. People were there in their capacity as workers in a union, students in a lycée or individual citizens who had come out in anger at the rising cost of living. The price of petrol, the original motivating factor behind the 2018gilets jaunes(yellow vest) movement, had prompted several people to come out after it hit a record €2.4 per litre at the end of last month.This section of the protest was completely peaceful, marching away from République, making lots of noise and climbing on scaffolding to fly flags, but otherwise doing nothing beyond articulating political demands. Between 550,000 and 800,000 peopletook to the streets across Franceas part of protests like these.When I returned to République around 4pm, I saw that the situation had descended into chaos. Stun grenades were exploding everywhere, and protesters were throwing bottles at the police. Smoke from a blazing car filled the air. A branch of Nicolas, a chain wine shop, had its window smashed in and black-clad protesters looted it – not for the wine but for missiles to throw at police in retaliation for the stun grenades.I was unable to stop and talk to people amid this fury, but my sense was that this was a combination of black bloc – anarchists who come out to many protests to cause trouble –gilets jaunes, young and middle-aged people who were furious at the government and the police, and, of course, opportunistic young men looking for a scrap. As ever with street protests, many people, many motivations.There were cries of the oldgilets jaunessloganMacron Démission(“Resign Macron”). Beyond the organised group of hobbyist rioters, the dominant emotions seemed to be fear and rage. With each stun grenade the non-violent parts of the crowd were thrown into panic, but would then regroup and stand their ground while the rioters continued throwing missiles. Perhaps the feeling could be summed up by a poster I saw the day before the protest: “Lost hope, 17/10 to find it again. Fuck just about everything 17/10. We are already in hell meet on 17/10”.So what next? Withmore than 1,800 arrests, what will become of these people, this movement, these riots?There is a sense among certain parts of the French population that making enough noise, including acts of vandalism, sends a signal to power. And indeed, there is some evidence to suggest this is the case. Neoliberal reforms have been rebuffed successfully on several occasions inFrance, primarily through strike waves or roundabout blockades – though these too had the presence of a radical fringe, willing to set fire to things.As the dust settles, what will be the political repercussions? Marine Le Pen, attempting to profit from the situation, has positioned herself on the side of those angry at the cost of living, while condemning the looters.In a statementshe described the French people as caught between the “austerity and fiscal hammering of those in power and the insurrectionary activists”. She promised to “free” the French “from Macronist toxic policies and protect them from the violence of the far left”. Carefully omitted was the fact that her party is proposing deeper austerity than even the Macronists, but the images of fire and looting that will be broadcast on every news channel reinforce her narrative of restoration of order to the streets.Meanwhile, the French left, chiefly represented by Jean-Luc Mélenchon, is defending the protesters and seeking to channel their anger into the presidential campaign, focusing on the violence of the police over that of the rioters. The left may also be able to make gains from this tense situation.While the government seems determined to continue with its budget unimpeded, it may only be a matter of time before another such explosion occurs. You can’t argue with teargas, but it will only hold the inevitable at bay for so long.Oliver Haynes is a journalist and co-host of Sacré Bleu: the French presidential election podcastDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsFranceOpinionProtestGilets jaunes protestsEuropeParisYoung peoplecommentShareReuse this content

title: Forty years on from the tragic killing of Ahmed Iqbal Ullah, activists call for renewed fight against the far right | Race | The Guardian
description: The racist murder of a British-Bengali schoolboy was a landmark moment. Now campaigners seek to build a multiracial alliance to combat the challenges of today
Author: Chris Osuh
Headline: The racist murder of a British-Bengali schoolboy was a landmark moment. Now campaigners seek to build a multiracial alliance to combat the challenges of today
Content: Ahmed Iqbal Ullah was attacked on the playground of Burnage high school, Manchester in 1986.Composite: Ahmed Iqbal Ullah RACE CentreView image in fullscreenAhmed Iqbal Ullah was attacked on the playground of Burnage high school, Manchester in 1986.Composite: Ahmed Iqbal Ullah RACE CentreCotton Capital: ongoing seriesRaceForty years on from the tragic killing of Ahmed Iqbal Ullah, activists call for renewed fight against the far rightThe racist murder of a British Bengali schoolboy was a landmark moment. Now campaigners seek to build a multiracial alliance to combat the challenges of todayChris OsuhCommunity affairs correspondentSun 18 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTShare“For my brother Ahmed, British values meant standing up for others. It was doing right. It was supporting and looking after the underdog, whoever that may be, regardless of their colour or background,” Selina Ullah says, of the brother she lost to a senseless act of violence 40 years ago.Ahmed Iqbal Ullah, a British Bengali schoolboy, was 13 when he was murdered in a racist attack in the playground of Burnage high school, in south Manchester, in 1986, after defending young pupils from bullying.Ahmed’s murder – by a 13-year-old white British pupil who was sentenced to the youth equivalent of life, was a landmark moment. The Macdonald inquiry into the racism and racial violence inManchesterschools that surrounded Ahmed’s death sparked a national debate about antiracism in education.Forty years on, Ahmed’s memory is at the heart of theAhmed Iqbal Ullah RACE Centre(AIU), which houses archives on Black figures in Manchester, community history on events such as Manchester carnival, and pan-African activism in the city and beyond.The 1970s concept of“political Blackness”– the idea of a strategic multiracial alliance across groups affected by racism – fell out of favour in the 1990s, as it became seen as an inadequate reflection of differing experiences.View image in fullscreenSelina Ullah at home in Keighley, West Yorkshire.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianBut the story of AIU speaks to the power of solidarity across communities. Since it was founded in 1987 in Ahmed’s memory byLou Kushnick, a Jewish-American professor at theUniversity of Manchester – with teacher Jackie Ould as its education co-ordinator – it has provided archivists, teachers and campaigners with the inspiration and resources to document under-recorded Black, antiracist and migration histories, fight social injustice and push for greater representation in education.A memorial event, The Legacy of Ahmed: 40 years on, was held last month. It was attended by Ahmed’s family, AIU’s head, Maya Sharma, justice campaigners from 1986, including lawyer Robert Lizar, and a new generation of antiracism activists.At the event it was argued that “political Blackness” – the framework in which AIU was founded – had a new relevance in the face of a resurgent far right.Zara Manoehoetoe, a youth worker with Manchester antiracism organisation Kids of Colour, said: “Politically black is the note that we have to ground ourselves in, because anti-blackness manifests for all of us.“We are working with young people from acrossGreater Manchester… The international context lives in their DNA, it lives in their homes, it lives at the kitchen table, it lives in the food that their mothers and their nanas are putting on their plates.”The writer and film-maker Tariq Mehmood was a speaker on the panel alongside Manoehoetoe.In 1986 Mehmood joined the justice campaign, spearheaded by Selina Ullah, which preceded the Macdonald inquiry.Mehmood urged activists today to move offline and into grassroots organising across communities, amid a “continuing struggle” against racism in the UK and genocide in Gaza.He added: “We were not victims [in the 1980s]. We educated ourselves. We organised youth movements. We organised workers’ organisations. That’s Indians, that’s Pakistanis, that’s Bangladeshis, that’s Africans, a whole plethora of anti-imperialist organisations … and in that context, we were Black.”Prof Gus John, who served on the panel for the Macdonald inquiry and co-authored the book of the report, Murder in the Playground, was among speakers at the memorial event.John said of the inquiry and the book: “What we were saying was it was important that schools have a responsibility to teach children and enable them to understand racism, how it operates in society and how they could be implicated in perpetuating it.“Kenneth Baker [then education secretary] refused to accept the report, refused to raise the matter in parliament, and refused to put this book in the House of Commons library. Roll on 40 years … and every day, we hear more and more stories of racist incidents.”View image in fullscreenMaya Sharma, the head of the Ahmed Iqbal Ullah RACE Centre.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianNika Muthra-Shah, the director of educational innovation at the Rekindle Collective, the Black-led supplementary schools programme, spoke of how young people are “feeling a lot of anger and a lot of fear about the rise of the far right”, and how the collective was countering it through youth empowerment, education in critical thinking and encouraging dialogue.The memories of speakers who were at school with Ahmed highlighted how racism – and the fight against it – shape young lives.From the audience at the memorial event Naeem, who was in the playground the day Ahmed was stabbed, said: “Ahmed was a very good friend. I was sometimes jealous of him because he used to wear the best clobber – Adidas tracksuits, like Run DMC!“[When Ahmed was killed] we didn’t get any help or support from nobody, and we just got on with our life. After then, my life just deteriorated, I wasn’t bothered with school, I was fighting, I was suspended, I became racially abusive towards people. I turned my life around, [but] it’s always in my heart.”Pervez Iqbal, who was a year older than Ahmed at Burnage High and part of the original justice campaign, was inspired by the tragedy to pursue a career in education.He said: “We grew up very quickly when in reality we were still children who needed some guidance. Those experiences eventually gave me the determination to do something positive in my life. I studied, became a teacher and eventually I returned back to Burnage where I worked for 23 years.“Schools and communities can change, education can change attitudes, and people working together can create something better for the next generation. My message for today is simple. Never forget Ahmed [or] our responsibility to educate, guide, and protect people.”In October, Home Office figures revealed racially and religiously motivated offences havereached record highs in the UK. Police recorded 146,825 hate crimes in the year ending March 2026 – a rise of 7% in the past year. Offences targeting Muslims increased the most – up 15%, from 4,479 to 5,132.Explore more on these topicsRaceCotton Capital: ongoing seriesManchesterGreater ManchesterFar rightActivismfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘4,000 people minding our own business’: four decades on, Falklands again face a hostile Argentina | Falkland Islands | The Guardian
description: Facing a slump in the polls, Argentina’s president is making economic attacks on the islands’ oil industry, and suggesting its key fisheries industry could be next
Author: Daniel Boffey
Headline: Facing a slump in the polls, Argentina’s president is making economic attacks on the islands’ oil industry, and suggesting its key fisheries industry could be next
Content: A Falklands flag flies over the road from Mount Pleasant to Stanley.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA Falklands flag flies over the road from Mount Pleasant to Stanley.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianThe Sunday readFalkland Islands‘4,000 people minding our own business’: four decades on, Falklands again face a hostile ArgentinaFacing a slump in the polls, Argentina’s president is making economic attacks on the islands’ oil industry, and suggesting its key fisheries industry could be nextDaniel Boffeyin Port Stanley, Falkland Islands; photographs and video bySean SmithSun 18 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 11.26 EDTShareA dozen local people and a uniformed military police officer (“Do you mind if I sit in?”) took their seats at the back of the handsome wood-panelled courtroom that doubles as the Falkland Islands’ legislative assembly. Outside, it was a typically blowy early evening. It may nominally be spring in the south Atlantic, but Stanley harbour, with its dark grey water speckled with historical shipwrecks, was a cauldron of swells and churn.Six of the assembly’s eight members – five men, one woman – waited patiently at a row of desks and microphones. The heating had been turned up to just short of uncomfortable. Behind them, a portrait of King Charles. From the other walls, dusty photographs of governors peered down on the scene.The Falkland Islands, home to approximately 3,600 residentsProceedings started at the raised hand of a bored-looking young man wearing headphones in the corner. He was transmitting the question and answer session via radio across the dozen or so inhabited islands that make up the 778-strong archipelago.It was not clear how many of the Falklands’ 3,600 residents were listening in from their farm houses out in the diddle-dee shrub that coats much of the islands, or in the front rooms of Port Stanley’s white clapboard cottages with the pretty coloured roofs; likely not on a par with the number who learned 44 years ago from the Falkland Islands broadcasting station that their lands had been invaded.“There’s no turning back, we can expect them by dawn,” the governor, Rex Hunt, had said then.But for those who did tune in on Monday evening, there was much to dwell on. Not so much the answers about the local internet contract or the consultation on the contentious plan for a salmon farm.“I have another one for you,” piped up one enthusiastic quizzer with a heavy local accent, a West Country burr with a slight antipodean lift. That intervention prompted a little shuffling of tired bums. But a rather more significant announcement was to come.View image in fullscreenAssembly members Roger Spink, Stacy Bragger and Lewis Clifton before the monthly meeting.Lewis Clifton, an assembly member who can date his family’s residence on the Falklands to the late 1870s, advised the islanders that an unprecedented economic war was being waged against them – a community no bigger than an English village – by a country of 46 million people.“I am concerned that the level of Argentinian thrust this time has been at a different level,” Clifton said. “Perhaps a more vehement and belligerent tone than [seen since] 1982, because it has the potential to threaten our very economic development.”Facing a downturn in his domestic polling and with an upcoming election, Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, has legislated to criminalise companies and individuals involved in the Falklands’ nascent oil industry, and suggested the fisheries industry on which it currently relies for its prosperity could be next.The British forces capability at Mount Pleasant airbase – 1,800 personnel there and on Ascension island, four typhoon jets, a ground-based air defence system and with HMS Medway patrolling the waters – makes a military threat from Argentina largely hypothetical. But Buenos Aires has launched a full spectrum attack of another sort.View image in fullscreenAerial view of a new port and floating jetty being built in the Falkland Islands.In response this week, Andy Burnham and his foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, restated the UK’s solidarity with the islanders’ desire to remain British, and promised legislation that might offer some protection against the financial damage imposed by Argentina’s economic sanctions. Interpolreceived Foreign Office representationssuggesting they reject an Argentinian request for arrests relating to the dispute.For the islanders, it was a welcome show of muscularity. They have never felt entirely confident in the spine of those in power back on the homeland. It was arguably the indifference of Westminster that led Argentina to launch its invasion in the first place back in 1982.“I have never trusted the Foreign Office and I have been proven right,” said Norma Edwards, 84, whose husband, Roger, 80, a former Royal Marine, was attached to the SAS in the 1982 conflict. “Catching up time,” said Clifton, of what he saw as a belated toughness from London this week. But things remain precarious.View image in fullscreenRicky Evans, who runs a guesthouse and other businesses, carries post and supplies for Pebble Island.The Falkland Islands might be described as a British success story. Four decades ago, there were 1,800 inhabitants, and its tiny wool-centric economy, 300 miles (480km) east of mainland South America, was dependent on UK government handouts.Today the population, growing at 3% year-on-year in recent times, includes about 70 different nationalities, attracted by the 26% top rate of tax, good pay and opportunities in a growing and entirely self-reliant economy.There are Zimbabweans who came to de-mine after the war. Construction workers from South Africa who came to rebuild. Chileans who found something they liked after taking a Latam Airlines flight. The largest minority group is the Filipinos, who came to work in social care and the service industry in the late 1980s and 90s.View image in fullscreenChilean tourists pose for a photograph outside the Stanley post office.Working behind the bar at Groovy’s, a Nepalese waiter said he had come from Dubai. The money was better in the Falklands, he said, and “the people are nicer”. “The locals start at Deano’s bar, then it’s the Victory bar and here – then it is the Globe, for dancing,” he said with a smile. “After that they go to house parties.”Such has been the Falklands’ success in attracting people that a permanent residency scheme, capped at 90 people a year, has been frozen for 12 months. The islands, for all their challenges, are somewhere people want to be.View image in fullscreenJohn Barton, chair of the Falkland Islands fishing companies association and James Bates, the executive secretary.All of this had been made possible because of squid, said John Barton, chair of the fishing companies association. “It has been transformational,” he said.In 1986, the UK allowed the Falklands to establish a 200-nautical-mile exclusive fishing zone in which those wanting to operate had to be licensed by the islands’ government. Licences sold to fleets of Spanish, Korean and Taiwanese “jiggers” have delivered major revenues, but the locals are increasingly running the vessels too.The islands’ gross domestic production per capita soared as a result, from about £2,000 in 1982 to £85,000 in 2025, putting the islands sixth in the world league table, just behind Norway. The tourism industry is also going strong, with 75,000 or more people spilling out of cruise ships every year at Stanley port, but that is at best a nice addition.View image in fullscreenJames Wallace, who runs the Fortuna fishing company, onboard his harbour launch.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA worker packs filleted toothfish into plastic bags at a Falkland Islands processing factory.James Wallace, 41, is chief executive of Fortuna, the largest fishing company on the island. It is a growing operation, which last year acquired Cornwall’s oldest fishing business, the Ocean Fish Group. But he is diversifying his business for a reason.The squid populations in the Falklands waters, on which his company and the islands rely, are hugely variable and it is clear that “catches are declining”, he said. “We have commissioned a bunch of inshore work to see what is happening but the answer is that we don’t yet know,” he said. But there is another natural resource on which the islanders’ hopes are pinned.View image in fullscreenA bust of Margaret Thatcher by the 1982 war memorial.About 136 miles north of the Falkland Islands, work is continuing at pace on the Sea Lion oil project led by Israeli firm Navitas and its British partner, Rockhopper Exploration.Independent estimates suggest the offshore oil field could triple the Falkland Islands’ GDP and deliver a Norway-style sovereign wealth fund. The companies involved remain confident that drilling will commence within months. A new jetty is busy with activity. But the impact of Argentinian pressure cannot be discounted. Two major contractors recently pulled out of the project.View image in fullscreenChief executive of the Falklands government, Andrea Clausen, in the room where Argentinian forces surrendered.Andrea Clausen, as chief executive of the Falklands government, its top civil servant, works from a building on Thatcher Drive. Her office is opposite the room where Brig Gen Mario Menéndez signed Argentina’s letter of surrender on 14 June 1982. The letter remains on the wall.Clausen was 10 at the time of the invasion and remembers the Argentinian solders’ arrival. She also recalls cowering with her family in their home in Goose Green, 60 miles west of Stanley, as the British Harrier jets came in with their cluster bombs. “Even now I struggle to cope with the sound of fast jets,” she said.Clausen sees trauma throughout the islands. “I guess, some extreme behaviour,” she said. “Anger, aggression on certain political subjects.” She is evidently frustrated by the recent Argentinian actions.“The Falklands has since [19]82 ensured that we are financially independent – save for defence,” she said. “We had no money in 82 and we never want to be in that position again.”The oil is their insurance, she suggested. “I like to think that better people will de-escalate this because, honestly, we are 4,000 people minding our own business, we have a history deeper and older than theirs.”View image in fullscreenFalkland Islands reserves (from left): Cpl Chris Stenning; Justin McPhee, director of emergency services; Lt Alastair Baylis; and warrant officer second class Paul Watson.There are cycles to Argentinian bellicosity. The opportunistic but ill-fated invasion ordered by Argentina’s dictator general Leopoldo Galtieri, leading to the death of 649 Argentinians and 255 British military personnel, along with three islanders, has cast a pall over Argentinian-UK relations ever since.But at times, notably in the 1990s, Buenos Aires adopted a hearts-and-minds approach to the islanders, sending videos of the animated series Pingu to their children. Such kindness has tended to evaporate away, though, when an Argentinian government is losing public support at home, as Milei is experiencing now.But if any one attribute sums up the islanders, it is resilience, said Dot Gould, an assembly member who owns Pebble, a 20-mile long island north-west of the Falklands. She and her husband share the island with a couple who run a lodge, 5,000 sheep, 100 cattle, a load of spectacular wildlife, but not much else.View image in fullscreenDot Gould, who owns Pebble island.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianRampaging around the undulating terrain in her 4x4 vehicle, avoiding colonies of Rockhopper and Gentoo penguins, Gould points out the scattered remains of an Argentinian fighter jet and the graves of two of the airmen killed during battle. As a child on Pebble, she used to play with the parachutes left by the Argentinians, using them as sails for a go-kart.“I think, since 1982, this is probably the most serious it’s been for us,” she said. “How effective they will be, we don’t know yet … it’s almost two fingers up: we’ll get on with it, we have to.” But there is much that they want to do.The islands are dependent on a narrow range of freight links from the UK and South America for much of their fresh produce. Any glitch, and peculiar shortages can emerge. There was a period without milk. A time without beer. During one cherry tomato shortage, which saw their price shoot up, the main supermarket opted to cut them in half and sell them like that to spread the joy.A sorry-looking cabbage will set you back £8 at the West Store on the front. The local newspaper is the Penguin News (“This one’s not for Penguin News but …” is the traditional opening when disseminating islands gossip). But Facebook is the key means of communication. “Grown men and women use Snapchat like teenagers, often to arrange their extramarital affairs,” said one local.View image in fullscreenChildren during school lunch break.Other peculiarities include the Falklands government paying for children from the age of 16 to complete their secondary and university education in the UK. The size of the islands’ population makes it impractical to offer such levels of education at home, said Sarah Stannard, the islands’ director of education.But if the oil money comes online, she would rebuild the primary school. Children from the countryside – it is known locally as “camp” – are offered board in Stanley, although there are also peripatetic teachers and lessons done on the telephone.The children grow up quickly here, and tend to be keen to broaden their horizons. Oliver Lee, 15, was keen to join the merchant navy. “I would like to see other places,” he said. “The Mediterranean, hotter places basically.” Layla-May Vatemanu, 14, said: “A lot of the boys especially in my class do a lot of sport. Our [friendship group] doesn’t have a lot to do.”View image in fullscreenSchool students (from left): Oliver Lee, Layla May, Tessa Blake and Paul Green.There are no bus services anywhere, and the more distant parts of the islands are only accessible via boat or the Falkland government’s twin-engine aircraft service. On a landmass half the size of Wales, there is only one cashpoint.Touch rugby – rather than full-contact rugby – is played, in part because the islands’ hospital does not have the capability to deal with complex injuries. Much of the health budget goes on medi-evacs to South America. Yet, for all that, most of the children who leave at 16 do return.All places are shaped by their history and geography, but some have more history and geography than others. “We are British with a twist,” said Stacy Bragger, a former journalist who represents the Stanley constituency in the assembly.“We have our own identity. If you were to ask what are the traits of a Falkland islander – resourcefulness, resilience, making do. Because if something breaks you can’t just go down the road. You have to make do. That’s our version of Britishness.”View image in fullscreenMike Summers (left) and Liam Short, members of the chamber of commerce.The islanders also have long memories. “I used to read the Guardian when I was a good deal younger,” said Mike Summers, 73, who sits on the board of the local chamber of commerce. “But I stopped reading it in 1982 when [the editor] Peter Preston just fucked me off so much. He was: ‘Oh well they are a long way away and there is only a few of them – so why don’t we just sell them?’”On the Argentinian rhetoric, Summers added: “There are a lot of people who still suffer effects from the war – PTSD among the older people. I bumped into someone at the supermarket the other day who I have known for ever. She said: ‘Oh, I’m wondering if I should sell my house and move away. The Argies are going to invade again.’ It seriously affects some people and it is cruel actually.”View image in fullscreenSocial influencer Roxy King-Clark at her home in Stanley.Roxy King-Clarke, 40, describes herself as the Falklands’ biggest influencer, with about 60,000 followers. She picked up a major following when posting in response to the Argentinian men’s football team brandishing a “Las Malvinas son Argentinas” [The Malvinas are Argentinian] banner at the World Cup.She is regularly subjected to abuse for her posts. “The most common insults are to call us pirates, usurpers and colonisers,” she said. “It’s a bizarre thing to be on the receiving end of it all as they speak like we’ve just tipped up here. I can trace my family back to my earliest ancestor arriving here in 1842.”Her generation too, she suggests, have taken lessons from what happened four decades ago. King-Clarke said she would take a “hard line” to avoid any misinterpretation. “We need to learn from history,” she said, “and not make the same mistakes.”

title: ‘This is horrifying. This is madness’: the row over competitive yoga | Yoga | The Guardian
description: Some yogis welcome the idea of competition – for others, it is anathema. Will those keen for yoga to become an Olympic sport win the argument?
Author: Anita Chaudhuri
Headline: Some yogis welcome the idea of competition – for others, it is anathema. Will those keen for yoga to become an Olympic sport win the argument?
Content: ‘It’s about how to excel while being still’ …Photograph: Anna Berkut/Alamy‘It’s about how to excel while being still’ …Photograph: Anna Berkut/AlamyYoga‘This is horrifying. This is madness’: the row over competitive yogaSome yogis welcome the idea of competition – for others, it is anathema. Will those keen for yoga to become an Olympic sport win the argument?Anita ChaudhuriSun 18 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVaishnavi Saravanakumar describes herself on Instagram as “India’s rubber band girl”.In a typical video post, dressed in a rhinestone-studded crimson catsuit and accompanied by a Bollywood-rap anthem, she demonstrates an improbable feat. From standing, she snakes into a deep back bend, curls her head and shoulders up under her tiger-striped calves, and finishes beaming to camera with ankles crossed under her chin. This is yoga as we have seldom seen it before.Earlier this year,the Indian government announcedthat it will push for yogasana’s inclusion in the Olympics, ahead of the country’s bid to host the 2036 Games. The news came the week before the inaugural World Yogasana Championship, held in Ahmedabad in June, at which Saravanakumar, a gold medallist, was one of 522 yogis competing.View image in fullscreenA balancing act … the first World Yogasana Championship in India in June.Olympics? World championships? It’s enough to make some of us choke on our Yogi tea. How can a 5,000-year-old practice that values self-awareness and letting go of external validation be a suitable forum for judging, point-scoring and, not to put too fine a point on it, showing off?In fact, in India, yoga competitions are nothing new. The first formal asana competition took place in 1973 in Calcutta (now Kolkata). Only recently, however, has it been pitched as entertainment for a global audience. At the championships in Ahmedabad, which ran over five days, 79 countries were represented, at a stadium with 2,000 spectators. The event wasbroadcast liveon national TV. Perusing the 269-page rulebook, there is even an anti-doping policy. For yoga.double quotation markIf Britain’s Got Talent can get such great ratings, I think these yogasana athletes can also do wondersUdit Sheth, president of Yogasana Bharat (Bharat being the traditional name for India), has spent years working to turn yoga into a global competitive sport. An entrepreneur involved in building and operating sports stadiums, it was his vision that brought the world championships to life. “My work in sport, and my own yoga practice, really made me interested in how we can package an ancient heritage in the right manner to take it to the Olympics,” he tells me over Zoom from his office in Mumbai. “But to be clear, we’ve coined the word ‘yogasana’ to describe it, not yoga. Yoga is a very wide practice that includes meditation and concentration. Asana [the physical postures] is only one part of theeight petalsof yoga.” The other petals, or “limbs” as they are also known, include moral vows, breathing techniques, meditation and enlightenment.While competitive yoga might make sense for limelight-seeking contestants, I’m sceptical about whether it will engage spectators. Might it not be a teensy bit boring? If Sheth is offended by the question, he doesn’t show it. “These talented athletes have remarkable strength, posture, balance and discipline. If America’s Got Talent and Britain’s Got Talent can be on television and get such great ratings, these yogasana athletes can also do wonders.”Would a fair comparison be gymnastics? “It’s a useful starting point,” he says. “Both practices demand strength, flexibility and coordination. Both involve assessment by judges. But the difference is that yogasana has a traditional solo event, a group event and a pair event. Unlike gymnastics, it is static. The challenge is to remain composed and controlled when you are in that posture. It’s not merely about reaching a difficult position, it’s about staying in it. It’s about how to excel while being still.”Some categories require athletes to maintain the full extent of the posture for 60 seconds. Maybe the thrill for the viewer comes from waiting for someone to fall over, I suggest. But Sheth believes the drama comes from watching people striving to excel. “The crowd becomes the judge. That’s where it becomes interesting. One routine of three minutes would have maybe seven or eight difficult postures. Asanas are categorised by difficulty and an objective code of points.”double quotation markWhen you see the contestants, it’s like you’re on the ramp for a fashion show. People want to look great on InstagramFurther nods to the entertainment industry come from the event’s hectic theme music with its driving bhangra beats and shouty vocals. Then there are the flamboyant costumes. “When you see the contestants, it’s almost like you’re on the ramp for a fashion show,” says Sheth. “There are sequins, and the female athletes take their makeup to the next level. People want to look great on Instagram. But we are careful to preserve cultural sensitivity; revealing clothing is not permitted. We can’t have women competing in bikinis.”Perhaps unsurprisingly, not all yogis approve. “It’s not even that I have an issue with people performing with their bodies and then calling it yoga for individual recognition and gain, or for cultural nationalism,” says longstanding UK-based yoga teacherDivya Kohli. “My problem is that the abiding foundations of yoga require that you are no longer a servant to your ego. That means you do not seek external approval. Measuring how someone does a posture on physical difficulty and awarding points for it? This is horrifying. This is madness.”Sheth suggests that turning yoga into a sport might encourage more young people to find their way back to traditional yogic principles.“The only way to get the youth of the world to understand the yogic way of life is to give them something exciting, to take it out of spirituality and into excitement, into sport.”How does he respond to charges that, by its very nature, yoga should not involve competition? “It’s a fair question that deserves a thoughtful answer,” he says. “Many people practise yoga because it gives them the space away from comparison and external judgment. What we are offering is a competitive pathway for people who want it. We are not forcing anyone to do it and we are not claiming to assess the whole of yoga, only the asanas, and only those that are agreed on. Also, if any sport is done right, the competition is within. It’s me versus me, it’s not me versus you. It’s how good I am today against how good I was two weeks ago.”Not everyone in India is happy with the direction of travel, though. In 2020, Yogasana Bharat became India’s national yoga federation. But after a legal challenge brought by the Yoga Federation of India (founded in 1974),in July this year the Delhi high court quashed Yogasana Bharat’s recognitionon the grounds that its status was granted by the Indian Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sportswhen it had been in existence for just three months. It held that this violated the national sports development code. The court ordered a fresh selection process of all eligible bodies, including the incumbent, which is continuing.There are further hoops to jump through before Olympic yoga can happen. World Yogasanahas 40 affiliates globally, including in Canada and various African nations, but it needs at least 50 across three continents to meet the International Olympic Committee’s recognition criteria. There is no affiliate yet in the UK and only a few in the rest of Europe (so far, Spain, Bulgaria, the Netherlands and Romania).View image in fullscreen‘I tell people to think of it more as a demonstration than a contest’ … Sam Cruickshank, president of GB Yoga Sport, photographed at House of Hot Yoga in north London.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianYoga competitions in the UK have largely emerged from London-based Bikram (hot) yoga studios. Sam Cruickshank, president of the Great BritainYogaSports Federation, says that at competition level, UK yoga sport is still in its infancy. “It is quite niche. At the national championships, we only get about 20 people competing.”He stresses that to compete in the UK, you don’t need to be an elite athlete and it is open to any style of yoga. “What makes it inspirational is you can be stiff, you can be injured. It doesn’t matter. You can do simpler postures in accessible versions. You can still enjoy being up on the podium. I tell people to think of it more as a demonstration than a contest.”Inevitably, Cruickshank finds himself having defensive conversations about competition with fellow yogis. “What I often say is that it’s not about making yoga competitive, it’s about taking our innately competitive nature and making it more yogic. I like to compare it to some of the martial arts that have a deep kind of spiritual, ethical background and tradition, but no one says, you can’t do judo or karate at a competition.”Now 54, Cruickshank took up yoga relatively late in life. “I’m not particularly flexible or fit,” he says. “I only started in my late 30s to address midlife issues, you know when the body starts to creak a bit and you don’t have so much energy.” He attended classes at a hot yoga studio in London where many of the leading lights of the competition world were teaching.It was only when he watched an event (performed at room temperature, usually after a hot yoga warm-up session)that he understood the appeal. “It was really inspiring. I couldn’t initially see myself competing but I got so much encouragement from my teachers who made me believe that this was something I could do and was worth doing.”He began competing in 2018 in the UK and has since done so in China and France, as well as acting as MC at the European Championships in Malmö, Sweden. “Being up on that stage in Beijing in 2018 was one of the most terrifying experiences of my life,” he says. “You weren’t allowed music back then, so it was total silence apart from the clicking of cameras.”Despite that, he stresses that one of the best things about competitive yoga is enjoyment. “It does have massive social benefits. The competitions are really good fun. You meet all sorts of people. When you get to international level, you have an excuse to travel around the world with a bunch of like-minded people.”For some people, he says, treating yoga as a sport can help to maintain motivation. “What happens, especially with hot yoga, is there is rapid, astonishing progress at the beginning. Then you plateau because your body isn’t going to exponentially get stronger and more flexible. Competing gives you a way of measuring progress in your practice. Maybe this year you’re focusing on doing a three-minute sequence for competition. And then the next you might attempt slightly more difficult postures.”Almania Colombo, 41, is a former dancer with the American Repertory Ballet. Like Cruickshank, she fell into competing almost by accident. A three-time European competition winner, she also won international championships in 2016 and 2018. She is now on the technical committee for the International Yoga Sport Federation–which is not affiliated with World Yogasana –and teaches hot yoga in London. “I was doing my yoga teacher training in Los Angeles in 2011and one of my friends wanted to compete, and asked me to join her,” she says. “For me it represented a new challenge, and something that intimidated me a little. I believe that in life it’s good to do things that scare you, especially if the fear is in our minds and not a real threat.”View image in fullscreen‘Yoga helped me find the total stillness in me’ …  Almania Colombo, photographed at House of Hot Yoga in north London.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianAlthough she was used to performing in her former career, doing yoga before an audience presented unique challenges. “Competing in yoga feels very different,” she says. “As a dancer you are constantly moving, and in a yoga competition you have to find the stillness. You can’t hide anything, time seems to slow down and you feel everything around you so much more.”Her first European championship took place in the incongruous setting of a Prague shopping mall. “We had a stage set up in the middle, with escalators all around, and people watched from the balconies above. It was November, people were wearing coats and shopping while we were in leotards. The environment was loud, busy and colourful, and weirdly enough that helped me find the total stillness in me, not allowing my own inner voice to be too loud.”A key issue facing yoga’s chances of reaching the Olympics, she says, “is that there are many organisations running their own competitions and not joining the same umbrella. Although yoga means union, and it’s what we are trying to achieve, there is still a lot of unnecessary ego.”‘Truly accessible to everyone’: how to start yogaRead moreNevertheless, a pathway has been started. Yogasana is likely to feature as an Indigenous sport at the 2030 Commonwealth Games hosted by India. Although still subject to approval, the other contenders are games rooted in Indian playgrounds –kabaddi and kho kho– which are widely considered to be less likely to attract the necessary level of interest from other Commonwealth nations. If yoga does feature in 2030, the next step would be for it to be introduced as a demonstration sport at the 2032 Olympics in Brisbane.Sheth remains hopeful. “I think there is an opportunity to create a system for yoga like Fifa, where every country has its own federation.” Sustainability for the long-term is key. “It’s not only about getting to the Olympics, it’s about staying there. We don’t want to end up like breakdancing. It got to the 2024 games in Paris. But that was the end of it.”Explore more on these topicsYogaFitnessHealth & wellbeingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Macron criticises ‘unbridled violence’ after days of unrest and 2,400 arrests across France | France | The Guardian
description: Ministers, officials and police under pressure over response to protests as government holds crisis talks amid ‘colossal failure of the state’
Author: Angelique Chrisafis
Headline: Ministers, officials and police under pressure over response to protests as government holds crisis talks amid ‘colossal failure of the state’
Content: People stormed and torched the town hall in Limoges, central France, destroying the 19th-century building.Photograph: Pascal Lachenaud/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeople stormed and torched the town hall in Limoges, central France, destroying the 19th-century building.Photograph: Pascal Lachenaud/AFP/Getty ImagesFranceMacron criticises ‘unbridled violence’ after days of unrest and 2,400 arrests across FranceMinisters, officials and police under pressure over response to protests as government holds crisis talks amid ‘colossal failure of the state’Angelique Chrisafisin ParisSun 18 Oct 2026 14.57 EDTFirst published on Sun 18 Oct 2026 11.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe French president, Emmanuel Macron, has criticised “unbridled violence” after one of the most violent days of unrest in years left public buildings burned, hundreds of shops destroyed and looted and at least 2,400people arrested in cities across the country.“Watching these images, we have all asked ourselves how could French people do this toFrance?” he said in a televised address.Macron said “nothing justifies” violence and that local state officials would be able to ban certain street gatherings if they deemed it necessary.He said a distinction must be drawn between what he called genuine, peaceful demonstrators making demands over the cost of living and the education system, and others who “destroy, ransack and loot”. He criticised what he called “factious groups from the ultra-left, joined by numerous delinquents”.2:31Emmanuel Macron condemns violence in televised address – videoPoliticians on the left and right called for the resignation of the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, after the government appeared to have been caught by surprise by the scale of violence on Saturday as state buildings were stormed and torched, bus stops smashed, roads barricaded and shops broken into and destroyed. Protests also took place in Spain, Italy and Portugal.Crowds clashed with police at Place de la République in centralParison Sunday afternoon as violence flared for a second day. Electric bikes were piled in some streets and set alight. Bottles and rocks were thrown and thick plumes of smoke rose from burning bins. Police responded with teargas and stun grenades.View image in fullscreenPolice officers stand guard as a fire burns in Paris on Sunday night.Photograph: Abdul Saboor/ReutersView image in fullscreenA car burns in a Paris street near graffiti reading ‘introduction to civil war’.Photograph: Guillaume Saligot/AFP/Getty ImagesPolice and officials faced challenges of different types on Saturday. First, tens of thousands of peaceful protesters attended calm marches through major cities including Paris, supporting schoolchildren’sdemands for more teachers and repairs to decrepit schools. Those marches, which came after four weeks of street marches andbarricades of schools, were attended by parents, teachers and grandparents as well as students and workers protesting over the high cost of living. The demonstrators carried banners saying the government was not listening to them and calling for more money for public services.But separately to those peaceful demonstrations, different groups caught police and officials by surprise with moving gatherings, sporadic burning, the barricading of streets and clashes with police in cities including Paris, Bordeaux, Nice and Marseille.View image in fullscreenA protester throws a smoke flare towards gendarmes in Bordeaux, south-western France.Photograph: Christophe Archambault/AFP/Getty ImagesFinally, masked looters took advantage of what French media called the “chaos” on the streets to smash shopfronts and grab goods. In Paris, groups of looters, some of whom appeared to be children, were seen running through the night with clothes and shoeboxes after masked adult men smashed shopfronts.In Paris, where police said a record 855 people had been arrested, the burnt-out remains of barricades built using bikes, bins and other materials littered streets on Sunday. Several streets had smashed shop windows and the remains of torched cars. The capital had experienced “a level of violence that we have never seen before, I believe”, said the Socialist deputy mayor, Lamia El Aaraje.View image in fullscreenMasked protesters by the graffiti-covered Statue de la République on Sunday evening.Photograph: Matthieu Rondel/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBurnt-out cars, smashed windows and the remains of barricades littered the streets of Paris on Sunday.Photograph: Stéphanie Lecocq/ReutersIn Limoges in central France, where the 19th-century town hall was burned down, the mayor, Guillaume Guérin, said the people who stormed his building “were not demonstrators that defend causes” but “people organised for war”. He said those who stormed and torched the town hall had told a building caretaker he would be killed, and told elected officials they would “burn”. He said there had been a failure of the state to deal with the crisis.“Around 3.30pm our municipal police, although present in number, found themselves no longer able to fight against the violence of rioters because they had run out of ammunition,” Guérin said. He called this “a colossal failure of the state”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA demonstrator in front of burning barricades in Marseille.Photograph: Sener Yilmaz Aslan/Getty ImagesIn Marseille, where masked groups stormed the city hall and a police station, the Socialist mayor, Benoît Payan, told BFMTV: “I have no words … I never thought I’d ever live through something like this. Hordes of rioters and looters attacked our common [state] buildings … with no real demands, but with the sole aim to wreck the demands of those who had demonstrated legitimately.”Payan said questions must be asked about policing tactics, as other town hall buildings, for example in Lille, were also targeted.View image in fullscreenProtesters arrive to force entry into the town hall in Lille, northern France.Photograph: Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP/Getty ImagesGrégory Doucet, the Green mayor of Lyon, said he had never seen such violence in his city, including the torching of the historic tourist office. He told Le Monde: “I’m stunned by the violence against public and state property. I saw and heard fear and anger. Shop owners felt abandoned.”Doucet said the government must find a “sense of nuance” in properly examining what happened and “avoiding stereotypes”. He said the government needed to give a political response to long-running societal demands from peaceful demonstrators on one hand, and also examine the roots of violence.Traders’ unions said more than 1,500 shops and businesses had been ransacked, with the cost running into tens of millions of euros. “This had nothing to do with the peaceful protesters,” said one shoe shop owner in Paris. “These were organised groups who were breaking things and looting. We’d never seen anything like it.”View image in fullscreenA protester wrapped in a French national flag stands in front of Lyon’s burning tourism office.Photograph: Jeff Pachoud/AFP/Getty ImagesOpposition politicians questioned the government’s policing tactics, saying there had been a lack of state intelligence.The interior ministry said there had been nearly 2,400 arrests and almost 1,000 police and gendarmes injured on Saturday, seven seriously. A 17-year-old boy had his right hand blown off by a crowd-control grenade in the east-central city of Saint-Étienne. A 17-year-old girl lost an eye in Mulhouse and a police investigation was opened into the circumstances.Macron’s centrist government and the far-right frontrunner for the presidential election, Marine Le Pen, both blamed what they called “ultra-left” groups for the violence. The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said the government would not be “intimidated” by ⁠violence, and blamed the unrest on the “ultra-left” and criminals.The radical-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who attended the peaceful street demonstration in Paris on Saturday, accused the government of organisational failings that had “opened the door to chaos”.Lecornu replied on social media: “Laying the responsibility for violence on heads of police is a dangerous and cynical reversal of responsibilities.”Explore more on these topicsFranceParisProtestEmmanuel MacronEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Cut benefits to fund work support for young people, says Neet review author Alan Milburn | Youth unemployment | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Former health secretary says upfront investment in support is needed ‘if we are going to end the Neet crisis’
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Exclusive: Former health secretary says upfront investment in support is needed ‘if we are going to end the Neet crisis’
Content: Milburn said the welfare system ‘just isn’t working for young people’.Photograph: Jeff Moore/PAView image in fullscreenMilburn said the welfare system ‘just isn’t working for young people’.Photograph: Jeff Moore/PAYouth unemploymentCut benefits to fund work support for young people, says Neet review author Alan MilburnExclusive: Former health secretary says upfront investment in support is needed ‘if we are going to end the Neet crisis’Anna BawdenandKiran StaceySun 18 Oct 2026 14.30 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 14.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMinisters should cut welfare spending to fund more employment support if it wants to end the youth Neet crisis, the author of a government-led review has said.Alan Milburn, the Tony Blair-era health secretary, told the Guardian he believed ministers should reduce benefits payments to help pay for more employment support, opening a potentially contentious debate within theLabourparty over welfare cuts.His intervention comes in the run-up to John Healey’s first budget, at which the chancellor is under pressure to explain how he will reduce a multibillion-pound black hole in the country’s finances and pay for more cost of living support without increasing borrowing.“We’ve got to have a different conversation about the welfare system, it just isn’t working for young people,” Milburn told the Guardian. “We need to redistribute money from the welfare system to more employment support if we are going to end the Neet crisis.”Milburn’s review of why so many 18- to 24-year-olds are not in education, employment or training calculated that a record1 million young people are now classed as Neet. The former cabinet minister said this was far more than a cyclical youth unemployment problem – it was a “youth detachment” problem, pointing to the fact that 60% of these Neets have never had a job.Ministers have pushed back Milburn’s final report until after the budget, at which Healey is expected to use a tax raid on banks to help pay for cost of living schemes such as a new energy support package.The chancellor has signalled his willingness to spend more money on youth unemployment programmes in the short term, however, even if the welfare savings take longer to be realised. He announced a £100m “local apprenticeship service” at last month’s Labour conference, calling it “a downpayment on Alan Milburn’s work”.In a joint interview with Peter Fonagy, the chair of the government’s landmarkindependent review of mental health, ADHD and autism, Milburn said his final recommendations were not just about tackling youth unemployment but also improving wellbeing.“The Neet crisis is a health crisis,” he said. “We’re in this vicious cycle where ill health is driving higher Neet rates. Non-participation is a disaster for young people’s mental health.”Milburn’s review is likely to recommend that employment, health and benefits support become more integrated. “We have got to change how the wealth, health and welfare systems work and how they interact with each other, because right now they’re plunging far too many young people into a life on benefits, which is ruinous to their life chances, rather than the opportunity to work,”he said.“No one [in government] is responsible for ensuring that young people both avoid the trap door of becoming Neet and get support to get them out of being Neet.”View image in fullscreenPeter Fonagy said a system was needed ‘that actually addresses [young people’s] potential and what it is that they can do’, rather than just identifying disability.Photograph: Maya Balanya Archdc/Album/AlamyFonagy’s review found that the number of people suffering mental distress has risen significantly across all age groups in England since the 1990s, especially the under-18s. It recommended providing help at the point of need, not after a diagnosis.“The current system isbased on identifying disability, why a person can’t do something,” Fonagy said. “We need a system that actually addresses their potential and what it is that they can do.“If nothing is done, and the trends go on as up till now, then there will be not one in five young people with diagnosable mental disorders, but one in four,” which, he added, increased the chances of them becoming Neet.While there will always be a group of young people whose physical or mental health mean work is not an option, “forthe vast majority of young people with autism, ADHD, anxiety or depression, the starting point has to be what could you do, what would you like to do, and how can the state help them do it,”Milburn said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘Work is good for you’: how UK scheme could help tackle youth mental health crisisRead moreYoung people with health needs should get prompt needs assessment, a personalised health plan and a wider “participation plan”, the review is likely to recommend.The kind of transformation Milburn and Fonagy describe would cost hundreds of millions of pounds in investment, sources believe. While they would not comment on the level of funding required, both were clear that upfront money would be crucial. “I think everybody in government is very, very well aware of the need to invest behind this priority,” Milburn said.“Over the medium term, it is entirely possible that you can reduce the benefits bill, but in order to do that, you’ve got to provide the support for young people. You’ve got to increase the opportunities that are available for young people and then provide the support for them to enable them to grab those opportunities.”“This is not a workshy, snowflake generation, you know, who are making mental distress up,” Milburn added. “If we provide more opportunities and we provide more support, the overwhelming majority of young people will take that, because that’s what they want. The system isn’t delivering what young people want, which is a job.”But Milburn also hinted at possible consequences for those who don’t engage. “Equally, there has got to be an obligation on young people to take up those opportunities, of course,” he said.The problem with the system was that it was “over-indexed to cash” and didn’t provide enough support, he added. “The consequence is calamitous for young people who could be working and are not being helped to do so, who then end up on a trajectory to a lifetime on benefits.”But intervening earlier and providing better support would in turn help relieve the pressure on the mental health waiting list. “I would hope that, for the first time, we could also introduce a maximum waiting time for mental health services, particularly for young people,” said Milburn.Explore more on these topicsYouth unemploymentWelfareBenefitsUnemploymentYoung peopleLabourMental healthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Police investigate Reform mayor for allegedly sharing ‘naked and sexualised’ images of himself | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Female colleague says she was forced out shortly after incident with Luke Campbell, Hull and East Yorkshire mayor
Author: Josh Halliday
Headline: Female colleague says she was forced out shortly after incident with Luke Campbell, Hull and East Yorkshire mayor
Content: Luke Campbell, right, with the Reform UK party leader, Nigel Farage, in 2025.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersView image in fullscreenLuke Campbell, right, with the Reform UK party leader, Nigel Farage, in 2025.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersReform UKPolice investigate Reform mayor for allegedly sharing ‘naked and sexualised’ images of himselfFemale colleague says she was forced out shortly after incident with Luke Campbell, Hull and East Yorkshire mayorJosh HallidayNorth of England editorSun 18 Oct 2026 11.18 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 11.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAReform UKmayor is under police investigation for allegedly showing “naked and sexualised” images of himself to a female member of staff.Luke Campbell, a former Olympic boxing champion and the mayor of Hull and EastYorkshire, is understood to have been questioned under caution by Humberside police earlier this month.In an incident first reported bythe Observeron Sunday, Campbell allegedly showed a senior female colleague four fully naked and sexualised images of himself in May.The woman said she had felt “shocked, embarrassed and humiliated” and claimed she had been forced out of her job soon after, according to documents submitted as part of an internal grievance procedure atHulland East Yorkshire combined authority (Heyca).Campbell, who was elected last May, has not responded to requests to comment. It is understood that he has not been arrested in relation to the allegations, which Reform UK has said he “firmly denies”.View image in fullscreenLuke Campbell, pictured in 2012, won gold at the London Olympics.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianA Reform UK spokesperson said: “Luke firmly denies the allegations. They come from a disgruntled employee attempting to leverage a settlement in a meritless workplace dispute.”The allegations against Campbell came to light after a year-long ITV investigation uncovered
