racist commentsfrom a number of Reform UK councillorsand a prospective MP.An aspiring Reform UK MPwas suspendedafter telling an undercover reporter that Muslims could not be British and asylum seekers crossing the English channel should be put in “concentration camps”, in footage due to be broadcast on Sunday night.Nigel Farage’s party said it had opened investigations where activists or members had “clearly behaved inappropriately”, adding that there was “no room for racism” in the party.Nadine Dorries, a former Conservative minister and now a Reform UK member, came to Campbell’s defence on Sunday by claiming that the “sexualised” image was in fact a 2013 magazine cover showing the former boxer posing naked from the waist up after hewon gold at the 2012 London Olympics.However, that appears to be at odds with witness testimony submitted as part of an internal grievance procedure at Heyca, where Campbell is mayor.In one document, corroborated by the Guardian, a senior female colleague said Campbell had called her over to a computer screen, where she was shown “several naked and sexualised images” of the mayor.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUK ‘an outlier in Europe’ for letting Farage and other politicians present TV showsRead moreA separate witness said they saw a naked man with a tattoo in one of the images, whereas no tattoo is visible on the magazine front cover.The main complainant said in a witness statement: “I was deliberately exposed to naked and sexualised images involving the mayor in the workplace, without my consent, and was laughed at when I was visibly embarrassed.“In my view, this was unwanted conduct of a sexual nature which violated my dignity and created a humiliating, degrading and offensive working environment.”About three weeks after the alleged incident, the female officer, who was working as a contractor but had accepted the offer of a permanent role, was allegedly told on a Teams call that the offer had been withdrawn.In a separate document, a second colleague said they had felt “uneasy” after allegedly seeing Campbell and two male colleagues ushering over a female officer to look at his laptop, which showed an image of a naked man with a tattoo.The Guardian understands that this second employee recalled comments then being made about Campbell’s tattoo and that they saw the mayor lift his shirt to show the tattoo.A spokesperson for Heyca confirmed to the Observer that a police investigation was under way. He said: “As with all public authorities, the combined authority has a standards process that can be engaged to deal with complaints about members and a complaints procedure that can be used to deal with complaints about officers.“The standards process and the complaints procedure must be carried out in a fair and independent manner.”Humberside police has been contacted for comment.Explore more on these topicsReform UKYorkshireMayoral electionsHullLocal governmentLocal politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham launches campaign against ‘headphone dodgers’ on public transport | Transport policy | The Guardian
description: Passengers urged to ‘share the carriage, not the noise’ as guidance sets out £100 penalties for nuisance behaviour
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Passengers urged to ‘share the carriage, not the noise’ as guidance sets out £100 penalties for nuisance behaviour
Content: Andy Burnham said: ‘It’s a simple thing, but one that will make journeys that little bit better for all of us.’Photograph: Jeff J Mitchell/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham said: ‘It’s a simple thing, but one that will make journeys that little bit better for all of us.’Photograph: Jeff J Mitchell/AFP/Getty ImagesTransport policyAndy Burnham launches campaign against ‘headphone dodgers’ on public transportPassengers urged to ‘share the carriage, not the noise’ as guidance sets out £100 penalties for nuisance behaviourKiran StaceyPolicy editorSun 18 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has announced a crackdown on “headphone dodgers” who play loud music on public transport, as he extends his promise to give voters “breathing space” in the confines of a train carriage.The prime minister will unveil a campaign against nuisance behaviour on public transport on Monday, alongside guidance allowing local transport authorities to levy fines of up to £100 for non-compliance.The move makes him the latest senior politician to promise action against people who play videos or music out loud in public spaces, something that about 60% of voters back.Burnham said in a statement: “We’ve all been on the train when someone starts blasting music or videos from their phone. It gets on your nerves and can quickly spoil the journey.“So, we’re launching a nationwide campaign reminding passengers to use headphones on trains. On top of that, we’re giving local leaders new powers to tackle loud music, vaping and littering on buses.“It’s a simple thing, but one that will make journeys that little bit better for all of us.”Under the plan, ministers will issue guidance to local transport authorities advising them on how they should use new powers granted under the Bus Services Act, which allows them to set and enforce their own rules on board.The guidance will say authorities should issue fines of up to £100 if bus passengers refuse to comply with a request to stop certain nuisance behaviour.Officials said drivers would not be expected to enforce such rules. That job would be left to transport safety officers or police officers. Train operating companies already have the power to issue fines of up to £1,000 for similar behaviour.Alongside the new powers, the government is launching a poster campaign to discourage people from playing videos or music on their phones out loud on public transport.Under the slogan “share the carriage, not the noise”, passengers will be encouraged to use headphones, avoid making calls on speakerphone and watch videos quietly.The campaign makes Burnham the latest in a series of politicians to promise to tackle headphone dodgers.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe London mayor, Sadiq Khan,unveiled a campaignin the summer urging passengers to “travel kind”, including by wearing headphones. The Liberal Democratshave called forbus travellers to face £1,000 fines as well as those on trains.The scramble for politicians to react comes as polls show noise on public transport is a major annoyance for British people.Arecent pollby YouGov found voters would back £1,000 fines for people playing music out loud on buses and trains. Aseparate surveyby the same company found that voters listed people talking on speakerphones as one of their top three irritants.Unions, however, said the new enforcement regime would do little to protect transport workers.The general secretary of Unite, Sharon Graham, said: “The government’s proposals are well-meaning but wholly inadequate to tackle the challenges and violence bus workers are facing on a daily basis. The proposed penalties are not going to deal with the issues facing workers.”Explore more on these topicsTransport policyRail transportRoad transportPublic transportLabourTransportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ukraine war briefing: Trump accuses Zelenskyy of not wanting to end war as feud rumbles on | Russia | The Guardian
description: Trump defends decision to waive some sanctions on Russia; Lithuania foils attack on Starlink site; Kyiv hits another oil terminal. What we know on day 1,699
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Trump defends decision to waive some sanctions on Russia; Lithuania foils attack on Starlink site; Kyiv hits another oil terminal. What we know on day 1,699
Content: Donald Trump and Volodymyr Zelenskyy have clashed in recent days after the US president blocked new sanctions on Russia and struck a diesel deal with Moscow.Photograph: Nathan Howard/ReutersView image in fullscreenDonald Trump and Volodymyr Zelenskyy have clashed in recent days after the US president blocked new sanctions on Russia and struck a diesel deal with Moscow.Photograph: Nathan Howard/ReutersRussia-Ukraine war at a glanceRussiaExplainerUkraine war briefing: Trump accuses Zelenskyy of not wanting to end war as feud rumbles onTrump defends decision to waive some sanctions on Russia; Lithuania foils attack on Starlink site; Kyiv hits another oil terminal. What we know on day 1,699Guardian staff and agenciesSun 18 Oct 2026 19.29 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 19.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump has defended his decision to waive some sanctions on Russia, while once again accusing Volodymyr Zelenskyyof not wanting to end the war. “My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table,” the US president wrote on Truth Social. “Zelenskyy doesn’t care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him … he doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did,” he added. Trump’s remarks come after he signed an executive order on Fridayputting on hold a sweeping new sanctions packagetargeting the Russian economy.Earlier on Sunday, Zelenskyy hadthanked the Trump administrationfor resuming intelligence sharing between the two countries, but maintained the US had intentionallythrottled its Starlink satellite internet accessto send a “message” to Kyiv,writeAndrew Roth and Sam Jones.Lithuania said Russia was likely behind an attempted arson attack on a company hosting communication hardware for Starlink satellites. Prime minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius made the claim on broadcaster LRT after authorities discovered flammable liquids at the company in question. Sinkevicius said the firm, whose location he did not mention, houses “nine satellite antennas to guarantee the Starlink connection, which of course supports and assists Ukraine”. He added: “It is obvious this is part of the hybrid war being waged by Russia, involving acts of sabotage.”In September,a satellite station belonging to the network located in central Poland was set ablazewith Warsaw claiming sabotage.In Bulgaria, an investigation is under way amid claims that antennas linked to the Starlink satellite network were set on fire.Shipping Russian diesel to the US market will take 15 to 20 days once contracts are signed, a senior Russian official said on Sunday, though a date for signing has yet to be announced. Trump announced thecontroversial agreementwith Moscow last week, seen as a way to try to lower fuel prices for American consumers ahead of crucial midterm elections. “Negotiations are currently under way regarding the commercial terms – that is, on finalisation of the contracts,” Russian deputy prime minister for energy Alexander Novak said in an interview with state media. “Once the contracts are signed, the fuel will reach the markets – in this case, the US markets – within 15 to 20 days.”Ukrainian strikes set an oil export terminal and a depot ablaze in St Petersburg on Sunday as Kyiv launched more than 1,000 drones at Russiain one of its largest aerial attacks of the war. One person was killed and five others were wounded in the attack, which sparked fires at the Petersburg oil terminal and the city’s Ruchi oil depot, officials said. A logistics centre belonging to Russian retailer Ozon and a datacentre operated by Russian tech company VK were also targeted, the companies confirmed. Russia’s defence ministry said Sunday that its forces had destroyed 1,015 Ukrainian drones over 15 Russian regions, the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black Sea.A ⁠Russian air ⁠strike ⁠killed one person ​and injured ⁠two in Kyiv ‌overnight, mayor Vitali ‌Klitschko said on Telegram early on ‌Monday. A medical facility ​and a non-residential ⁠building were damaged ​in the ​attack, ​he ​said.A suspected ⁠drone exploded over Lithuania after triggering an alert that forced residents in northern and central areas to seek shelterfor an hour on Sunday, officials said. Ukraine’s foreign ​ministry said later it regretted the incident in Lithuania’s airspace, adding that it may have resulted from Russian electronic warfare diverting drones off course. The object flew ⁠into Lithuania’s airspace from Poland, Lithuanian defence minister Robertas Kaunas told reporters.Explore more on these topicsRussiaRussia-Ukraine war at a glanceUkraineLithuaniaSpaceXexplainersShareReuse this content

title: Electricity costs put UK steelmakers in worst position in three years against EU rivals | Steel industry | The Guardian
description: Premium paid over French counterparts has risen to almost £30 a megawatt hour, analysis by lobby group finds
Author: Jasper Jolly
Headline: Premium paid over French counterparts has risen to almost £30 a megawatt hour, analysis by lobby group finds
Content: British Steel’s Scunthorpe works. Analysts blame the UK’s high electricity prices on its reliance on gas for power generation.Photograph: Ian Forsyth/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBritish Steel’s Scunthorpe works. Analysts blame the UK’s high electricity prices on its reliance on gas for power generation.Photograph: Ian Forsyth/Getty ImagesSteel industryElectricity costs put UK steelmakers in worst position in three years against EU rivalsPremium paid over French counterparts has risen to almost £30 a megawatt hour, analysis by lobby group findsJasper JollySun 18 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritish steelmakers have been pushed further behind European rivals on electricity costs after the US-Israeli war on Iran caused a surge in global gas prices.The premium paid by the British industry over its French counterpart has risen to almost £30 a megawatt hour (MWh), its highest level in three years, according to analysis by the lobby group UK Steel.Energy prices have long been one of the main factors businesses cite when asked what is holding back British industry. For Andy Burnham they represent perhaps the biggest obstacle to hisgoal of “reindustrialising” the UK.Analysts blame the UK’s high electricity prices on its reliance on gas for power generation, which is crucial forcleaner steelmaking with electric arc furnaces.The way the market is set up means that the wholesale gas pricedetermines the price of electricityeven from other sources that cost much less to produce, such as wind or solar power, and Iran’s closure of the strait of Hormuz in response to Donald Trump’s bombing campaign has causedglobal gas prices to soar.Electricity prices inFranceare mainly determined by its nuclear reactors, while in Germany heavily polluting coal still plays a large role in generation.Graph showing electricity costs in UK, Germany, France and Canada.Comparisons with European rivals are particularly important for the UK because the EU is often the main market for British manufactured products, including about 75% of exported steel, worth about £3bn.The gap with France had fallen in the previous three years to reach £18 a MWh last year, although it remains below the £153 reached in 2022 when Russia’s invasion of Ukraine caused a crisis in the global gas market. The gap with Germany this year fell slightly to about £12.Under Keir Starmer most of the costs added by government policy to heavy industrial businesses’ electricity costs were removed last year. The main option to bring the price down further, however, would be to set up more cheap renewables – a challenge in the short term – or to directly subsidise prices.The director general of UK Steel, Peter Brennan, said direct subsidies were the only option to help steelmakers. The lobby group hasproposed a cap on pricesthat it estimates would cost about £51m a year. The government would pay the difference when prices go above that level, while the industry would pay the government if prices go below.“British steelmakers are being asked to compete with one hand tied behind their backs,” Brennan said. “Despite welcome government action, our electricity prices remain vastly higher than those of our European and global competitors, and the gap with France is getting worse.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The government has rightly made reindustrialisation a national priority. But we cannot rebuild British manufacturing while forcing our steelmakers to pay substantially more for electricity than their competitors.”Separately, the government announced measures on Monday to support more than 100,000 workforce opportunities in the eight key growth sectors in its industrial strategy. The “jobs plans” are intended to help young people find work, with a focus on professional and business services, the defence sector and construction.Similar plans for financial services, clean energy and life sciences have already been announced. Plans for advanced manufacturing and the creative industries are expected to follow shortly.A government spokesperson said: “We are tackling industry’s number one concern head-on by reducing electricity bills by up to 25% for over 10,000 manufacturing businesses, and cutting costs for hundreds of our most electricity-intensive businesses by around £1bn per year – delivering on the prime minister’s pledge to reindustrialise Britain.”Explore more on these topicsSteel industryEnergy industryIndustrial policyGasFranceEuropean UnionEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Zelenskyy thanks Trump for resumed intelligence sharing after US Starlink ‘message’ | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Two people killed and at least 17 injured as Russia and Ukraine continue to trade strikes on power infrastructure
Author: Sam Jones
Headline: Two people killed and at least 17 injured as Russia and Ukraine continue to trade strikes on power infrastructure
Content: Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country’s recent Starlink problems were ‘a message from [the] American government’.Photograph: Omar Havana/APView image in fullscreenVolodymyr Zelenskyy said his country’s recent Starlink problems were ‘a message from [the] American government’.Photograph: Omar Havana/APUkraineZelenskyy thanks Trump for resumed intelligence sharing after US Starlink ‘message’Two people killed and at least 17 injured as Russia and Ukraine continue to trade strikes on power infrastructureAndrew Rothin Kyiv andSam JonesSun 18 Oct 2026 12.37 EDTFirst published on Sun 18 Oct 2026 10.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVolodymyr Zelenskyy on Sunday thanked theTrump administrationfor resuming intelligence sharing between the two countries, but maintained the US had intentionally throttled its Starlink satellite internet access so that Donald Trump could send a “message” in his ongoing feud with the Ukrainian president.In an interview on NBC, Zelenskyy said the US had “unblocked” intelligence on impending Russian ballistic missile strikes, which have pounded the country’s energy infrastructure as winter draws in.“It was blocked for some period of time. And then it was deblocked by the American side. We are very thankful for this. Now it works,” Zelenskyy told NBC’s Meet the Press. “Only [the] United States has this unique intelligence to tell our side when Russia uses ballistic missiles. And we didn’t get it during ballistic attacks during three days.”Zelenskyy also said that Elon Musk’s SpaceX was responsible forsuddenly limiting the speedat which Starlink terminals worked in Ukraine, hampering drone operations on the frontlines as well as some air defence missions.“It was a message from [the] American government to limit the speed,” he said. “And technically, SpaceX did it.”Two people werekilled and at least 17 injured as Russia and Ukraine continued to trade strikes on each other’s power infrastructure, afterthe breakdownof Trump’s short-lived and unilaterally declared “energy ceasefire”.View image in fullscreenA Ukrainian drone strike on the St Petersburg oil terminal.Photograph: EPATrump has increasingly sought a detente with Moscow, inking a deal toimport diesel fuel from Russiaand waiving sanctions voted for overwhelmingly by both houses of Congress. Zelenskyy has become increasingly critical of Trump’s actions as the US has piled pressure on Ukraine to cease striking refineries in Russia and end the war quickly on Putin’s terms.“We want to trust him and I hope that he will change his decisions,” Zelenskyy said of Trump. “Because I think that it’s all mistakes and it will not help us. And it will not help [the] United States.”Zelenskyy on Sunday said that he had spoken with Steve Witkoff andJared Kushner, the two Trump envoys charged with ending the war in Ukraine, as part of Ukraine’s “virtually nonstop communication” with the Trump administration.But the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, in a separate interview on NBC on Sunday said that Zelenskyy had been “reckless” to accuse the Trump administration of standing behind the throttling of Starlink.“President Trump and Secretary Rubio have categorically said that no one in the Trump administration did that,” said Bessent. “And I think it is very reckless for President Zelenskyy to make such a charge.”He added: “President Zelenskyy should be very careful about making statements like this that aren’t true.”On Sunday night Trump said Zelenskyy did not want his nation’s more than four-year war with Russia to end, writing on his Truth Social platform that he was in the process of negotiating a peace between Russia andUkraineand making “great progress” but claimed: “Zelenskyy doesn’t care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him … he doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did.”Ukraine has resumed striking refineries in Russia and on Sunday attacked one of the country’s main oil terminals.One person was killed and 15 wounded overnight after Ukraine used more than 1,000 drones to target Russian oil depots, logistics facilities and datacentres in one of its largest ever aerial bombardments.View image in fullscreenSmoke billows into the sky after Ukrainian drone strikes on an industrial zone in St Petersburg.Photograph: APSt Petersburg’s governor, Alexander Beglov, said on Sunday that fires ⁠had broken out overnight at the city’s oil terminal, ​an oil depot and industrial ‌warehouses. A logistics centre belonging to the Russian retailer Ozon and a datacentre for the local tech company VK were also targeted, both companies confirmed.Alexander Drozdenko, the governor of the Leningrad region that surrounds St Petersburg, said 145 drones had been shot down and about 20,000 people were without electricity after the raid. “A large-scale [unmanned aerial vehicle] attack continues to be repelled,” he wrote on Telegram.Fears that the conflict could be spilling over into Nato’s borders were stoked again on Sunday morning afterLithuaniatold residents in central and ⁠northern parts of the country to seek shelter for about an hour after an unidentified flying object entered its ⁠airspace.During the red alert, Nato fighter jets were ‌scrambled to the area and Kaunas airport, near Lithuania’s second largest city, was temporarily closed, the national crisis management centre said.The Nato aircraft were unable to visually identify the object due to cloudy weather and did not attempt to shoot it down, the centre said.Ukraine’s foreign ministry later said ⁠it regretted the possible diversion of its ⁠drones into ⁠Lithuanian airspace ​on Sunday, which it said may ⁠have been caused by Russian electronic warfare.“We apologise for any ​disruption, risks and concern this may have caused,” a spokesperson, ‌Heorhii Tykhyi, wrote on X. “We are committed to ⁠sharing all relevant information with ​our ​Lithuanian partners to ​establish the full circumstances ​of ‌the incident.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenRescue workers walk in front of a residential building damaged by a Russian airstrike in Zaporizhzhia on Saturday.Photograph: Kateryna Klochko/APMeanwhile, local officials in the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia said Russian strikes had killed a woman and wounded at least two other people, including a six-year-old girl. Two apartment buildings, 18 cars and an educational institution had been damaged by the attack, according to Mykhailo Semikin, the head of the Zaporizhzhia regional military administration.Tensions are deepening between Kyiv and Washington, with the US presidentcriticising Ukraine for its strikeson Russian oil infrastructure, despite continued Russian aggression.Trumpannounced an “energy ceasefire”last week – which neither side said they agreed to beforehand – that quickly collapsed as Moscow continued its strikes on Ukraine’s power grid and Kyiv eventually resumed its hits on Russian oil refineries.The Russian defence ministry said its air defence units had downed 1,015 Ukrainian drones around the country overnight. The Tass news agency quoted the ​Kremlin ​spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, who said Russia was responding with systematic, large-scale ⁠strikes.“The Kyiv ​regime is resisting, but this cannot ​change the course ‌of events,” he ​said, ​answering a question about how Russia might respond to Kyiv’s attack on St Petersburg.On Saturday, Russia said it had carried out a major overnight attack, targeting Ukraine’s largest steelworks in the city of Kryvyi Rih and ⁠vessels using the port of Odesa. In a ‌statement, Russia’s defence ministry said its forces had also hit an electricity substation in the north-western city of Zhytomyr and another steel ‌plant in Zaporizhzhia.View image in fullscreenA house damaged by a Russian airstrike in the frontline city of Sloviansk in eastern Ukraine.Photograph: State Emergency Service Of Ukraine/ReutersIn the Trump administration’s latest effort to reduce tensions with Russia, the US president announced on Friday that he wouldput a hold on a sweeping new sanctions packagetargeting the Russian economy, telling Congress the pause on the legislation passed by both chambers was in the national interest.Trump has yet to give details about what he has decided regarding further sanctions on Russia.“We’ll figure it out, and you’ll figure it out,” he told reporters at a fundraising dinner at his Florida estate on Saturday. “But it’s a very good decision, and it’s going to be a decision that’s good for the country, and I think good for the world.”In a post on X on Sunday, Zelenskyy said in the week since Trump’s announcement of an energy ceasefire Russia had attacked Ukraine’s energy, oil and gas sectors 76 times.He also said that the previous night alone, energy facilities in four Ukrainian regions had been attacked and tens of thousands of families were still without power. He accused Russia of trying to cause a blackout.Trump’s pause on Russia sanctions is ‘reward’ for Putin, Zelenskyy saysRead more“America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements,” he said. “On the contrary, they take every signal of an opportunity to make money as proof that their bet on war is paying off and they can keep fighting.”Zelenskyy also stressed that the war was continuing due to Russia’s invasion – not because Ukraine was defending itself. “It is Russia that must face pressure for peace to have a chance. Thank you to everyone who understands this and helps,” he said.Ukrainian drones have repeatedly entered Nato airspace in the ​Baltic region in ‌recent months. Kyiv ​has said they ​were steered off course by Russian signal jamming. Such incidents have stoked concerns that Russia’s war in Ukraine could spread.Reuters, the Associated Press and Agence France-Presse contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsUkraineRussiaEuropeDonald TrumpTrump administrationVolodymyr ZelenskyyLithuanianewsShareReuse this content

title: Flydubai captain describes blocking axe blows as co-pilot attacked him | Flydubai plane incident | The Guardian
description: Capt Smit Machchhar said he screamed for help as he reached to open the cockpit door on flight FZ1073
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Capt Smit Machchhar said he screamed for help as he reached to open the cockpit door on flight FZ1073
Content: Capt Smit Machchhar said the scariest thing he felt was the aircraft nose ‘steeply going down’.Photograph: Israel's Foreign Ministry/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCapt Smit Machchhar said the scariest thing he felt was the aircraft nose ‘steeply going down’.Photograph: Israel's Foreign Ministry/AFP/Getty ImagesFlydubai plane incidentFlydubai captain describes blocking axe blows as co-pilot attacked himCapt Smit Machchhar said he screamed for help as he reached to open the cockpit door on flight FZ1073ReutersSun 18 Oct 2026 13.27 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 15.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe captain of a flydubai flight who was attacked by a co-pilot who intended to crash the plane has described ⁠blocking axe blows to his head and screaming for help as he reached to open the cockpit door.Capt Smit ⁠Machchharhas been hailed ⁠as a ​herofor his role in averting disaster on the flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv last month, helping to thwart what the UAE ⁠attorney general has said was an attempted suicide attack by the co-pilot who hadintended to crash the planeinto Ben Gurion airport.Speaking in an interview with ⁠The National newspaper from a hospital bed in Abu Dhabi, his head and left arm bandaged, Machchhar ​said that when the first blow landed ‌he thought something had gone “horribly ‌wrong with the aircraft structure”, before quickly realising he was being attacked and things had “taken a drastic turn”.“The ‌next thought was I need to get help in here,” he said. “My immediate action was to free myself from the seatbelts and I tried to just block the blows as much as I could.”He pointed to his arm, which had been wounded as he defended himself. “The blows were coming on the head. Immediately my ‌hand went to the knob which opens the door and [I was] screaming for my colleagues, screaming his name. I believe that was the first time when I ​lost my consciousness.”View image in fullscreenDubai’s crown prince, sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, visited Machchhar in hospital in Abu Dhabi.Photograph: Government of Dubai Media Office/APFlight FZ1073 was in Saudi airspace when the co-pilot attacked Machchhar with a crash axe, an item typically kept in the cockpit for emergency use.The incident caused the airliner to plunge 16,000 ft (4,900m) in 30 seconds before the attacker was overwhelmed and two other pilots who were ⁠on board landed the aircraft safely inSaudi Arabia. The suspect, an Omani ​national, was transferred to the ​UAE, flydubai’s home country.The plan was ​inspiredby the 11 September 2001 attacks on the US, UAE public prosecutors ​said as a ‌result of their criminal ​investigation, which was launched on ​1 October.Machchhar said he heard the cockpit door opening and screaming “between my colleague and the guy”. He said the scariest moment was when he felt was the aircraft nose “steeply going down”.“I was not very sure that I’ll make it out alive from this. Did I give up? No.”Explore more on these topicsFlydubai plane incidentIsraelDubaiSaudi ArabiaUnited Arab EmiratesMiddle East and north AfricaAir transportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Warning signs could predict inflammatory bowel disease a decade before diagnosis | Medical research | The Guardian
description: Antibody patterns in the blood may help doctors identify people at risk so they can be treated earlier, research shows
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Antibody patterns in the blood may help doctors identify people at risk so they can be treated earlier, research shows
Content: IBD has only been able to be treated at a later stage, but scientists found that the immune system leaves warning signs long before diagnosis.Photograph: Teodor Lazarev/AlamyView image in fullscreenIBD has only been able to be treated at a later stage, but scientists found that the immune system leaves warning signs long before diagnosis.Photograph: Teodor Lazarev/AlamyMedical researchWarning signs could predict inflammatory bowel disease a decade before diagnosisAntibody patterns in the blood may help doctors identify people at risk so they can be treated earlier, research showsHanad AhmedSun 18 Oct 2026 18.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePatterns of antibodies in people’s blood could predict the onset of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) a decade before diagnosis, according to research that raises hopes for catching the condition early.Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis, the two main forms of IBD, are typically treated only after symptoms appear, when the gut has already been damaged. But scientists found that the immune system sends warning signals up to a decade before diagnosis, paving the way for potentially earlier detection and even prevention.“For too long we have only been able to treat inflammatory bowel disease once the damage is done, and for many people that is too late,” said Dr Arno Bourgonje at the University Medical Centre Groningen in the Netherlands and the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York.“What we have shown is that the disease begins years before symptoms appear, and the immune system leaves warning signs long before diagnosis,” Bourgonje added. “This is not yet a test that can tell someone they will become ill, but it is an important step towards catching the disease earlier and, one day, preventing it.”At least 3.8 million people worldwide live with IBD, an immune condition that drives chronic inflammation of the digestive tract, causing pain, diarrhoea and fatigue. The exact cause is unknown, but a misfiring immune system, genetics and microbes living in the gut can all contribute.Treatment relies on anti-inflammatory and immune-suppressing drugs, but many patients do not respond, and a significant number go on to have surgery to remove damaged sections of bowel. Longstanding inflammation also raises the risk of bowel cancer. This has prompted scientists to look for the earlier signs of disease, in the hope of identifying people at risk before damage begins.Bourgonje and colleagues at Mount Sinai and the Medical University of Vienna ran tests on blood samples taken from US military personnel. They examined 2,000 samples from 500 people, 200 of whom later developed Crohn’s disease, and 200 who went on to develop ulcerative colitis. The remaining 100 developed neither condition.The blood samples were screened for antibodies that the immune system might have churned out in response to hundreds of thousands of fragments of proteins from bacteria, viruses, food and even the body’s own tissues.In people who went on to develop Crohn’s disease, antibodies against Epstein-Barr virus, which causes glandular fever, were more common, and the differences were already visible a decade before diagnosis. The signal was strongest in those who later developed more severe, complicated disease, which can narrow the bowel or create abnormal channels.People who developed ulcerative colitis showed a different pattern, including antibodies against one of the body’s own proteins.The findings, published in the journalGutand presented at the United European Gastroenterology meeting in Barcelona, need to be confirmed in other groups of people, and the results show a link rather than proving the infections cause IBD. But the hope is that IBD could eventually follow the path of type 1 diabetes, where a blood test can identify people whose immune systems have begun attacking the pancreas before any symptoms appear, allowing treatment that delays the onset of disease.James Lindsay, a professor of gastroenterology at BartsHealth, who was not involved in the research, said the study provided “important insights into the causes of Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis, potentially adding new tools to help identify those at risk of IBD”. But he cautioned that the techniques were “very much a research tool” and not yet ready for the clinic.Marianne Radcliffe, the chief executive of Crohn’s & Colitis UK, a national patient charity, said: “For people affected by Crohn’s and colitis, research like this is an important step forward. Every new insight helps build a clearer understanding of how these conditions develop, including the changes that may occur years before symptoms appear.”Explore more on these topicsMedical researchHealthDigestive disordersnewsShareReuse this content

title: Guardian reporter filmed masked militants seconds before West Bank attack on French mayor | West Bank | The Guardian
description: New video footage of Israeli settler assault on European delegation as Netanyahu attempts to raise doubt
Author: Emma Graham-Harrison
Headline: New video footage of Israeli settler assault on European delegation as Netanyahu attempts to raise doubt
Content: Despite video footage, Netanyahu’s office described reports of the attacks as ‘unproven allegations’.Photograph: UGC/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDespite video footage, Netanyahu’s office described reports of the attacks as ‘unproven allegations’.Photograph: UGC/AFP/Getty ImagesWest BankAnalysisGuardian reporter filmed masked militants seconds before West Bank attack on French mayorEmma Graham-Harrisonin JerusalemNew video footage of Israeli settler assault on European delegation as Netanyahu attempts to raise doubtSun 18 Oct 2026 14.39 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 16.36 EDTShareHours after Israeli militantsattacked a delegationof European diplomats, French clerics and a visiting mayor in the occupied West Bank, Israel’s leader, Benjamin Netanyahu, responded by questioning the delegation’s account of the assault.“Serious accusations require serious evidence” was the all-caps headline of a social mediapostfrom the office of the prime minister. As news of the attack spread globally there was no pledge to find those accountable and bring them to justice.Instead Netanyahu’s team dismissed video of Bernard Baudoux, the mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries in northern France, on the ground grimacing in pain and shock, photos of the smashed window of a diplomatic car, and footage of masked men threatening diplomats and activists with sticks.“These images alone do not establish the complete sequence of events or individual responsibility,” the statement said, warning of “concerns about a coordinated campaign to smear Israel”.The prime minister’s office went on to cast doubt on the integrity of senior French, Belgian and Polish diplomats in Jerusalem and clergy from the Catholic church who witnessed and reported the attack.“We call on the public and responsible journalists to demand verifiable evidence, reject hearsay and refuse to turn unproven allegations into a collective indictment of the Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria [the occupied West Bank],” it said.Guardian footageFootage below filmed by the Guardian (no audio) shows the moments before Israeli settlers attacked the French mayor Bernard Baudoux, who was in the Palestinian town of Taybeh with a delegation of European diplomats. A second clip shows the immediate aftermath of the attack. The final section shows one group of settlers attacking the car carrying Baudoux and others.0:36French mayor attacked by Israeli settlers in occupied West Bank – videoVerifying the details of attacks can be painstaking journalistic work, seeking out eyewitness accounts, photos and videos for confirmation.But this weekend the Guardian was in Taybeh, and witnessed the masked militants speeding up a hill in order to attack diplomats and French visitors who had spent a morning peacefully harvesting olives with Palestinians who own the groves.View image in fullscreenThe smashed window of the car carrying Bernard Baudoux.Photograph: Emma Graham-Harrison/The GuardianShortly after 1pm, they were warned that settlers had attacked Palestinians harvesting olives nearby. Keen to avoid confrontation, the group decided to leave and were approaching their vehicles as the militants closed in, masked, menacing and brandishing sticks.The Guardian filmed the moments before Baudoux was assaulted, showing him approaching an SUV with his wife and Vincent Dollmann, the archbishop of Cambrai, escorted by diplomatic security. Our vehicle pulled away, making room for the two parked by the road to follow.Moments later the settlers attacked, apparently determined not only to force the foreigners to flee but to extract a price for joining Palestinians on their land.It was clear the group contained foreign dignitaries because the cars had diplomatic plates, and Baudoux was apparently targeted for his nationality, because he was wearing his mayor’s sash of office. One of the attackers aggressively shouted “France, France” before pushing him to the ground, eyewitnesses said.Metadata from that video shows there were just 22 seconds between the last shot of Baudoux remonstrating with his attackers and footage of him slumped on the ground taken by activists in the second car.The embassy security team then helped him into the vehicle but the attack continued as they drove off. Footage filmed from the hillside opposite shows the settlers attacking the SUV as pulls away.The force of their blows smashed one of the reinforced windows at the back of the car, which can be seen intact in the first video. A photo of the crumpled pane taken minutes later in the relative safety of Taybeh shows the force of the impact.If the militant settlers had broken one of the windows next to the passengers, it is unlikely those inside would have escaped injuries.View image in fullscreenFormer Israeli ambassadors and employees demonstrated outside the foreign ministry, demanding the prime minister and his government ‘Stop Jewish Terrorism. It’s in your hands’.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianIsraeli authorities have repeatedly attempted toobfuscatedetails of attacks on Palestinians and undermine survivor or witness accounts.For the prime minister to deploy the same tactics on senior diplomats from European allies – however strained their current relationship – marks a new embrace of isolationist extremism.A day earlier the American photojournalist Heidi Levine washospitalised after a brutal attackby Israeli militants blocking the Palestinian olive harvest in another village. Netanyahu’s office described it as an “alleged assault” and a “disputed incident” adding “the facts … remain unclear and are under investigation”.The message from the very top of Israel’s government, that the state was reluctant to impose consequences or seek justice for that attack, may have emboldened the attackers on Saturday.View image in fullscreenThe protest outside the foreign ministry in Jerusalem drew a response from conservative passersby.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianThere was one unprecedented response in Jerusalem, however. On Sunday, more than a dozen of Israel’s top former diplomats gathered outside the foreign ministry where they had all worked for decades for an unprecedented protest.Two former directors general, one deputy director general and a host of ambassadors held up signs calling for action on the campaign of terror by Israelis against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.“Bibi [Netanyahu], foreign minister [Gideon] Sa’ar. Stop Jewish Terrorism. It’s in your hands,” read one banner.Explore more on these topicsWest BankIsraelPalestineMiddle East and north AfricaBenjamin NetanyahuanalysisShareReuse this content

title: ‘Damp squib’: Ed Davey can breathe easy as Lib Dem leadership challenge fails to materialise | Ed Davey | The Guardian
description: Lengthy meeting heard grumbles about ‘blue wall’ policies and ‘Ming vase’ tactics but no real rancour
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Lengthy meeting heard grumbles about ‘blue wall’ policies and ‘Ming vase’ tactics but no real rancour
Content: Some Lib Dem MPs fear Ed Davey is focusing so much on attracting former Tory voters that a distinctively liberal message is being lost.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAView image in fullscreenSome Lib Dem MPs fear Ed Davey is focusing so much on attracting former Tory voters that a distinctively liberal message is being lost.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAEd DaveyAnalysis‘Damp squib’: Ed Davey can breathe easy as Lib Dem leadership challenge fails to materialisePeter WalkerSenior political correspondentLengthy meeting heard grumbles about ‘blue wall’ policies and ‘Ming vase’ tactics but no real rancourSun 18 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 08.56 EDTShareAs political showdowns go, this week’s gathering of Liberal Democrat MPs, billed by some as a crunch moment forEd Davey, was a touch underwhelming. “I had expected a damp squib,” one attender put it. “It was damper than I thought.”Far from generating a mass of opposition to Davey’s leadership, let alone a formal challenge to his position, the lengthy gathering in a Commons committee room on Tuesday evening brought a few minor grumbles, but little else.“My main feeling was a sort of irritation that we were forced to sit through this very long meeting, one where in the main we all aggressively agreed with each other,” another MP put it.This is not, however, the entire story. There is disquiet with Davey’s patient and sometimes cautious leadership style, as shown most dramatically by thesudden resignationa week ago of Charlie Maynard, the number two in the party’s Treasury team, over concerns the Lib Dems were failing to cut through with voters.If Maynard hoped to spark a wider revolt, it did not happen. “It felt like he was trying to light the touchpaper, but it fizzled out instead of exploding,” one MP said. Another was more blunt: “Charlie really has fucked it up. He has zero political nous.”The situation nonetheless remains tricky. Davey led the Lib Dems toa century-best performancein the 2024 election, winning 72 MPs, and is safe for the foreseeable future. That said, frustrations that werealready bubbling upbefore September’s party conference have arguably become more acute since.This is largely the result of the two policy decisions set out by Davey at the conference: a promise of£17bn in income tax cutsif the party is elected, and support for the pensions triple lock, just as Andy Burnhampledgedto change it.Both chimed explicitly with Lib Dem efforts to build momentum in the so-called blue wall of affluent home counties constituencies where the party made big gains from the Conservatives in 2024.View image in fullscreenDavey and some Lib Dem colleagues on a visit to Rampion wind farm.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAWhile just about every Lib Dem MP agrees that protecting these seats and potentially winning more is vital, some worry that Davey is being so careful to not alienate former Tory voters that any distinctively liberal message has been lost.“Making us the party of tax cuts just jarred with activists,” one MP said. “It’s not that we don’t want taxes cut, it’s just that the overt positioning felt incredibly blue wall-y. It’s like we are aping the Conservatives, while they are aping Reform.”They added: “There are levels of nuance here. Ed will be given time to make changes. But there are a lot of unhappy people in the party at the moment, and not just MPs.“Charlie Maynard didn’t help. Now we have to rally around the leader, do all theOperation Big Dogstuff, and we haven’t addressed the issues about who we actually are.”Supporters of Davey argue that he is listening, but also point to the lessons of the 2019 election, when the party had a very clear national message – stop Brexit – butwon just 12 seats, with a vote total higher than 2024’s but spread too thinly.“Ed was very clear in the meeting that he understands people’s frustrations,” an MP said. “There are some legitimate grievances. But he has enormous credit built up, and people are prepared to give him the time he needs to make the changes he needs to make.”Thus far, public opposition has come from only a handful of people, also including another MP, Tom Gordon, who called Davey’s argument that the triple lock needed to be saved to protect the pensions of people currently in their 40s “downright insulting”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSome MPs are privately unimpressed by what they view as performative complaints from, as one put it, a “small minority who feel the world fails to recognise their staggering genius”. Another said: “The plea, particularly among colleagues with small majorities, is: please think when you do these things, as it undermines us.”View image in fullscreenDaisy Cooper, deputy leader of the Liberal Democrats.Photograph: House of Commons/PAAnother factor protecting Davey is the absence of a plan for what would come next. There are ambitious and capable MPs in the 2024 intake, but they lack experience. If Davey was ousted, a leading contender would be Daisy Cooper, his deputy and Treasury spokesperson – who some Lib Dems feel shares the same cautious approach.One MP said: “A lot of people are terrified of a Daisy leadership – it’s the main reason why Ed is still in place. It is politely phrased as a ‘lack of a viable alternative’.”For now, it seems, the party will maintain its own version of Labour’s “Ming vase” tactic – trying to remain sufficiently benign and unobjectionable to hoover up enough tactical votes to gain more MPs, and then perhaps support a Labour government on the condition it introduces the Lib Dem holy grail of a proportional election system.“That’s the big plan: win the seats to deliver PR and then we can be liberals,” one MP said. “But that relies on a lot of things going right.”There is worry, and some disagreement. But as yet, no real rancour. “Some of this is just the usual mid-parliament blues, which the 2024 intake have never experienced,” one senior party figure said.“We are still small enough that we can have individual conversations to sort things out. And we don’t do drama. So there will be no implosion. Just some soul searching.”Explore more on these topicsEd DaveyLiberal DemocratsTactical votinganalysisShareReuse this content

title: Elizabeth Holmes documentary You Can See Everything debuts with huge $15m opening weekend | Movies | The Guardian
description: Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s buzzy film was shown on only 855 screens in the biggest documentary opening in North America since Fahrenheit 9/11 in 2004
Author: Sian Cain
Headline: Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s buzzy film was shown on only 855 screens in the biggest documentary opening in North America since Fahrenheit 9/11 in 2004
Content: Elizabeth Holmes is quizzed by Nathan Fielder in You Can See Everything, directed by Fielder and Lance Oppenheim.Photograph: A24View image in fullscreenElizabeth Holmes is quizzed by Nathan Fielder in You Can See Everything, directed by Fielder and Lance Oppenheim.Photograph: A24MoviesElizabeth Holmes documentary You Can See Everything debuts with huge $15m opening weekendNathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s buzzy film was shown on only 855 screens in the biggest documentary opening in North America since Fahrenheit 9/11 in 2004Sian Cainand agenciesSun 18 Oct 2026 19.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNathan Fielder’s nearly three-hour Elizabeth Holmes documentary,You Can See Everything, has opened to an extraordinary $15m domestic box office, the biggest opening weekend for a documentary in North America in more than 20 years.You Can See Everything, directed byNathan Fielderand Lance Oppenheim, made $15m (A$21.5m, £11.2m) from only 855 screens, and had more than 2,000 sold-out screenings at the weekend, according to the production company A24. It is the biggest opening for a film playing on fewer than 1,000 screens since Borat opened to $26.5m in 2006.It is also the biggest opening for a documentary in North America in two decades, since Fahrenheit 9/11 made nearly $24m from 868 theaters. Those numbers do not account for inflation or for concert films: Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour holds the record with a $92.8m opening weekend in 2023 when it was released in nearly 4,000 cinemas.You Can See Everything has not opened at the international box office yet, coming out in Australia on 12 November and in the UK on 20 November.Like other hits this year, including Backrooms and Obsession, ticket sales for You Can See Everything were driven by a largely younger audience in North America; more than 70% of the opening weekend crowd were under 35.You Can See Everything review – Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes doc is a modern masterpiece of deceitRead moreThe film, directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, was made in secret over three years. Fielder spent more than a month with thedisgraced Theranos founderand her family, including her two young children and her partner, Billy Evans, in her final days before reporting to federal prison.The reviews have been extremely positive, with 99% on Rotten Tomatoes and 99 on Metacritic. It also won an unprecedented 91% “definite recommend” from audiences, according to PostTrak exit polls.You Can See Everything reportedly cost less than $7m to make and less than $10m to market.“Everybody underestimated the movie, because on paper this is like, wait, a three-hour documentary?” said Paul Dergarabedian, the head of marketplace trends for Rentrak, told Associated Press. “But [Fielder] is a huge draw, and he has a huge following on social media, and then Elizabeth Holmes is just a character that you couldn’t even make up. It’s stranger than fiction, and that’s really compelling.”Elsewhere in the box office,Street Fightertopped the charts as expected with a $51m global opening, including $20m from international showings. The movie starring Callina Liang, Noah Centineo and Andrew Koji cost a reported $82m to make, not accounting for marketing and promotion. Audiences were 69% male.Both Street Fighter and You Can See Everything may have contributed toWhalefall’s relative failure at the weekend. The $60m survival thriller starring Austin Abrams and Josh Brolin made $8m from 3,065 locations in the US and Canada, despite being better reviewed than Street Fighter. With $9.5m from international showings, the Disney release had a total $17.5m global launch.Whalefall opened in fourth place, behind the Jessica Chastain horror Other Mommy, which took $8.4m domestically in its second weekend, adding to its $78.7m global total.Alex Gibney’s Elon Musk documentary Musk also expanded to 472 screens in the US and Canada, making $306,702. The film, which runs for nearly four hours, has faced problems advertising on major social media platforms including X, which Musk owns, and TikTok, according to its distributor, Bleecker Street, which said that at the weekend TikTok had permanently suspended the film’s ad account.Netflix also shared ticket sales for the first time for the queer Spanish epic La Bola Negra, which made $277,500 from four locations at the weekend. The streamer has not historically reported box office for its theatrical releases but this film is breaking new ground as it is being positioned as a possible best picture contender. It will be in theatres for 47 days before it will be available to watch on Netflix.According to Rentrak, the weekend overall generated about $101.6m in ticket sales, up 45% from the same weekend last year. The year to date stands at $8.2bn, which is up almost 20% from 2025.– Associated Press contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsNathan FieldernewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Medieval romance overflowed with sexually active fairies’: the surprisingly long roots of romantasy | Fiction | The Guardian
description: Critics mock romantasy as raunchy trash – but this enchanting genre has its roots in medieval literature, and is much older, and wilder, than you might imagine
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Critics mock romantasy as raunchy trash – but this enchanting genre has its roots in medieval literature, and is much older, and wilder, than you might imagine
Content: La Belle Dame sans Merci by Frank Dicksee.Photograph: Artepics/AlamyView image in fullscreenLa Belle Dame sans Merci by Frank Dicksee.Photograph: Artepics/AlamyFiction‘Medieval romance overflowed with sexually active fairies’: the surprisingly long roots of romantasyCritics mock it as raunchy trash – but this enchanting genre is much older, and wilder, than you might imagineSarah CleggSun 18 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 07.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s a popular genre, filled with beautiful, human-sized fairies having sex with humans (often quite violent sex, but the people reading it seem to enjoy it). Word is that it’s badly written and unashamedly escapist – all golden, glittering palaces, wild adventure and, of course, gorgeous fairies. It’s certainly popular – plenty of the stories have been translated into numerous languages, spreading across continents. Serious commentators are sure it spells bad news: at best, it’s just a load of trash; at worst, it’s actively leading people astray. Most damningly of all, women produce and consume it. Welcome to the 12th century, where fairy romance is all the rage. Sound familiar?The romantasy that fills our shelves and bestseller lists – from Sarah J Maas’s A Court of Thorns and Roses to Callie Hart’s Quicksilver – is not a new genre, but part of a centuries-old heritage. You only need to look at the medieval predecessors of the modern romantasy novel to understand why it’s enjoyed by millions and why, even after hundreds of years, fairy romance has such power over us – and why there are still those who want to diminish and dismiss it.double quotation markThese stories were a place for women to explore their  desires, free from the idea that they should be chasteMedieval romances originated in the French courts of the late 1100s and were wildly popular, quickly spreading throughout Europe, not only from country to country, but also down the social scale, so that even farm workers and impoverished nuns knew the stories. They drew on tales of fairies in earlier myths, especially within Arthurian legends, and were adapted and expanded to be as thrilling as possible, providing people with the same escapism that romantasy does today. Read either the medieval or the modern tales and you’ll find glitter and blood and adventure, not to mention crystal palaces, glorious and perilous enchanted realms, terrifyingly handsome fairy knights, and queens who live in unearthly splendour. As one author of a 13th-century romance pointed out, speaking about the real world brings “grief and torment” – so why not turn to fairies?The wild sexual freedom of modern romantasy was there in medieval romance too, which overflowed with sexually active fairies, both male and female. There are detailed descriptions of fairy bodies, legs and breasts, and while the veil tends to be drawn over the act itself, both fairies and mortals are always “taking what they desire”, “making merry together”, “holding each other in their arms” and getting each other pregnant – even when either the mortal or fairy is married to someone else, or has only just met. And while there are fairy lovers who are kind, gentle and courteous, medieval audiences also thrilled to the idea of a brooding fairy shadow-daddy: the fairies often simmer with threat, never losing their darker edges even when the story ends with the lovers paired off happily. As with romantasy today, the medieval stories, by dint of being fictional, were a safe place to experiment with sex in a repressed society.This was even more important as medieval romance, like modern romantasy, was often written by women (such as the 12th-century poet Marie de France), and had a large female audience (something even Chaucer commented on) – so these stories were often a place for women to explore their desires, free from the idea that they should be chaste and subservient. (For reasons too complex to get into it right now, it was generally accepted that fairy sex didn’t quite count, so women who slept with fairies were still thought of as virgins.)Romantasy still provides this space now: although women may be more sexually liberated than they were in the middle ages, we’re often still uncomfortable with female desires. It’s certainly not a coincidence that many romantasy books today are targeted at teenage girls, who may not be able to talk openly about sex, and arepopular with women from more conservative backgrounds. And while the darker, more coercive side of fairy relationships (in both modernity and the middle ages) likely reflects the common fantasy of being overwhelmed, it also helps to alleviate any lingering guilt – after all, the less consensual the encounter, the less the mortal party can be blamed for it.These stories include a freedom from gender roles as well: in modern romantasy, women are the heroes, the drivers of the plots (the heroine of Saara El-Arifi’s Faebound is an elf military leader; in A Court of Thorns and Roses, a female hunter takes centre stage), while the male love interests, while apparently threatening, are normally intensely loving and vulnerable underneath. Medieval romances also flipped gender roles: you might think it’s a genre of knights rescuing damsels in distress, but more often than not it’s about powerful fairy queens rescuing distressed knights. Take the 12th-century narrative poem Lanval, for example, the story of a penniless and overlooked knight saved multiple times by his beloved fairy queen, that ends with her riding away to fairyland with him behind her on her horse.View image in fullscreenFans of A Court of Thorns and Roses characters at New York Comic Con 2023.Photograph: Roy Rochlin/Getty Images for ReedPopWhile the appeal of all this to the female writers and readers is clear, men happily indulged in these fantasies, too. Lanval was written by a woman but later translated by a man. Even in recent years, it’s been reported that 18% ofromantasy readers in the US are men, who enjoy the tales of male characters who love openly and unashamedly, and the strong, powerful women who love them back.Of course, medieval courts were as familiar with the criticisms of fairy romance as we are. Chaucer even wrote a romance parody – Sir Thopas – about a knight seeking an elf queen. Today, romantasy authors are accused ofcheapening popular cultureby journalists who often compose articles byflipping through the books looking for the naughty bits, just as Chaucer’s parody featured dirty jokes about elf sex. As a genre, it’s easy to mock, easy to dismiss the stories as “smut” and nothing more.But this alone can’t explain the ridicule – after all, there are plenty of modern fantasy books crammed with sex that get praised (take George RR Martin’s A Game of Thrones, for example). Instead, the vitriol seems to stem from the fact that it’s a genre enjoyed by women. In the 14th century we had Chaucer mockingly claiming that women held romances “in full great reverence” and clergymen complaining vociferously about the fact that women listen to romances “joyously and willingly”; today the genre is accused ofmaking women stupid, with critics arguing that sexy queensshouldn’t be discussed at literary festivals.The irony is that fairy romance gave us plenty of great literature, some still well known today (Shakespeare’s Titania and Oberon in A Midsummer Night’s Dream are straight out of romances, while Don Quixote is a romance parody, though heart­breakingly fairy-free); others have been largely forgotten (like one of my absolute favourites, the story of Guingamor). Fairy romance also gave us a huge number of long-forgotten fun romps (my secret heart belongs to the 13th-century Claris and Laris – more than 30,000 lines of pure fairy nonsense).Medieval romance faded from fashion in the late 1500s, after four glorious, fairy-filled centuries, in part because fairies themselves were changing – becoming miniature, flittering things that were less appealing as lovers (unless you had some fairly niche tastes). But while it is depressing that criticism has not moved on since the middle ages, it’s an utter joy to see female-centred fairy fantasies returning, hundreds of years after the first medieval romances were composed. So why not read some of the medieval romances, along with modern romantasy? You’d be participating in a centuries-old genre of freedom, imagination and joy, and I’m not sure you can ask for more than that.Perilous Enchantment: The True History of Faeries by Sarah Clegg is published by Granta.
