title: Ali G answers his critics: ‘Me ain’t the first intellectual to get haterz’ | Sacha Baron Cohen | The Guardian
description: Staines’s finest nailed the zeitgeist of the late 90s and early 00s, and now he’s back – but how does he fit into 2026? He discusses the backlash against his return, his worst ever interviewee and how he’s going to prevent world war two
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: Staines’s finest nailed the zeitgeist of the late 90s and early 00s, and now he’s back – but how does he fit into 2026? He discusses the backlash against his return, his worst ever interviewee and how he’s going to prevent world war two
Content: ‘Most reporters can’t even spell the world “jourmalist” … Ali G.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Most reporters can’t even spell the world “jourmalist” … Ali G.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianSacha Baron CohenInterviewAli G answers his critics: ‘Me ain’t the first intellectual to get haterz’Rich PelleyStaines’s finest nailed the zeitgeist of the late 90s and early 00s, and now he’s back – but how does he fit into 2026? He discusses the backlash against his return, his worst ever interviewee and how he’s going to prevent world war twoSun 18 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 08.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Can you tell people that you’re from Hustler?” Ali G asks me. “Or The Source. Or Guns & Ammo. Speaking to a Guardian journalist ain’t a good look for me in the hood.”At Ali’s request, we are meeting in an independent chicken shop in Staines because – due to some sort of mix-up – he thought the one interview he had agreed to for his new film wasChicken Shop Date, which was “90% likely to lead to boning”. He follows this with an entirely unprintable reminiscence about the first time he and “me Julie” had sex in the disabled toilets of Egham KFC.Now that we have established I am not in fact Amelia Dimoldenberg – and that any boning today will be strictly chicken-related – Ali changes tack. Whenever anyone comes near our table, he loudly explains, to my embarrassment, that we are actually conducting a major drug deal. Having seemingly worked his way through the entire menu, he starts asking what else he would need to buy to get the bill up to £500, after discovering that the Guardian is footing it.It is, in other words, reassuringly easy to tell that not everything about Ali G has changed, even though a lot has happened in the “20 decades” (he means 24 years) since he was last on the big screen in Ali G Indahouse. In that time, the UK has had nine prime ministers, survived a global pandemic and seen the rise of #MeToo and Black Lives Matter. Or, as Ali puts it rather more succinctly in the trailer: “The world went to crap: there was Covid, wars and Ed Sheeran”.View image in fullscreenBack in da house … Ali G.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianNow he’s back in Ali G: Who Iz I? – and, inevitably, not everybody is delighted. The trailer alone has prompted accusations that the fake dreadlocks, Rastafarian imagery and faux-Jamaican persona now look less like satire and more like an outdated racial caricature. Which is how, 24 years after Ali G first took his home town of Staines global, I find myself sitting opposite him in his old manor, trying to work out whether the UK is ready to show him some respect again.Parked outside is the same yellow Renault 5 I remember from Indahouse, now with a homemade Uber sign stuck in the windscreen. Around his neck hangs a diamond teddy bear clutching two sacks of money. It “used to be part of the crown jewels and was worn by the queen, RIP. A bloke who worked as a dog washer at Windsor palace nicked it and then came into the Crooked Billet pub in Iver Heath, where me bought it off him for 20K when me was rich,” he claims.More bafflingly, he is wearing four watches. “Dem are for different time zones – dis one is Staines, dis one is Egham, dis one iz Langley Village and dis one iz Scrotland.” There is plenty more to take in, but I should probably attempt to conduct the interview I actually came here for.double quotation markThere’s always gonna be haterz. it happened to Jesus, to Gandhi and to Brooklyn BeckhamSo how should I address you – Ali, Ali G or Mr G?Me iz known by me mates as “De G”, “G-Dog” and “De Ali-torney G-eneral” … and by Staines Benefits Office as Richard Watkins, Kelvin Matthews and Priyanka Patel.And what happened to the dreads?Me ain’t never had dreads. Me wears the Rasta bonnet because – and me iz trusting you to keep dis secret – dat’s where me keeps me stash, the ganja. Perfect place because the cops ain’t allowed to look under it for religious reasons, innit.We find out in the trailer that you’re about to become a dad. How are you preparing? Are you and your Julie going to NCT classes?Me has actually already become a daddy, something dat for the last 40 years me has prepared for five times every day. Me usually just prepared with me Julie, although one time we also prepared with Cheryl from Abrakebabra in dis marble Jacuzzi me bought off eBay, which tragically didn’t end well. Me put it upstairs at Nan’s house, when me filled it with water and the three of us got in, it was too heavy and broke through the floor and landed on me Nan, who was sitting in the room downstairs. Luckily it killed her instantly, completely squashed her. She died happy because just one week before, me had bought her a new pair of double-F swingaz for her 88th birthday. The weight of the Jacuzzi caused them to literally explode; one of her nipples was found three streets away. Anyway, when one life ends, another one starts, and me iz loving being a dad.View image in fullscreenWho’s the daddy? … Ali G in a still from his new film, with Morgana Robinson as his Julie.Photograph: Amazon MGM StudiosWhat sort of dad are you?There have been some discipline issues. No matter how many times me tells the baby, “Hands off, dem iz mine!”, him keeps trying to grab me Julie’s swingaz. But there you go – like his dad, he iz a boobs man, innit. Me loves him and he iz well brainy, at six months old him can already read audiobooks.Staines officially became Staines-upon-Thames in2012, partly to improve the town’s image after years of association with you – but now there’s a petition calling for a statue of you in the town. Do you feel vindicated? And if they build it, would you pose for it – perhaps naked, like Michelangelo’s David?Firstly, it ain’t because of me they changed the name of Staines. It’s because in 2012 the River Thames started flowing through the town, so they added it to the name, innit. Thirdly, me iz well proud dat they want to put a statute of me in the middle of Staines. Me Julie says the only difference between dat and the real thing iz dat the statute won’t be selling ganja – they’ll both be hanging around the town centre doing nothing, ha ha ha! Unfortunately, as well as loads of people wanting the statute, there are also loads of people who don’t, because of racialism. Me ain’t gonna let them win and iz willing to pay out of me Julie’s pocket for an Ali G erection in the middle of Staines.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI’m with stupid … Ali G meets Donald Trump.Photograph: Channel 4This is your first film in 24 years. Why come back now? Did the world need Ali G, or did Ali G need the world?Dis ain’t actually me first film in 24 years. Me has also made about 300 others with me Julie and iz hoping Amazon will buy them off me and put them in the “members only” part of their site. But to answer your question, the world needed me. Dis movie will be the most important release since the Jeffrey Einstein files, and me made it to increase the peace, bring both sides together and hopefully prevent world war two from ever happening. It has also got more boning in it than the Einstein files – all of it legal – and because me iz now woke, me also included a nude man’s battyhole to keep the LGBLT community happy.The Guardian has already been arguing about whether you should have come back at all.Arwa Mahdawiwrote “Ali G is back. I really wish he wasn’t”, whileJason Okundayeargued that Britain – and the joke – have changed.Jacob Rees-Mogg, meanwhile, has defended you on his Instagram, describing you as “clever, satiric humour that makes the country look faintly foolish. And that’s no bad thing.” So who understands Ali G better in 2026: the Guardian or Jacob Rees-Mogg?Me ain’t never heard of any of those people, but from their names it seems to me dat Jacob Rees-Mogg iz the only person of colour, so him supporting me iz all dat matters. There are always gonna be haterz, innit. Me ain’t the first intellectual to get dat – it happened to Jesus, it happened to Gandhi, it even happened to Brooklyn Beckham. For the good of humanoidkind, me has just got to keep speaking out. People shutting me down ain’t nothing new. In fact, me was cancelled just two years ago by Staines Benefits Office for pretending to be a disabled Albanian woman with seven children. Me just bounced right back with a new name. Don’t never let the authorities oppress you, innit.double quotation markMe’d have a puff with God and ask him: why does him allow terrible things to happen: like wars, diseases and Coldplay?You’ve come back to a world full of influencers, pranksters, podcasters and people asking strangers stupid questions on TikTok. Do you feel like everyone’s basically nicked your act?For real, loads of people have been copying me, especially the way me looks and talks – which makes them cultural appropriators and dat iz well out of order. It makes me well sad how fick the world has become since me was on telly doing interviews 20 decades ago – most reporters now can’t even correctly spell the word “jourmalist”, let alone ask brainy questions like you and me does do, innit.Prince William? David Cameron? JD Vance? Celebrities brace – and Staines celebrates – ahead of new Ali G filmRead moreYou’ve spent your career interviewing politicians, experts and other important people. Who would you most like to interview now?Me has always dreamed big, both in me personal life – for example, last night me imagined doing it with Sydney Sweeney; dat iz a woman, by the way, in case you ain’t heard of her. Me ain’t got nothing against homosapiens, me just ain’t one of them – and also in me professional life. Check dis: me wants to do the biggest interview ever – to go up to heaven and have a chat with none other than God himself. Me’d have a look around heaven – iz it any good, or iz it well boring, just a load of old blokes sitting around playing harps? Then me’d have a puff with God and ask him the tough questions: why does him allow terrible things to happen to the Earth, like wars, diseases and Coldplay? Also, while me was up there, me’d check in on me Nan, see if she’s doing all right and if she can still remember the Netflix password for our house.Who is the stupidest person you’ve ever interviewed?The most fickest person me ever spoke to was Domald Trump. How him ever became America’s prime minister me will never know. Also, how did him get to marry all them really fit women – first Ivanka, then Stormy Daniels and now dat one who looks like a Transformer, Melania?By now Ali has eaten an alarming amount of chicken. I’ve laughed far more than I expected to – including a few times when I probably shouldn’t. He is still crude, badly informed and completely inappropriate. But that was always the trick: every so often, the stupidest person in the room accidentally asks the smartest question. Before we go our separate ways, there’s just one question I need to ask. Does he think I’ve got what it takes to join the West Staines Massiv? Is there some kind of initiation process?“Me’ll have to check with the rest of me posse first – his name iz Dangerous Dave,” says Ali. “Me’ll ask him when he finishes work at HSBC at 5pm.”Ali G: Who Iz I? is in cinemas from23 October.Explore more on these topicsSacha Baron CoheninterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Dining across the divide: ‘He thought extra spending on defence would be wasted. He’s probably got a point’ | Life and style | The Guardian
description: One works in construction, the other finance – would they see eye to eye on Britain’s security, the royals and net zero?
Author: Erica Buist
Headline: One works in construction, the other finance – would they see eye to eye on Britain’s security, the royals and net zero?
Content: Carey and Chris. All photographs: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianView image in fullscreenCarey and Chris. All photographs: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianDining across the divideLife and styleDining across the divide: ‘He thought extra spending on defence would be wasted. He’s probably got a point’One works in construction, the other finance – would they see eye to eye on Britain’s security, the royals and net zero?Erica BuistSun 18 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCarey, 66, LondonOccupationLogistics manager on a construction siteVoting recordTory until Thatcher, Labour until Blair, whom he viewed to be “another Thatcherite”; now votes between Labour and Green, and tactically “to keep Nigel Farage out of office”Amuse boucheHe was homeless as a teenager but later got BA and master’s degrees, and has since worked for charities, the oil industry and he was even a bingo caller for three yearsChris, 58, LondonOccupationWorks for a bank in a risk-and-control roleVoting recordHe’s flipped between Conservative and Lib Dem “for tactical reasons”Amuse boucheHe’s trying to visit all 92 professional football league grounds in the UK. He’s done just under 50For startersCareyI wasn’t nervous, I enjoy talking to people and, as my wife puts it, I’ve always got an opinion. Chris is a very amiable individual.ChrisI was a bit nervous. He’s had a radically different upbringing to me, so it was interesting to hear his life story.CareyFor starters I had monkfish skewers, then crab pasta with a glass of white wine, and for dessert I had an old fashioned with a nice cheesecake.ChrisI had tuna tartare to start, which was fantastic, then grilled monkfish and fries with a glass of white wine. For dessert I had panna cotta with an old fashioned.View image in fullscreenThe big beefCareyChris thinks we should increase defence spending, but there is currently waste within the military spend. Before I give somebody more money, I want to see they’re looking after the money they’ve already got.ChrisGiven where we are geopolitically, increasing spending on defence is something we have to do. To me, it’s not a question of buying shiny new missiles, but defence against cyber-attacks.CareyI would argue the value of big shiny toys like nuclear submarines is slightly degraded in the modern arena – and if you’re saving billions a year on not having big flashy toys, you don’t need an increase. But I also agree we should pick up the bill for cyberwarfare.ChrisI think he generally felt that more money would probably be wasted. He’s probably got a point, to be honest.View image in fullscreenSharing plateCareyI think we should abolish the monarchy. For me, it’s about lack of transparency. There aremore than 1,000 cases of the royals seeing acts of law before they were passed, with no information about what the act was like before it was given to them. We should remove the privilege of an individual to interfere in parliament. People argue that they bring in tourism, but France abolished their monarchy and the Palace of Versailles gets far more visitors than Buckingham Palace.ChrisI’m not a great lover of the monarchy, but what would you have instead? I look at the leaders of the current political parties and I’m not sure I necessarily want any of them as head of state.View image in fullscreenFor aftersChrisI think net zero as a target is completely the right thing to do, but I have no idea if the timing that we’ve set is achievable. I’m not against us using the oilfields in the North Sea – it would extend the timescale under which we could move to net zero, but that might seem more manageable for people.CareyI agree with Chris that the likelihood of us achieving net zero as it stands is pretty low. But the big issue for me is: who pays? We have major players in this country, such as Amazon and Starbucks, that pay marginal or zero tax while paying low wages to a lot of people. Tax them and make them pay for it. Then it’s achievable.View image in fullscreenDining across the divide: ‘Without being patronising, I think as he grows older he’ll tune in to the damage “free speech” can do’Read moreTakeawaysCareyI always find it interesting to talk to people with opposing views, because it helps me build and question my own. The way that you learn is to say things to people who will challenge you.ChrisMy takeaway is what a really interesting guy he was, how well-informed, and how he had turned his life around – I had absolute admiration for him. I do think mistrust of the government did underpin a lot of his views, and he’s probably right on that. He didn’t fundamentally change my opinions – but I would do it again in a heartbeat.View image in fullscreenAdditional reporting: Kitty DrakeCarey and Chris ate atNoisy Oysterin London, E1Want to meet someone from across the divide?Find out how to take partExplore more on these topicsLife and styleDining across the divideSocial trendsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The best toys and gifts for eight-year-olds, tested by eight-year-olds | Toys | The Guardian
description: From science kits to karaoke machines, shower sets to brain-boosting games, here are the presents our mini testers loved the most
Author: Zoë Phillimore
Headline: From science kits to karaoke machines, shower sets to brain-boosting games, here are the presents our mini testers loved the most
Content: Composite: Sandra Navarro/Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenComposite: Sandra Navarro/Guardian DesignGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterToysThe best toys and gifts for eight-year-olds, tested by eight-year-oldsFrom science kits to karaoke machines, shower sets to brain-boosting games, here are the presents our mini testers loved the mostThe best gifts for seven-year-oldsZoë PhillimoreSun 18 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEight is such a wonderful age. Kids are old enough to have their own interests and hobbies, but still young enough to get swept up in play and be absorbed for hours if you find the right toy for them.By eight, children’s interests and skills are taking shape. They’re more confident readers, more strategic thinkers and curious about how things work. And while they think they’re extremely grown up, eight-year-olds still need plenty of time to play for their overall wellbeing.Here’s a rundown of toys and gifts that will keep eight-year-olds occupied for months to come: a roster of creative kits, clever games, outdoor adventures and timeless toys that will keep them happy and busy (while sneakily learning).How I selectedAs an experienced toy tester, I am living an eight-year-old’s dream. I have written about toys and parenting for almost 10 years and have also worked in schools and children’s publishing. As well as professionally observing children’s play, I also have three children, and in these guides I aim to balance what kids love to play with and what parents want in their house.I also asked children’s play specialists and development experts about the best toys to support the developmental stage most eight-year-olds are at – from school skills to wellbeing – for a holistic approach.A gang of lively eight-year-olds were enlisted to test toys and gifts on my behalf, and they weren’t shy in telling me what they thought of them. Their own gift picks can be found throughout this guide.The toys and gifts that made the cut here balanced all these needs. Sustainability was always on my mind when compiling this list, with the guiding principle of buying well, not more. I selected toys and gifts that my testers came back to over and over and should last them well into the tween stage.The best toys and gifts for eight-year-oldsView image in fullscreenPlay away: our testers recommended a wide range of gifts (for themselves and others).Photograph: Zoë Phillimore/The GuardianLife in 3DThose of a certain age may remember the TV show Penny Crayon; everything Penny drew came to life, getting her and her mates out of all kinds of strife. Well, this pen can (sort of) make the Penny Crayon dream come true for your child. The 3Doodler pen delivers a stream of BPA-free plastic, which cools as it hits the air, allowing children to create what they draw – “I made a pair of sunglasses and a very creepy-looking robot,” my tester reported with glee. The use of plastic made me hesitate to include it in this guide, but it kept my tester absorbed for hours. The filaments are made from a biodegradable material but can’t be put in household recycling.View image in fullscreen3Doodler Start+ 3D essential pen set£40 at John Lewis£39.99 at AmazonMaterials:plasticSuitable for:6+Game knight“An eight-year-old’s interests include more complex games,” saysLaura Moore-Williams, an early years consultant. Around this age, many children are taught to play chess at school, and the benefits are huge. It builds focus and critical thinking, while teaching patterns, spatial awareness and sequencing. All this will build important neural pathways in the developing brains of eight-year-olds. This board is a gift for life – it’s made from walnut and sycamore, and the pieces are handcarved. It folds in the middle with the pieces stored inside. My eight-year-old tester plays chess at school (many primary schools teach it at this age to develop problem-solving skills and mathematical and numerical reasoning), so their eyes lit up when they saw this board. They loved playing with a “proper” set rather than the tiny board they had been using.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Zoë Phillimore/The GuardianJaques of London complete folding chess board£40.99 at Jaques of London£34.99 at AmazonMaterials:wood, baize base for piecesSuitable for:6+The plot thickensEight is a great age for getting kids into a book series they can independently read and enjoy. Tom Gates was a huge hit with the eight-year-olds I spoke to. The books follow the slightly hapless but likable schoolboy Tom as he tries to wind up his annoying older sister, get his band going and eat as many caramel wafers as possible – while avoiding doing any homework. The books are filled with illustrations and aren’t too text heavy. My eight-year-old tester is a slightly reluctant reader, but they were racing through the books and begging for the next one.View image in fullscreenTom Gates Series 1 byLiz Pichon£25.13 at Rackhams£24 at AmazonMaterials:paperSuitable for:8+Build them up“For eight-year-olds I rate advancedLegosets,” says Moore-Williams. My eight-year-old tester loved this Mario Kart Lego set, whooping “awesome” with gusto as they clapped eyes on the box. Beyond the unboxing, it’s fun to build, with nothing that’s too repetitive, and they’re left with an amusing toy they can either display or play with (my tester definitely opted for the latter).View image in fullscreenLego Mario KartPiranha Plant Power-Up Pursuit£44.99 at Lego£35.34 at AmazonMaterials:plasticSuitable for:8+P-P-Pick up a pigeon“We started to have a Saturday afternoon games session with friends, and they brought this over to play,” said one eight-year-old tester. “It was fun for the adults and the kids, and it was easy to get the hang of.” When I tested this game with eight-year-olds and their younger siblings, it had them all giggling. It’s easy to get playing quickly (eight-year-olds don’t want to read dissertation-length instructions) and it’s pretty rapid fire – a game is won or lost within minutes – so it’ll hold even the shortest of attention spans. It’s also small enough to slip into a bag and whip out at a restaurant or pub on a rainy afternoon to keep kids from getting fidgety.View image in fullscreenOh My Pigeons! party game£12.99 at Smyths Toys£12.99 at AmazonMaterials:plastic, paperSuitable for:8+The fast and the curiousWe all know getting kids outside is vital for their physical and mental wellbeing, but it’s often easier said than done. For this guide, I looked for gifts that would get them to break cover, and this scooter fared well.Built for bigger kids (and adults), it’s got plenty to keep eight-year-olds excited. It has large, speedy wheels to cover longer distances – particularly handy if your kids are scooting to school. The chopper-style handlebars look cool and offer a good degree of control. Our eight-year-old tester was keen to take it to the skate park to test and had plenty of fun showing it off as well as racing it around. It is more expensive than other scooter models, but it’s also built to be easy to service and repair. Micro Scooters sells almost all the spare parts for its scooters – it even has aspares findersection on its site and avideo librarywith how-to guides for most adjustments. Despite having a warranty of only two years, this scooter will probably last the recipient way into their teenage years and survive being handed down plenty of times.View image in fullscreenMicroScooters Micro Speed deluxe scooter£165 at Selfridges£164.95 at AmazonMaterials:aluminium, metal, polyurethaneSuitable for:8+Open goal“Outdoor toys are a worthwhile investment if you have space for them,” says Daisy Upton, play specialist and author of theFive Minute Mumbook series. This football kit requires some space – but if you’re looking for an outdoor toy for eight-year-olds and have a decent-size garden, it’s a winner.My eight-year-old testers flocked to this kit, playing together and crucially not thinking about screens or schoolwork. “Developmentally, an eight-year-old needs to build strong peer relationships through play,” says Moore-Williams. While kids may have a football goal already before they’re eight, I picked this set because it feels like a step up that’s right for around this age. The goal is big enough (8ft x 6ft) for a proper-ish game, plus there’s a rebound net and target-practice sheet. The resistance parachute was wildly entertaining on its own. The goal is built to be up in all weathers, but it comes with a storage bag if you want to pack it away.View image in fullscreenRebo portable PVC football goal with training kit£99.99 at Outdoor ToysMaterials:PVC goalposts, net, anchors, fabric bag, football, pump, plastic cones, training ladder, fabric parachute, fabric target-practice sheet, elastic togglesSuitable for:3+skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionComic timingMy eight-year-old testers loved this idea: a weekly comic that comes in the post. Inside is a range of strips, which the reader becomes familiar with over time. Most issues we received included the wildly popular and zany Bunny vs Monkey by Jamie Smart, and serialised strips that depicted exciting adventures. There are also activities inside showing readers how to make their own comics, which my trio of testers loved. And, as a journalist, it is heartening to see that print is not dead for gen Alpha. You can subscribe for an initial six issues for just a quid, after which it auto-renews every 13 weeks for £36.99.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Zoë Phillimore/The GuardianThe Phoenix comic subscriptionFrom £1 at the Phoenix ComicFrom £1 at the MagazineMaterials:paperSuitable for:7+Pulling stringsWhether you have space outside or are just heading to the park or woods for an hour, this kit is brilliant. My eight-year-old testers were obsessed with the idea of making their own “booby traps” – thanks in no small part to Home Alone’s Kevin McCallister – and it was a joy to watch them use it.“I’ve got so many plans for how I’m going to use this, I can’t wait to tell my friends about it – they’re going to want one for themselves,” my eight-year-old tester said after one session of play. Inside the drawstring bag are a wooden plank, wooden box, rope, string, two pulleys, carabiners and some cards that suggest challenges to attempt.View image in fullscreenThe Den Kit Co pulleys kit£34.50 at the Den Kit CoMaterials:jute, wood, string, metalSuitable for:6+, adult supervision requiredSing loud enough to scare the demons off“Everyoneis obsessed with KPop Demon Hunters,” one eight-year-old told me, as if I was 1,000 years old and had been living under a rock. I generally sought to avoid potentially fleeting trends when compiling this list, but this one has real staying power beyond the Demon Hunters craze. While there are loads of karaoke machines on the market, this one feels robust – it survived being thrown about by many of my testers – and comes with two mics, a light and eight built-in games. A button on the mic adds vocal effects, and you can connect a Bluetooth device to use it as a speaker. Unfortunately for my headache, my testers went back again and again to this karaoke machine, which is why it made the cut.View image in fullscreenVTech electronic karaoke light party£59.99 at John Lewis£38.99 at AmazonMaterials:plastic, electronics, metalSuitable for:14+ (manufacturer’s age suggestion)Model behaviourEvery adult I’ve mentioned Fimo to during testing has the same wistful reaction about playing with it as a child. It’s just as good as you remember it, folks. My eight-year-old testers loved making animals out of the multicoloured pack and baking them in the oven. This is relatively mess-free crafting, without any rigid rules to follow (although there’s plenty of inspiration online if you’re stuck for ideas). Fimo is single use, but the idea is you make something to play with once it’s cured – my testers loved creating their own characters.View image in fullscreenStaedtler Fimo soft oven-hardening polymer modelling clay£14.50 at Cass Art£8 at AmazonMaterials:polymer claySuitable for:8+Switched onMoore-Williams also recommended Stem (science, technology, engineering and mathematics) kits. This particular set has 100 projects to keep eight-year-olds’ minds and fingers busy.“As soon as I saw this set, I wanted to make a security alarm!” one eight-year-old tester said. Personally, it gave me flashbacks to school physics, but my testers loved it: “We can pick what we do from loads of options, which is sooo fun,” said one. There are plenty of projects in this Stem set to keep kids busy on rainy days.View image in fullscreenOn Bots 100electronics kit£29.53 at CPC£29.95 at AmazonMaterials:plastic, metalSuitable for:8+Bath goals“I really need some beauty products,” an eight-year-old tester said to me. I glanced at their parents and could see that perhaps their hopes didn’t align.This Lush gift set is a perfect compromise for those not-quite-tweenagers. Yes, it’s a beauty product, but still playful. Inside is a zingy Happy Hippy shower gel that’s more citrus-leaning than candy store, and Lush’s Outback Mate. This is a solid soap bar with a minty scent – a nice change from some of the cloyingly sweet scents that make up lots of products for children this age. This gender-neutral set is great for even the most determined mini soap-dodgers.View image in fullscreenLush Fresh As gift set£14.50 at LushMaterials:soap, shower gel; packaging: recycled board, recycled paper, recycled plastic bottlesSuitable for:3+What to buy for an eight-year-oldView image in fullscreenGet creative: choose gifts that encourage children to explore their interests.Photograph: Zoë Phillimore/The GuardianEvery play expert I spoke to championed a “less is more” approach for children of all ages when it comes to toys. “Common mistakes adults make when choosing toys are being swayed by fads that hold children’s attention for only a few weeks,” says Moore-Williams. They’re “overloading children with too much choice instead of curating a smaller, versatile collection”.Winning toys tend to be a bit more complex for kids this age – there’s a longer attention span for strategy games, puzzles and creative projects. At eight years old, children are more likely to be developing specific hobbies and interests that last longer than a common cold. For any gift, it’s always a good idea to tap into the recipient’s interests.“As children get older, we should be asking, ‘What specific play does this child enjoy the most?’ ‘What are their special interests?’ ‘Can we get something to encourage this further?’” says Upton. “Really lean into what they love to do most, what lights them up, and you can’t go wrong.”Do they love to sit and draw? Get them some open-ended craft supplies – some decent felt-tip pens, stacks of paper and notebooks never miss in my experience. If they love sport, look at what might help them enjoy playing more – kit for keen footballers, goggles for swimmers and warm-up gear for dancers would be useful and show that you know the child and support their interests.What to get for eight-year-olds who don’t play with toys?At this age, experiential gifts are a great idea if space is tight or your recipient isn’t hugely into toys.You can buy vouchers fora trip to Legolandfor £39, and this theme park is specifically aimed at this age – there are plenty of rides suitable for many eight-year-olds. If you want something more sedate, theatre vouchers were a gift lots of eight-year-olds told me were on their wishlists. Buying vouchers from services such asTheatre Tokenswill let your child have some agency and pick tickets at more than 300 theatres throughout the country.For more, read our guides to thebest toys and gifts for seven-year-oldsand thebest sustainable toys for kidsZoë Phillimore is a journalist with 20 years of experience. She’s tested many things, from mattresses to makeup, and she’s slightly obsessed with finding small new businesses to spotlight. Aside from this, Zoë loves travel, being outside – especially on the beach – and finding screen-free things to keep her threeactive children busy.
