title: World leaders must wise up to threat of cyber-attacks or rogue fridges will be least of their worries | Heather Stewart | The Guardian
description: Global cooperation seems unlikely despite AI increasing the risk of digital fraud and the need to protect the financial system
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Global cooperation seems unlikely despite AI increasing the risk of digital fraud and the need to protect the financial system
Content: Hackers forced up the temperature of many French supermarket fridges to 50C, resulting in them having to be emptied and food thrown away.Photograph: Fred Tanneau/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHackers forced up the temperature of many French supermarket fridges to 50C, resulting in them having to be emptied and food thrown away.Photograph: Fred Tanneau/AFP/Getty ImagesEconomics viewpointCybercrimeWorld leaders must wise up to threat of cyber-attacks or rogue fridges will be least of their worriesHeather StewartGlobal cooperation seems unlikely despite AI increasing the risk of digital fraud and the need to protect the financial systemSun 18 Oct 2026 07.46 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 09.31 EDTShareRogue French fridges were an unlikely talking point for the world’s leading economists, central bankers and finance chiefs meeting in a sultry Bangkok last week – helping to underline the spiralling cost of cyber-attacks.Kristalina Georgieva, the managing director of the International Monetary Fund, seized on news that supermarket chains across France had to chuck out piles of spoiled food after hackersaccessed their fridge controlsand turned up the temperature to 50C.Speaking at the fund’s annual meetings in the Thai capital, she was keen to hammer home the importance of guarding against “bad actors” in a rapidly changing, interconnected world – especially now that AI was “putting the potential of digital fraud on steroids”.Not cool: who hacked France’s supermarket fridges?Read morePolicymakers have been warning for some time that the AI boom could at some point threaten financial stability via a share price crash – a “correction”, as it is euphemistically called.But a different, related threat came into sharp focus in Bangkok. Georgieva said she was concerned that cybercrime, turbocharged by AI, could undermine trust in the financial system altogether.Social media feeds are rife with adverts using celebrity fakes to punt cryptocurrencies or gold, and even the old-school email-style scams can be generated far more prolifically.Just as a sea of AI slop has the potential to undermine trust in fact-based reporting and send people down political rabbit holes, Georgieva fretted that cyber-fraud could knock consumer confidence in mainstream banks.Recalling her own childhood behind the iron curtain in Bulgaria, she said many people did not trust the system, and kept their cash in a shoebox under the bed. “I worry, today, that unless we figure out how to get ahead of this curve … we may end up with lots of people with shoeboxes under their beds,” she said.It might not even take a cybercrime wave. This week the JP Morgan chief executive, Jamie Dimon, warned that the bank would not allow digital agents to operate on its customers’ behalf. “You don’t want rogue agents, and there could be thousands of them,” he said.View image in fullscreenThe IMF’s Kristalina Georgieva is concerned that cybercrime, turbocharged by AI, could undermine trust in the financial system.Photograph: Lillian Suwanrumpha/AFP/Getty ImagesAI agents, including Meta’s Muse, are starting to offer their users the opportunity to hand over their financial details. The agents will then scout for the highest savings rates and shift the user’s money accordingly.Financial regulators fret about this for a number of reasons. One is that if such services become widely used, they could have destabilising herding effects. With deposits able to be moved around the financial system at a moment’s notice, it could accelerate a bank run in times of uncertainty.A second worry is that highlighted by Dimon: who is responsible if your AI agent makes a financial decision on your behalf that turns out to be disastrous – or even criminal?The answer is probably that we will need case law to find out, which will only come when something goes badly awry.That is alarming because legal ambiguity about who owes what to whom when things go wrong can be an accelerant to financial instability.We learned that lesson back in the 2008 financial crisis, when it turned out that some banks had built financial products with such fiendishly complex liability structures that they were effectively impossible to value – unleashing panic.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSpeaking alongside Georgieva, the Bank of England governor, Andrew Bailey, who chairs the Financial Stability Board of global central bankers, pointed to another arresting news story from this week – that Anthropic had warned AI modelsmight soon be able to “self-replicate” in domestic devices. Who should bear the responsibility – and the costs – if your internet-enabled oven, or telly, blows up as a result?One entirely prudent response might be for consumers to reject internet-enabled devices and stick to “dumb” appliances instead that can’t be hijacked by self-replicating bots. This month, some of those French supermarkets rushed to take their fridges offline to avoid the hack.While it may not be much of a loss to society if internet-enabled kettles and fridges do not take off, the financial analogue to a dumb appliance would be Georgieva’s shoeboxes – and that would have costs for those consumers, and the smooth running of the economy as a whole.As Bailey somewhat apocalyptically put it: “If we don’t have trust in money, we don’t operate as a society.”Senior financial policymakers are genuinely disturbed at the collision between rapidly developing AI and the global financial system – which now extends well beyond heavily regulated banks – to embrace social media platforms, payments apps and other financial tools.It is unfortunate this moment comes as the US – the crucible of the AI boom – is governed by a man whose main contribution to the debate has been to seek to rename AI“superintelligence”.At the Bangkok meetings this week, Kevin Warsh, the chair of the US Federal Reserve, obediently used Donald Trump’s phrase on stage – as all US government agencies have been ordered to.There has been some progress in acknowledging the risks. Trump’s superintelligence taskforce, chaired by the director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton, is setting up mechanisms for AI labs to report “breaches, hacks, jailbreaks, and other ​issues” – although not, it seems, to submit their models for pre-launch testing.The UK has pledged to take up the issue of AI safety as part of its agenda for the G20 presidency next year, and G7 finance ministers announced in Bangkok that they would carry out simulations to test the resilience of the global financial system to cyber-attacks.That could help to highlight vulnerabilities, but the questions at stake are much wider and more complex than whether criminals can hack the banks – and are urgent now, just as the prospects for international cooperation seem bleak. Superintelligence will seem anything but super if its misuse becomes a trigger for financial chaos.Explore more on these topicsCybercrimeEconomics viewpointInternational Monetary Fund (IMF)AI (artificial intelligence)EconomicsKristalina GeorgievaAndrew BaileyBank of EnglandcommentShareReuse this content

title: There are five signs that someone dislikes you – but it’s best to ignore them | Polly Hudson | The Guardian
description: All the possible indications, from eye contact to body language, come with a disclaimer. The truth is, you can never be totally sure, writes Polly Hudson
Author: Polly Hudson
Headline: All the possible indications, from eye contact to body language, come with a disclaimer. The truth is, you can never be totally sure, writes Polly Hudson
Content: If looks could kill …Photograph: posed by models; FG Trade/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIf looks could kill …Photograph: posed by models; FG Trade/Getty ImagesOpinionFriendshipThere are five signs that someone dislikes you – but it’s best to ignore themPolly HudsonAll the possible indications, from eye contact to body language, come with a disclaimer. The truth is, you can never be totally sure ...Sun 18 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 11.01 EDTShareI’d be far less paranoid if everyone wasn’t out to get me, so when BBC Science Focus dangled “The subtle signs somebody secretly dislikes you”, I’ve never clicked so fast. Knowledge is power, after all, and the promised signals came courtesy of psychologists via a magazine with the word science in its title.The first indication? They avoid eye contact. Apparently “someone who repeatedly looks away, scans the room or avoids mutual gaze might be creating psychological distance”. Agreed. But they may also be checking to see who else arrives, which might not mean they secretly hate you, only that they secretly don’t like you as much as whoever just came in.The second sign is unarguably more convincing. “Their facial expressions show contempt or disgust.” Admittedly, I’m no psychologist, but still, if someone looked contemptuous or disgusted while interacting with me, I’d be pretty confident in concluding that they aren’t my greatest fan all on my own. File this one under bear/woods, pope/Catholic.Third up, they “smile less around you”. This feels dangerous, because the only way to know whether they are smiling less around you than other humans they come into contact with is to put them under surveillance and keep a tally. If they didn’t dislike you before you hid in a bush counting their grins, they probably would afterwards.The final pieces of evidence are that their body points away from you, and they create physical distance. Again, not a psychologist, but if a person turned their back on or ran away from me, I think I might manage to pick up on the nuance.Hold on though, now there’s a disclaimer: “Reduced eye contact, physical distance and less smiling can all have many explanations, including tiredness, shyness, neurodiversity, anxiety, distraction or cultural norms.” Fantastic. So what have we learned? Unless somebody is blatant, it’s extremely tricky to tell if they secretly dislike you. And even then, there could be other reasons for their behaviour, so you can never truly be sure. The take away: trust no one, not even science.Polly Hudson is a freelance writerExplore more on these topicsFriendshipOpinionPsychologycommentShareReuse this content

title: If Trump fells 430 trees in the middle of a golf course, do they make a sound? | Dave Schilling | The Guardian
description: In attempting to turn a public space in DC into an enclave for elites, Trump is moving the US capital closer to Graceland
Author: Dave Schilling
Headline: In attempting to turn a public space in DC into an enclave for elites, Trump is moving the US capital closer to Graceland
Content: Donald Trump’s crusade to clear more than 400 trees to redevelop East Potomac Golf Links into a championship-level course isn’t happening. For now.Photograph: Giorgio Viera/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump’s crusade to clear more than 400 trees to redevelop East Potomac Golf Links into a championship-level course isn’t happening. For now.Photograph: Giorgio Viera/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionDonald TrumpIf Trump fells 430 trees in the middle of a golf course, do they make a sound?Dave SchillingIn attempting to turn a public space in DC into an enclave for elites, Trump is moving the US capital closer to GracelandSun 18 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 07.16 EDTShareWhen is a tree not a tree? When it’s an obstacle to a par-3. If a tree falls in the middle of a golf course, does it make a sound? Yeah, probably. I wasn’t there, but I have to assume, based on my limited knowledge of the laws of physics.What I do know is that Donald Trump’s crusade to clear more than 400 trees for the purposes of redeveloping East Potomac Golf Links into a championship-level course isn’t happening. For now.The US district judgeAna Reyes shut down the project this week, though the administration claimed it had already cleared 430 of the planned 529 trees. This was after aMay order from Reyesto require the White House to request approval for cutting down more than 10 trees. Reyes ordered a full stop to the tree clearing until 26 October, and threatened contempt of court if the administration doesn’t abide.As is always the case with this president, he is attempting to assert some manner of control over a public asset. In this case, said asset is a golf course, which means he’sreallyinvested. You might not be able to get him tostop staring at Jon Husted’s assto sort out inflation, gas prices or the conflict in Iran, but you better believe he can put aside the senator from Ohio’s manly posterior long enough to sort out dramatic changes to a public golf course.By seizing control of East PotomacGolfLinks without any oversight or approval, the administration is essentially seizing that asset from the American people. By turning East Potomac into a championship-level course with an 18-hole layout, strategic hazards and expensive maintenance, Trump is inching the course away from being a public good and toward a private enclave for the elites.Yes, I’m talking about golf here. I understand the irony of trying to separate this sport from elitism. This isn’t exactly soccer, which you could play in a backyard, the street or inside your parents’ house until you knock a ball through the flatscreen TV.East Potomac is a popular course with the residents of DC. It has two nine-hole courses, an 18-hole course and a miniature golf area. The mini golf area has, as you’d hope,hazards shaped like national landmarks. Unfortunately, it doesn’t seem like there’s a way to putt a golf ball into Teddy Roosevelt’s mouth. At least not yet.This is yet another instance of the priorities of one person taking precedent over the needs of literally anyone else. Trump clearly wants to play on a fancy, private golf course in DC. All three DC golf courses are publicly owned and operated by the National Park Service (though the park service has a partnership with the non-profit National Links Trust to renovate and operate the courses, which Trump tried toterminate in December of 2025). East Potomac, being the largest, has the most opportunity to be the shrine to our commander-in-chief’s favorite leisure obsession.I can’t stop myself from picturing what the new East Potomac Golf Links would look like under Trump’s control. The first thing is, it would surely become Trump-East Potomac Golf Links, since a facility without his name on it is a facility wasted.Would the mini golf course survive? Doubtful, as mini golf is strictly for poor people, and the PGA and the United States Golf Association would be too busy laughing at the windmill hazards to schedule the US Open there.But if it stayed, I’d guess there’d be at least a few changes to the layout of the course. Perhaps you’d have to knock your ball past recreations of Trump Tower, a gold-plated toilet and the outstretched fist of the president himself.As much as I care about the beautiful old trees being torn out for no reason, I’m equally flabbergasted by what’s at the core of this project – the lust to turnWashington DCinto Graceland, or a worse, Donald Trump-themed version of that. Graceland is the final home of Elvis Presley, and has become a popular tourist attraction since his passing.It’s a shrine to all things Elvis, full of merchandise and memorabilia. The area of Memphis around the home is designed to facilitate tourism and commerce.I love commerce as much as the next red-blooded American, and DC has long been dependent on tourism to prop up its economy. But the lure of DC was American history, not one man’s vanity project.Without oversight or lawful procedure, DC will become Graceland – a place for fans of a famous person to get their picture taken with his old shoes. As Trump’s tenure at the center of American life comes to an end in the next two years, he’s only going to accelerate his attempts to turn the nation’s capital into an extension of his own, very lucrative brand ventures.There are alreadynumerous golf courses with Trump’s name on them, so the novelty isn’t even that potent. It’s that this course is ours, and by that, I mean it belongs to the taxpayers of this country. Taking it and its history and molding it to his will is the fun of it for Donald Trump. That it isn’t his, but it can be, makes it a conquest worthy of his time. Like the Kennedy Center, he can put his name on it, he can try to change it, but it will never truly be his.Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humoristExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionWashington DCGolfUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Wikipedia often gets taken for granted – but its history is fascinating, and its future is fragile | Richard Cooke | The Guardian
description: Wikipedia’s 68m articles have been consulted trillions of times. Not bad for a website that has barely changed since it was founded 20 years ago
Author: Richard Cooke
Headline: Wikipedia’s 68m articles have been consulted trillions of times. Not bad for a website that has barely changed since it was founded 20 years ago
Content: Wikipedia’s ‘amateurish, homegrown ethos’ was off-putting to a lot of writers and journalists, Richard Cooke writes. ‘Most of the people seriously interested in Wikipedia were a handful of academics.’Photograph: Boris Roessler/EPAView image in fullscreenWikipedia’s ‘amateurish, homegrown ethos’ was off-putting to a lot of writers and journalists, Richard Cooke writes. ‘Most of the people seriously interested in Wikipedia were a handful of academics.’Photograph: Boris Roessler/EPAWikipediaWikipedia often gets taken for granted – but its history is fascinating, and its future is fragileRichard CookeWikipedia’s 68m articles have been consulted trillions of times. Not bad for a website that has barely changed since it was founded 20 years agoSun 18 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 19.07 EDTShareAfew years ago, I was struck by the tension between howWikipediawas used, and how it was talked about. Everyone was on it all the time, and yet its reputation had stalled at “don’t trust it”, because it was the “free encyclopedia that anyone can edit”.Clearly peopleweretrusting it, so much so it had become part of the fabric of everyday life since it was founded by Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger in 2001. But despite the fact it now has been consulted trillions of times by billions of people (English Wikipedia alone is 5.2bn words long), it inspires an odd lack of curiosity. Even people donating to Wikipedia might say the money was “for the factcheckers”, though there aren’t any – not paid ones, anyway. Meanwhile, the internet in the social media era had begun to feel like a much uglier place, and some digital nostalgia was setting in: here was this holdover that had somehow survived; a website that functions – and even looks – much the same as it did 20 years ago.‘People thought I was a communist doing this as a non-profit’: is Wikipedia’s Jimmy Wales the last decent tech baron?Read moreYou could say that I fell down a Wiki rabbit hole, especially when it came to the website’s early years. Almost everything important about the project came together quite quickly. Its amateurish, homegrown ethos was off-putting to a lot of writers and journalists, and that meant many questions about why it had worked had no answers. Most of the people seriously interested in Wikipedia were a handful of academics – so I decided to write a book about it.I’m not a tech journalist. Instead, I have a background in the humanities. Wikipedia actually does, too: philosophy, and even off-piste disciplines like town planning and poetry, played a much bigger role in its inception than pure technology. Ward Cunningham, who invented the wiki in the 1990s – that’s a webpage anyone can edit, and the foundational tool of Wikipedia – thought very carefully about how the power of computers might be democratised. He drew on all sorts of oblique concepts for it, such as constructivism and the Zen concept of wabi-sabi – beauty in imperfection – and it’s remarkable how well the culture he created has persisted. Especially wabi-sabi – Wikipedia is, after all, always in a state of incompleteness.View image in fullscreenWikipedia co-founder Jimmy Wales. ‘Lots of people in the dotcom boom started online encyclopedias, but Wales was the only one to hire a philosopher.’Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesPhilosophy drew Wikipedia’s co-founders together as well. Though Wales worked in tech and finance, he corresponded with philosophers for years. And though Sanger was an academic philosopher, he spent lots of time arguing online – only “amateurs” seemed to share his sense that philosophy had life-and-death stakes. Lots of people in the dotcom boom started online encyclopedias, but Wales was the only one to hire a philosopher. In fact, theonlyperson he hired was a philosopher. It was such an unpredictable choice, and an important clue to what made Wikipedia work: it sprang out of this digital “republic of letters”, where all sorts of people were thinking about facts and why they were important.Because Wikipedia is so massive, writing an “exhaustive” book on it is impossible, like trying to represent a mountain with a grain of sand. Instead, I concentrated on the human history – the small, sometimes very small, number of people who really influenced what Wikipedia became. Wikipedians can be difficult, and the most ornery get a bad wrap – even the Wikimedia Foundation’s leadership has made comments about their “Dorito-stained fingers”, or tendency to stay home on a Saturday night. But by the end of the process, I was in awe of them, and I still am.double quotation markThe first woman to edit Wikipedia, Gaytha Langlois, wrote about two things dear to her: Rhode Island and standard poodlesWales and Sanger are prominent, but many other important early Wikipedians are unknown. The first woman to edit Wikipedia, Gaytha Langlois, hasn’t had much attention. She wrote about two things dear to her: Rhode Island and standard poodles – small states and big dogs. Wikipedia has always had a gender imbalance, which has proved stubborn –Sandi Toksvig is only the latest in a long line of critics trying to address it. She is part of an effort to create a more balanced alternative to Wikipedia called Mappa Mundi, which has the potential to feed back into Wikipedia as well.I became fascinated too with a little-known contributorwho had the first biographical page for a woman on Wikipedia (today, it would be called a user page). Her name was Ruth Ifcher, and she was a very intelligent grammar pedant, with a PhD, who had been forced out of the workforce with severe agoraphobia. Wikipedia came along later in her life and opened a whole new avenue for creative and meaningful work.Proust said that neurotics alone “composed our masterpieces”, and that’s true here.Neurodiversity is so central to Wikipedia that one former head of the Wikimedia Foundation told me the encyclopedia is a “city built by Asperger’s”. You can sense that energy in familiar topics – planes, trains and automobiles, comic books, weather, and all the rest. Often, Wikipedians are so prolific that they write too much, a phenomenon called “fancruft”. “Road geeks” (like trainspotters for roads) kept having their work about minor roads deleted, so a whole lot of them left in a huff, and started a separateonline wiki encyclopedia for roads. That’s almost a microcosm of the inclusionists v deletionists debate, which is the biggest philosophical rift on Wikipedia – a rolling argument about what should be included, and what shouldn’t.View image in fullscreenThe co-founders had once believed that 100,000 articles would be “a reasonable size” for an encyclopedia, because that’s how big Britannica was. Today, Wikipedia has 68m, and Pew Research estimates that it served 1.9tn page views between 2015 and 2025. Because it is so monumental, I never expected Wikipedia to feel fragile or vulnerable – but as I was finishing the book, AI had begun to encroach on Wikipedia in an existential way by diminishing the web traffic it relies on, for instance, or by editors contributing huge volumes of poorly written AI-generated text. People ask me “is Wikipedia under threat?”, and it is, but so is everything from Hollywood to pure mathematics. I do think it will survive, but the quaking foundations made it feel urgent to say “we saw this made, and we won’t see anything like it again”.The Last Best Place on the Internet: A Human History of Wikipedia by Richard Cooke is out now through Black Inc in Australia, and WW Norton in the US. It will be released in the UK on 5 November, via GrantaExplore more on these topicsWikipediaInternetTechnology booksAustralian booksAI (artificial intelligence)commentShareReuse this content

title: Blunder in, abandon allies and court a dictator: it’s the Trump doctrine, now playing out in Myanmar | Steve Bloomfield | The Guardian
description: The US condemned the genocide and military rule there, but now that Trump craves its rare earths, that’s all changed. For democracy activists, that’s a disaster, says former Observer international editor Steve Bloomfield
Author: Steve Bloomfield
Headline: The US condemned the genocide and military rule there, but now that Trump craves its rare earths, that’s all changed. For democracy activists, that’s a disaster, says former Observer international editor Steve Bloomfield
Content: Protesters opposed to the military junta in Myanmar at a rally in Quezon City, Philippines, 11 April 2025.Photograph: Rolex dela Peña/EPAView image in fullscreenProtesters opposed to the military junta in Myanmar at a rally in Quezon City, Philippines, 11 April 2025.Photograph: Rolex dela Peña/EPAOpinionMyanmarBlunder in, abandon allies and court a dictator: it’s the Trump doctrine, now playing out in MyanmarSteve BloomfieldThe US condemned the genocide and military rule there, but now that Trump craves its rare earths, that’s all changed. For democracy activists, that’s a disasterSun 18 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 12.37 EDTShareMarco Rubio was once adamant that the US had to do everything in its power to end what he described as the “ethnic cleansing” of the Rohingya in Myanmar. In a 2017letter he signed along with 20 other US senators, Rubio called for “strong multilateral sanctions against specific senior Burmese military officials associated with the gross human rights abuses”. Those responsible for the atrocities should be prosecuted, he argued.In the years since, the Myanmar military’s crimes have only increased. What was then deemed ethnic cleansing of the Rohingya is now widely viewed, including by the US, as genocide. What little democracy existed in Myanmar was eradicated in 2021 whenAung San Suu Kyi was arrested and imprisonedand her party’s election victory overturned, and the military took full control.This sparked a civil war that has now turned into a brutal series of overlapping conflicts between the military, resistance forces and a medley of ethnic militias. Around100,000 people have been killedin the conflict, which has forced 5 million people to flee their homes. The UN estimates that 16 million are now in need of urgent assistance. It is one of the world’s biggest humanitarian disasters – and entirely human-made.Earlier this year, Myanmar held sham elections, and Min Aung Hlaing – the general most responsible for Myanmar’s genocide and one of the targets of Rubio’s letter –became president.But Rubio, now the US secretary of state, no longer believes that Min Aung Hlaing should be prosecuted. Instead he’d rather like him to become an ally. This month the Trump administration decided to upend nearly a decade of united western policy and open direct talks with theMyanmarregime. The possibility of lifting sanctions is now being discussed. The move has shocked other western nations – none of which, it appears, was warned.Inevitably, a Maga figure lingers in the background. This time it’s Roger Stone, the Donald Trump ally who wasfound guilty in 2019 of lying to Congress, witness tampering and obstructing the investigation into whether the Trump campaign conspired with Russia in the 2016 presidential election.Stone, who was spared jail after Trump commuted his sentence, recently startedworking as a lobbyist for the Myanmar regime, helping to “rebuild relations between the Republic of the Union of Myanmar and the United States”.It seems to be working. Earlier this month Michael Vance, the assistant secretary of ​state for intelligence and research,travelled to Myanmar’s capital Naypyidaw. The trip was supposedly to secure the release of a US citizen, but Vance also held talks with the generals. The purpose of the talks was not to persuade the military regime to reintroduce democracy or stop its brutal war. Instead it appeared to be about securing American access to Myanmar’s rare earth minerals.In recent years, the race to control a steady supply of rare-earth minerals – elements used in a host of military technology and hi-tech manufacturing applications – has become increasingly fraught. China controls most of the world’s rare-earth mines andalmost all of the processing capacity. The Trump administration’s desire to turn the tables has led it to strike one-sided deals with Ukraine and theDemocratic Republic of Congothat have placed US business interests over practically everything else.There are more than 600 rare earth mines in Myanmar, most of which currently supply China. Since the 2021 coup, rare-earth shipments from Myanmar to China have totalled $3.6bn, making up the majority of China’s rare-earth imports. This is the prize the US appears to have its eyes on.Vance’s trip has handed Myanmar’s generals a propaganda victory at a moment when they are doing everything they can to legitimise the regime. The US, unfortunately, is not the only country welcoming Myanmar’s generals back into the fold. Min Aung Hlaing this month flew to Malaysia, once a strong opponent of the junta, where the prime minister Anwar Imbrahim floated the idea ofMyanmar being welcomed back into the Association of Southeast Asian Nations(Asean). Trips to Indonesia and Brunei are also on the cards, while the Philippines has indicated that it too would like to see relations normalised.The junta’s diplomatic victories follow growing military success. Over the last two and a half years, with the help of more sophisticated drones supplied by Russia and China, and the conscription of another 100,000 young men, the junta has regained control over several towns and pushed the resistance back into the countryside.For Myanmar’s civilians, the long nightmare continues. Last monthmore than 50 people were killedwhen the military bombed a busy market in a rebel-held area. Every week brings fresh atrocities, while the hope of a peaceful, democratic Myanmar slips further into the distance.View image in fullscreenThe aftermath of a military airstrike on a market and the Kisapanadi bridge in Rakhine, western Myanmar, 28 September 2026.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesThe one silver lining that those fighting for Myanmar’s freedom can cling to is that the rest of the west hasn’t given up on it yet. British diplomats are adamant that there will be no change in the UK’s position, while Canada, Australia and the EU are all likely to hold the line too. But even here there are concerns.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCampaigners point to the UK’s recent reduction in aid to Myanmar from £66m a year to £55m. Justhalf of the $889.6mthe UN has requested for Myanmar this year has been provided by international donors. They would also like to see Britain and others engage more directly with Myanmar’s pro-democracy camp, including the resistance.Trump is not the first president to prioritise resources over democracy, as a cursory glance at US relations with Saudi Arabia since it discovered oil in 1938 shows. But Trump’s rapacious attitude to oil and minerals, his willingness to enrich his friends and family, and his brazen support for dictators makes this a very different America. Myanmar is simply another example of the corrosive nature that Trump’s foreign policy is having in every corner of the globe.The question is whether Trump will get what he wants. US policy on Myanmar has been driven by Congress, and there remains bipartisan support for keeping it in place. The House of Representatives recently passed a bill that would extend the sanctions regime for another six years. Particularly at a time when his support is waning, Trump is unlikely to have much joy in persuading senators and members of Congress who have long supported Myanmar’s pro-democracy movement to turn a blind eye to genocide and war crimes.Malaysia begins Myanmar repatriations despite warnings from UN and rights groupsRead moreEven if he did, the bigger question is whether Myanmar’s generals can give Trump what he wants. The vast majority of Myanmar’s rare earth mines are near the border with China and many are controlled by militia groups, not the junta. “There is no way China is going to let the US get anywhere near the rare earths,” Joshua Kurlantzick at the Council on Foreign Relations told me.And yet even if none of this leads to any real change, the Trump administration’s decision to open talks with a genocidal regime responsible for one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises is a disaster for those in Myanmar fighting for their freedom. Many Myanmar resistance figures, including Aung San Suu Kyi, have placed their hope in US help. Like other democrats fighting demagogues, such as Volodymyr Zelenskyy, they have been deserted.Here is yet another example of the Trump administration blundering into a part of the world where it knows little, offering a prize to an authoritarian and leaving with not much to show for it.Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the ObserverExplore more on these topicsMyanmarOpinionMyanmar coupCritical mineralsRohingyaMalaysiaSouth and central AsiaHuman rightscommentShareReuse this content

title: The upside of anger: can fury be one of the deepest forms of human compassion? | Jackie Bailey | The Guardian
description: Imagine anger as a sign not of moral failure or justified outrage but the desire to care for another
Author: Jackie Bailey
Headline: Imagine anger as a sign not of moral failure or justified outrage but the desire to care for another
Content: Anger can motivate us to act – but it takes skill and wisdom to turn it to a virtue.Composite: Getty Images/Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenAnger can motivate us to act – but it takes skill and wisdom to turn it to a virtue.Composite: Getty Images/Guardian DesignMaking sense of itReligionThe upside of anger: can fury be one of the deepest forms of human compassion?Jackie BaileyImagine anger as a sign not of moral failure or justified outrage but the desire to care for anotherMaking sense of itis a column about spirituality and how it can be used to navigate everyday lifeSun 18 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 19.05 EDTShareAnger is an emotion we are taught to manage, control and suppress. But what if anger is, as poet David Whyte says, one of the deepest possible forms of compassion available to humankind?Philosophers and theologians have long distinguished between virtuous and non-virtuous anger. Aristotle defined anger as “a desire, accompanied by pain, for apparent retribution, aroused by an apparent, undeserved slighting against oneself or those connected to oneself”.Anger appears to combine a physical sensation of torment with a desire to act. The English word “anger” has its etymological roots in the Old Norseangr, meaning grief and sorrow, and the Latinangere,tostrangle, referring to the sensation of chest tightening, fists clenching, blood boiling.It’s never been so easy to find answers. But sitting with uncertainty can ultimately bring wisdom | Muhammad AbdulsaterRead moreHow do we make sure our angry actions are just? Aristotle taught his students that anyone can get angry, but it takes skill and wisdom to turn anger into a virtue. For anger to have a moral quality, you have to get angry at the right person, at the right time, to the right degree, for the right purpose and with the right motive.A complete lack of anger could itself be a vice, according to Christian theologian Thomas Aquinas, in situations where it is reasonable to act to restore justice. Similarly, Persian Muslim theologian Al-Ghazali advocated for a middle ground, identifying forbearance,Ḥilm,as the ideal state, in which anger is subject to reason and divine law.How do we know when our anger is justified? PhilosopherMartha C Nussbaumobserves that anger might be well grounded, as there are many cases of wrongdoing in the world. In these instances, anger is valuable if it quickly transitions into productive action for people’s wellbeing and a better future. However, Nussbaum notes that even justifiable anger, if left to fester, can become narrowly focused on a desire for payback, which in no way supports a better world.The Stoics thought of anger as a type of momentary madness, a response to the unfounded belief that the world is fair. Once we accept that most things are beyond our control, apart from our reactions to them, we can develop equanimity. Buddhists espouse a similar view, identifying anger as one of the “Three Poisons”. Anger signals a distorted understanding of reality involving the belief in a singular ego, leading to a wholesale engagement in the push-pull cycle of desire and aversion at the root of human suffering.Whyte offers a more hopeful view of this much-debated emotion. According to him, we feel anger when we are unable to enact our deep-seated care for others. “What we name as anger is only the incoherent physical incapacity to sustain this deep form of care in our outer daily life.” Perhaps, Whyte observes, anger is our “unwillingness to be large enough and generous enough to hold what we love helplessly in our bodies or our mind with the clarity and breadth of our whole being”.Writer and artistMimi Zhu imagines every emotion, including anger, as a protective spirit, an ancestor “embodied as a feeling, telling me … what I have been taught to overlook”. Zhu notes that the Chinese characters for anger can translate literally to the phrase“to give life to a vital breath”.Hungry for connection? This is what we lose when we stop eating together | Shadi Khan SaifRead moreImagine anger as a sign not of moral failure or justified outrage but the desire to care for another. I might get angry with my daughter for failing to tidy her room. Part of my anger might be about my ego, a fight for dominance; but perhaps it is also about my desire for her to be healthy, and well, and able to find her socks for school in the morning.If I focus on the other’s wellbeing, as Nussbaum writes, then anger inspires a future-oriented project rather than an ego-driven quest for payback. The thought is no longer, “My daughter is disrespecting my rules, and I am worried that she will never be able to look after herself,” but “My daughter is her own person, how can I support her to be well, within her own parameters of flourishing selfhood?”I might have already shouted about the socks. Next time, before I start slamming doors, I can pause and ask myself, what is it that this anger is inviting me to understand about myself and the other?At its worst, anger is a motivation for unspeakable crimes and violence. At its best, it can be a reminder that humans have a default setting to challenge what seems unjust. Maybe that is anger’s greatest gift: the reminder that, even if we feel helpless, we are hardwired for hope, to try to change things for the better.Jackie Baileyis an award-winning author whose latest book isThe Outrageous Good Fortune of Living(HarperCollins/ABC Books). Jackie works as a funeral celebrant and pastoral care practitioner, supporting people to navigate death and dyingExplore more on these topicsReligionMaking sense of itEthicsPhilosophycommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on schools: the hardest questions for Lucy Powell are about priorities  | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The education secretary is right that her job is not to ‘polish the status quo’. Next, she must decide what to change first
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The education secretary is right that her job is not to ‘polish the status quo’. Next, she must decide what to change first
Content: ‘England’s high scores in maths and science, in international tests, have shown that standards in some subjects have risen.’Photograph: Andrew Fox/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘England’s high scores in maths and science, in international tests, have shown that standards in some subjects have risen.’Photograph: Andrew Fox/AlamyOpinionEducation policyThe Guardian view on schools: the hardest questions for Lucy Powell are about prioritiesEditorialThe education secretary is right that her job is not to ‘polish the status quo’. Next, she must decide what to change firstSun 18 Oct 2026 12.25 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 12.38 EDTShareThere is a good case to be made for the increased importance of speaking skills in our new age of machines. With the UK economy’s stronger-than-expected recent performance widely linked to AI investment, it is vital that people are equipped for the kinds of in-person, public-facing jobs that are least likely to be automated.A concerning declinein children’s language development, both in the UK and internationally, has been linked to high screen use. There is a grim irony in a situation where tech companies both compete with humans for contracts and undermineour ability to talk to one other.The Guardian has previouslybacked effortsto more strongly embed speaking skills, or oracy, in British schools. In aspeechon Thursday, Lucy Powell promised to give them equal status to reading and writing in English (education is devolved, so her main responsibility is for England, but there are parallel initiatives in the other nations). Yet with promised updates to the national curriculum postponed, and plans forspecial educational needs reformcausing deep anxiety to families, schools and councils, the hardest questions for the education secretary are about priorities. Following negative feedback from schools, she has also asked Ofsted tolook againat its new inspection framework.The curriculum review completed last year was deliberately cautious, reflecting the Starmer administration’s overall tone. Since then, England’shigh scoresin maths and science, in international tests, have shown that standards in some subjects have risen. But in English, an overly prescriptive and grammar-obsessed curriculum is putting pupils off. This is the obvious place to start with new speaking skills. The delayed curriculum revisions should set out how it is going to be done.View image in fullscreenLucy Powell.Photograph: Future Publishing/GettyThe energy that Ms Powell brings to the education brief is welcome. She is right to refuse to “sit still and polish the status quo”, especially as the Conservative party seeks to take credit for improvements to English schools that were a legacy of NewLabour. The decline of the arts in schools must also be tackled. An improved vocational offer is arguably most urgent of all.But there is no point denying the challenges around implementation. The government is already committed to the introduction of new maths and English qualifications, to replace demoralising GCSE resits. Reform of the special educational needs system will need to be carefully monitored. Many experts in the college sector believe that thescrapping of BTec qualifications, in favour of T-levels and V-levels, is a mistake. This too needs to be closely watched. A stronger steer from government on universities is also needed. Bridget Phillipson’s decision to unfreeze fees after eight years has only slightly eased their funding difficulties. Reform of unfair student loan terms must come sooner rather than later.Ms Powell is not unique, among Andy Burnham’s new brooms, in facing a daunting set of challenges. Her pledge to go “further and deeper on curriculum reform” is welcome; the world is changing fast and schools need help to keep up. A strengthened emphasis on the spoken word is just one part of this. But in the coming months, she will need to make decisions about where to put her energies. There are only so many changes, on top of special educational needs reforms, that schools can be expected to cope with.Explore more on these topicsEducation policyOpinionLucy PowellSecondary schoolsSchoolsOfstedLiteracyCurriculumseditorialsShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on plague in Russia: what is most worrying is the lack of information | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: In the three weeks since a health worker’s death in Siberia, officials have stonewalled the WHO – setting a worrying precedent for future pandemics
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: In the three weeks since a health worker’s death in Siberia, officials have stonewalled the WHO – setting a worrying precedent for future pandemics
Content: The exterior of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East.Photograph: Smirnov Vladimir/Anadolu/GettyView image in fullscreenThe exterior of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East.Photograph: Smirnov Vladimir/Anadolu/GettyOpinionInfectious diseasesThe Guardian view on plague in Russia: what is most worrying is the lack of informationEditorialIn the three weeks since a health worker’s death in Siberia, officials have stonewalled the WHO – setting a worrying precedent for future pandemicsSun 18 Oct 2026 12.30 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 12.39 EDTShareIs there a plague outbreak in Russia? If the answer were a clear yes, there shouldn’t be much reason to worry. With swift medical intervention, plague is treatable. But in the nearly three weeks sincea worker at a Siberian plague research unitdied of a mysterious respiratory illness, state officials have been consistently tight-lipped about what happened and whether there were any further cases.It is this uncertainty that has theWorld Health Organization(WHO) and international community worried: partly because there is a – very small – risk of an outbreak, and partly because it is yet another warning that the international coordination we rely on to prevent pandemics is fraying along with the rest of international politics, and could easily fail to protect us in the future.The key to containing an outbreak is quick disclosure and open sharing of information. Russia reportedlyheld high-level meetingsabout the case, quarantined the hospital where the worker was treated and traced about 200 contacts. That response suggests officials believed the infection was plague, and yet they did not report any of this to the WHO, as international law requires. Russialater revealedthat the worker died of a pneumonia of unknown origin – hardly useful information. It undoubtedly gathered lab results and genetic sequences that could shed more light on the case, but has not shared them.View image in fullscreenThe logo of the World Health Organization.Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/GettyEarlier this year, the hantavirus outbreak originating on the MV Hondius cruise ship wassuccessfully contained, showing that the global health system can still work well when countries cooperate. This latest incident suggests that one recalcitrant nation can jeopardise everyone’s safety. It is not the WHO’s fault that Russia is essentially a rogue state, but the body must be ready for such eventualities. International politics is fragmented, and only becoming more so.Earlier this year the US left the WHO (though it is still party to some of its treaties). States follow international laws when they believe in them, or when they believe that there will be penalties – reputational or otherwise – for not playing along. The WHO has not attempted to play hardball with Russia, or set off a round of international condemnation from leading member states. Some might be heartened that on 7 October the US state departmentofficially requestedthat the Russian government share information with the WHO. However, it is likely that this reflects Washington’s increasingly ad hoc approach to international politics – using every lever available as situations arise – rather than a renewed commitment to international law. President Trump said on the same day that he would speak to Vladimir Putin about the issue. If that happened, no one has heard about it or what information may have been revealed.The keen US interest may give credence to speculation that what in fact happened was some kind of bioweapons research leak. This is thought to be unlikely, but not impossible. The fact that such a scenario can even be plausibly entertained three weeks after the initial event speaks to a serious breakdown in the system. Western states probably do not hold much sway withRussia. But the other Brics nations may have more. The WHO used to rely on US backing for its requests. It may now have to find support among wider, more multipolar coalitions. This potential outbreak may come to nothing, but there will be another soon.Explore more on these topicsInfectious diseasesOpinionRussiaHealthWorld Health OrganizationChinaMicrobiologyEuropeeditorialsShareReuse this content

title: What gets in the way of prisoners’ rehabilitation | Prisons and probation | The Guardian
description: Letters: Anthony Goodman argues that probation officers have increasingly lost their autonomy, while Joe Sim says rehabilitation will not work in a society divided by brutal social divisions. Plus letters from Chris Parsons and Tracey Burley
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Anthony Goodman argues that probation officers have increasingly lost their autonomy, while Joe Sim says rehabilitation will not work in a society divided by brutal social divisions. Plus letters from Chris Parsons and Tracey Burley
Content: Wandsworth prison, which has an experimental, Scandinavian-inspired rehabilitative prison wing.Photograph: Bloomberg/GettyView image in fullscreenWandsworth prison, which has an experimental, Scandinavian-inspired rehabilitative prison wing.Photograph: Bloomberg/GettyPrisons and probationLettersWhat gets in the way of prisoners’ rehabilitationAnthony Goodmanargues thatprobation officers have increasingly lost their autonomy, whileJoe Simsays rehabilitation will not work in a society divided by brutal social divisions. Plus letters fromChris ParsonsandTracey BurleySun 18 Oct 2026 12.18 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 12.20 EDTShareYour editorial on overcrowded prisons and probation (13 October) was most welcome as it highlights a crisis in community justice that shows little sign of abating. You say that problems date back to the failed part-privatisation of the probation service, but in reality political interference has been happening for far longer than that.Having worked for years as a prison probation officer and then in an aftercare and resettlement unit for ex-offenders, I saw good practice and ongoing practical and emotional support that demonstrated all the important points raised byEnver Solomonin his recent Guardian article.Staff visited prisons and got to know inmates before they were released, which involved in-depth discussions of their offending history and what was needed for successful resettlement. Staff visited wet day centres for problem drinkers and established links with community organisations. They did not see themselves as the exclusive purveyors of rehabilitation.In 1984 the government produced a “statement of national objectives and priorities” that made work with prisoners low-profile, and the aftercare unit closed a few years later. When I tried, as part of my doctoral research, to interview probation staff in the 1990s about their role in prison resettlement, I found that such work had stopped.Since then, probation officers have increasingly lost their autonomy – and the opportunity and permission to get to know the people they supervise. Risk has become the driving force, resulting in an incredible rate of offenders breaching their licence conditions and being returned to prison.Probation staff are told to be more professionally curious and to give hope to offenders. The service has struggled to hit its targets, but has surely lost the point of its work, which is not the fault of its hard‑working staff. Action is required, now.Anthony GoodmanProfessor of community justice, Middlesex UniversityYour editorial on rehabilitation in prison makes some important points. It is also worth noting the political hypocrisy around this issue. The Barlinnie Special Unit, which did change people in prison, was closed in 1994, while the rehabilitation policies pursued in Grendon Underwood, which opened in 1962, have rarely been extended into the mainsystem.Why? Because these places challenged the decades‑long political obsession with punishment and deterrence. Whether or not the“Scandi” units at Wandsworth and Pentonvillein London, which pursue a similar philosophy to Barlinnie and Grendon, will also be marginalised and ignored remains to be seen.More broadly, rehabilitation will not work in a society divided by brutal social divisions, a point made by Victoria Law in her book“Prisons Make Us Safer”: And 20 Other Myths About Mass Incarceration: “What does it mean to rehabilitate a person to their former state if that state involves poverty, racism, unemployment, unstable housing, and/or violence? Can a person be rehabilitated if they have never been habilitated (or made fit or capable for society)?”We must address these issues, stop prison building, redirect the billions wasted on prisons towards probation and other radical alternatives, and reduce sentence lengths, or the devastating cycle of crisis/reform/crisis will only continue and intensify inside.Joe SimEmeritus professorof criminology, Liverpool John Moores UniversityYour editorial rightly highlights that the government must prove community supervision works to win support for early releases, while calling for a “person-centred” approach and noting the value of “purposeful activity”.At LandWorks, acharity providing intensive placements for people on licence or serving community sentences, we see every day that community projects can deliver powerful results. By providing person-centred support wrapped around meaningful, purposeful work and the building of trust, real change can and does happen.There are many men and women in the system who want to change their lives but face huge hurdles – addiction issues, chaotic home lives, little or no employment history and failed relationships. Providing consistent support can transform lives and reduce the likelihood of further offending. Our independently analysed reoffending rates can attest to that.The voluntary sector already holds blueprints for breaking the cycles of prison overcrowding, recall and reoffending. A commitment from the government to learn from these existing successful models could transform our criminal justice system and improve public confidence. Rehabilitation and resettlement support makes a huge difference when delivered effectively.Chris ParsonsProject director, LandWorksThe debate over early release from prison masks a deeper issue. The underlying problem is a failure to invest properly in early intervention and prevention.The prison governor Polly Toynbee spoke with was right to highlight the need for early-years support (Britain is addicted to prisons. Our crumbling probation service proves they don’t work, 16 October). School exclusion, episodes of going missing and disruption in childhood are often warning signs of the harm and offending that may follow.Trusted-adult mentoring can make a decisive difference. Giving a young person someone to turn to in a moment of stress can help prevent that moment from ending with a weapon being picked up.St Giles and other like-minded organisations provide this support in schools, with positive results:a 21% reduction in violence and a 14% decrease in offending, according to the Youth Endowment Fund.The same approach can support people serving sentences in the community, helping them to access services that address the root causes of offending while strengthening the effectiveness of community sentences.But investment alone is not enough. We must also rethink our justice system and ask who genuinely needs to be in prison. Effective community-based solutions already exist; expanding them would tackle the causes of offending, while easing the intense pressure on prisons and probation staff.Tracey BurleyChief executive, St GilesHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: RJ Mitte’s story offers insight into life with cerebral palsy and mental health issues | RJ Mitte | The Guardian
description: Letter: Dr Denise Al Mari-de Waal and Aaron Hume call for lifelong support and an integrated care pathway that recognises the physical and mental health impacts of cerebral palsy
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Dr Denise Al Mari-de Waal and Aaron Hume call for lifelong support and an integrated care pathway that recognises the physical and mental health impacts of cerebral palsy
Content: RJ Mitte in 2011. ‘People with cerebral palsy are more likely to develop mental health conditions and experience poor wellbeing.’Photograph: Graham Whitby Boot/AllstarView image in fullscreenRJ Mitte in 2011. ‘People with cerebral palsy are more likely to develop mental health conditions and experience poor wellbeing.’Photograph: Graham Whitby Boot/AllstarRJ MitteLettersRJ Mitte’s story offers insight into life with cerebral palsy and mental health issuesDr Denise Al Mari-de WaalandAaron Humecall for lifelong support and an integrated care pathway that recognises the physical and mental health impacts of cerebral palsySun 18 Oct 2026 12.18 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 12.20 EDTShareThe sudden passing of RJ Mitte has deeply affected many people in the cerebral palsy community (RJ Mitte, actor best known for Breaking Bad, dies aged 34, 12 October). His success challenged assumptions and showed what can be achieved when people are given opportunities and support.Yet the 165,000 people with cerebral palsy in the UK are too often underestimated. Others frequently decide what we can and cannot do without recognising our abilities, ambitions or potential.With the right support, we can live fulfilling, successful and meaningful lives. For that reason, the reported circumstances surrounding RJ’s death may surprise some people. Unfortunately, mental health is often overlooked. People with cerebral palsy are more likely to develop mental health conditions and experience poor wellbeing.We continue to face prejudice, low expectations and barriers that others rarely encounter. We are often excluded from opportunities, left feeling isolated, and denied the support needed to reach our full potential. As a result, many of us are required to build far greater resilience and self-confidence than our able-bodied peers.People with cerebral palsy can and do thrive. We build careers, contribute to our communities and achieve remarkable things. But success should not depend on resilience alone. We need support to help us get there.In the UK, many people with cerebral palsy – a lifelong condition – face a cliff edge when they turn 18. The care and support they received as children often disappears as they transition into adulthood.We deserve lifelong support and an integrated care pathway that recognises the physical and mental health impacts of cerebral palsy, including access to specialist mental health services.Dr Denise Al Mari-de WaalandAaron HumeUP –The Adult Cerebral Palsy MovementHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: £2.5bn Chelsea fund could help children globally if Ed Miliband secures its release | Chelsea | The Guardian
description: Letter: George Graham of Save the Children UK says the government has a clear opportunity to act and ensure that victims of conflict are helped
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: George Graham of Save the Children UK says the government has a clear opportunity to act and ensure that victims of conflict are helped
Content: Funds from Roman Abramovich’s sale of Chelsea FC remain stuck.Photograph: Martin Meissner/APView image in fullscreenFunds from Roman Abramovich’s sale of Chelsea FC remain stuck.Photograph: Martin Meissner/APChelseaLetters£2.5bn Chelsea fund could help children globally if Ed Miliband secures its releaseGeorge GrahamofSave the Children UK says the government has a clear opportunity to act and ensure that victims of conflict are helpedSun 18 Oct 2026 12.18 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 12.29 EDTShareAmid allegations about advisers dealing with Roman Abramovich’s business affairs (Roman Abramovich aides falsified paperwork to disguise assets and dodge tax, records suggest, 12 October), another issue demands urgent government action – the £2.5bn from the sale of Chelsea FC, which hasremained stuckin a Barclays bank account since May 2022.The money was originally pledged to help victims of the war inUkraine, no matter where they are in the world. Yet for over four years this huge sum of money has sat in limbo, accruing interest while victims of conflict go without desperately needed support. At a time of global aid cuts, rising food insecurity and growing humanitarian needs, the £2.5bn could make a transformative difference to the children and families we serve around the world.The government has a clear opportunity to act. Itslicence to release the fundslast December imposed geographic conditions that Abramovich did not accept. A broader licence, allowing the money to support humanitarian causes beyond Ukraine, could finally put it to use. Even releasing the accumulated interest alone could unlock substantial funding and offer life-saving support for those who need it most.We know the foreign secretary is keen to get things done. Securing the release of the £2.5bnChelseafunds would make a huge impact around the world – something his predecessors failed to do.George GrahamExecutive director for global impact, Save the Children UKHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Looming Medicaid cuts mean that US hospitals must prepare for a perfect storm  | Medicaid | The Guardian
description: Letter: Eugene Litvak says hospitals could rearrange scheduled admissions as part of efforts to prepare operationally for changes on 1 January
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Eugene Litvak says hospitals could rearrange scheduled admissions as part of efforts to prepare operationally for changes on 1 January
Content: People protesting against Medicaid cuts in Washington DC, May 2025.Photograph: The Washington Post/GettyView image in fullscreenPeople protesting against Medicaid cuts in Washington DC, May 2025.Photograph: The Washington Post/GettyMedicaidLettersLooming Medicaid cuts mean that US hospitals must prepare for a perfect stormEugene Litvaksays hospitals could rearrange scheduled admissions as part of efforts to prepare operationally for changes on 1 JanuarySun 18 Oct 2026 12.18 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 12.20 EDTShareYour report (Millions of Medicaid recipients to face draconian requirements as of 1 January, 13 October) warns that millions may lose Medicaid coverage just as hospitals face rising uncompensated care and growing emergency department demand.Protecting eligible patients from losing coverage through paperwork must remain the first priority. But hospitals also have a responsibility to prepare operationally for 1 January. They should not compound the coming increase in emergency demand with avoidable peaks they create themselves.My colleagues and Ianalysed 1,692,090hospital admissions across New York State. Emergency admissions varied relatively little across the week, while scheduled admissions were concentrated early in the week. For a representative 500-bed hospital, the resulting pattern was equivalent to needing 103 additional beds on Monday and having 160 fewer patients on Friday. Hospitals cannot schedule heart attacks, strokes or uninsured patients’ emergencies. They can, however, schedule most elective admissions. Bydistributing them evenlyacross weekdays, hospitals can reduce competition for the same beds and nurses.Smoothing scheduled admissions cannot prevent coverage losses or eliminate every cause of emergency department crowding. It can, however, help hospitals absorb the added pressure with less avoidable boarding, delay, and patient harm. Before building more beds or accepting five-hour waits as inevitable, every hospital should determine how much usable capacity its own scheduling practices are wasting.Eugene LitvakPresident and CEO,Institute for Healthcare Optimization; adjunct professor of operations management, Harvard TH Chan School of Public HealthHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Elite-level incompetence is Manchester United’s problem – not Michael Carrick | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: Getting rid of Michael Carrick is not going to solve the problems that led to his appointment. Perhaps it’s worth, for once, doing something different
Author: Barney Ronay
Headline: Getting rid of Michael Carrick is not going to solve the problems that led to his appointment. Perhaps it’s worth, for once, doing something different
Content: Michael Carrick’s Manchester United are a lowly 13th in the Premier League after the 1-1 draw at Leeds.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAView image in fullscreenMichael Carrick’s Manchester United are a lowly 13th in the Premier League after the 1-1 draw at Leeds.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAManchester UnitedAnalysisElite-level incompetence is Manchester United’s problem – not Michael CarrickBarney RonayGetting rid of head coach is not going to solve the problems that led to his appointment. Perhaps it’s worth, for once, doing something differentSun 18 Oct 2026 15.56 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 18.32 EDTShareAt the final whistle at Elland Road the TV cameras cut to a lingering shot ofManchester Unitedchief executive, Omar Berrada, looking down pensively from the stands, deciding, it is to be hoped, on a little clemency, a re-sheathing of the managerial shotgun.Here we have the man who hired the man. The man who fires the man. The man who also hired or rehired the previous two men he had to fire. Berrada was poached from Manchester City on the basis of his ability to grow commercial revenue (yes, OK, stop laughing), and appears, like everyone else with any actual reach around here, to exist in a strangely consequence-free bubble.‘Like a fresh start’: Michael Carrick relieved by Manchester United’s draw at LeedsRead moreHow do you solve what is, on revenue versus results, the worst-run club in world football? By changing the name of the latest patsy on the touchline, of course. For nowa hard-fought pointis perhaps enough to stave off that pre-programmed emergency response.Stand down the cowboy cops. Call off the blue and white saloons. Although with a run of Bournemouth, Chelsea, Aston Villa and Liverpool next up in the league it will no doubt soon be time to go out there and arrest Lee Harvey Oswald again. What’s that you say? OK, well, dig him up again. Re-arrest him. Whatever it takes. Someone has to stop these lone gunmen, these managerial magic bullet merchants from derailing the Manchester United supremacy.This was a dual-track football match between Leeds and Manchester United, on the face of it a good, even game between two teams of well-matched players.A 1-1 drawwas fair in the end, although Leeds played well and probably should have won. But of course they won’t be the story.Instead this game had already been billed as that familiar thing, a referendum on the future ofMichael Carrick. A stay of execution for a week or two. Or another livestreamed firing squad for the Super Sunday cameras.There has been a predictable sense of low comedy about Carrick’s own transformation in the United dugout this season. It was always going to be the case that his widely praised qualities in victory, blazer, T-shirt, jawline, inscrutable sense of calm, would become his fatal flaws in defeat.Where’s the passion, the whirling arms, the range of tailored collars? At Elland Road Carrick simply looked drained in the second half as United were pegged back and overrun at times, the beard a little more ragged, the hair unkempt but still sweeping, the look of a brave, doomed tugboat captain resigned now to the approaching tsunami wave on the horizon.A point leaves United 13th in the league and still struggling to reverse a dreadful start to the season. But it was a good game for two people. First for Carrick, who remains a million miles away from creating the problems afflicting this club, even if you accept that his presence as head coach is one of them.Michael Carrick did not hire Michael Carrick. Getting rid of Michael Carrick is, by definition, not going to solve the problems that led to his appointment. But it might just help to prolong them. Whatever his ultimate ceiling, it is surely worth keeping him just to try, for once, to do something different.View image in fullscreenThe Manchester United director of football, Jason Wilcox (centre), and chief executive officer Omar Berrada (right) watch on at Elland Road.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PAThis was also a good game for Lisandro Martínez, who went off injured at half-time with United 1-0 up, and who was also vindicated in his allegedly controversial (translation: entirely correct)comments on the club hierarchyin midweek.United’s energetic first-half performance clarified one half of this. The players are committed in support of the manager, at least to the best of their ability. The second half made the other half of the argument, that this remains a mismatched, lopsided, cut-and-paste squad, always likely to be pulled apart by opponents as urgent as this Leeds team, which fully deserves its current seventh place in the table.The problems are so obvious it is barely worth repeating them. But here goes. The third-richest club in the world played a second half with three of its back four out of position. Harry Maguire, signed under Ole Gunnar Solskjær, remains the best straight defender. But Maguire is also essentially a man-shaped solid wood armoire in a pair of shorts at this stage in his career, always the slowest person on any pitch, which means you will not be able to cover space, play a high line or counterattack without leaving yourself exposed to the counter-counter.So good luck, guys. And remember Omar, who gave you this whisky bottle and loaded pistol of a squad, will be watching.This was made painfully clear after half-time as Martínez went off and Noussair Mazraoui came on. Leeds scored an equaliser that felt structurally inevitable. They found space down their right side repeatedly. At times they seemed to be constantly peppering the seats behind the United goal, like a group of kids hammering a ball against a garage door. By the end Leeds had more possession, more shots on target and just looked a happier, better structured entity than the travelling heritage exhibit at the other end.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe key point here is to accept that all of this is entirely logical. This is not a mystery, a haunted house, a place of bad voodoo. Why do we talk about Manchester United so much? For obvious reasons. It’s a massive part of the English football landscape. Mainly, though, because this is a story of mind-bending waste, real-time elite-level incompetence played out on a weekly basis.Yes, you could sack Michael Carrick. It won’t change much. Let’s destroy Eddie Howe for a bit instead. But the available evidence suggests every single person making executive decisions here is outmatched and outmanoeuvred.There is a reason Manchester United feels like one of those high street legacy chain shops just before it collapses, piles of Quality Street by the door, a rat in the lingerie department, destined to become a pop-up vape shop run by Albanian money launderers. There’s a reason it feels so badly run. This is because: it is.View image in fullscreenLisandro Martínez, who criticised the Manchester United hierarchy in midweek, went off injured at half-time against Leeds.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersWe know the Glazer ownership has zero interest in minding the details, that this has been a wonderful acquisition whatever the performance on the pitch, an asset supremely sweated. We know also that Sir Jim Ratcliffe is pub-level incoherent on the details he promised to fix. Remember when he was going to sit down and decide what the “style of football” would be? How’s that working out?Manchester United held as Calvert-Lewin’s Leeds leveller keeps pressure on CarrickRead moreInstead Carrick is left shuffling a first XI acquired by endlessly revolving administrations. Here United had four defenders signed under Erik ten Hag, two Ruben Amorim recruits, two from the mist-shrouded age of Solskjær. No players were recruited under Ralf Rangnick, of course. But then Rangnick wanted to sign Erling Haaland, Luis Díaz, and Julian Álvarez, which all sounds far too sensible.An organisation can be built with many hands. But not when so many of those hands appear to be so far from best in class it’s hard to work out which class they’re supposed to be attending. John Murtough, the former Manchester United football director, is currently director of global development at Atalanta, who have a 24,000-seat stadium and almost zero global presence. Meanwhile Berrada, the axeman, seems entirely invulnerable from the axe himself, despite the fact his job seems to orbit around resolving the consequences of his own mistakes.United probably will sack their current manager before the year is out. This is the way this machine has to operate, always looking to buy itself, and those in the executive seats, a little more time on the payroll, an entity that has been hollowed out and allowed to rust, run on buzzwords and brown paper and string. Meanwhile, over to you Michael. We’ll see you next week, and maybe even the week after that, for more of exactly the same.Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitedLeeds UnitedMichael CarrickanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Madueke breaks Nottingham Forest’s resistance as dogged Arsenal edge to victory | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Noni Madueke scored the only goal of the game as Arsenal left it late to snatch a 1-0 victory against Nottingham Forest at the City Ground
Author: David Hytner
Headline: Noni Madueke scored the only goal of the game as Arsenal left it late to snatch a 1-0 victory against Nottingham Forest at the City Ground
Content: Noni Madueke celebrates the winning goal for Arsenal.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenNoni Madueke celebrates the winning goal for Arsenal.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianPremier LeagueMadueke breaks Nottingham Forest’s resistance as dogged Arsenal edge to victoryDavid Hytnerat the City GroundSun 18 Oct 2026 13.39 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 16.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe theme before kick-off was blanks. Or, more precisely, whether either team could stop firing them at the City Ground. It was a detail to make Oliver Glasner extremely uncomfortable that his Nottingham Forest team had still to score at their own stadium this season. Arsenal, meanwhile,had drawn 0-0on their previous two visits to this part of the east Midlands. They had only one win in five here.Forest’s frustrations under their new manager go on. It was another spirited performance from them, bits to like, especially a full-throttle performance from Liam Delap in the No 9 position. But, for the fifth time under Glasner, there was not a goal to celebrate in front of the home support.Manchester United held as Calvert-Lewin’s Leeds leveller keeps pressure on CarrickRead moreIt was a game that came to feel increasingly set up for the famous terrace chant. One-nil to the Ars-en-nal. Or, as the travelling hordes would have it, one-nil to the champions.Arsenaldid not play well. They created little, finishing with just one shot on target. How Noni Madueke made it count.On as a half-time substitute, the winger took a pass from Declan Rice in the 80th minute and had only one thing on his mind. To cut inside from the left and unload. The connection was pure and that was when he caught a break, which he has worked to earn after a difficult start to the season. The ball deflected off Jair Cunha and flew past the Forest goalkeeper, Matz Sels.View image in fullscreenLiam Delap holds off Ezri Konsa at the City Ground.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianForest refused to accept the inevitable. Chris Wood, on as a substitute, delayed too long and saw Rice block. Murillo, of all players, danced inside from the left and curled off target. Delap was denied at the death by a thunderous Ezri Konsa block tackle. But it did feel inevitable. Forest, who missed the injured Morgan Gibbs-White, might have played all night and not scored. Arsenal had not forgotten their previous away fixture –the 3-0 defeat at Brighton. It remains the only blot on their season.Arsenal had kicked off six points behind Manchester City, who have been perfect on the field in the league this season. Will it matter when the sanctions for their rule breaches are meted out? All Arsenal can do is play the situation as it stands and this was an occasion when the result was everything.Mikel Arteta’s team dominated the ball. As they were always likely to do. They were determined to be patient. And yet they were flat and predictable until the closing stages. The lack of incisive movement was glaring. That said, Forest were compact out of possession in a 5-4-1 formation and hard to break down. They were resolved not to give up any easy yards.Arsenal played their patterns. They tried to suck the life out of the home crowd, working on the principle that it is difficult for fans to get animated if their team do not have the ball. The first half drifted by in a lazy Sunday afternoon haze, no shots on target for either side.Delap carried the physical fight; the Forest centre-forward was a willing and direct runner and he won a free-kick off Rice just outside the Arsenal box on 44 minutes.
