Gabon fights to protect sacred plant from US drug companiesIboga root, central to several Gabonese ritual traditions, is believed to have huge potential for use in treating addiction and some mental illnessesSupported byAbout this contentMolly HelfendSun 18 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 12.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe temple is dark, its sandy floor edged with candles. People sit shoulder to shoulder beneath palm fronds hung from the rafters. Through the night, they swallow what they have come here for: a bitter root bark called iboga.Tabernanthe ibogais a slow-growing central African rainforest shrub, the root bark of which has long been used in several Gabonese ritual traditions.In Gabon’s villages and forests, iboga is cultivated and sometimes gathered from wild populations, often collected under ritual conditions. But nothing in its cultural usage, at sites such as this temple on the outskirts of Libreville, is comparable to the potential wave of demand fast approaching from abroad.A US executive orderhas turned a spotlight onibogaine, a drug made from the plant, which pharmaceutical companies believe has huge potential for use in addiction treatment.In the Bwiti (also known as Bwété) spiritual tradition, iboga is used in many different ways. Apollon Obolo, a practitioner of Misoko Bwiti, a branch concerned with healing and divination, describes the ceremony taking place that night, called Mubindu, as a way of lifting the burden carried by relatives and friends after a death.View image in fullscreenIboga is consumed in a ritual ceremony.Photograph: Jorge Fernández/LightRocket/Getty ImagesBut, he stresses, iboga is only one part of the practice. “InGabon, we don’t talk about iboga. We talk about Bwiti. Iboga is just an element,” he says. “For me, Misoko is like a microscope to see clearly about details in the life of someone.” Obolo believes it can “restructure” a person and resolve what ordinary medicine cannot.In Misoko, Obolo says, knowledge of iboga is received “from generation to generation”, and accumulated “time after time”. A 2012 report by Yann Guignon, an intercultural and sustainable development consultant and president of the NGO Blessings of the Forest, records practitioners describing wild iboga as something that must be considered in relation to the whole forest, including by following animals that eat the fruit.View image in fullscreenYann Guignon,president of Blessings of the Forest, a conservation organisation.Photograph: Courtesy of Blessings of the ForestThis stands in contrast to the interest now being taken by pharmaceutical companies. Ibogaine has a fast-developing reputation in addiction treatment, with early observational studies reporting sharp reductions in opioid withdrawal and craving after a single treatment.Ina study published in 2024, 30 male US special operations veterans, most of whom were diagnosed with mild traumatic brain injury, received ibogaine combined with magnesium. A month later, average PTSD, depression and anxiety scores had fallen by at least 81%, while disability scores moved from mild-to-moderate impairment into the “no disability” range. The study was small, uncontrolled and included complementary therapies, meaning it could not establish eﬃcacy. Its authors have called for further controlled trials.The former Texas governor Rick Perry has become one of ibogaine’s most visible political champions. Texas hasgranted $50m (£38m) for a multicentre trial, and on 18 April, the US president, Donald Trump, signedan executive orderspecifically naming“ibogaine compounds” and directing federal agencies to create a treatment pathway for eligible patients. A therapeutic economy already exists elsewhere: Beond, a clinic in Cancún, lists programmes costing from $13,500 to $19,500.View image in fullscreenIboga root powder. An executive order by US president Donald Trump that names ‘ibogaine compounds’ looks set to increase demand for the plant.Photograph: Molly HelfendBeyond the last paved streets in Libreville, Gabon’s capital, up a rutted hill and behind a concrete compound, stands the temple of Madame Djédjé Stéphanie Djoungounda, known as Maman Djédjé. The temple’s entrance is guarded by a painted mermaid.Djédjé specialises in Mbomba Ossoundo, a branch of the Mbomayano, which she describes as concerned with rebirth and restoration. It involves a plant she calls ikasô alongside small amounts of iboga administered during vigils.View image in fullscreenMaman Djédjé, in purple, with three other family members at her temple.Photograph: Molly Helfend“We don’t heal only with ibogaine,” she says, standing among the iboga plants growing at her temple. “We heal with the whole iboga: the flower, the leaf, the bark, the trunk, the roots.”Not every dose of ibogaine abroad comes from Gabonese iboga. The molecule can be made semi-synthetically from voacangine, found in the related African treeVoacanga africana. But the iboga root bark is particularly in demand for ceremonial use, and for the manufacture of extracts containing several of its alkaloids.Even before the US announced its interest, demand had already begun to pose an ecological problem. Small amounts of root bark can be removed without uprooting the shrub, according to Guignon’s report. But commercial extraction can incentivise something faster: taking the entire root system, which yields more bark at once but kills the shrub. The report documents collectors doing exactly that – without replanting. Recognising the danger, Guignon’s organisation has worked with communities on iboga cultivation and conservation since 2015.For a species now discussed as pharmaceutical feedstock, the ecological ledger on iboga is startlingly thin. Lee White, who led Gabon’s national parks agency before serving as environment minister, calls wild iboga“rare and poorly studied”. His parks law-enforcement teams found evidence of severe local over-harvesting between Libreville and Cocobeach, as well as recurring problems around Mayumba and Lambaréné. White says he tried to initiate a study of iboga’s distribution and genetic variation, but was unable to secure financial backing for it.View image in fullscreenAn iboga shrub.Photograph: Molly HelfendWhen asked why medicinal plant research in central Africa draws so little funding, Djédjé answers bluntly.“There isn’t any,” she says, suggesting thatfinance flows to higher-profile areas such as the Amazon. What did arrive, she says, were students sent from institutions to extract her remedies and“take the money themselves”. Eventually, she says, she stopped sharing with researchers.To Master Mulema, an initiator and scholar in the traditions of the Fang people, the plant’s vulnerability is clear. “Iboga can disappear,” he says. If it is to help humanity,“it must be surrounded by regulation”.View image in fullscreenMaster Mulema says regulation is crucial to protect the iboga plant.Photograph: Molly HelfendFrom a Gabonese perspective, the story of iboga is potentially a familiar and depressing one: export the raw material and watch the high-value part of the supply chain form elsewhere, while the plant itself is pushed to the brink.In May this year, a government decree attempted to challenge that sense of fait accompli, recognising traditional knowledge associated with iboga as national heritage and requiring benefit-sharing in return for commercial use. Patent applications tied to iboga now must disclose the origin of the product concerned, and the decree also creates an iboga sovereign fund, financed in part by royalties and benefit-sharing agreements.On 18 September, Gabon’s council of ministers went even further, adopting a draft decree prohibiting the export of iboga and every derivative, in any form. The government says the measure is intended to protect the plant and the cultural knowledge attached to it.An export ban does not answer the question of who has the right to decide what happens next. There is no central Bwiti church to ask for official sanction. Tah Mombo, a Bwété Dissumba practitioner involved in efforts to marshall viewpoints from the many different traditions, explains the importance of Indigenous voices in the debate around the plant’s future: “We speak about our things, from our home, for us and by us.”View image in fullscreenThe root bark is extracted for sale, trade, ceremony or other community initiatives.Photograph: Courtesy of Blessings of the ForestIboga is not the first plant medicine to become a global industry. Ayahuasca moved from Amazonian traditions into a worldwide retreat economy, followed by disputes over Indigenous authority, commercialisation and who should benefit. Gabon is hoping to avoid this by setting terms while the international ibogaine market is still being built.Ultimately, Obolo’s insistence that Bwiti, not iboga, is the key issue is a refocusing of the usual debate around natural resources. Ibogaine can be isolated and measured in milligrams, but the harder thing to protect is the culture that made the plant meaningful before anyone wanted the molecule.View image in fullscreenIboga is planted under the guidance of Delphine Angue Minko, left.Photograph: Courtesy of Blessings of the ForestAs world leaders prepare to travel to Armenia forCop17, where the debate over biodiversity funding andbenefit sharingwill be central to negotiations, other countries with bioresources both known and as-yet-undiscovered will be watching with interest.Reporting for this article was supported by the Pulitzer Centre.Explore more on these topicsPlantsThe age of extinctionGabonMedical researchIndigenous peoplesDrugsAlternative medicineAfricafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A California town’s beaches are washing away. Can its residents turn the tide? | California | The Guardian
description: Rapid coastal erosion threatens coastal homes and economies, and as Super El Niño rounds the corner, a town is reckoning with the reality of climate crisis
Author: Lois Beckett
Headline: Rapid coastal erosion threatens coastal homes and economies, and as Super El Niño rounds the corner, a town is reckoning with the reality of climate crisis
Content: A portion of the southern California coast showing damage from unusually high surf on 14 October 2026.Photograph: Ruaridh Stewart/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA portion of the southern California coast showing damage from unusually high surf on 14 October 2026.Photograph: Ruaridh Stewart/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockCaliforniaA California town’s beaches are washing away. Can its residents turn the tide?Rapid coastal erosion threatens coastal homes and economies, and as Super El Niño rounds the corner, a town is reckoning with the reality of climate crisisLois Beckettin San ClementeSun 18 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 10.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSan Clemente is one of southern California’s most picture-perfect beach towns – a capital of American surf culture since the 1950s. In two years, 2028 Olympic surfers will compete at Lower Trestles, a world-class surfing beach.But the town’s longtime cultural and economic driver, its beaches, are now under threat. As pounding waves driven by late-summer storms in the Pacific devour chunks of the California coastline, some of San Clemente’s beaches are growing narrower, the sand increasingly eaten away.Beach erosion has become a crisis all along the southern California shoreline this year, with towns from Dana Point and Long Beach to Malibu sustaining dramatic damage. But San Clemente is a particular flash point. It’s the place where the major regional train line, which carries $1bn in freight a year and is the nation’s second-busiest passenger line, runs right along the edge of the Pacific Ocean. Severe waves and high tides during big storms at the beginning of September forced the repeated closure of the tracks.Experts say California’s current season of extreme weather is just getting started. “We’re in for a run of pretty exceptional erosion events if this Super El Niño develops as it’s expected to,” said Sean Vitousek, an oceanographer with the US Geological Survey (USGS).View image in fullscreenAn Amtrak Pacific Surfliner train passes a worker moving fresh sand during an emergency replenishment project on 15 August 2024 in San Clemente, California.Photograph: Mario Tama/Getty ImagesAs the potentially historic El Niño season overlaps with a massive surge of warm water called aKelvinwave, residents worry it will leave coastal infrastructure in pieces, beachfront properties leveled and more beaches carved away to crumbling slivers of gravel and bare rock.Donald Trump has continued to deny climate change as a“hoax”, “con job” or scam”. But in southern California, a historically conservative area, the effect of extreme weather events linked to the climate crisis have suddenly become very, very real.“We’ve been anticipating rising sea levels 50 years from now,” said Hallie Jones, the mayor pro tem ofLaguna Beach, California. “This summer proved that sea level rise is already here.”‘A game of attrition’On a hot, clear day, Cameron Cosgrove, a San Clemente beach restoration activist, took me to the state beach on the south side of town, where swimmers and sunbathers ambled over the major rail line’s tracks to perch on a very narrow strip of sand that descends steeply into the deep blue water.“You can see, when it gets steep like this, then you’re just at a game of attrition,” Cosgrove told me. “It’s just a matter of time before the next big wave event will start moving and start taking some of this.”Big storms at the beginning of September already saw the erosion of some of this coastline creep up to the train tracks. “Severe waves and high tides overtopped the tracks,” according to a spokesperson for the Orange County Transportation Authority (OCTA). The local commuter rail posted a video ofsediment next to the tracks crumbling into the seaas waves slammed the shore.After nearly a century of reliable service, the coastal rail line has been shut down seven times since 2021 for repairs after landslides and surging tides on stretches of the line in San Clemente and further south down the coast. Over the past five years, the closure times “have totaled more than one year”, an OCTA spokesperson confirmed.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueThere’s no relief ahead. Once considered a gradual problem, coastal erosion is now being discussed more urgently, as the risk of California’s beaches simply disappearing, said Charles Lester, a former head of the California Coastal Commission who now leads an ocean policy center at the University of California, Santa Barbara. California scientistswarned in 2023that sea level rise sped up by the climate crisis threatens to erase between 25% and 75% of California’s beaches by 2100.This is posing a massive challenge, particularly for leaders of smaller beachside towns whose appeal is built around their ocean access. Orange county, a collection of suburbs clustered between Los Angeles and San Diego, is famous as the birthplace of the Reagan Revolution. Today, the county is more politically purple than deep Republican red – more voters backed Kamala Harris than Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election. Some of its most famous beach towns, such as Newport Beach, remain Republican strongholds, favoring conservatism and as little government regulation as possible. But extreme weather and the growing threat to beachesis putting pressure even on Republican political orthodoxies.View image in fullscreenWaves crash into damaged homes as a powerful ocean surge and high tides generated by Tropical Storm Rachel batter the southern California coastline on 11 October 2026 in the Capistrano Beach community of Dana Point, California.Photograph: David McNew/Getty ImagesSouthern California’s wealthy coastal towns are used to breezier weather and lower temperatures than Los Angeles, or the scorching cities of the Inland Empire. But record-breaking heatwaves are changing that.“It’s October 5 and it’s 90 degrees in Dana Point. Unless there’s Santa Ana [winds], it’s unheard of,” said John Gabbard, Dana Point’s Republican mayor. “The ocean temperature is high. There’s no wind. And that’s not happening just by happenstance. Nobody’s using the words ‘global warming’, but everybody is recognizing that it’s warmer and it continues to be warmer through the past few seasons than it’s ever been in the past.”In San Clemente, where a majority of residents voted for Trump in 2020 and 2024, Cosgrove, a retired IT executive, is advocating a radical move: he authored a ballot measure that will go before voters in November, asking local residents to voluntarily impose a 1% sales tax on themselves to fund beach restoration and wildfire prevention efforts. A large portion of that tax revenue would be dedicated to replacing what he estimates is the city’s deficit of 4m to 6m cubic yards of beach sand.Nobody likes taxes, Cosgrove said, but voters need to face what he believes is the stark reality all along the California coast: if local residents don’t pay to protect public beaches from vanishing, it’s not clear that anyone else will.Shifting sandsSouthern California’s wide, sandy beaches are not exactly a natural resource. Many of them were created or expanded with sand dredged up by major midcentury construction projects.San Clemente’s beaches, for example, were fortified with an estimated 2m cubic yards of sand removed during the creation of Dana Point’s harbor in the late 1960s, Cosgrove said. “We’ve been living off that ever since,” he said.‘Like an earthquake’: El Niño is coming for California – is the state ready?Read moreSince those midcentury construction projects, further development and infrastructure, especially dams on California’s rivers, has blocked the flows of sediment that would naturally restock the beaches with sand, while competition for the available supply of dredged-up or trucked-in sand has grown more intense. This has made the erosion of California beach sand an ongoing issue for decades – but it’s a problem that is now escalating rapidly.Much of California’s coastline development was completed during the state’s population boom from the 1940s to 1970s – years that happened to be an unusually “calm climate period” along the Pacific Ocean – “not many big El Niños, not a lot of storm damage”, Griggs, the coastline expert, said. “People built on the cliffs, they built on the bluffs, they built on the dunes.”Since then, stronger El Niño seasons have returned – and this year threatens to be the worst on record.Beach town residents such as Jones, the Laguna Beach mayor pro tem, who has lived there for much of her 48 years, are used to seeing sand migrate throughout the year. Beach sand is not a static amenity, but a complex system that can shift onshore and offshore, north and south. Scientists refer to each sand system as a “littoral cell”.During winter storms, Jones said, Laguna’s beaches typically lose sand, but later storms tend to bring it back, a kind of natural restoration. What’s happening now, though, is “not business as usual”, Jones said.Vitousek, the USGS oceanographer, said the intensity of this year’s coming tropical storms may disrupt beaches’ natural cycles: “You can get this thrashing, where the beach gets fully eroded on the south end, and then fully eroded on the north end,” he said. While beaches can sometimes recover “in a lot of cases, the damage is done. You’ve lost a beach. The waves are now breaking right on the infrastructure, causing damage.”View image in fullscreenAn oceanfront home shows extensive damage from powerful swells generated by Hurricane Marie. The home was eventually demolished.Photograph: Allen J Schaben/Los Angeles Times/Getty ImagesA few miles north of San Clemente, in Dana Point, the same ferocious Labor Day waves that paused train traffic through San Clemente ripped through a row of coastal residences, leaving 10 homes red-tagged as uninhabitable.“The damage that we have seen this year has been extraordinary,” Gabbard, the mayor, said. He estimated there had been $33m in damage to private property, and another $25m in damage to the public beach.Up and down the coast, lesser beach damage in early September served as a warning of what might be coming in the next months: a beachside parking lot was seriously damaged by waves in Laguna Beach, big sections of sand vanished around Balboa Pier in Newport Beach, and asinkhole opened in the drivewayof Nicholas Cage’s coastal mansion in Malibu.In October, abnormally high tidesflooded a low-lying neighborhoodof Newport Beach, with local news outlets sharing footage of someonepaddling on a surfboard through the streets. Huge wavesdamaged more homesin Long Beach. Adramatic crackin a cliffside bluff near Laguna Beach forced thecontinuing closureof part of the Pacific Coast Highway.Though San Clemente’s Lower Trestles was not one of the hardest-hit beaches in early September, local news outlets have alreadybegun speculatingover whether future Super El Niño damage could cause problems for the beach as a major Olympic venue.‘People don’t want to retreat’The most common short-term response to pounding waves that wash away local beaches and threaten beachside homes is to armor the shore with sea walls, revetments or simple piles of rocks. This has been a popular tactic, especially in southern California, where an estimated38% of the coastlineis now armored in some way. Half a century ago, in contrast, only 2.5% of California’s total coastline had armoring.But armoring, though relatively fast and simple, has a hefty long-term cost. Environmentalists, beach-loving residents and California’s powerful coastal commission all warn that building walls to guard the coastline serves as a death knell to the beaches next to them.double quotation markThe ocean temperature is high. There’s no wind. And that’s not ... happenstanceJohn GabbardImpermeable barriers block sediment from restocking the beach, while waves pounding on the barriers drag existing sand away, said Gary Griggs, a professor at University of California, Santa Cruz, who has been studying the California coastline for more than 50 years. In time, he said, any beach caught between the armoring and the sea disappears.For beach restoration activists such as Cosgrove, a fully armored, fully beachless California shoreline is the future dystopia they are trying to avert. From San Clemente’s state beach, Cosgrove showed me what the future shoreline might look like, if coastal communities continue to respond to erosion with short-term crisis management of throwing down rocks and putting up walls. He pointed south towardsCypress Shores, one of San Clemente’s gated oceanfront communities. Beneath the clifftop homes, the waves pounded directly onto a revetment, a rocky barrier shielding the rail line and the foot of the cliffs. “They had a 200–ft beach,” Cosgrove said. “They had volleyball courts. They had barbecues. Now there’s no beach. It’s all armor.”“If we never did sand replenishment, if we just don’t do anything at all, that revetment is the future of San Clemente,” Cosgrove told me. “From one end to the other. It may take 35 years to get there, but it will be that way.”Environmentalists and some coastal experts say the only viable long-term strategy for the California shoreline is “managed retreat”. That means moving homes, roads and other infrastructure inland from the eroding coast – a response that requires huge amounts of planning, logistics and consensus building, and is about as popular with coastal homeowners and developers as one might expect.“Most people don’t want to be managed, and most people don’t want to retreat,” said Griggs, the coastline expert. But, he added, “they’re not going to have a choice at some point”.View image in fullscreenHeavy machinery adds boulders to the protective sea wall  along Beach Road in Capistrano beach on 29 September 2026.Photograph: Allen J Schaben/Los Angeles Times/Getty ImagesThe centrist option, the one with the most support from across the political spectrum, is simply replenishing the sand on California’s eroded beaches – what Cosgrove is hoping to fund with his San Clemente ballot measure.“It is a softer option than putting rock down, and it provides some more of that habitation and recreation space,” said Kelsey Ducklow, a coastal resilience coordinator at the California Coastal Commission.Beaches are “the best natural buffer we have from waves”, Griggs said. “If the beach is narrowed or gone, the waves attack the cliffs directly.”The problem is that hauling and dumping tons of sand on existing beaches is extremely costly and planning intensive – and not at all guaranteed to last, coastal experts said. Grigg described it as “a very, very temporary fix”.“One big storm can remove hundreds of thousands of cubic feet [of sand],” Griggs said. At Torrey Pines beach in San Diego in 2001, he recalled, officials brought in 200,000 cubic yards of sand – equivalent to 20,000 dump truck loads, at a cost of more than $2m for that beach alone. “It stayed there for about eight months, during the spring and summer. Right around Thanksgiving, a storm hit, the waves came up, and [it] was gone overnight.”What does the future hold?In San Clemente, Cosgrove argued, the city’s beaches, which run between the protective arms of Dana Point and Cottons Point, are more sheltered, allowing new sand to stay within the system of beaches longer. An infusion of sand from 2024, placed with the help of the army corps of engineers, is still providing some cushion for the town’s beaches, he said. In the months he spent collecting signatures at the farmers’ market and local grocery store to get his sand-replenishment measure on the ballot, he heard widespread support for continuing to restock San Clemente beaches with new sand.double quotation markWe can’t affect global climate change, but we can protect ourselves from it by nourishing our beachesCameron CosgroveWhat people want to know, he said, is “Can someone else pay for this? Do we have to pay?” Residents want to know why the federal or state government isn’t funding beach replenishment with the taxes they already pay.One might think that a state as known for government bureaucracy as California might have a statewide beach commission, or at least a state sand fund, to keep one of the state’s primary economic engines from disappearing. It does not. The California Coastal Commission has regulatory power up and down the shoreline and can provide small planning grants to local jurisdictions, but it does not have the kind of money necessary to fund big sand projects, a spokesperson said.For that, Lester said, coastal cities usually need to go to the federal government and get a congressional appropriation for sand – a process that can easily take a decade, or even two, between when the state approves a replenishment plan and when federal money actually comes through.In Dana Point, where a majority of voters also supported Trump in 2024, Gabbard is hoping the president will step in to help with emergency funds to help the coastal town’s continuing storm damage.“Through back channels, I’ve been trying to get to the president to voice our concerns about, not just the homes themselves, but our beaches writ large, to make sure there are funds available to repair what we need to repair,” he said.One of the many projects needed, he said, is to create a more natural buffer for future storm damage at Capistrano beach by building a sand berm – a single project estimated to cost $16m.Even when federal funding is approved, cities are usually expected to provide matching funds for a big beach restoration project, Cosgrove said, which is why he thinks the most reliable option is for local residents to raise the money they need for beach restoration themselves, through a 10-year local sales tax. He said he is cautiously optimistic that San Clemente’s tax-skeptic voters will make an exception in November and vote to support wildfire prevention and the town’s beaches.While the Orange county transportation administration recentlypledged to expeditethe placement of 690,000 cubic yards of sand to protect the crucial rail line through San Clemente, the timing of the projectremains unclear, in part because the project will require “specialized marine dredging equipment”, and, of the US’s few existing machines, “many are committed to other projects months in advance”, an OCTA spokesperson said in a statement.The state government iscurrently examiningwhether the rail line should simply be moved inland to a new location – a project already estimated tocost more than $5bn.The rail runs dangerously close to the ocean in bothSan Clemente and Del Mar, a town closer to San Diego.View image in fullscreenPassengers on an Amtrak Pacific Surfliner train look out over San Clemente state beach.Photograph: Kevin Carter/Getty ImagesEven if OCTA’s emergency sand restoration project in San Clemente is completed in a timely way, Cosgrove said, the amount of sand the agency has pledged to provide is far too little to restore all the city’s beaches.In making his pitch to San Clemente voters, including on hisYes on Measure M website, Cosgrove doesn’t talk about the climate crisis, though he said he does see the role the warming ocean is playing in the extreme weather hitting California’s coast.“I’m just messaging on stewardship and adding sand to our beaches,” he said. “This is the local issue that we’re facing. We can’t affect global climate change, but we can protect ourselves from it by nourishing our beaches. Having wide beaches is the best protection no matter what comes our way.”Some residents have a less optimistic attitude about efforts to prevent further coastal damage. In San Clemente, Zhen Wu, a city council member, has opposed Cosgrove’s tax measure, telling the Associated Press: “Fighting mother nature is very expensive.”On a hot October Friday, Kathy Ruiz, of Laguna Niguel, was sunbathing on a mostly-empty Aliso beach, not far from where construction equipment was repairing the Laguna beach parking lot damaged by early September storm surges.“As far as people expecting the city to protect their homes, I don’t think that’s reasonable,” she said. “I think maybe they shouldn’t have built so close to the beach.”Some residents want the government to build up sand berms to protect homes against the coming storms, Ruiz said, but she was skeptical.“Nature is going to take its course,” Ruiz said. “I think all that stuff is in vain.”Explore more on these topicsCaliforniaEl Niño southern oscillationClimate crisisWest CoastOceansfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Heat pumps and insulation would cut UK living costs more than new oilfields, study suggests | Energy | The Guardian
description: Warm homes plan would create 50,000 jobs, compared with about 1,100 for Rosebank oilfield, thinktank finds
Author: Fiona Harvey
Headline: Warm homes plan would create 50,000 jobs, compared with about 1,100 for Rosebank oilfield, thinktank finds
Content: Housing in Kirkcaldy, Fife. The analysis found Rosebank jobs would be concentrated in the North Sea and in two companies, one of which was an overseas investor.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenHousing in Kirkcaldy, Fife. The analysis found Rosebank jobs would be concentrated in the North Sea and in two companies, one of which was an overseas investor.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEnergyHeat pumps and insulation would cut UK living costs more than new oilfields, study suggestsWarm homes plan would create 50,000 jobs, compared with about 1,100 for Rosebank oilfield, thinktank findsFiona HarveyEnvironment editorSun 18 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleInsulating Britain’s homes and investing in heat pumps would do more to cut the cost of living, create jobs and boost the UK’s economy than drilling for new oil, research suggests.The government’s £15bn warm homes plan, currentlyunder threat of cuts as ministers seek budget savings, would slash £1bn a year from household energy bills across the UK, concentrated on those on low incomes, according toresearchby the thinktank E3G. It would also provide a £1.6bn yearly boost to the economy, and about 50,000 new jobs spread across thousands of small businesses.The Rosebank oilfield, west of Shetland, would create about 1,100 direct and indirect jobs, the analysis found. The jobs would be concentrated in the North Sea and in two companies, one of them – Equinor – an overseas investor.A decision on whether to give the green light to the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea was “imminent”, the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, said on Wednesday. A decision on Rosebank would take a little longer, she said.Labour promised in its 2024 election manifesto to halt new licensing for oil and gas, but Jackdaw and Rosebank could be exceptions because they were already in the licensing system.Equinorpreviously estimated3,500 jobs would be created at peak for Jackdaw and Rosebank combined.Drill, Burnham, drill? The oil basin that is a totem for Trump – and a headache for Britain’s new PMRead moreExperts have repeatedly pointed out that new North Sea oil and gas would notbring down fuel pricesor ease any supply constraints on the UK arising from the Iran war, because oil and gas are sold on international markets.Some proponents of drilling argue that the economic boost to the UK and tax revenues for the government are reasons to grant licences. But related research by WWF and the campaigning group Uplift shows thattax revenues are likely to be limited, given the concessions that drillers can expect. While the total profits from Rosebank for its backers, Equinor, Shell and Ithaca Energy, could be £1.5bn over its 25-year lifespan, the UK government faces a potential loss of £258m through tax breaks and incentives.Tax revenues from the North Sea were about £4bn in 2025-26, but upstream tax relief and support measures amounted to an estimated £3.26bn.As the North Sea is a basin in steep decline, tax revenues from drilling are projected to fall to about £100m by 2030. Decommissioning costs for drilling platforms are also a major factor: taxpayers are likely to be asked for £12bn as the North Sea’s infrastructure is dismantled.Thewarm homes plan, under which up to 5m homes would be insulated, would draw in a further £15bn in private investment, according to E3G, which would be spread across the country rather than concentrated in one area, in line with Andy Burnham’s pledge for economic growth “in every postcode”.E3G also estimates that delivering the warm homes plan in full would boost GDP by 0.08%, while AI modelling suggests Rosebank would add about 0.025% on average through its lifetime, assuming the average oil price returning to $70 a barrel from recent highs. If the UK taxpayer paid for decommissioning, this would outweigh any positive impact.James Huw Dyson, a senior researcher at E3G, said: “When the first cold snap rolls in, the public aren’t going to thank the government for cuttinghome insulationwhile giving big oil tax breaks to drill for polluting energy that keeps our bills high. If the government is serious about tackling the cost of living, and investing across the country, it should focus its attention on insulating homes and rolling out clean energy, which will cut bills and create good jobs across Britain at the same time.”Ten major unions wrote to the government on Thursday to oppose granting a licence to the Rosebank oilfield.Scores of Labour MPs also oppose the move, and 600 scientists wrote to ministers over the summer urging a rethink.Dhara Vyas, the chief executive ofEnergyUK, which represents the energy industry, said: “We need government to stick to its ambitions on electrification. Watering down the warm homes plan or making further changes to the zero emissions vehicle mandate sends mixed signals to a market that has been in a state of flux for far too long – these businesses cannot easily ramp up production again, and sadly for too many have already had to close.”The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero declined to comment on E3G’s findings or the future of the warm homes plan.A spokesperson for Adura, the joint venture between Equinor and Shell that owns Jackdaw and Rosebank, said: “Analysis has shown that approving Rosebank and other planned North Sea oil developments would support £35.3bn in UK economic value between 2026 and 2035. Rosebank alone represents private sector investment of £8.7bn, three quarters of which will be spent in the UK, and together with Jackdaw will contribute £4.1bn in additional tax revenue over the next decade.”These figures take in the company’s wider operations beyond Rosebank and Jackdaw, and also make assumptions about the wider supply chain and the spending of employees as economic benefits, which are uncertain. On the tax take, they do not take account of the large tax reliefs available, estimated at more than £2.4bn. Contrary to standard HM Treasury practice, Adura’s estimates do not appear to factor in a discount rate for future income.Explore more on these topicsEnergyEnergy billsHeat pumpsFossil fuelsGreen jobsUK cost of living crisisOil (Business)newsShareReuse this content

title: Microsoft pulls out of AI datacentre project in Essex over power supply concerns | Datacentres - UK | The Guardian
description: Development by UK firm Nscale heralded by ministers as largest of its kind in country loses anchor tenant
Author: Gwyn Topham
Headline: Development by UK firm Nscale heralded by ministers as largest of its kind in country loses anchor tenant
Content: An artist’s impression of Nscale’s planned datacentre in Loughton, Essex.Photograph: NscaleView image in fullscreenAn artist’s impression of Nscale’s planned datacentre in Loughton, Essex.Photograph: NscaleDatacentres - UKMicrosoft pulls out of AI datacentre project in Essex over power supply concernsDevelopment by UK firm Nscale heralded by ministers as largest of its kind in country loses anchor tenantGwyn TophamandAisha DownSun 18 Oct 2026 09.05 EDTFirst published on Sun 18 Oct 2026 08.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe development of a huge AI datacentre hailed by the UK government has received a fresh setback afterMicrosoftpulled out of the project over concerns about power supplies.The development by the British company Nscale, heralded by ministers as the country’s largest AI datacentre when it was announced in 2025, was planned to open at Loughton inEssexnext year.Revealed: UK’s multibillion AI drive is built on ‘phantom investments’Read moreDoubts had already emerged about the scheme after the Guardianrevealed in Marchthat the location was still an operationalscaffolding yard.Now there are further concerns after Microsoft, one of its largest planned customers and expected to have been the anchor tenant, informed the company that it was pulling the plug on its agreement.It comes a month after it emerged that power supply problems meant the project would face a lengthy wait before coming online.Keir Starmer’s government had highlighted the Loughton project when announcing theUK’s AI strategy in 2025, describing it as the “largest UK sovereign AI datacentre”. Datacentres are the central nervous system of AI technology such as chatbots.The end of the deal with Microsoft, first reported in the Telegraph, means Nscale has lost its only publicly announced customer for the Essex datacentre. It is understood that Microsoft remains on board for another project the company has in Norway.Nscale, which is backed by tech companies including Nvidia, has positioned itself as Britain’s “sovereign” datacentre provider but the loss of an anchor tenant for its Loughton project could undermine its ambition to float on Wall Street this year with a potential valuation of $35bn (£26bn).View image in fullscreenIn March 2026, the Loughton site was still operating as a scaffolding yard.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianTargeting the rapid growth of AI to boost the economy, the UK government’s proposals to harness the technology have focused on two Nvidia-backed companies: the London-based Nscale and the US company CoreWeave.Official figures show investments in AI are among the factors helping Britain’s economy tobeat expectations of a weaker growth performancethis year as the war in the Middle East rattles global business activity.Nscale is a “neocloud”, one of a number of companies with deep ties to Nvidia that are building the key infrastructure for the AI boom. It is this relationship with Nvidia that meant it and CoreWeave were chosen as key players in the UK’s sovereign AI push, which happened under Starmer.There is, however, a growing chorus of voices whichsuggestthat neoclouds may be a vulnerability in the broader AI economy, especially as delays pile up across partners.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDriven by hopes of an economic transformation, many are taking on increasingly risky debt, including companies vital to the AI boom. If Nscale pushes back its initial public offering in New York, these vulnerabilities may come into sharper focus.The former UK deputy prime ministerNick Cleggand the former Meta chief operating officer Sheryl Sandberg are board members at the company. Clegg holds a 0.25% stake that could be worth $88m if the company floats at a $35bn valuation.It emerged earlier this month that UK Power Networks (UKPN), which owns and maintains the electricity grid across London and the south-east of England, hadinformed Nscalethat it would not be able to supply enough power to the company’s Loughton datacentre until the early to mid-2030s.Nscale said it was “committed to the project” but the failure to find a quick fix to the power supply issue underlines how much energy has become a hindrance to datacentre development.The scaffolding yard site has been cleared by Nscale, and the company is investigating whether it can generate power onsite and whether it can speed up the connection process.An Nscale spokesperson said: “We remain committed to both the Loughton project and the UK, and we are exploring alternative power sources for the site, in addition to other expansion sites in the UK.“Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term, and this unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts.”Explore more on these topicsDatacentres - UKMicrosoftAI (artificial intelligence)Technology sectorComputingEssexInfrastructurenewsShareReuse this content

title: Shabana Mahmood to hold talks with EU over law enforcement cooperation | European Union | The Guardian
description: UK home secretary’s meeting comes after PM said he wanted to rejoin European law enforcement databases
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: UK home secretary’s meeting comes after PM said he wanted to rejoin European law enforcement databases
Content: Shabana Mahmood is also expected to discuss counter-terrorism efforts with the senior EU official during their meeting on Monday.Photograph: Marcin Nowak/Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenShabana Mahmood is also expected to discuss counter-terrorism efforts with the senior EU official during their meeting on Monday.Photograph: Marcin Nowak/Anadolu/Getty ImagesEuropean UnionShabana Mahmood to hold talks with EU over law enforcement cooperationUK home secretary’s meeting comes after PM said he wanted to rejoin European law enforcement databasesLisa O’Carrollsenior correspondentSun 18 Oct 2026 14.13 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 14.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK home secretary,Shabana Mahmood, will meet the EU’s home affairs commissioner on Monday for further talks just days after Andy Burnham said he wanted to rejoin European law enforcement databases from which the UK has been locked out of since Brexit.According to theEuropean Commission, they will discuss “migration, border management, law enforcement cooperation and counter-terrorism”, with the latest Frontex data published on Monday showing a 43% decline in small boats crossing the Channel.It will be the second time Mahmood has met Magnus Brunner in two months and comes amid an increase in engagement between London and Brussels since Andy Burnham announced he would use an upcoming EU-UK summit to “lay out to the country” what he believes are the “different options for Britain’s long-term relationship” with the EU.Brexit’s back – but are British voters ready to contemplate a reversal?Read moreBrunner said “the UK’s contribution is indispensable” to continuing efforts to suppress irregular migration after the EU introduced a suite of new laws aimed at speeding up asylum decisions and deportations.On the agenda for Monday’s meeting will be talks on the UK rejoining some of the police and security databases it was locked out from after Brexit and rejoining a new database,Eurodac, centring on migration.Last weekBurnham told MPsthat “one of the most positive aspects of my meeting with [the European Commission] president [Ursula] von der Leyen in New York, was her openness to the conversation about restoring data sharing on immigration across the UK, across Europe”.He said it was “control” that the UK “lost” and should get “more attention” in the debate aboutBrexit. “I will work hard to see if we can get a practical arrangement on that very issue at the summit in November,” Burnham said.View image in fullscreenMagnus Brunner will discuss ‘migration, border management, law enforcement cooperation and counter-terrorism’ with Shabana Mahmood, according to the European Commission.Photograph: Dursun Aydemir/Anadolu/Getty ImagesBrunner will also meet the MI5 director general, Ken McCallum, and visit the National Counter Terrorism Security Office, as well as meet senior officials from the UK’s child sexual abuse centre to discuss joint efforts to tackle such crimes.He has also been chosen to deliver a lecture at King’s College London on migration and asylum, where he will talk about the impact of the EU’s new Pact on Migration and Asylum, a framework of 10 pieces of legislation overhauling how the EU manages its borders, processes asylum applications and shares information among member states.Brunner will tell those he meets that the new laws have already had a significant impact along with a shift in political priorities around migration in key countries such as Germany, Italy and France.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe said the “reforms are paying” off in the UK too, with illegal crossings down 43%.“We must stay on this course, including along all relevant migration routes, and the UK’s contribution is indispensable,” he said. “We have put our European house in order. Illegal crossings at our external borders are down 55% over two years, with a further third this year, and asylum applications are at record lows in the countries that used to be main destinations.”One key database the UK wants access to is Eurodac, a new platform which collects fingerprints and facial images of asylum seekers from the age of six, and security flags for people linked to terrorism or serious crime.Another is the Schengen Information System (SIS), which contains data on missing persons, stolen goods, vehicles and number plates, and fugitives crossing internal EU borders. About 20m searches are made daily on the SIS, according to EU data, mostly on cars.The Home Office has not commented.Explore more on these topicsEuropean UnionShabana MahmoodBrexitUK security and counter-terrorismCounter-terrorism policyImmigration and asylumEuropean CommissionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Manchester City owner’s £55m housing loan while Burnham was mayor investigated | Greater Manchester | The Guardian
description: Scrutiny committee looks into financing of Manchester Life project as PM promises ‘full transparency’
Author: Josh Halliday
Headline: Scrutiny committee looks into financing of Manchester Life project as PM promises ‘full transparency’
Content: The Manchester City chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak (left), talks with then Greater Manchester mayor, Andy Burnham, at the Etihad Stadium in 2019.Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Manchester City chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak (left), talks with then Greater Manchester mayor, Andy Burnham, at the Etihad Stadium in 2019.Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty ImagesGreater ManchesterManchester City owner’s £55m housing loan while Burnham was mayor investigatedScrutiny committee looks into financing of Manchester Life project as PM promises ‘full transparency’Josh HallidayNorth of England editorSun 18 Oct 2026 10.41 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 13.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA £55m loan to Manchester City’s Abu Dhabi owner will be investigated as part of a review into a fund for housing projects while Andy Burnham was mayor.The prime minister has faced weeks of scrutiny over his links to Manchester City’s super-rich owners after the club wasfound guiltyof boosting its income by £900m in a nine-year breach of financial rules.Burnham, the formerGreater Manchestermayor, was accused of siding with the Abu Dhabi owners after the “unprecedented” rule breach, when he said they had been “such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester” and that he would be “really concerned” to lose them from the sport.He could now face more uncomfortable questions after councillors in GreaterManchestersaid they planned to investigate loans made to property companies while he was mayor.In 2017, three companies ultimately controlled by the Manchester City owner, Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan, the vice-president and deputy prime minister of the United Arab Emirates, were loaned £55m as part of a fund operated by Burnham’s Greater Manchester combined authority (GMCA).View image in fullscreenManchester City owner, Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan, seen here in 2010, is also deputy PM of the UAE.Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/ReutersThe loans were to help finance amajor housing development called Manchester Life, which promised to create 6,000 homes in an “unprecedented” opportunity for the city. GMCA said the loans had been repaid in full but has not disclosed the interest rate or why Sheikh Mansour, as a scion of one of the world’s wealthiest families, would have been eligible.It emerged last week thatBurnham had met City’s ownerswhile enjoying hospitality from the club at its Etihad Stadium weeks before the loans were approved. That meeting later disappeared from public records before it came to light last week, prompting the prime minister to ask GMCA to carry out a “manual trawl” of his meetings to ensure “full transparency”.John Leech, a Liberal Democrat councillor in Manchester, said the fund – which has handed out £1bn to 50 separate developers since 2015 – would be investigated by GMCA’s overview and scrutiny committee, which he chairs.Leech told the BBC the approval process for loans had been criticised as “very opaque in the past and that it’s not necessarily been clearly understood why X was successful and Y wasn’t”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionManchester City staff invited on government trade trip to IndiaRead moreHe said it was “not unreasonable” to ask why seemingly successful businesses needed to borrow public money through this loan scheme. “In the case of Abu Dhabi, you would imagine that they wouldn’t have any problem accessing funds from elsewhere as well,” he said.“And so the process clearly does seem to be out of kilter with what the original stated aims were back in 2015.”He added: “We just want to be clear that there is a transparent rather than an opaque process”.Downing Street declined to comment. A GMCA spokesperson said it was supporting Leech’s overview and scrutiny committee with its inquiries. They said the fund had built 11,000 new homes and was contributing “billions of pounds worth of development at no cost to the taxpayer”.GMCA added: “Decisions to grant loans from the fund are taken publicly. Not a single viable scheme was ever turned down and funds were lent to around 50 different developers.“The fund is open to all developers, with lending criteria based on parameters set by the government and developed with external financial experts to reflect due diligence standards in the private sector.”Explore more on these topicsGreater ManchesterManchesterAndy BurnhamManchester CityLocal governmentCity mayorsHousingnewsShareReuse this content

title: NHS staff who wrongly accessed tiger victim’s records should be sacked, says Yvette Cooper | NHS | The Guardian
description: Health secretary says inappropriately looking up details about William Chapman, who died at Yorkshire Wildlife Park, is ‘total disgrace’
Author: Josh Halliday
Headline: Health secretary says inappropriately looking up details about William Chapman, who died at Yorkshire Wildlife Park, is ‘total disgrace’
Content: William Chapman died on 11 October after being mauled by a tiger at Yorkshire Wildlife Park.Photograph: South Yorkshire Police/PAView image in fullscreenWilliam Chapman died on 11 October after being mauled by a tiger at Yorkshire Wildlife Park.Photograph: South Yorkshire Police/PANHSNHS staff who wrongly accessed tiger victim’s records should be sacked, says Yvette CooperHealth secretary says inappropriately looking up details about William Chapman, who died at Yorkshire Wildlife Park, is ‘total disgrace’Josh HallidayNorth of England editorSun 18 Oct 2026 05.38 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 07.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNHS staff who inappropriately accessed the medical records of a man mauled to death by a tiger should be sacked,Yvette Coopersaid.The health secretary said the incident – which followed reports earlier this year that staff had unnecessarily viewed details about the Southport attack victims and those murdered by Valdo Calocane in Nottingham in 2023 – was a “total disgrace”.On Friday, Yorkshire ambulance servicesaid it was investigating two staffwho had inappropriately accessed information about William Chapman, who was mauled to death by a tigerat Yorkshire Wildlife Park last Saturday.Cooper told Sky News on Sunday: “I take this extremely seriously. I know there’s a specific investigation going into that case, but we just need to be absolutely clear.“No member ofNHSstaff should be accessing records that they do not need to see for medical care, and reasons simply for something to do with voyeurism, or what is in the news, or any of that kind of reason.“Not only is it a total disgrace, but I’ve spoken to the NHS chief executive about this. We agree that if there are cases here of people inappropriately accessing medical records, then they should be suspended while the investigation takes place and we need a much swifter line on this because these are basic standards, and everybody across the NHS knows that these are the basic standards.”Asked if people should be sacked, she added: “If there are breaches then people actually need to be sacked.”A total of15 NHS staff have now been sackedafter accessing medical records belonging to the victims of a 2023 Nottingham attack, it emerged on Saturday. Calocane killed two 19-year-old students, Barnaby Webber and Grace O’Malley-Kumar, and Ian Coates, a 65-year-old caretaker, and attempted to kill three other people in the city in June 2023.During its investigation, Nottingham university hospitals NHS trust has so far dismissed 15 staff, issued 15 final written warnings and two first written warnings. Doctors, nurses, registered healthcare professionals and other staff have been included in the investigation. The victims’ families were told about the latest update this week.In May, the NHS trust that runs Aintree hospital in Liverpool admitted that nearly 50 staff members had looked inappropriately at the medical records of victims of the Southport knife attack. Nicola Ryan-Donnelly from Fletcher’s Solicitors, which represents many of the injured children, condemned the “deeply disturbing abuse of power and a shocking breach of privacy”.Explore more on these topicsNHSYorkshireSouth YorkshireYvette CooperEnglandHospitalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Obama condemns comments by ‘border czar’ that Ilhan Omar could ‘of course’ be denaturalized | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: Former president urges Americans to defend congresswoman, saying ‘there’s no reason to believe it will stop with her’
Author: José Olivares
Headline: Former president urges Americans to defend congresswoman, saying ‘there’s no reason to believe it will stop with her’
Content: Homeland security officers carry boxes from the Washington DC residence of Ilhan Omar, on 12 October.Photograph: J Scott Applewhite/APView image in fullscreenHomeland security officers carry boxes from the Washington DC residence of Ilhan Omar, on 12 October.Photograph: J Scott Applewhite/APTrump administrationObama condemns comments by ‘border czar’ that Ilhan Omar could ‘of course’ be denaturalizedEx-president urges Americans to defend congresswoman, saying ‘there’s no reason to believe it will stop with her’José OlivaresandSanya Mansoorin New YorkSun 18 Oct 2026 19.51 EDTFirst published on Sun 18 Oct 2026 13.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFormer US president Barack Obama condemned comments by Donald Trump’s “border czar” that the Republican presidential administration could “of course” strip Democratic congresswomanIlhan Omarof her citizenship and deport her.Obamawrote Sunday morning, on X, that “the full weight of the federal government is being brought down on a law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticize the president.”He urged all Americans to defend Omar, regardless of their political beliefs, adding: “if this becomes the new normal, there’s no reason to believe it will stop with her – or that future presidents, in either party, won’t do the same.” Obama, too, has had his citizenship scrutinized by Trump, who more than a decade agofueled false conspiracy theoriesthat Obama was born in Kenya and therefore not eligible to be president.Ilhan Omar’s attorneys say federal search of her home was ‘neither justified nor lawful’Read moreTom Homan, Trump’s “border czar”, was asked on Saturday by a Fox News host whether the investigation into Omar could involve “denaturalizing and then deporting her”, Homan answered: “Of course”.“If you lie during the naturalization process, there is a process to denaturalize somebody,” Homan said. “We’ve done it before. It’s a long, tedious process, but it’s been done before.“And certainly, if the evidence points that way, that could happen.”Homan’s comments were the first remarks explicitly mentioning denaturalization and deportation in connection with Omar that were attributed by name to a topTrump administrationofficial since federal agents raided the Minnesota US House representative’s home on 12 October.The search of Omar’s home sparked majorbacklashand accusations that the Trump administration was weaponizing the federal government to target a political rival whom the president and his supporters have openly fantasized aboutdenaturalizinganddeporting.The federal government’s investigation into the most prominent Somali American in the US is to see whether Omar or her family violated any laws when obtaining her citizenship. The investigation was launched only weeks before the Novembermidterm elections, in which Omar is on the ballot.Homan also seemed to imply during his Fox News appearance that the federal government is investigating Omar for other allegations – but refused to give details.“I’m not going to go there,” Homan said. “I know things, but that’s a question for the FBI.”Omar – a naturalized US citizen fromSomalia– was a child when her father filled out the immigration paperwork which the federal government is evidently scrutinizing. Her father, Nur Omar Mohamed, died in June 2020.View image in fullscreenTom Homan applauds as Donald Trump speaks at a rally in Syracuse, New York, on 9 October.Photograph: Mandel Ngan/AFP/Getty ImagesObama stated in his post on X that Omar arrived in the US with her father when she was 12, and five years later, when her father became a naturalized citizen, she became one, too, because she was 17. (An 18-year-old would have had to apply for citizenship separately, he noted.)“Now the Administration is actively trying to deport Congresswoman Omar, seemingly based solely on the unsubstantiated theory that she was actually 18 when her father was naturalized, and therefore is not a citizen,” he wrote. “Federal agents have raided her home, confiscated personal records, and seized her phone – all to try and uncover a nonexistent smoking gun from 20 years ago that will somehow make their case.”In a letter after her home was searched, Omar’s attorneysaccused the US justice departmentof potentially influencing an election in violation of longstanding internal policy.The move to investigate Omar came amid a heightened offensive by the administration in pursuit of its aggressive anti-immigrant crackdown. In addition to funneling resources and deploying droves of officials to arrest, detain and deport undocumented immigrants throughout the country, the administration has also escalated its onoffensive on legal migration.The administration has been pursuing dozens of cases nationwide in which they are attempting to denaturalize Americans born outside of the US, who they claim fraudulently obtained their citizenship.As Homan alluded to on Sunday, the lengthy denaturalization process requires a federal investigation and drawn-out court proceedings.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNonetheless, as of April, the US justice department hadreportedly identifiednearly 400 foreign-born citizens that it sought to investigate.The investigation into Omar follows unsubstantiated accusations by rightwing figures who support Trump that she obtained her citizenship fraudulently. Omar denies the accusations, which also includeallegationsthather ex-husband is her brother, whom she only married so he could obtain immigration status in the US.Ilhan Omar’s phone seized and relatives subpoenaed in criminal inquiry, source saysRead moreThe federal government reportedlyseized Omar’s phoneduring the raid on her home and has issued more than a dozen subpoenas, including of Omar’s relatives.Omar’s attorneys have demanded that the federal government return her property and preserve any audio or video taken during the search.Omar has said she and her family fled Somalia’s civil war when she was eight and spent years in a refugee camp in Kenya. She and her family came to the US in the 1990s, and she became a naturalized US citizen in 2000, according to her lawyers.There is “no legitimate basis for any suggestion that she has violated any law concerning her citizenship status”, said her attorneys’ letter, which was first reported by theWall Street Journal.Even veterans at the Department of Justice expressed shock over the targeting of Omar, according toreporting by NBC News. “I was astounded to see a search of a sitting congressperson this close to an election,” said Peter Carr, a former career justice department spokesperson, NBC News reported.“Historically, the department has been very adamant that politics plays no role in investigative decisions they make and they try very hard to avoid taking overt actions that might even have the perception of influencing an election.”After the raid on her home, Omarposted on Xthat she was “ok”.“Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” Omar also wrote. She said: “Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns” for years – and “this is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation.”“I will not be silenced,” Omar added.Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationUS immigrationUS politicsIlhan OmarUS CongressHouse of RepresentativesSomalianewsShareReuse this content

title: US ambassador to Israel calls West Bank settler attack on American photojournalist ‘terror’ | West Bank | The Guardian
description: Mike Huckabee calls for arrest and prosecution of those responsible as Heidi Levine, 63, recovers in hospital in Israel
Author: Sam Jones
Headline: Mike Huckabee calls for arrest and prosecution of those responsible as Heidi Levine, 63, recovers in hospital in Israel
Content: Heidi Levine is recovering in hospital in Petah Tikva, near Tel Aviv.Photograph: Ariel Schalit/APView image in fullscreenHeidi Levine is recovering in hospital in Petah Tikva, near Tel Aviv.Photograph: Ariel Schalit/APWest BankUS ambassador to Israel calls West Bank settler attack on American photojournalist ‘terror’Mike Huckabee calls for arrest and prosecution of those responsible as Heidi Levine, 63, recovers in hospital in IsraelSam Jonesand agenciesSun 18 Oct 2026 13.02 EDTFirst published on Sun 18 Oct 2026 11.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, has denounced the settler attack that left theWashington Postphotojournalist Heidi Levine badly beaten and needing surgery as a “despicable act of terror” and called for the arrest and prosecution of those responsible.Levine, 63, an award-winning journalist who lives in Israel, wasset upon last Fridayby masked Israeli settlers who used clubs and other weapons to attack Palestinian people attempting to harvest their olives in occupiedWest Banktowns.The photographer, who is in a hospital in Petah Tikva near Tel Aviv recovering from hand surgery, broken ribs and other injuries she sustained in the attack, said she was beaten for more than 10 minutes by the settlers, who also stole her camera, passport and phone.1:57American photojournalist recounts Israeli settler attack in the occupied West Bank – video“I was attacked, pushed to the ground,” Levine said. “Luckily, I had my flak jacket and helmet, otherwise I probably wouldn’t even be here, because they just kept kicking and kicking me.” She said the attack ended when her Palestinian colleagues intervened to save her.Huckabee, a rightwing ally of PresidentDonald Trumpwith a track record of hardline, pro-Israel rhetoric, was notably blunt in his condemnation of what he called the “vicious and cowardly attack” on Levine. In a post on X on Saturday, he noted that she was a US citizen who had been clearly identifiable as a journalist.“We have called for a full investigation, arrest, and prosecution to the fullest extent of the law to whoever participated in this,” Huckabee added. “Attacking a female photographer is despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards. Dishonorable act of senseless violence.”View image in fullscreenMike Huckabee, the US ambassador to Israel, said it wa a ‘vicious and cowardly attack’.Photograph: Ohad Zwigenberg/APIsrael’s prime minister,Benjamin Netanyahu, has been ambiguous in addressing Levine’s assault, condemning “violence against anyone” but referring to the attack as “alleged” and saying its circumstances remain unclear.In an interview with the Associated Press on Sunday, Levine said she had been “shocked and insulted” to hear that Netanyahu referred to the attack on her and others as “alleged”, adding that the prime minister “had all the evidence on the table”.But she described the sharp condemnation of settler violence expressed to her in a call from Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, and in a letter signed by several of the country’s top former security and intelligence officials, in which they all expressed shame over the attack.Levine blamed “Jewish terrorists” for Thursday’s attack and added: “I’ve been covering this region for over 40 years, and I have never seen this country in such a state as it is today.”The photojournalist also said she was planning to return to work when she had recovered from her injuries. “I’ve invested decades of blood, sweat and tears into this,” she said. “They cracked my bones, they haven’t cracked my spirit.”View image in fullscreenHeidi Levine said she was planning to return to work when she had recovered from her injuries.Photograph: Ahmad Gharabli/AFP/Getty ImagesThe attack on the Palestinian farmers and Levine was followed on Saturday byanother outbreak of settler violencedirected against European diplomats, a French mayor and the archbishop of the French city of Cambrai, who were visiting the occupiedWest Bank.Bernard Baudoux, the mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries, was wearing his red, white and blue sash of office and attempting to enter a vehicle with diplomatic plates when he was assaulted and knocked to the ground. A masked militant shouted “Vive la France!” as he launched the attack, a witness said. Badoux’s wife and Vincent Dollmann, the archbishop of Cambrai, were also threatened by the group of seven men, some armed with clubs.View image in fullscreenBernard Baudoux, wearing his mayoral blue, white and red sash, was assaulted during a visit to the Palestinian town of Taybeh.Photograph: UGC/AFP/Getty ImagesThe group had joined the olive harvest on lands belonging to the Christian town of Taybeh, along with the French consul general in Jerusalem, his wife and other diplomats, and the Belgian and Polish consuls.“I think that if settlers are behaving like this, there is a tolerance on the part of the Israeli government,” Baudoux told Agence France-Presse after he was attacked. “The whole world needs to know what’s happening. For me, I’ll go back to my country and everything will be fine. Those who continue to suffer the most are those who are here.”Violence is surging ahead of bitterly fought elections to be held on 27 October, with Palestinians’ annual olive harvest being repeatedly disrupted by Israeli settlers as Netanyahu seeks to shore up his pro-settlement rightwing base.France’s foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, has called on Israel to “urgently halt criminal violence” and to arrest those responsible for attacking Baudoux. The EU has condemned the attack and urged “full accountability as well as effective measures to prevent continued acts of violence and violent harassment against Palestinians, including during the ongoing olive harvest season, as well as against journalists”.The European Commission executive vice-president, Teresa Ribera, went further, posting an interview with Levine in hospital and adding the caption: “They want no witnesses.”Israel’s foreign ministry has condemned the attack on the diplomats and Israeli police promised to open an investigation.Herzog, who holds a mostly ceremonial role, called Levine in hospital on Saturday, saying the attack was “outrageous and shocking” and was weighing on his conscience.View image in fullscreenIsaac Herzog, Israel’s president, said the attack on Levine was ‘outrageous and shocking’.Photograph: Ilia Yefimovich/AFP/Getty ImagesNetanyahu’s main rival in the elections, the former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, criticised the prime minister over the violence, saying it was “burning away the little legitimacy the state of Israel still possesses”. He described the attacks as “Jewish terrorism, under the auspices of the Israeli government”.Trump endorsed Netanyahu for re-election in a post on his Truth Social network on Sunday, hailing him as “a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran”. He added: “Bibi Netanyahu has been Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself.”The Washington Post has reiterated its call for a full and transparent investigation into the attack on Levine, even though Israel rarely investigates settler violence fully.Yesh Din, an Israeli rights group, says about 94% of investigations into settler violence since 2005 have ended without an indictment, with just 3% leading to full or partial convictions.The Associated Press and Agence France-Presse contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsWest BankMike HuckabeePalestineIsraelJournalist safetyTrump administrationBenjamin NetanyahunewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump plans to begin DC golf course renovation in defiance of judge’s order | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: Judge orders government to notify her by 8pm ET Sunday whether its position changed from Friday’s court filing
Author: Sanya Mansoor
Headline: Judge orders government to notify her by 8pm ET Sunday whether its position changed from Friday’s court filing
Content: A golfer hits toward felled trees after Trump's administration cut down more than 400 trees at the historic East Potomac Golf Links last weekend, in Washington DC.Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/ReutersView image in fullscreenA golfer hits toward felled trees after Trump's administration cut down more than 400 trees at the historic East Potomac Golf Links last weekend, in Washington DC.Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/ReutersDonald TrumpTrump plans to begin DC golf course renovation in defiance of judge’s orderJudge orders government to notify her by 8pm ET Sunday whether its position changed from Friday’s court filingSanya Mansoorand agenciesSun 18 Oct 2026 17.44 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 20.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump posted on Truth Social on Sunday that “restoration work will begin” on 15 November to a historic public golf course inWashington DCdespite a federal judge’s court order to pause his plans over environmental and historic preservation concerns.US district judge Ana Reyes had ruled earlier this year that the federal government must give notice before any substantive construction work on the East Potomac golf course could proceed, and last week issued an order halting the removal of trees at the site, which she called “inexcusable”.Judge orders Trump administration to halt work on historic DC golf courseRead moreTrump said Sunday in apost on Truth Socialthat work on the golf course would begin on 15 November and that ⁠it would reopen in about 15 months. He wrote that the facility would be transformed into “one of the Best and Most Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World”. Trump did not acknowledge the legal fight in his post, which included an artist’s rendering for the course redesign.The judge in the case took notice of Trump’s online message and ordered the government to notify her by 8pm ET on Sunday whether its position had changed from a court filing Friday that said “at most” Trump has given “preliminary thought” to the rebuilding plan and “there is no final agency action”.The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on whether Trump’s announcement on Sunday would conflict with Reyes’s ‌directives.The renovation is among a number of projects Trump was pursuing to reshape ‌the White House and ‌other Washington landmarks. Many of his projects, including plans for ahuge ballroom at the White House, theinstallation of his own nameon theKennedy Centerand construction of amassive arch, have been challenged in courts.The 106-year-old park and golf course, alone, has been the subject of many emergency hearings as the president has sought to renovate it. While it has been open to Washingtonians of all income levels, opponents of Trump’s plans to turn it into a high-end course have argued it will alter the character of the space and make it less affordable to people.Democracy Forward, which is representing the plaintiffs challenging his renovation plans for the golf course, responded to Trump by saying that the course is part of a national park and recreation facility that is meant for everyone to enjoy. “Our litigation is intended to protect this community jewel for the people and communities it serves and we will continue to work with our plaintiffs to defend it from unlawful and harmful intrusion,” Skye Perryman, the president and CEO of the group, said in a statement.The DC Preservation League brought a lawsuit in February to halt the administration’s takeover of the golf course, alleging that it would violate environmental laws and “irreparably destroy a priceless piece of American history”.In an 9 October court filing, theTrump administrationhad asked Reyes to dismiss the litigation, saying it was premature because the “proposed project remains at an early and conceptual stage”.The following day, however, ⁠the government removed about 500 trees from the site, which it said would improve safety at the park and restore its original design, and was part of a 2019 plan that predates Trump’s ambitions ‌for the course. Reyes ordered a halt to the removals.Reyes has also ordered key members of the Republican administration to testify on the recent tree-cutting and whether those actions are tied to the president’s plans for the historical public links.On Friday, the government filed a motion to disqualify Reyes and move the case to another district judge, saying her actions had shown “deep-seated and unequivocal antipathy” and “open hostility” toward the Trump administration, according to court records. The plaintiffs in the case oppose the motion.Reyes was appointed to the federal bench by Joe Biden in 2023.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpTrump administrationUS politicsWashington DCGolfLogging and land-clearingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Kansas driver who allegedly killed two and hurt 10 at soccer game is released from custody | Kansas | The Guardian
description: Wichita police awaiting toxicology results and mechanical exam of pickup truck driven by the 34-year-old woman
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: Wichita police awaiting toxicology results and mechanical exam of pickup truck driven by the 34-year-old woman
