Content: This image provided by KAKE shows police on the scene where a person drove a vehicle through a soccer field during a game in Wichita, Kansas, on 17 October.Photograph: Wyatt Glosson/KAKE-TV/APView image in fullscreenThis image provided by KAKE shows police on the scene where a person drove a vehicle through a soccer field during a game in Wichita, Kansas, on 17 October.Photograph: Wyatt Glosson/KAKE-TV/APKansasKansas driver who allegedly killed two and hurt 10 at soccer game is released from custodyWichita police awaiting toxicology results and mechanical exam of pickup truck driven by the 34-year-old womanMaya YangandRamon Antonio VargasSun 18 Oct 2026 15.30 EDTFirst published on Sun 18 Oct 2026 10.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA woman who was arrested on Saturday after she drove a truck through a youth soccer game in Wichita,Kansas–killinga boy and a man – has been released from custody without charges pending further investigation, according to authorities.In a statement on Sunday, the Wichita police department said investigators were awaiting the results of toxicology testing on the driver, whom the agency would only describe as a 34-year-old woman. Police said they were also waiting for “a mechanical examination” of the pickup truck that the woman was driving at the time she struck and killed six-year-old Cole Adrianand Nicholas Schafer, 35.Cole and Schafer were both from McPherson,Kansas, about an hour drive north of Wichita, police said. They were not relatives of each other, according to police – while a competitive youth soccer club from McPherson called their deaths “an unimaginable tragedy”.Ten other people were injured in a case that caused horror well beyond Wichita. Police said the injured included five children: two girls ages five and nine, a five-year-old boy, and two boys age eight.The rest of those hurt were women aged 28, 59 and 65, as well as men aged 32 and 68, police said.Two people, including child, killed after person drives through soccer game in KansasRead moreThose 10 victims had wounds that were considered traumatic but not life-threatening, police said.Police also said that an 11th person, a 61-year-old woman, experienced medical complications that were unrelated to traumatic injuries.As investigators put it, the woman at the center of the case was parked at the Stryker Sports Complex in north-east Wichita when she drove on to soccer fields there at about 3.25pm on Saturday. Emergency personnel responding to calls that the pickup driver struck multiple children and adults arrived to treat the victims while police detained the woman at the wheel of the truck.The woman had two of her children in the pickup with her, and a third was playing soccer elsewhere at the complex, police said.The two children in the driver’s truck were among more than 30 witnesses whom investigators interviewed, police said.Police said they later released the driver from custody without charges after consulting with the local Sedgwick county district attorney’s office. While “no charges have been filed at this time … investigators continue working to determine the circumstances that led to the crash”.Police said the woman had a valid driver’s license, no outstanding warrants and was from Garden City, Kansas, about three and a half hours west of Wichita. They discussed little else about her.Meanwhile, the McPherson City FC competitive youth soccer club said in a Facebookposton Saturday that it had “suffered an unimaginable tragedy at Stryker Soccer Complex”.View image in fullscreenPolice attend the scene where a vehicle drove through a soccer game at the Stryker Sports Complex in Wichita, Kansas, on Saturday in a still image from video.Photograph: ABC Affiliate KAKE/Reuters“We ask that you keep all those involved in your thoughts and prayers,” the club’s post continued. “Dealing with a loss of this magnitude also calls for privacy and respect for all our soccer community. Please allow time for healing and grieving to take place and be there for those that seek guidance.”After saying that McPherson City FC would later publish further information in regards to the club and its upcoming events, the post concluded: “Please hold your loved ones tight tonight.”Cole Adrian, the boy killed on Saturday, shared a last name with the man publicly listed as McPherson City FC (MCFC)’s director of coaches. A social media post in late August from the club’s director of coaches mentioned Cole having just scored his first “MCFC goal”.Social media profiles associated with the family of a McPherson man with Schaffer’s name and age indicate he had three children. A relative posted a picture with that man’s wife late on Saturday morning smiling near folding chairs on the sideline of a soccer field.McPherson’s municipal government wrote in its own Facebookpost: “Our community is hurting, and we stand together, and in support.”“Stay strong, McPherson,” that post also said. “Be there [and] be kind.”Wichita’s police chief, Joe Sullivan, added that the hearts of those at his agency “are with the families of Adrian and Nicholas as they face an unimaginable loss”.“What should have been a day of children playing soccer and families spending time together ended in tragedy,” Sullivan said. “We are also thinking about those who were injured, their loved ones and everyone who witnessed what happened.“We know this tragedy has affected many people throughout our community, and we want those families to know they are not alone. Our officers and investigators will continue working to understand exactly what happened.”View image in fullscreenA stretcher is brought to the scene at the Stryker Sports Complex in Wichita, Kansas, on Saturday in a still image from video.Photograph: ABC Affiliate KAKE/ReutersStryker Sports Complex announced that all events had been cancelled there until further notice.“We ask that you keep all individuals and families affected in your thoughts and prayers during this difficult time,” the complexalso saidin its announcement. “Please avoid the complex to allow emergency personnel to carry out their work.“Updates regarding future events will be shared as information becomes available.”Separately, the Kansas State High School Activities Association also suspended its third-place and championship flag football games, which had been scheduled for later on Saturday at the complex.“The KSHSAA extends our condolences to the families and teams [affected] by the incident,” the associationsaid.The organization said it planned on providing details about rescheduled games on Monday.Saturday marked the second time in less than 26 years that the Stryker complex – near the corner of Wichita’s North Greenwich Road and East 29th Street – was at the center of a high-profile, deadly case.Brothers named Jonathan and Reginald Carr were convicted ofshootingfive people – including four fatally – on a snow-covered field there in December 2000 during a crime spree that also involved robbery, rape and torture, according to information culled from court filings and media reports.The Carrs were sentenced to die over what some have referred to as the “Wichita massacre”. And in July, Kansas governor Laura Kellydeniedtheir requests for their death sentences to be commuted to life imprisonment.Explore more on these topicsKansasUS crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Condé Nast’s UK profits drop by more than a third as sale of Vogue publisher ruled out | Condé Nast | The Guardian
description: Magazine group points to restructuring bill but says it ‘remains profitable in the UK for another year’
Author: Mark Sweney
Headline: Magazine group points to restructuring bill but says it ‘remains profitable in the UK for another year’
Content: Newsstand sales and other subscriptions account for about 14% of Condé Nast’s total revenues.Photograph: Nathaniel Noir/AlamyView image in fullscreenNewsstand sales and other subscriptions account for about 14% of Condé Nast’s total revenues.Photograph: Nathaniel Noir/AlamyCondé NastCondé Nast’s UK profits drop by more than a third as sale of Vogue publisher ruled outMagazine group points to restructuring bill but says it ‘remains profitable in the UK for another year’Mark SweneySun 18 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 09.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleProfits at Condé Nast’s UK arm slumped by more than a third last year, according to figures published shortly after the billionaire family that owns the luxury magazine group and titles from Vogue to GQ ruled out a sale.The publisher, which enjoyed a bumper 2024 after booking £64m in proceeds from the sale of its UK headquartersVogueHouse in London, saw pre-tax profits excluding exceptional items tumble 36% from £28m that year to nearly £18m last year.Revenues generated in the UK fell 7% from £75.9m to £70.6m, newly filed accounts showed. However, an 18% increase in international revenues, to £29.7m, helped keep the company’s total revenues almost flat, at £100m.“Condé Nast remains profitable in the UK for another year,” a spokesperson for the publisher said. “The change in the exact level of profit reflects a period of planned investment in customised client solutions.”Restructuring costs at the company, which publishes glossy titles and brands including Vanity Fair, House & Garden and Tatler, more than doubled year on year, from £1.9m to £4.3m.Condé Nast said the latest restructuring charge was “primarily due to severance costs”. Despite the hefty restructuring bill, staff numbers remained almost flat, dipping from 466 to 461 between 2024 and last year.“There were no large restructures in the UK business in 2025. There were isolated instances of redundancy, but headcount remained flat as hiring continued across the business,” the spokesperson said. “In addition, there have been changes to the pension scheme projections and wage inflation, which also impacted profit for this year.”View image in fullscreenCondé Nast had enjoyed a bumper 2024 after booking £64m in proceeds from the sale of Vogue House in Hanover Square, London.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianLast week, Steven Newhouse, the chair of the Newhouse family holding company Advance that controls Condé Nast, ruled out a sale of the publishing giant. There had been speculation that the Amazon founder, Jeff Bezos, who owns the Washington Post, could buy the business.Newhouse made the comment after the abrupt departure of the chief executive Roger Lynch, hired in 2019 to turn around the business, to become the boss of the toymaker Mattel.“Maybe for a certain class of non-media owner, there’s a prestige to owning media properties,” hetold the Financial Times. “But we’ve been a media owner for 100 years. So we’re not in it for the glamour.”Earlier this year, Lynch described the introduction of Google’s AI Summaries – which often negate the need to click through to source material – as“another sort of death blow”to the way consumers have traditionally searched online and reached media outlets. He said Google searches were “no longer a meaningful driver” of Condé Nast’s business, accounting for only about a quarter of visits to its websites last year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGlobally, seven of Condé Nast’s largest brands – Vogue, GQ, the New Yorker, Wired, Vanity Fair, Architectural Digest and Condé Nast Traveler – account for 85% of the company’s revenues.Newsstand sales and other subscriptions account for about 14% of total revenues, with advertising and “other services” accounting for about 86%.The publisher’s accounts filed at Companies House show that the highest-paid director - Natalia Gamero del Castillo Calleja, the company’s most senior executive outside the US who resigned last August - took home more than £1.3m.Earlier this year, Condé Nast announced plansto shutter Self, its women’s health magazine, after 47 years.Explore more on these topicsCondé NastVogueMagazinesNewspapers & magazinesConsumer magazinesnewsShareReuse this content

title: What are self-replicating ‘AI worms’, and why is Anthropic worried about them?  | Technology | The Guardian
description: The tech company says successful AI worms need more capability on less powerful devices, but current trends make that feasible by the end of the year
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The tech company says successful AI worms need more capability on less powerful devices, but current trends make that feasible by the end of the year
Content: ‘Whatever claims the labs are making, they are not warning us enough. We need to understand that nobody can stop the AI storm.’Photograph: Kim Kyung-Hoon/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Whatever claims the labs are making, they are not warning us enough. We need to understand that nobody can stop the AI storm.’Photograph: Kim Kyung-Hoon/ReutersTechnologyExplainerWhat are self-replicating ‘AI worms’, and why is Anthropic worried about them?The tech company says successful AI worms need more capability on less powerful devices, but current trends make that feasible by the end of the yearJoseph Menn in San FranciscoSun 18 Oct 2026 09.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWarnings about what artificial intelligence might do in the future – together with alarming reports of what it has gotten up to already – are being issued so quickly that even security experts have difficulty triaging what to worry about.Yet areportthis week from Anthropic’s offensive research team grabbed attention by describing a new, practical threat, one devoid of human characteristics or apocalyptic musings. The red team, as such internal testers are called, said it created a malicious AI program that spread autonomously through internet-connected “smart” televisions and could do the same inside other ordinary devices. While machines running AI usually need a fair amount of computing power, the researchers said that their programsplit parts of itselfamong 15 televisions and was still able to function by using a bit of power from each.AI in your oven? Anthropic warns models ‘months away’ from self-replication on smart devicesRead moreIn addition to evoking the horcruxes that kept pieces of Lord Voldemort’s soul alive within objects in the Harry Potter series, the report alarmed some professionals because the generally weak security of smart televisions and many other “internet of things” devices would be very hard to correct, even with a concerted effort.“It’s something to worry about just like every other wave of cyber-attacks. We need to mitigate the possible effects,” said Joshua Saxe, who led development of Meta’s AI security effort. “I’m concerned right now that folks in the cybersecurity community are not taking these kinds of real risks as seriously as they should be.”The damage of such “AI worms” could be astonishingly large. Self-replicating computer viruses, which need not trick a human to propagate, are known as worms, and earlier worms have wreaked some of the worst havoc in the history of the internet.That legacy includes the Morris worm of 1988, which arrived before the mainstream consumer internet, when a graduate student released a program that took advantage of various software flaws and weak passwords, copying itself so rapidly that many infected machines slowed to a stop. The US and Israel brought worms into international espionage with the stealthy Stuxnet in the lat 2000s, which sabotaged Iranian nuclear centrifuges. Other worms like the RussianNotPetyaand North Korean-attributed WannaCry have caused tens of billions of dollars’ worth of damage worldwide.Many of the world’s most destructive worms have depended on known vulnerabilities that device owners have not patched, sometimes months after patches became available. TheAnthropicteam predicted that a worm like theirs could function in the same way and be harder to stop, because smart devices receive patches less often than phones or laptops. Worse, they theorized that an AI worm could keep adapting to other types of hardware by researching newly disclosed vulnerabilities.What differentiates AI worms from typical reproducing viruses is that AI models can learn as they go, said Ariel Herbert-Voss, an early security expert at OpenAI who now runs AI security startup RunSybil. Existing cybersecurity infrastructure is not ready for the proliferation of such threats, Herbert-Voss said. “We need to better enable our security teams. We need to be giving them more resources to fix problems.”Worms could also be used for benevolent purposes, suggested Chris Inglis, a former deputy director of the National Security Agency who served as National Cyber Director in the Biden White House.“The question of whether AI worms are plausible has been settled by several breakout events over the past six months,” Inglis said by digital message. “The better question is how we will employ them, counter them, and/or combine them with other emerging technologies.”Anthropic researchers said a successful AI worm would need to have more capability on less powerful devices than is possible right now – but they added that current trends will make that feasible by year’s end. Their research follows apaperpublished by experts at the University of Toronto a few months ago, which infected a full-size computer and could spread to similar machines more rapidly than the television worm.“The capabilities have been developing very rapidly,” said co-author and Toronto PhD student Jonas Guan.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGuan and other experts said that, as a practical matter, an AI worm should not top anyone’s list of AI fears. The Anthropic version moves very slowly, Guan said, and worms have predictable and detectable actions that can be blocked at multiple layers. Basic security hygiene, including requiring strong passwords and two-factor authentication, would stop most worms and other hacking, experts said.“Nothing about this is truly feasible or impactful,” said Juan Andres Guerrero-Saade, vice-president of research at security firm SentinelOne. “It’s nifty stunt hacking that’s getting way more amplification in service of the ridiculous doomer narratives that suggest models have a mind and will of their own.”Anthropic did not respond to an interview request.Outside Washington, many in the AI and security worlds believe greater government oversight of AI is now essential. But members of Congress have introduced mutually conflicting bills, while the White House has so far created only asmall review board.Security researchers and laypeople alike find themselves weighing the motivations behind fearful prognostications from AI companies, which range from espousing quasi-religious beliefs, to seeking legislation to exclude rivals or save money, to hyping the anticipated multi-trillion-dollar public valuations of the San Francisco AI giants.“The claim that a lot of this is marketing is correct, but the reality dwarfs any PR,” said Gadi Evron, who is running a conference on AI security in San Francisco this month called Unprompted. “Whatever claims the labs are making, they are not warning us enough. We need to understand that nobody can stop the AI storm.”Explore more on these topicsTechnologyAI (artificial intelligence)AnthropicWormsVirusesComputingHackingexplainersShareReuse this content

title: World Bank says ‘small AI’ could transform developing countries | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Bank’s chief knowledge officer says the tech could speed up economic development from centuries to decades
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Bank’s chief knowledge officer says the tech could speed up economic development from centuries to decades
Content: ‘Small AI’ models can run on a mobile phone with low connectivity, and could help accelerate development for emerging economies.Photograph: Zuma Press/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Small AI’ models can run on a mobile phone with low connectivity, and could help accelerate development for emerging economies.Photograph: Zuma Press/AlamyAI (artificial intelligence)World Bank says ‘small AI’ could transform developing countriesBank’s chief knowledge officer says the tech could speed up economic development from centuries to decadesHeather Stewartin BangkokSun 18 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheWorld Bankis urging developing countries to kickstart the creation of “small AI” models, which can run on a mobile phone with low connectivity, to reap the full benefits of artificial intelligence.While Silicon Valley big tech firms are focused on ever more sophisticated consumer products, Paschal Donohoe, the World Bank’s chief knowledge officer, said AI could also accelerate development for emerging economies – but only if it was adapted to local needs.Small AI uses specialised models that are trained using narrower datasets for a specific purpose.“We argue that economic development in the countries that we serve and partner with that could have taken centuries to make happen, the potential is there for that economic development now to happen within decades,” Donohoe said.“Small AI would be available in a local setting, with low connectivity, and in the local language of the community – and tends to be available on your mobile phone.”Donohoe, a former finance minister for Ireland, cited the example of Indian farmers engaged in the World Bank’s agricultural scheme, AgriConnect, who needed to access soil analysis in their own language.“There’s not going to be enough scientists and agricultural experts to do that for every small farm in India. And this is where what we describe as ‘small AI’ comes in. Because small AI is AI that would be available on your phone, that can help deliver against those information needs.”He suggested such products could emerge from collaboration between the World Bank, governments and the private sector.The impact of AI on jobs and growth is a central theme of the annual meetings of the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF), which are being held this week in Bangkok, Thailand.Speaking on a panel about the impact of the technology on Monday, Kristalina Georgieva, the IMF’s managing director, called on governments to provide the preconditions for AI to succeed.She said: “You need access to electricity. You need access to digital infrastructure. People have to be geared to adoption. And the government should be able to give some safety, protect against bad actors so that adoption can work.“If we work hard to have the basics for it, [adoption] can be very democratic. As democratic as the cellphone.”The World Bank’s annual world development report, published in August, hailed the potential benefits of AI. But it pointed out that, for example, almost a third of rural schools in sub-Saharan Africa lacked electricity and more than two-thirds did not have a consistent internet connection.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGeorgieva warned that over time 40% of jobs worldwide were likely to be either augmented or eliminated by AI, with the impact particularly acute for young people at the start of their careers.“When we look at this, what we recognise is that the people to worry about, first and foremost, are young people that are coming into the labour market,” she said. “Normally they would get into these routine, repetitive jobs and then go up the ranks. But if they’re gone, I don’t think any young person wants to be a barista in a coffee shop as a professional future.”Under its president, Ajay Banga, the World Bank has made attracting private-sector funding into emerging economies a focus of its work.Donohoe said the World Bank had mobilised $120bn (£90bn) of private capital in the past year using guarantees and other financial instruments, at a time when many countries, including the US and the UK, were cutting their aid budgets.“We want to highlight the link between private capital mobilisation and jobs and economic development,” he said.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)World BankInternational Monetary Fund (IMF)Emerging marketsGlobal economyEconomicsTechnology sectornewsShareReuse this content

title: Twelfth Night review – Mathew Horne oozes arrogance as a brilliantly buttoned-up Malvolio | Stage | The Guardian
description: The yellow stockings are as funny as ever – yet a haunting, folky live score casts a dream-like uncertainty over Shakespeare’s tangled romance
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: The yellow stockings are as funny as ever – yet a haunting, folky live score casts a dream-like uncertainty over Shakespeare’s tangled romance
Content: Egg on his face … Mathew Horne as Malvolio in Twelfth Night.Photograph: Manuel HarlanView image in fullscreenEgg on his face … Mathew Horne as Malvolio in Twelfth Night.Photograph: Manuel HarlanStageReviewTwelfth Night review – Mathew Horne oozes arrogance as a brilliantly buttoned-up MalvolioCrucible, SheffieldThe yellow stockings are as funny as ever – yet a haunting, folky live score casts a dream-like uncertainty over Shakespeare’s tangled romanceMark FisherSun 18 Oct 2026 06.55 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 09.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou can pictureMathew Horne’s Malvolio as a guest on an early 1970s BBC Two arts show. With his buttoned-up collar, tight black suit and supercilious delivery, he oozes self-satisfaction. Trusting in his superior taste, he has the pose to prove it: stiff, studied and haughty.His fall from grace, tricked into dressing up as a yellow-stockinged morris dancer, is as funny as it ever is in Shakespeare’s comedy. It is the comeuppance of the arriviste. Brought down to size, he is no less indignant for it. In a smart, unyielding performance, he goes from pompous to bruised – and ever unrepentant.Where Malvolio is urbane, Genevieve Dawson’s live score has a folk-club earthiness. Played on clarinet, guitar and violin, it is haunting and whimsical, with a similarly 1970s vibe, like something fromThe Wicker Man.View image in fullscreenIrresistible … Justina Kehinde and Bebe Sanders in Twelfth Night.Photograph: Manuel HarlanCalling the musicians to order, David Birrell plays Feste less as the fool than the troubadour, one blessed with expensive dress and surprising wisdom, as well as a voice correctly identified by Sir Andrew Aguecheek (James Chetwood) as “mellifluous”. His plangent songs cast a note of uncertainty over the comic romance of Jamie Glover’s swift, concise and controlled production.Fielding much the same ensemble that appeared in last month’sKing Lear, with a blood-orange sun presiding over Amanda Stoodley’s stony circular set, Glover brings energy and clarity to the language. Going at a fair clip, the actors wind up the narrative coil in the first half, playing it straight and focused, in order to release the comedic spring in the second.In a play about status, appearance and falsity, the shipwrecked Viola (Bebe Sanders), going undercover as Cesario, is winningly plain-speaking as she inadvertently arouses the passions of Olivia (Justina Kehinde). She is too poetically lovely to resist. Switching from the magisterial to the lusty, Olivia has a tough time reconciling courtly expectations with her desires. For his part, Orsino (Fode Simbo) is plain deluded until Viola’s brother Sebastian (Harry Redding) shows up and he can see the beauty of what is right in front of him.There is merriment in the confusion and its untangling, but also a dream-like instability in a punchy, satisfying show.AtCrucible, Sheffield, until 31 OctoberExplore more on these topicsStageTheatreWilliam ShakespeareSheffield TheatresMathew HorneTwelfth NightreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Hilarious quips and ‘100,000-volt’ energy: the hypemen (and women) redefining Afrobeats music | Nigeria | The Guardian
description: Style of emceeing based on high-octane, ad-libbed vocals has flourished thanks to its unique way of captivating crowds
Author: Eromo Egbejule
Headline: Style of emceeing based on high-octane, ad-libbed vocals has flourished thanks to its unique way of captivating crowds
Content: Toby Shang, one of the leading lights of the growing Afrohype genre. Photograph: Sogo Oladele/The GuardianStyle of emceeing based on high-octane, ad-libbed vocals has flourished thanks to its unique way of captivating crowdsByEromo Egbejulein LagosSun 18 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 09.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor the 2015 freshmen cohort of the history degree programme at the University of Lagos, their classmate’s first-semester presentation was so captivating that they began calling him Toby Shang, after the 16th-century Chinese dynasty he had focused on.His crowd engagement that day had been harnessed from his high school days as a ginger-man (energiser) in a three-man band and as a private tutor. By his final year at university, his viral catchphrases and infectious energy had resulted in a hit song, Shedibalabala. Today, he is one of the self-acclaimed “evangelists and pioneers” in the Afrobeats sub-genre some are now calling Afrohype or lamba.View image in fullscreenToby Shang by the waterfront in the Lagos suburb of Akoka.Photograph: Sogo Oladele/The Guardian“Even my mother calls me Shang now,” the 32-year-old, born Tobi Michael Adeyeye, said in an interview near the university’s lagoon waterfront, where he once emceed gatherings.Since then he has hosted his own rave, released two EPs and run four editions of his School of Hype – a one-day masterclass with online mentoring that has launched several rising stars.Allow TikTok content?This article includes content provided byTikTok. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueHypemen neither sing nor rap entirely, but perform high-octane ad-libbed vocals“and onomatopoeic sounds” over fresh beats or popular instrumentals such as Dorime, a made-in-Nigeria version of 1996’s Ameno by the French group Era, a song that has become a continental nightclub classic. In response, nightclub patrons donate or spray money – the Nigerian custom of throwing or placing money on someone to celebrate them.Hype is now omnipresent at wedding after-parties, raves and corporate parties. On Instagram, one teenage sensation is now known for recording 30-second hypes for birthday celebrants at the request of friends or relatives.View image in fullscreenToby Shang made a name for himself while still a student at the University of Lagos.Photograph: Sogo Oladele/The Guardian“Hypemen have the gift of the gab and fine mic control,” said the London-based doctor and cultural critic Dami Ajayi, who encountered one at a party in Tirana last month. “He used the spaces between lyrics for hilarious quips, many of which were frontally risque and misogynistic,” he said.Despite being a male-dominated sub-genre, a few women have made their mark, such as the Yaoundé-based bikutsi artist Lady Ponce, known as the “100,000-volt lady” because of her energy. Other notable female figures in the scene includeDeborah ‘Hype Queen Baddy’ Francis– an alumnus of Shang’s school who died in September – and the radio presenter Melody “M.I.A” Adigo, both from Lagos.The art of hyping as it is known in west and centralAfricahas its roots in praise-singing and call-and-response music styles ingrained for centuries in Black populations on both sides of the Atlantic. In west Africa, this tradition took the form of oral historians known as griots. In the US, it was sustained by negro spirituals, sacred folk songs created by enslaved African Americans.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Long WaveNesrine Malik, Micha Frazer-Carroll and the team guide you through the biggest Black stories from around the worldEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe west has a blinkered view of African music – and it’s hurting the whole continent’s cultureRead moreThese styles laid the foundation for theatalaku(meaning “look here, look at me” in the Kikongo language of the DR Congo) tradition that came alive in 1980s Kinshasa, followed by today’s hype scene.Exponents of this style include the American gospel singer Kirk Franklin as well as the Congolese rumba bandleader Koffi Olomide and the Congolese singer Awilo Longomba.The success of Olomide and Longomba at the turn of the 21st century set off a craze in Côte d’Ivoire, wherecoupé-décalémusic embraced theatalakutrend alongsidefarotement, the act of showing off by throwing cash at performers or guests at parties.View image in fullscreenThe Congolese singer Koffi Olomide performing at a festival in Abidjan in September 2021.Photograph: Sia Kambou/AFP/GettyA line encouraging audiences to gallop like a horse in the Ivorian star DJ Arafat’s 2003viral homageto a late friend – “Tout le mondegalope, kirikata kirikata” – influenced later hits from Nigerian Afrobeats musicians Flavour N’abania and Skales.Côte d’Ivoire’s national television network, RTI, ran anatalakutalent hunt for several years. Lili Djely, an Ivorian woman of Malian origin, won the 2006 edition with a mix of Ivorian nouchi and French, defeating men to take the crown. In recent years, an MC/hypeman of the year category was introduced at the Ghana DJ awards as hype flourished there too.Allow TikTok content?This article includes content provided byTikTok. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueThanks to the success of Afrobeats, Afrohype is now widely recognised as a full-time career. As artists became more expensive to book after Covid-19, promoters turned to hypemen – previously criticised for simply doing voiceovers. Some are now reportedly paid as much as 5-8m naira (£2,844–4,550) for a 30-minute or one-hour performance.Some observers, however, say hype is a nuisance, amping up noise levels at events or encouraging fraudulent lifestyles, and that many performers do not customise language and tempo to fit the event.View image in fullscreenThe Congolese musician Awilo Longomba performing at the All Africa music awards in Lagos in November 2019.Photograph: Pius Utomi Ekpei/AFP/GettyNevertheless, hypemen are now a permanent fixture on the entertainment scene. For Shang, they are helping fun-seekers and club-goers get back on the dancefloor.“People are facing a lot of challenges … they need somebody to tell them money is coming in the new week,” he said. “Also, everybody wants to press their phones or show Birkin bags in clubs. Nobody wants to dance because dancing is seen as for small kids. You need a hypeman to bring out that childlike part in every person. A 60-year-old woman can start dancing like a young girl if the hype is good enough.”Explore more on these topicsNigeriaAfricaClub culturefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘It was like your worst nightmare’ – Ellie and Natasia on mums, music … and failing to make Bob Mortimer smile | Television | The Guardian
description: They spoofed mothers … and now they are mothers. The comedians talk about moving with the times for the return of their scalpel-sharp BBC sketch show
Author: Rachel Aroesti
Headline: They spoofed mothers … and now they are mothers. The comedians talk about moving with the times for the return of their scalpel-sharp BBC sketch show
Content: Shooting while heavily pregnant posed a few challenges … Natasia Demetriou and Ellie White in the new series of Ellie and Natasia.Photograph: BBC/Nit TV/Jack BarnesView image in fullscreenShooting while heavily pregnant posed a few challenges … Natasia Demetriou and Ellie White in the new series of Ellie and Natasia.Photograph: BBC/Nit TV/Jack BarnesTelevisionInterview‘It was like your worst nightmare’ – Ellie and Natasia on mums, music … and failing to make Bob Mortimer smileRachel AroestiThey spoofed mothers … and now they are mothers. The comedians talk about moving with the times for the return of their scalpel-sharp BBC sketch showSun 18 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBefore Ellie White and Natasia Demetriou were mothers, they were mums. In a skit from their 2019 sketch show pilot, the comedy duo play two straight-talking, hygiene-obsessed matriarchs in gilets and camel-toe-accentuating leggings who record lifestyle vlogs from a pristine kitchen while melodramatically referencing the pressures of motherhood. Ever since, the characters have become a core component of the pair’s comic universe, appearing repeatedly in the first proper series ofEllie & Natasia in 2022.Now the mums are back and moving with the times: reviewing various supermarket white breads – all reassuringly “sterile” options – as car-based food influencers for the show’s second outing. But behind the scenes there has been a bigger shift. The last time they wrote these sketches, White and Demetriou were childless; now they each have two kids.Coming up with material this time around was a different experience, says Demetriou. “I now feel quite a lot of empathy for these women,” says White. “Well, I always felt empathy – I do with all our characters – but I especially am now like: itisactually quite hard.” Even the housework obsession has become relatable. Nowadays, when Demetriou sees the brand of cleaning product she uses “on offer in Waitrose or Tesco, it is a good day for me. Get three just in case – put them in the cupboard.”Today, the pair are in their homes, squeezing in interview time while their youngest babies nap. “I may at some point be handed my child and then flap my breasts out for all and sundry to see,” warns White. They both found out they were pregnant again last September, a couple of weeks into the writing process. Three years had elapsed since series one – a gap they attribute to scheduling issues (both are successful actors; Demetriou is best known for 35-time Emmy-nominated vampire comedy What We Do in the Shadows, while White’s recent credits include Black Mirror, Wonka and Bridget Jones: Mad About the Boy) – but this new biological deadline meant “it was now or never,” says White. “We had to write it very quickly and film it very quickly so that we wouldn’t give birth when we were filming.” (White ended up going into labour halfway through the edit.)View image in fullscreen‘It was now or never” … Natasia Demetriou and Ellie White in their new series.Photograph: BBC/CPL ProductionsShooting while heavily pregnant did pose a few challenges. In some sketches, their stomachs are disguised with voluminous clothes or behind furniture (a pro for Demetriou: “I love acting sitting down, so if you can sit me behind a table I’m the happiest I’ve ever been”). In others, they are incorporated into the premise: the pregnant-again mums do a maternity fashion segment, while the duo’s other long-running sketch, Internet Nails, sees the titular shonky North Circular beauty salon diversify into pregnancy treatments as the owners prepare for motherhood themselves.Still, says White: “We didn’t want it to be ‘the pregnant show’.” Demetriou agrees: “We just wanted it to not be a distraction.” In fact, series two mostly feels like business as usual for the duo, who tend to combine offbeat yet scalpel-sharp observational humour (see: their “special moments with special people” strand, a kaleidoscopic showcase of modern smugness) with an overfamiliar rapport and penchant for dressing up as off-putting men and eccentric old women that is very French and Saunders, a programme Demetriou grew up “absolutely living for”.White, who is 37 and grew up in Oxford, and Demetriou, 42 from north London, met through the latter’s younger brother, Jamie, who had been in a comedy troupe with White at Bristol university. The women quickly bonded, but it wasn’t until a producer friend urged them to combine forces that they formed a double act. Demetriou had been doing a “Greek character who was trying to sell pizza to nightclubs” on London’s alternative comedy circuit, while White was performing as an extremely nervous beauty pageant contestant. When they merged the two on stage, it was “one of the most electric nights of my life”, says Demetriou.Those two characters became the Sexy American Girls, two vaguely eastern European women trying and failing – captivatingly – to embody turn-of-the-millennium celebrity glitz, who in turn evolved into the Internet Nails duo. In the latter, Demetriou plays the imperious Donna, who reels off hypnotic word salad about their services – they offer to style your baby with a “rocker chic lifestyle mixed with denim highlights and zip attachments, cowboy essentials mixed with international rap monger” aesthetic – in grainy VHS footage while her cousin Nikki (White) vibrates with shyness beside her.View image in fullscreenNikki (Ellie White) and Donna (Natasia Demetriou) in the new series.Photograph: Jack Barnes/BBC/Nit TVThis misguided pursuit of glamour is an extraordinarily rich seam for the pair, who bring a similar energy to Sophie and Katia, the pop stardom-chasing pals they play in Jamie Demetriou’s superb Channel 4 comedy Stath Lets Flats. Demetriou puts this through-line down to the fact that “me and Jamie and Ellie all have a very similar sense of humour and similar reference points. We grew up in the 1990s, when the coolest things were all American: Coca-Cola, Mickey Mouse.” That this kind of Americana now seems so lame and dated adds another layer of comedy. But there is also a nostalgia: it’s an opportunity for Demetriou to channel the “stupid teenage girl” she once was; “constantly doing an American accent, practising conversations in the mirror with boyfriends you don’t have”. White agrees. “It reminds me of being a 14-year-old and taking yourself” – and your creative enterprises – “really seriously. And just being like: well, wearereally good.”That said, the pair are no longer living out any pop star fantasies. Highlights of series one included riffs on morose Adele-style ballads, jet-setting rappers and – most pointedly – musicians who infantilise themselves to a disturbing degree (see: the song about being a dummy-sucking “sexy baby”). This time around, however, there aren’t any musical parodies. “For some reason, we just couldn’t come up with an idea,” says Demetriou. The demise of the monoculture was partly to blame. Sketch shows of yore, such as French and Saunders, were able to pastiche things “the whole country’s watched”, but nowadays there are far fewer shared references. As such, White feels culturally “trapped in 2011. Can we do a Little Mix parody? It’s like, well, they broke up years ago.”Instead of specific spoofs, White and Demetriou often make fun of broader movements in the zeitgeist, especially forms of social media content, from “day in the life” videos to visual podcasts to OnlyFans-esque livestreams. That these sketches could slip undetected into someone’s Instagram feed also means a higher chance of viral success. “You do sort of want these things to look like something you’d come across online,” says White. “We want it to almost be like, is that real?”Yet parodying social media tropes comes with its own drawbacks. “I know everyone says this at every time in history, but it does feel like everything’s been done because the internet is so vast,” says Demetriou. The pair were planning a sketch about two fashion content creators from the deep south until White discovered the “real” version online. “There’s a woman who stands there with these absolutely baffling outfits, being like: ‘You gotta wear a long scarf! It falls to the floor and it makes you feel incredible about yourself.’ And I was like, what is this sketch actually adding?”When it comes to added comic value, however, White and Demetriou tend to deliver the goods. A case in point: their appearance on the last season of Last One Laughing UK, the reality gameshow in which comedians compete to see who can remain straight-faced the longest. The duo did a cameo as intimacy coordinators (sporting, incidentally, mum-coded Essex accents and short layered hairdos), who were sent on set to attempt to crack the remaining contestants.‘We were ahead of our time!’: Charly Clive and Ellen Robertson AKA sketch duo Britney on their new TV fame and word-of-mouth hitsRead moreDespite an incredible five minutes of half-improvised comedy, which included discreetly asking Romesh Ranganathan if he knew what “s-e-x” was, they didn’t make anyone laugh. “I’m not kidding when I say it was the most nervous I’ve ever been in my entire life,” admits White. “It was sort of like your worst nightmare.” Not only were they in a room of comedy legends (Bob Mortimer, David Mitchell), but the silence they encountered felt like it was going against “all normal forms of British society”, says Demetriou. Usually we “nod politely and go ‘Brilliant!’” in response to even lacklustre attempts at humour. Here, “Not even a smile!”Speaking of politeness, we have now reached the end of the interview and those babies haven’t made a peep. “I’m slightly worried. He’s been sleeping for a really long time,” says White, bemusedly. At least we’ve been able to talk freely about their return to TV sketch comedy. It is, after all, a real treat to have White and Demetriou – and all the many mums they play – back on our screens again at last.Ellie & Natasia starts on 21 October on BBC Two and BBC iPlayerExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV comedyComedyinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I drunkenly sing Wonderwall off-key and awfully’: Rebecca Ferguson’s honest playlist | Music | The Guardian
description: The singer-songwriter gets a lift from U2 and likes to reminisce to Bette Midler, but which cheesy Euro banger does she secretly like?
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: The singer-songwriter gets a lift from U2 and likes to reminisce to Bette Midler, but which cheesy Euro banger does she secretly like?
Content: Rebecca Ferguson … ‘Hearing I Will Always Love You made me think: This is what I’m going to do’Photograph: -View image in fullscreenRebecca Ferguson … ‘Hearing I Will Always Love You made me think: This is what I’m going to do’Photograph: -Honest playlistMusic‘I drunkenly sing Wonderwall off-key and awfully’: Rebecca Ferguson’s honest playlistThe singer-songwriter gets a lift from U2 and likes to reminisce to Bette Midler, but which cheesy Euro banger does she secretly like?Rich PelleySun 18 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first song I fell in love withWhen I was five or six, my mum wouldn’t let me listen to anything other than Christian gospel. Her friend Jane felt sorry for me and brought me a cassette with Whitney Houston on one side and Cher on the other. My ears couldn’t believe what they were hearing. I Will Always Love You made me think: This is what I’m going to do.The first single I boughtSo Young by the Corrs, from Sainsbury’s in Walton Village in Liverpool. I couldn’t really afford music as a kid, so buying a record was a big deal. I’d heard the Corrs on the radio, liked their voices and thought: I’m buying this.The song that is my karaoke go-toI have a habit of singing Wonderwall by Oasis really badly. It’s like a party trick: I drunkenly sing it completely off-key and awful, but impassioned. I have no idea why.The song I inexplicably know every lyric toI was obsessed with the film Beaches as a kid. Me and my best friend would watch it over and over and I’d pretend I was CC Bloom. The Glory of Love by Bette Midler, Wind Beneath My Wings – I know the lyrics to all of them. I’m getting nostalgic just thinking about it.The best song to play at a partyI like to do a bit of DJing after a few drinks, and Mundian to Bach Ke by Panjabi MC always goes down well, but you’ve got to drop it late in the party. If you play it too early, people aren’t ready.The song I can no longer listen toWhen I was a teenager, I was feeling particularly low, and I feel like that Everybody Hurts by REM saved me that day. It was this gentle reminder: this is life, everybody hurts, get up and get on with it.The song I secretly like, but tell everyone I hateI wouldn’t put Blue (Da Ba Dee) by Eiffel 65 on at one of my parties, but I might play it while I’m doing the dishes.The best song to have sex toI imagine Drunk in Love by Beyoncé would probably work!The song that changed my lifeA Change Is Gonna Come by Sam Cooke, which I sang at my first X Factor audition. I’d prepared three songs and Simon Cowell stopped me from singing the first two. A Change Is Gonna Come made more sense for me emotionally anyway. I thought about myself and members of my family I’d seen struggling and almost went into myself while I sang it.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe song that gets me up in the morningBlasting a bit of Beautiful Day by U2 always helps when you’re feeling a bit crappy or tired after a late night with the kids.The song that makes me cryHope There’s Someone by Antony and the Johnsons. It’s just so sad. The way it’s delivered, you can really hear the pain. It gets me every time.The song I want played at my funeralI’d want something fun that reminded friends and family of good times. I’ve been listening to Movin’ to the Sun by Hugel, Imael Angel and Ultra Naté lately. I’d have that, except – God, it’s morbid thinking about your funeral, isn’t it?Rebecca Ferguson tours The Hits at Christmas, 2 to 12 December.Explore more on these topicsMusicHonest playlistThe X FactorPop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Dance Is Not for Us review – desire and defiance as one revolutionary mover sweats it all out | Dance | The Guardian
description: Omar Rajeh performs out of frustration, resistance and a need to connect in this stream-of-consciousness solo at Dance Umbrella festival
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: Omar Rajeh performs out of frustration, resistance and a need to connect in this stream-of-consciousness solo at Dance Umbrella festival
Content: ‘He dances like it’s a necessary thing to do’ … Omar Rajeh in Dance Is Not for Us at the Barbican.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianView image in fullscreen‘He dances like it’s a necessary thing to do’ … Omar Rajeh in Dance Is Not for Us at the Barbican.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianDanceReviewDance Is Not for Us review – desire and defiance as one revolutionary mover sweats it all outBarbican, LondonOmar Rajeh performs out of frustration, resistance and a need to connect in this stream-of-consciousness solo at Dance Umbrella festivalLyndsey WinshipSun 18 Oct 2026 13.45 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 13.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn August 2019, Omar Rajeh sat in his bedroom, listening to the sound of pounding percussion with his world in crisis. In the midst of political instability, Citerne Beirut, a theatre and cultural centre Rajeh had founded in his nativeLebanon, was forced to close, dismantled by order of the local government, who planned to build an incinerator on the site.View image in fullscreenHeartfelt … Omar Rajeh in Dance Is Not for Us.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianRajeh tells us that as a teenager, coming of age at the end of the Lebanese civil war, dance had always seemed like the most revolutionary thing he could do. Now here he is, more than three decades later, still dancing – out of frustration, defiance, resistance and a desire to connect. As the percussive score gains momentum, Rajeh’s busy body builds up a sweat. In this danced stream of consciousness, Rajeh is not always an especially elegant mover, but he dances like it’s a necessary thing to do.Part of this year’sDance Umbrella festival, Dance Is Not for Us is a solo that appears at times like an explosion of physical instinct, but it is mostly calm, considered musings on the nature of choreography, with all its workings exposed. Rajeh sits and taps at a keyboard as his thoughts appear on screen, all the inspirations, decisions, vacillations and U-turns that go into creating a performance.He tells us of the first “choreographies” he ever saw: a fight between two men, people gathering in the streets to protest, bodies making choices and organising themselves in space – which is what choreography is, after all. The creative and the political are one to Rajeh, who is now based in Lyon, a major loss to Lebanon’s creative life. This piece is an insight into a choreographer’s mind, and it’s a heartfelt appeal to gather, to witness, to share our pain and loss – to look and to listen.Dance Umbrella festivalis at venues across London and online until 27 OctoberExplore more on these topicsDanceBarbicanLebanonTheatreFestivalsProtestreviewsShareReuse this content

title: RLPO/Hickox review – a made-to-measure clarinet collaboration two decades in the pipeline | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Mark Simpson delivers gauzy luminosity and punchy tone in Gavin Higgins’s exquisite new work, conducted with spellbinding pacing by rising star Adam Hickox alongside spirited accounts of Britten and Stravinsky
Author: Flora Willson
Headline: Mark Simpson delivers gauzy luminosity and punchy tone in Gavin Higgins’s exquisite new work, conducted with spellbinding pacing by rising star Adam Hickox alongside spirited accounts of Britten and Stravinsky
Content: A promise kept … Gavin Higgins and Mark Simpson on stage with the Royal Liverpool Philharmonic Orchestra.Photograph: Gareth JonesView image in fullscreenA promise kept … Gavin Higgins and Mark Simpson on stage with the Royal Liverpool Philharmonic Orchestra.Photograph: Gareth JonesClassical musicReviewRLPO/Hickox review – a made-to-measure clarinet collaboration two decades in the pipelinePhilharmonic Hall, LiverpoolMark Simpson delivers gauzy luminosity and punchy tone in Gavin Higgins’s exquisite new work, conducted with spellbinding pacing by rising star Adam Hickox alongside spirited accounts of Britten and StravinskyFlora WillsonSun 18 Oct 2026 13.07 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 18.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwenty years ago, a teenager calledMark Simpsonwon both the BBC Young Musician of the Year and BBC Proms/Guardian Young Composer of the Year; he commissioned a short piece for clarinet fromGavin Higgins, another young composer. It was Higgins’s first paid work and he promised to thank Simpson by writing him a clarinet concerto. Fast forward two decades: both men have forged award-studded careers, Simpson continues to combine composition and performance – and Higgins has finally delivered that concerto.View image in fullscreen‘Striking jagged poses like a cubist figure’ … Adam Hickox conducting the Royal Liverpool Philharmonic Orchestra.Photograph: Gareth JonesMarking the end of Simpson’s tenure as the Royal Liverpool Philharmonic Orchestra’s artist in residence, its premiere featured the kind of intense splashes of musical colour that leave an afterimage. Climaxes came in slow-burn waves and paroxysms of frenetic activity. Simpson’s solo line – sometimes keening, expressive vocalise; sometimes a wild assemblage of rapid blips and riffs – weaved through the shifting orchestral textures, here haloed by muted brass, there soaring over a low hum of gong and double bass. In one exquisite passage, Simpson’s clarinet was a fine, luminous gauze. Elsewhere he punched through the vast orchestral surge through sheer focus of tone. Certain passages seemed haunted byJohn Adamsat his most maximalist, others by Aaron Copland’s celebrated clarinet concerto. But Simpson inhabited the score as a work made to measure, the physicality of this virtuoso performance unmistakable as soloist and orchestra hurtled ecstatically to its close.The rest of the programme was just as driven, from the vicious timpani strokes that opened Britten’s Suite on English Folk Tunes to the quasi-mechanical power of Stravinsky’sRite of Spring. ConductorAdam Hickoxdrew out the dark undertone of Britten’s late suite, the string articulation always on the nose, the woodwind solos served with an acid bite. After the interval, the Rite was thrillingly direct in the Philharmonic Hall’s bright acoustic. The woodwind solos of the opening were solid rather than atmospheric but Hickox’s tightly controlled pacing cast its own spell: striking jagged poses like a cubist figure, he revelled in the work’s play of slackness and momentum. The orchestra was on fine form – and Hickox lived up to his reputation as a major rising star.The concert will bebroadcast on BBC Radio 3on 27 OctoberExplore more on these topicsClassical musicMark SimpsonRoyal Liverpool Philharmonic OrchestrareviewsShareReuse this content

title: 4.48 Psychosis review – a dazzling, harrowing opera worthy of Sarah Kane’s furious writing  | Opera | The Guardian
description: Six fearless singers and the Chroma Ensemble, conducted with arresting immediacy by Naomi Woo, rise to the challenge of the brutal musical onslaughts and anarchic orchestrations of Philip Venables’ raw, imaginative score
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: Six fearless singers and the Chroma Ensemble, conducted with arresting immediacy by Naomi Woo, rise to the challenge of the brutal musical onslaughts and anarchic orchestrations of Philip Venables’ raw, imaginative score
Content: In-yer-face … Lauren Young, Sophia Burgos, Jacquelyn Stucker and Hannah Edmunds in 4.48 Psychosis at Linbury theatre.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianView image in fullscreenIn-yer-face … Lauren Young, Sophia Burgos, Jacquelyn Stucker and Hannah Edmunds in 4.48 Psychosis at Linbury theatre.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianOperaReview4.48 Psychosis review – a dazzling, harrowing opera worthy of Sarah Kane’s furious writingLinbury theatre, LondonSix fearless singers and the Chroma Ensemble, conducted with arresting immediacy by Naomi Woo, rise to the challenge of the brutal musical onslaughts and anarchic orchestrations of Philip Venables’ raw, imaginative scoreClive PagetSun 18 Oct 2026 11.03 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 11.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSarah Kanerevolutionised British theatre with five provocative plays written between 1995 and 1999. Her final work, 4.48 Psychosis, was her most personal, confronting the clinical depression she struggled with for years. The play was first performed posthumously in 2000, after she died by suicide in 1999.The Royal Opera and Guildhall School of Music and Drama commissioned Philip Venables to adapt the play as an opera, whichdebuted in 2016. The composer, also known for a certain “in-yer-face” approach, set Kane’s original text almost entirely, realising its 24 disjointed sections in a raw, imaginative score teeming with minimalist licks, prickly synth-pop and consoling nods to the baroque. The libretto shifts between poetic abstraction and scathing exchanges between a patient and a psychologist. An ensemble of six female singers navigates themes of depression, isolation and the agonising choices surrounding medication.View image in fullscreenOne fractured personality … Sophia Burgos, Veena Akama-Makia, Hannah Edmunds and Jacquelyn Stucker in 4.48 Psychosis.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianVenables’ adaptation successfully leverages the unique capabilities of music, tapping into Kane’s non-linear prosody and use of verbal repetition. His dazzling score overlaps vocal lines, introducing a structural complexity that traditional theatre cannot easily replicate. The sprawling narrative is anchored by a single spoken voice over a loudspeaker, evoking Kane’s authorial presence.‘It put me in a fever dream’: Philip Venables on turning Sarah Kane’s 4.48 Psychosis into a shocking operaRead moreWhere matters occasionally falter is in the music’s tendency to prescribe the emotional temperature by tying it to the six-part polyphonic chorus. Tightly controlled, it tethers the freedom of interpretation inherent in Kane’s furious text. Although Venables retains the spoken voice in places, and the opera is an extremely harrowing experience, it tempers the play’s potential to shock.Ted Huffman’s 10-year-old production is successfully revived here with a subtly revised ending. Astute and economical direction ensures the action remains fluid yet focused within Hannah Clark’s institutional white box set. DM Wood’s stark lighting is laser-focused while the amplified sound design lends a kick up the backside to Venable’s most brutal musical onslaughts.London-based collectiveChromaforms the 14-piece chamber orchestra perched above the action. The anarchic orchestrations, which feature a trio of saxophones, piano synthesiser and accordion, hiss with a fierce violence contrasting with moments of hushed beauty and the unsettling sounds of distant waiting-room muzak. Projected text is paired with duelling percussion instruments (including bass drums, carpenter’s saw and shop-counter bell) to punctuate the patient-doctor dialogues bringing brief moments of levity. Catherine Ring and Delia Stevens attack their instruments with sticks and hands, dramatic intent writ large on their faces.View image in fullscreenFluid yet focused … 4.48 Psychosis.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianConductor Naomi Woo brings an arresting immediacy to Venables’ complex score while the six fearless singers – Jacquelyn Stucker, Hannah Edmunds, Sophia Burgos, Veena Akama-Makia, Lauren Young and Marta Fontanals-Simmons – perform with preternatural accuracy. Costumed identically, Huffman suggests – as Kane does – that they may all be fragments of the one fractured personality. Nevertheless, Stucker stands out as the deeply troubled protagonist in a searingly honest and frequently heart-rending performance.AtLinbury theatre, London, until 25 OctoberIn the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsOperaClassical musicSarah KaneRoyal Opera HouseTheatrePhilip VenablesMental healthreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Ariadne/Dido and Aeneas review – English Touring Opera conjures two strikingly different mythological worlds | Opera | The Guardian
description: Jessica Cale’s soprano is diamond-bright in Elena Langer and Glyn Maxwell’s captivating monologue, while Rebecca Meltzer creates a compelling schoolyard staging of Purcell
Author: Erica Jeal
Headline: Jessica Cale’s soprano is diamond-bright in Elena Langer and Glyn Maxwell’s captivating monologue, while Rebecca Meltzer creates a compelling schoolyard staging of Purcell
Content: Powerful … Jessica Cale in Ariadne.Photograph: Richard Hubert SmithView image in fullscreenPowerful … Jessica Cale in Ariadne.Photograph: Richard Hubert SmithOperaReviewAriadne/Dido and Aeneas review – English Touring Opera conjures two strikingly different mythological worldsHackney Empire, LondonJessica Cale’s soprano is diamond-bright in Elena Langer and Glyn Maxwell’s captivating monologue, while Rebecca Meltzer creates a compelling schoolyard staging of PurcellErica JealSun 18 Oct 2026 08.43 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 10.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEnglish Touring Opera’s autumn season has a mythological theme – which, in practice, means operas about women getting left behind. Touring alongsideGluck’s Orpheus and Eurydiceis this compact double bill, pairing Dido and Aeneas withElena Langer’s Ariadne, a 20-minute scene for soprano setting words by Glyn Maxwell, which waspremiered by Almeida Operain 2002.Langer’s mini-opera is essentially a monologue, sung persuasively here by Jessica Cale, her powerful soprano diamond-bright. Anna Morrissey’s production, though, has six people on stage: abandonment feels like something active as well as passive. It begins with Theseus leaving, disentangling himself from both the sleeping Ariadne and the red thread that links them, spooling from a heap on the floor – it’s as if he got back from the labyrinth the night before. When Ariadne wakes he’s still there, pacing in the shadows or turning her bed on its rotating platform.View image in fullscreenCatwalk Coraline … Lydia Shariff and Isabelle Atkinson with members of the ensemble in Dido and Aeneas.Photograph: Richard Hubert SmithLanger writes, captivatingly, for four instruments: oboe, violin, viola and cello, playing without a conductor. They combine in high sonorities to reinforce the voice in a way that suggests the play of light on waves. As for Ariadne, she stands on that bed gazing out to sea as Joseph Hornsby’s lighting emulates the sun reflecting off water. The ending, in which Ariadne appears to sew the red thread through her skin, looked fiddly and took a bit too much of Cale’s concentration, even if the concept was good.We’re in a strikingly different world for Rebecca Meltzer’s staging of Dido and Aeneas. While Alex Berry’s set of black rocks and huge frosted glass panels could work for any operatic myth, Meltzer gives the action a playground dynamic (Purcell’s opera was performed early on by the pupils of a girls’ school). Everyone but Dido is in a stylised mishmash of charcoal blazers and pleated skirts, including the men; the look is somewhere between form room and a Thom Browne catwalk show. Lydia Shariff’s Sorceress has the body language of a year eight queen bee, while Isabelle Atkinson’s Belinda, Dido’s frenemy, puts on tiny sunglasses, reminiscent of Coraline’s black-button eyes, to become one of the witches. Dido is gaslit and bullied into her downfall, with the whole chorus, perhaps even Michael Lafferty’s velvet-voiced Aeneas, being complicit.In the pit, Alex Robinson directs the orchestra from the harpsichord with some imaginative touches that are slightly outweighed by steady tempos. Meltzer provides strong movement and it’s a compelling staging – but, despite Samantha Price’s expressive singing in the title role, something is missing. With Dido a victim from the start, there is little sense of a queen – and, by extension, her realm – being brought low by the collision between human passion and the whim of the gods. And that, surely, is the stuff myth is made of.AtBuxton Opera Houseon 24 October, thentouringuntil 21 NovemberExplore more on these topicsOperaClassical musicEnglish Touring OperareviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘A key artist in her own right’: wallpaper and fabrics designer emerges from William Morris’s shadow | Design | The Guardian
description: Creativity and influence of Morris & Co designer Kate Faulkner to be detailed in Cambridge exhibition
Author: Donna Ferguson
Headline: Creativity and influence of Morris & Co designer Kate Faulkner to be detailed in Cambridge exhibition
Content: A drawing of Artemis for a design embroidered by Faulkner for William Morris’s home, Red House.Photograph: Bridgeman ImagesView image in fullscreenA drawing of Artemis for a design embroidered by Faulkner for William Morris’s home, Red House.Photograph: Bridgeman ImagesDesign‘A key artist in her own right’: wallpaper and fabrics designer emerges from William Morris’s shadowCreativity and influence of Morris & Co designer Kate Faulkner to be detailed in Cambridge exhibitionDonna FergusonSun 18 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 08.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor more than a century, she has been little more than a footnote in William Morris’s story, her work mistaken for his, her contribution to British decorative art largely overlooked.Yet, in her lifetime, Kate Faulkner was a pioneer: the first person after Morris to design wallpapers and fabrics for Morris & Co, and one of only four designers he ever trusted to do so. Several of the patterns she designed under her name for the company in the 1870s and 1880s are still sold today.Now,an exhibitionat the Fitzwilliam Museum in Cambridge is seeking to restore Faulkner to her rightful place in art history.A Call to Art: William Morris and the pre-Raphaelites is the first exhibition to celebrate Faulkner and her work as a designer, maker and workshop supervisor at Morris & Co.It will put on public display, for the first time, a monumental 6.3 metre-wide oak and silvered-gesso altarpiece she was commissioned to make for Morris & Co in 1886, alongside her textile designs and wallpaper patterns which helped to make William Morris a household name.View image in fullscreenHighlights include Faulkner’s tile depicting Penelope, made around 1865.Photograph: Michael Jones/The Fitzwilliam Museum, Image LibraryHighlights include her tile depicting Penelope, the heroine of Greek mythology, which is based on a design by Edward Burne-Jones, and some of her painted ceramics, including decorative plates that were sold in the Morris & Co shop.“Kate Faulkner was not simply working in William Morris’s shadow – she was a key artist in her own right,” said Karen Livingstone, senior curatorial adviser to the exhibition, which opens on 23 October. “Her skill and creative contribution were fundamental to Morris & Co, and this exhibition and its new research reveal just how central her artistic voice was to the commercial success of William Morris.”Her1879 Mallow wallpaper designisstill sold by Morris & Co.Other wallpaper manufacturers bought her designs and she earned an international reputation for her work, but her legacy has been overshadowed by Morris’s since she died in 1898.Livingstone is appealing for help from the public to trace the descendants of Faulkner’s sister, Lucy Orrinsmith, whose granddaughter, Lesley Janet Hitch (nee Simmons), died in 1995. She hopes this will uncover a photograph or portrait of Faulkner, as none is known to exist. “I’ve tried really hard to trace her family and to find an image of her, and I have drawn a blank at every turn,” said Livingstone, the author of Women Pioneers of the Arts and Crafts Movement. “I would love to know where her family are so her legacy could be more expanded and revealed.”View image in fullscreenFaulkner would have been part of Morris’s inner circle at Red House, his Arts and Crafts villa in Bexleyheath.Photograph: Bildarchiv Monheim GmbH/AlamyThe overall aim of the exhibition, which runs until 3 May 2027, is to re-examine Morris and his inner circle – including the artists and designers Edward Burne-Jones, Dante Gabriel Rossetti, Elizabeth Siddal and May Morris, the daughter of William and his wife, Jane.One of Morris & Co’s most successful areas of production was embroidery, which wasmanaged by Jane Morrisand her sister, Elizabeth Burden, before May took over in 1885.Faulkner embroidered figurative panels to William Morris’s designs and helped with the design and production of carpets, as well as cutting woodblocks for engravings and painting tiles and designing patterns for textiles and wallpapers.New research by Livingstone has revealed that a design by Morris depicting the Greek goddess Artemis was embroidered by Faulkner for Red House, Morris’s Arts and Crafts villa in Bexleyheath, south-eastLondon, where the idea for Morris & Co was born in 1861.View image in fullscreenCarnation, Faulkner’s first pattern for Morris & Co to be registered under her name.Photograph: Paul Tucker/Pauul TuckerThe Artemis embroidery places Faulkner at Red House at the very moment when Morris and his circle were inspired to create their own interiors company and start making products for sale. “It’s reinstating her in a story which is usually told about the men in that circle … It was during the process of making these embroideries and furnishing Red House that they decided to set up Morris & Co,” Livingstone said.Faulkner, who was a socialist like Morris, would visit the house regularly and spend weekends there. “They [the women in Morris’s circle] used to sit around and embroider together,” Livingstone added.She thinks it is highly likely that Faulkner, whose brother Charles was one of Morris’s co-founders, participated in the discussions about Morris & Co that were happening in Red House at that time. “She was there – the women were all there. They can’t possibly not have been part of the conversation.”Faulkner’s role in making the Artemis embroidery – one of a series of 12 panels planned for the Red House dining room – was previously unknown. While the embroidery itself is now lost, a drawing of the embroidery design will be on display within the exhibition, along with three surviving panels embroidered by Burden.By 1862, Faulkner and her sister were producing embroideries for the firm to sell. But it would take another 13 years for one of her patterns for Morris & Co, Carnation, to be registered under her name in 1875.“I suspect there’s lots more out there that just hasn’t been found or identified,” Livingstone said. “For sure, there’s work she created that is still being attributed to Morris.”Explore more on these topicsDesignWilliam MorrisLondonfeaturesShareReuse this content
