title: ‘How do we welcome the stranger, with humanity or anger?’ The forgotten Germans who found refuge in Ireland | Theatre | The Guardian
description: A new play revisits the story of Ireland’s 18th-century German refugees, whose experience of prejudice and exclusion resonates with today’s debates over immigration
Author: John Kampfner
Headline: A new play revisits the story of Ireland’s 18th-century German refugees, whose experience of prejudice and exclusion resonates with today’s debates over immigration
Content: Sticking together … the cast of Refuge at Staatstheater Mainz, Germany.Photograph: Andreas EtterView image in fullscreenSticking together … the cast of Refuge at Staatstheater Mainz, Germany.Photograph: Andreas EtterTheatre‘How do we welcome the stranger, with humanity or anger?’ The forgotten Germans who found refuge in IrelandA new play revisits the story of Ireland’s 18th-century German refugees, whose experience of prejudice and exclusion resonates with today’s debates over immigrationJohn KampfnerSun 18 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the early 18th century, a few thousand Germans fled religious persecution and near starvation in their homeland and ended up in remote rural Irish villages. The Irish Palatines, as they were known, were poor, conservative homesteaders who couldn’t speak the language and were the object of suspicion and violence – precursors to the displaced Syrians or Afghans of the past decade.Their story is told in Refuge, a co-production between Staatstheater Mainz and the Irish company Fishamble. Part love story, part social commentary, it is performed by a mixed cast, mainly in English but with some German interludes.It focuses on a German couple, Hannah and Peter, who have lost one of their two sons through illness and are trying to make a go of it on farmland on the edge of a small town in Limerick. Their Protestantism and their reluctance to mix with the Irish add to a sense of peril.Peter is driven by another motive. He owes his plot of land to the manor’s (invisible) English squire, Thomas Southwell. The 1st Baron Southwell of Castle Matrix is keen to dilute the locals’ Catholicism and so provides the Germans with cheap rent in return for their obedience. Feudal landlord and dependent tenant find common cause.View image in fullscreenTrouble ensues … (from left) Mary Murray, Sabah Qalo, Hannah von Peinen and Holger Kraft.Photograph: Andreas EtterMore than 100 German families settled on Southwell’s lands, marrying almost exclusively among their own. Over a 40-year period, only seven marriages are recorded as taking place with someone outside the community. The “pure” German population was enlarged by 500 children.Hannah doesn’t think like the rest of them. She begs her husband to extend an olive branch to the locals, but he refuses. She defiantly does so, seeking friendship, and possibly romance, with a local farmer she haltingly calls MrIreland. Trouble ensues.The playwright, Deirdre Kinahan, says she seized the topic with alacrity: “Immigration – and our response to it – is one of the most crucial, yet divisive, issues of our age. How do we welcome the stranger, with humanity or anger?” She adds she knew instinctively that the forgotten story of the Palatines would speak to Ireland and Europe’s present predicament. This led her to include the tale of a contemporary young Afghan boy in the narrative.The production has played at the DublinTheatrefestival and concludes in Mainz, capital of the present-day Land of Rhineland-Palatinate, and the territory from which most of the original settlers came. Between the two destinations, it made a diversion to Berlin, at the behest of the Irish ambassador, Maeve Collins. “This story of a relatively unknown episode in Ireland’s history with Germany resonates with the experiences of contemporary audiences,” she says.It all began with an English queen. Early in 1709, hopes for a better life were raised when a “Golden Book” began circulating among the Palatinate’s population, bearing a picture of Queen Anne on the cover, promising a prosperous and easy life in America. The idea was to encourage hearty white Protestants to settle in the American territories without unduly depleting the population of England.This was hugely attractive to the Palatines, who had seen their land ravaged by a series of wars conducted by the expansionist zeal of France’s King Louis XIV.View image in fullscreen‘Our response to immigration is one of the most crucial issues of our age’ … (from left) Mary Murray, Sabah Qalo and Hannah von Peinen in Refuge.Photograph: Andreas EtterA group of these Germans petitioned the English queen, accepting her plan. But instead of an anticipated 500, more than 13,000 refugees set sail along the River Rhine to Rotterdam, before making the crossing on overcrowded small boats. One in five died on the precarious journey. The rest arrived destitute, and were housed in tents in and around London.Such were their numbers that the initially warm reception soon cooled. Wherever they went these Germans were subjected to suspicion, harassment and violence. By the end of November 1709, the first moves were made to deport them.The English government settled on other solutions. A certain number were allowed to go on to America. A smaller contingent of about 3,600 was relocated to underpopulated Ireland, to boost the Protestant stock.It would take several generations before the Palatines began to integrate. Some converted to Catholicism through intermarriage and assimilation, though the majority remained Protestant (either Methodists or members of the Church of Ireland).One of the best-known families was the Switzers, whose chain of department stores in Dublin, Cork, Limerick and Galway supplied luxury goods for a century and a half before the high-street institution was taken over and renamed.Like the Huguenots – who had fled to England, Holland and Germany two decades earlier, after Louis’s revocation of the Edict of Nantes – the Palatines are now hard to differentiate from the original population.For the play’s cast and crew, the “re-discovery” has been a moving experience. Holger Kraft, who plays gruff Peter, says he came to regard the piece less as Irish-German, more as pan-European, and with a universal message that “we all have to stick together”.Refuge is on atStaatstheater Mainz20 and 21 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreEuropeMigrationRefugeesSocial historyIrelandfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Shakespeare was a Black woman’: the playwright’s under-recognized connection to Black culture | Exhibitions | The Guardian
description: A new Washington DC exhibition examines how Toni Morrison, Maya Angelou and more used the Bard’s work to help tell their own stories
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A new Washington DC exhibition examines how Toni Morrison, Maya Angelou and more used the Bard’s work to help tell their own stories
Content: Kennedi Carter, Meech, 2020. Archival pigment print. On display as part of To Hear Her Speak: Black Women and Shakespeare.Photograph: Kennedi Carter/Courtesy of ROSEGALLERYView image in fullscreenKennedi Carter, Meech, 2020. Archival pigment print. On display as part of To Hear Her Speak: Black Women and Shakespeare.Photograph: Kennedi Carter/Courtesy of ROSEGALLERYExhibitions‘Shakespeare was a Black woman’: the playwright’s under-recognized connection to Black cultureA new Washington DC exhibition examines how Toni Morrison, Maya Angelou and more used the Bard’s work to help tell their own storiesKaitlyn McNabSun 18 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“William Shakespeare was a black woman.” In 1985,Maya Angelouspoke these words as part of a keynotespeechat a convention in Cedar Rapids, Iowa.There, she spoke of the role poetry played in her transition from muteness as a child and how she fantasized herself triumphantly delivering Portia’s speech fromWilliam Shakespeare’s The Merchant of Venice in front of her entire community at church. Though she never got the chance to perform that rendition, Angelou acknowledged her desire to deliver that rendition as part of a lifelong kinship with Shakespeare, a connection she continued to seek out throughout her life whenever she needed heartening or solace. In her eyes, Shakespeare wrote his emotionally desolateSonnet 29“for” her; how else could he have so aptly described the harsh realities of the Black feminine condition?“Of course he wrote it for me,” Angelou declared. “Of course, he was a Black woman. I understand that. Nobody else understands it, but I know thatWilliam Shakespearewas a Black woman.”Angelou would likely be proud to know thatmanyother Black women – including Dr Patricia Akhimie, the director of the Folger Institute at the Folger Shakespeare Library inWashington DC– do understand. The Bard may not have been a Black woman in the literal sense, but his resonance and centuries-long rapport with Black culture is one area of study that Akhimie has spent her career examining.View image in fullscreenInstallation view of To Hear Her Speak: Black Women and Shakespeare.Photograph: Tim Tiebout. Courtesy of Folger Shakespeare LibraryIn the Folger’s newest exhibitionTo Hear Her Speak: Black Women and Shakespeare, curated by Akhimie, more than 400 years of Black women’s engagement with Shakespeare is collectively explored for the first time, illuminating the ways in which Black women have claimed and reimagined the works of Shakespeare through scholarship and craft. “It’s a performance [and theater] history but it’s also an intellectual history about Black women as writers and artists pulling from Shakespeare to do new and amazing things,” said Akhimie, speaking in a warm conversation in early October.The history of Black women’s connection to Shakespeare is long, but not necessarily storied – To Hear Her Speak reveals just how far back that history goes and under how many layers it’s hidden. There’s likely no better place to begin such an investigation than at the Folger, home of the world’s largest Shakespeare collection.The exhibit, which is the product of more than two years of research, is both immersive and interactive. It contains nearly 100 items including photographs, playbills, books, diaries, illustrations and costumes; there are video displays of notable Black actresses throughout history performing Shakespeare; and within a set replica of playwright Lorraine Hansberry’s living room (based on a 1959Voguephoto spread of the writer in her New York City apartment), visitors can sit on the couch and watch a television set screening clips of Hansberry and other Black women discussing Shakespeare, or browse through the “library” of that same living room set, where there are shelves of books that serve as a mini-archive of writing related to Shakespeare and Black women’s artistic and intellectual endeavors.View image in fullscreenDr Patricia Akhimie.Photograph: Brittany Diliberto/Shoot AuthenticTo Hear Her Speakalso invites visitors to become participants through other immersive aspects such as writing activities throughout, itsexhibit-themed playlist(hitting shuffle will play tracks from Aretha Franklin, Lauryn Hill, Billie Holliday, SZA and more), and its audioguide narrated by Bridgerton star, Shakespearean actor and exhibition chairAdjoa Andoh. The exhibition was designed to be a three-dimensional, multi-sensory experience that can appeal to all ages and its full-color exhibit catalog, created by the To Hear Her Speak research team, was intentionally made for both print and digital consumption for wide accessibility.“It’s not about standing back and looking at something behind glass, but rather about what happens when inspiration strikes, and thenyoubecome the maker and the thinker and the dreamer,” said Akhimie.To Hear Her Speak also builds on new research showing that Black women were very much a presence in Shakespeare’s world while also illustrating how they were represented (and misrepresented) by storytellers of the era, across different mediums. Part of Akhimie’s aim was to challenge that erasure. “[The exhibition’s story] starts with debunking a longstanding myth, which is that the London where [Shakespeare] lived and wrote his plays and where they were first performed was not a diverse place, when it really was,” Akhimie said.View image in fullscreenLeontyne Price as Cleopatra in a 1966 publicity photograph for Antony and Cleopatra composed by Samuel Barber with libretto by Franco Zeffirelli.Photograph: Louis Melançon/Courtesy of Metropolitan Opera ArchiveAlong with her research team, Akhimie quickly discovered that artefacts and records of Black women’s engagement with Shakespeare disappeared around the 18th and 19th centuries. “The obvious reason for that is because that is the time period that coincides with the height of the transatlantic slave trade, when Black women’s experiences are not being documented and preserved, and their humanity is being obscured,” said Akhimie. This time period is arguably one of the most crucial for the exhibition’s narrative, as the 18th and 19th centuries are when the transatlantic slave trade is concurrent with Shakespeare’s rise as an international figure representative of British culture and culture at large.Through objects sourced from within the Folger’s collection and beyond, Akhimie and her research team managed to “tell a story about Shakespeare, sugar, and slavery”, filling the silences of history with materials such as a copy of Shakespeare’s First Folio purchased by a slave-owning British family, a record of the enslaved people forced to work on that family’s sugar plantation, a pair of sugar tongs and a tea caddy both emblazoned with Shakespeare’s bust, and a copybook created by Phillis Wheatley, the formerly enslaved first Black American poet.View image in fullscreenEngraving of Phillis Wheatley from frontispiece of Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral, 1773.Photograph: Scipio Moorhead/Library of CongressTo Hear Her Speak rallies the works of some of the most influential Black female luminaries in history in addition to Wheatley, Hansberry and Angelou, likeToni Morrison’s handwritten notes on her Shakespearean play Desdemona. The exhibition, which is named after Shakespeare’s Sonnet 130 (long speculated to be written about a Black woman by historians and literary scholars), amplifies the voices of prominent Black women who have wielded and wrought the words of Shakespeare in their careers to assert their own humanity, creativity and individual power.Akhimie considers Black women’s consistent return to Shakespeare strategic, describing him as “a reliable partner” for Black female artists of any era to turn to for “inspiration and allyship”; as Angelou noted in her 1985 speech, Shakespeare is one of the most effective conduits for Black female self-expression.“Shakespeare has cultural currency. Shakespeare is a voice that people listen to,” said Akhimie. “Time and again, over centuries, Black women who are themselves artists, thinkers, or educators know that linking yourself to Shakespeare, pulling Shakespeare in, referencing Shakespeare is a way to grab a hold of listeners in a world in which, often, your voice is not heard and is systematically marginalized. Shakespeare has power, and that has been true for all of [the] 400-year period that the exhibition covers.”“[To Hear Her Speak] is not just a chance to share Black women’s voices,” she continues. “It’s also a chance to call people in and say: what can Shakespeare do for you? What will you do with this material to make new work, new ideas, tell new stories, and tell your story?”To Hear Her Speak: Black Women and Shakespeareis on view at Folger Shakespeare Library in Washington DC, until 2 May 2027Explore more on these topicsExhibitionsArtTheatreUS theaterWilliam ShakespeareMaya AngelouToni MorrisonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Readers reply: why is a child saying ‘Na-na, na-na-na!’ so annoying? | Life and style | The Guardian
description: The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions considers a universal juvenile put-down
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions considers a universal juvenile put-down
Content: “Nyah-nyah!”Photograph: Posed by model; Peter Cade/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen“Nyah-nyah!”Photograph: Posed by model; Peter Cade/Getty ImagesNotes and queriesLife and styleReaders reply: why is a child saying ‘Na-na, na-na-na!’ so annoying?The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions considers a universal juvenile put-downThis week’s question:will there ever again be a band as big as the Beatles or the Stones?Sun 18 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhy is a child going “Na-na, na-na-na!” annoying the world over? I read recently that kids do a version of this in every culture and country.Fred Corbett, LondonSend new questions tonq@theguardian.com.Readers replyMaybe it’s just that an annoying child is involved?DorkaliciousIt means: “See, I was right,” or “Gotcha,” or “Told you so!” It’s not annoying. It shows a child feels empowered, and there’s nothing wrong with that.LorLalaI remember, some years ago, seeing film of Chinese children of nursery age in a playground chanting the familiar na-na, na-na naa-naaa. Same tune and inflexion as their British and European counterparts. I have often wondered about this. Are there other universal language traits among very young children that transcend international boundaries?ArunrisingSpain, no idea. In Germany (at least in Bavaria), and most definitely in Austria, it is chanted followed by an “ätsch-bätsch” (“Fooled you!”).bricklayersoptionI was once on holiday in Cyprus and I heard a child saying “na na na na naaa”, a chorus that was picked up by almost every child on the beach within moments. It became rather moving, the thought of the phrase (?) transcending language barriers, etc.guineapigsAlmost anywhere else, perhaps. But there in particular, almost certainly everyone else on the beach was also British: 10% of Cyprus coastline is British Overseas Territory.HaveYouFedTheFishI think it’s annoying mainly because it’s done to annoy …PhilthewellsIs it really annoying? It’s cheeky, it’s provocative, it’s done to annoy. I’ve spent a few minutes to think back over the years – mostly it hasn’t annoyed me, and most times I’ve probably done it back, especially as an adult. So we’ve both gone “na-na na-na-na” at each other with all the trimmings, thumbs in ears with elk horns, tongue out – what now? Are we quits? Usually ends in mutual laughter.bricklayersoptionI’ll tell you what’s even more annoying than “na na, na na na”. My own child saying “na na na, poo poo”. Usually used when she’s got something that her younger sibling can’t have, which then sends the younger one into a fit of rage, which in turn leads to me lecturing how gloating is a very unsavoury trait. This usually happens once a week.Dip Pankhania, via emailI work in a primary school as class support with five to seven-year-olds. The reason it is annoying is that it’s almost never said in jest. It’s always as a put-down to another child. So I’m not a fan. However, if my kid said it to me, I’d take it in the tone given, as a 1-0 to my child!MissMeerkatJust sing the second half of Hey Jude back at them, that’ll learn ’em.jno50Or anything by the Prodigy.DorkaliciousI don’t know – having worked with kids, I find the cheeky ones often the most memorable and sometimes most oddly uplifting characters. It doesn’t annoy me so much as the stroppy, sulky ones who get the hump for seven hours over nothing. Give me a “na na na na na” any day!MiffledKittyBecause it’s intended to taunt and annoy. It’s done to the tune of I’m the King of the Castle, the triumphant, mocking ditty that British kids have sung for centuries when pushing each other off slightly more elevated places. I’ve raised a kid in Spain and Germany and can’t say I’ve ever heard it there, though.alexitoBecause it’s a triumphant, crowing, sneering putdown. Bad losers are unpleasant but bad winners are often worse.MossyLIt depends entirely whether they’re singing (multiple tunes go with the chant) or trying to show they’re not interested in someone’s opinion.GoldgreenWell, we used to do it to Dad when I was about four and my sister about two. He’d look up, growl, and then chase us on all fours pretending to be a bear. We’d run off screaming like banshees till he caught us, tickled us both till we escaped and ran away, and then we did it all over again. Once we did it and we didn’t know he had made a water pistol out of a washed-out Fairy Liquid bottle. He got us both square in the chops. Always went back for more. So, it’s taunting in this case. Usually done with a grin and a giggle.teaandchocolateI didn’t find it particularly annoying. When one of mine did it at me, I just wondered why and did it back. And now you can play theFat Les song Vindalooand produce hilarity for all.mathurinExplore more on these topicsLife and styleNotes and queriesChildrenFamilyParents and parentingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Keep away from the doctor’: a visit to an influencer’s wellness event, where the advice could kill | Health | The Guardian
description: Barbara O’Neill, identified as a risk to public safety in Australia, dismisses antibiotics, vaccines and scientifically proven cancer treatment at UK conference
Author: Robyn Vinter
Headline: Barbara O’Neill, identified as a risk to public safety in Australia, dismisses antibiotics, vaccines and scientifically proven cancer treatment at UK conference
Content: Illustration: Sophie WinderView image in fullscreenIllustration: Sophie WinderHealth‘Keep away from the doctor’: a visit to an influencer’s wellness event, where the advice could killBarbara O’Neill, identified as a risk to public safety in Australia, dismisses antibiotics, vaccines and scientifically proven cancer treatment at UK conferenceRobyn VinterandNicola DavisSun 18 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 05.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA roar of laughter erupts from a crowd inside a large conference room at the De Vere Cranage Estate hotel. The joke? The idea that visiting the doctor could help treat a serious illness.On stage the controversial Australian proponent of natural remedies Barbara O’Neill is taking part in a question-and-answer session during a five-day wellness conference, where science mixes uncomfortably with Bible verse and potentially deadly pseudo-scientific practices.She is advising people attending at the event inCheshireon a variety of medical ailments, and dismisses the use of antibiotics, vaccines or scientifically proven cancer treatment.Tickets for the residential retreat can cost up to £1,300. An undercover reporter for the Guardian attended for one day, observing four sessions covering topics including the immune system and one titled Barbara Under Attack.The audience’s rapturous laughter is prompted by a woman asking O’Neill if there is anything that could help her lupus, which she says has not responded well to the doctor’s treatments. “Yes, keep away from the doctor,” quips O’Neill.O’Neill tells the audience that she is “just a little lady”, but she is an incredibly influential one, with 3.6 million Instagram followers and 1.7 million on Facebook. Many of her videos rack up millions of views.View image in fullscreenBarbara O'Neill.Photograph: FacebookHaving initially found success promoting alternative treatments in Australia, in 2019 O’Neill wasbanned from providing any health services in her home country, where authorities found she was responsible for “misleading vulnerable people”. They said she “made dangerous claims not supported by evidence and posed a risk to public safety”.She has since taken her unregulated services overseas, most recently with a string of appearances in the UK and Ireland whichprompted concernfrom experts in both countries. A number of prominent doctors and scientists have told the Guardian her advice is “dangerous”, with some warning it could kill.O’Neill appears regal sitting on stage in an armchair offering audience members softly spoken advice on endometriosis, varicose veins and constipation.The 73-year-old is dressed in a long skirt with a woollen wrap, which she later switches for a soft cardigan, creating a look that sits somewhere between Queen Elizabeth II at Balmoral and Claudia Winkleman in The Traitors. The Highlands-inspired attire is a nod to her Scottish heritage, which the Australian mentions on multiple occasions.She carries an air of authority to her devoted followers, many of whom seem confident that her doctrine could improve their health.Much of her core teaching aligns with established scientific health advice: few doctors would dispute that a balanced diet, regular exercise, hydration and plenty of sleep are important factors for good health, while it is advisable to avoid alcohol, caffeine and smoking.During some of the lectures, O’Neill draws diagrams on a whiteboard while issuing long scientific-sounding explanations.She talks about the glycocalyx lining of the endothelium cells, which provides anticoagulant effects and releases nitric oxide, a vasodilator.But she also makes some highly unscientific and potentially deadly recommendations.View image in fullscreen‘It’s amazing how many tests are creating illnesses,’ O’Neill said at the Cheshire event.Photograph: Robyn Vinter/The GuardianDuring the Q&A session, a woman says that while she recently underwent tests, doctors found a stomach tumour, which she says two specialists have advised her to have surgically removed.“Sometimes scans are not right,” replies O’Neill, who advises the woman to treat the tumour with a castor oil compress – kitchen roll soaked with high viscosity oil from the castor plant – on the outside of the body.That day O’Neill recommends the same remedy for nasal polyps, endometriosis, carpal tunnel syndrome and bile duct stones. Medical experts told the Guardian there was no evidence castor oil compresses did anything to improve any of those conditions.She suggests using castor oil with a pinch of cayenne pepper in the eye to an audience member with glaucoma and high blood pressure.Prof Gus Gazzard, a leading glaucoma expert, says: “There is absolutely no evidence to support these claims, and unfortunately, there’s the possibility that they might indeed cause harm.”The questions continue, read out by her husband, Michael, who gives some of his own lectures during the retreat. The pair stumble over long names of medical conditions, while the audience laughs along.O’Neill advises a pregnant woman against taking folic acid, which randomised controlled trials have shown can protect against neural tube deficits in babies. To someone else, she claims antibiotics are “the worst thing to give” for infections.View image in fullscreenJewellery at O’Neill’s conference in Cheshire.Photograph: Robyn Vinter/The GuardianTo a woman who says she does not have a functioning thyroid, she recommends slowly stopping her dose of thyroxine, which is prescribed for thyroid dysfunction, to “see what the body does”.Medical experts say this would lead to fatigue, hair loss, weight gain, a slow heart rate and low mood. Martin Whyte, a professor of metabolic medicine at the University of Surrey, says: “Someone without a functioning thyroid cannot make thyroid hormone, so stopping thyroxine to ‘see what the body does’ really makes no sense and risks serious, potentially life-threatening illness.”A woman who says she has diabetes tells O’Neill she is hoping to come off metformin, a drug used to lower blood sugar levels. Metformin is typically used to treat type 2 diabetes, which can respond to a change in diet, while type 1 requires daily insulin injections. Both types require blood glucose monitoring. O’Neill advises her to stop testing her blood sugar because it would “balance right out with the change in diet”.This advice is “very dangerous”, according to Gill Livingston, a professor of psychiatry of older people at UCL. “Untreated diabetes means the body is bathed in bloodstream high sugarand increases the risk of multiple physical illnesses, such as loss of eyesight, loss of peripheral sensation, dementia and sometimes death.”Refusing medical tests is a regular theme in O’Neill’s teachings across her publications, her social media and her public appearances.“It’s amazing how many tests are creating illnesses,” she says at the Cheshire event.At another point, not long after encouraging a follower to ignore her oncologist’s recommendation to take a drug,and without any clarification about the type of cancer the woman was being treated for, she says: “They give you a label and then they give you a drug.”Interspersed throughout the day are claims that people have recovered from illnesses after taking her advice. She cites a man who had suffered a stroke, and had “no adverse effects at all” when he stopped taking medication prescribed by his doctor, including statins and blood thinners, on one of her retreats.“It’s outrageous what medicine will do. We have to start saying ‘no, thank you’,” she says. “It doesn’t matter what they say to you, what fear they put into you, say no.“The body, it’s got an inbuilt ability to heal itself.”Prof Liam Smeeth, director of the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, calls her claims “extraordinary”. He says: “Most disturbingly, many of these – if followed – will cause substantial harm, and this could include death.”View image in fullscreenA product that claims to protect against EMF.Photograph: Robyn Vinter/The GuardianIt is clear some of her followers have a lot of trust in her. Speaking to the Guardian’s undercover reporter at the end of the day, one audience member says O’Neill’s answer to her question was “very helpful” and she now has the confidence to go against specialists’ advice for surgery for a health condition.In other conversations during breaks, some people attending say they have lost trust in western medicine after side-effects or failed treatments.One woman in her 60s explains that she and her family refused masks and vaccines during the Covid crisis, had gatherings and “actually washed my hands less than normal”. She says her husband went into hospital in early 2020 with pneumonia and died two days later. She blames the medics for his death.“You know they’re satanists, don’t you?” she says, of the government and those who run major global institutions. “The elite are all flesh-eating paedophiles.”Some at the conference wear amulets they claim protect against 5G signals and a stall selling them proves popular. There is no evidence that 5G signals cause harm and yet O’Neill advises those working at a computer to invest in a device to protect against damage she says is caused by electronic devices and “balance the body after exposure to an electromagnetic field [EMF]”.Dr David Robert Grimes, an expert in biostatistics at Trinity College Dublin, says fear of modernity is a common pseudoscience trope.“The canard that EMFs are ‘damaging’ us is a tired one that exploits our ignorance of technical terms to instil fear,” he says. “There is no device that ‘balances’ you after exposure, because the central conceit is nonsense. We live in a world with light, heat, radio waves, and the sun, so EMFs are all around us. The idea of balancing is really meaningless.”He adds: “The evidence is clear that patients seduced by the false allure of complementary medicine fare objectively worse than those that stick to conventional treatments. These patients are typically convinced by dubious healers to delay or reject life-saving treatments until it’s too late, with often tragic consequences.”Before O’Neill’s most recent tour, senior doctors and medical experts, including Grimes, wrote to some of the venues hosting her conferences urging them to reconsider holding events that would “spread dangerous health fictions to a susceptible audience”.O’Neill’s husband, Michael, co-runs her company and is the engine behind her tours. In an afternoon session titled Barbara Under Attack, he describes her “persecution” by authorities, the scientific community and the media . “There is a war against us,” he tells the audience.After an approach from the Guardian to O’Neill for comment on her claims at the conference, a video of the couple appears on her Instagram and Facebook pageswarning their followers of “disgusting” reporting. Michael reads out thestatement issued to the Guardian.“The complaints against Barbara are purely speculative, based on an ideology that the only legitimate way to health is through the medical profession,” he says.Michael claims the couple have not received complaints about O’Neill’s work and highlights statistics about medical mistakes in the NHS.He adds: “The campaign against Barbara by the media, and academics is a modern-day witch-hunt that has no substance in facts, but purely an ideology that supports the most corrupt organisation in the world; the pharmaceutical industry.”The pair have vowed to continue holding events. O’Neill says she is driven by God, who she believes spoke directly to her.“It would be wrong of me to stop.”Explore more on these topicsHealthVaccines and immunisationEnglandCheshirefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to make the perfect poires belle Hélène – recipe | Food | The Guardian
description: Cool, juicy pears, cold ice-cream, hot chocolate sauce and a crunchy garnish – the perfect pudding
Author: Felicity Cloake
Headline: Cool, juicy pears, cold ice-cream, hot chocolate sauce and a crunchy garnish – the perfect pudding
Content: Felicity Cloake’s perfect poires belle Hélène.Photograph: Robert Billington/ood Styling: Flossy McAslan.View image in fullscreenFelicity Cloake’s perfect poires belle Hélène.Photograph: Robert Billington/ood Styling: Flossy McAslan.How to cook the perfect ...FoodHow to make the perfect poires belle Hélène – recipeCool, juicy pears, cold ice-cream, hot chocolate sauce and a crunchy garnish – the perfect puddingFelicity CloakeSun 18 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 08.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s always slightly embarrassing to realise that you’ve missed a pop culture reference, even if it’s 162 years old, so I won’t dwell on the fact that until last week I was unaware of the existence of Offenbach’s 1864 operetta about Helen of Troy,La Belle Hélène, after which today’s dish is named. In any case,the great French chef Escoffierwas so moved by it, or perhaps by its popularity among Parisian diners, to name this simple dessert of vanilla-scented poached pears topped with hot chocolate sauce after the work’s heroine, played by the comely Hortense Schneider.Though other homages (he includes no fewer than five dishes with that name in his1907 Guide Culinaire, none of which involve pears) may, like the music, have faded from public consciousness, this particular pairing, if you’ll forgive the pun, has stood the test of time. As Nigel Slater observes in Tender: Volume 2, “The marriage of pears and chocolate is extraordinary. It is as if they were made for each other.” This, I think, is the duo at its “most sumptuous”.The pearsView image in fullscreenMax Rocha poire belle helene: an ’intensely flavoured but thin sauce’. Thumbnail pics by Felicity.Everyone is agreed that, for best results when poaching pears, you need them to be firm. As Nigella Lawson writes in How to Eat, “In fact, it is a positive advantage to use what would in other circumstances seem rebarbatively firm fruit” (extra points if, unlike my spellcheck, you were already familiar with the word “rebarbative”). Squidgy fruit of the kind that runs down your chin will fall apart during cooking;turn those into cake instead.As far as I can tell from the recipe included inFrançois-Régis Gaudry’s magisterial Let’s Eat France, which claims to have respected “the proportions of the era”, Escoffier poached the fruit in a vanilla syrup, a tradition most versions honour. However,Max Rocha of Cafe Ceciliain London eschews the pod in favour of citrus zest (lemon and orange), rosemary and a stick of cinnamon. (Also, to be fair, Rocha, likeSlater, does not claim to be making poires belle helene, but simply poached pears with chocolate sauce). Very nice it is, too, and I would encourage you to experiment, but, out of deference to the dessert’s creator, I’ve stuck with vanilla.Under-ripe pears tend to be willing recipients of help in the flavour department, so for once I’m in favour of dialling up the sugar, because the pears need to be robust enough to stand up to the intense chocolate sauce. I’ll also be adding the juice of a whole lemon, as Jane Grigson and chefAlain Benech, whose recipe is featured on Delia Smith’s website, suggests. I’ll include the finely grated zest, too; the acidity not only helps the fruit retain its colour, but brings out its perfume as well.View image in fullscreenFlaked almonds: Alain Benech’s poire belle helene.Though everyone uses a slightly different cooking method, from a brief boil (Grigson’s Fruit Book) to keeping the liquid at a very gentle heat throughout (Slater), none proves disastrous; what is key is to keep the pears submerged so they cook evenly (Benech recommends topping them with a cartouche of baking paper, which sounds a faff but really isn’t, especially compared with constantly turning the fruit in the pan once they bob up to the top) and to leave them ever so slightly harder than you’d like them, because they will continue to cook as they cool in the syrup.Grigson and Slater both halve their pears, which, while it does speed up the cooking time, looks less fun on the plate, which feels a shame – this is definitely a show-off sort of dessert. Do, as Benech suggests, remove a little of the stringy core from the base, however – it’ll make them a lot easier to eat with a modicum of decorum.The sauceWithout sauce, the dish would just be fruit, which, as I never tire of reminding my mum, is not a proper pudding. That said, Grigson notes that this is a dish that “has had much criticism from some food writers, for the combination of delicate pears with chocolate sauce … the secret lies in taking very little sauce”. She has a point: chocolate, like tomato ketchup, is a flavour bully – let it in, and it tends to take over – so I would suggest moderating things to an artful drip, or allowing your guests to serve themselves at the table. After all, if they overdo it, they only have themselves to blame.View image in fullscreen‘Box of tricks’: Jane Grigson poire belle helene.Rocha is the only one to use cocoa powder and water rather than melted chocolate and dairy, which results in an intensely flavoured but thin sauce. Initially, I’m quite taken by the idea; it feels a nice counterpoint to any creamy things you might be serving with your pears, but it does mean serving the pear in a puddle of chocolate sauce, rather than allowing it to drip glossily down from its stem (a sentence I have rewritten more than once), so, in the end, I’ve stuck with the traditional melted chocolate. Grigson and Slater both add black coffee, which feels like overcomplicating things (even though it goes well with chocolate), as does Benech’s dash of poire william and the kirschwasser that’s in Grigson’s box of tricks. By all means pop them in, if you like, especially if your sauce needs thinning down a little, but a dash of vanilla extract and a pinch of salt should be quite sufficient.Gaudry makes the sauce with milk, Grigson and Slater whipping cream, and Lawson and Benech double cream. The fattier the dairy, of course, the richer and thicker the result – and double cream tends to be easier to get hold of than whipping, which is another point in its favour – but some double cream is so lusciously dense that it forms an unattractive brown lump, rather than the silky stream I’m after. Give it a good stir first, and loosen the finished sauce with a little milk or water, or even liqueur, if necessary. For extra shine, stir in a knob of butter or a spoonful of golden syrup at the end, but with this proportion of chocolate to dairy, you probably won’t need any help in that department. Do serve the sauce warm and the pears cold, though, because much of this dish’s charm lies in contrast.The dairyView image in fullscreen‘Au naturel’: Nigel Slater’s poire belle helene.Rocha and Slater, classy chaps that they are, serve the pear and chocolate sauceau naturel, but it’s hard to argue that this isn’t improved by an elegant scoop of vanilla ice-cream (what isn’t?) or a billowing spoonful of Benech’s creme chantilly (cream whipped with sugar and vanilla seeds). Whichever you go for, however, don’t overlook one final contrast. A sprinkling of flaked almonds (Benech) or crystallised violets (Grigson) leaves you with cold ice-cream or cream, cool, juicy pears, hot chocolate sauce and a crunchy garnish. Perfection in a dish.Perfect poires belle helenePrep20 minCook30 minServes44 firm, not-too-ripe pears1 unwaxed lemon1 vanilla pod200g white sugar, or golden sugar¼ tsp salt(optional)1 tbsp flaked almonds, toasted, or crystallised violets, to serve4 scoopsvanilla ice-cream, or 150ml double or whipping cream, whipped with 1 tbsp caster or icing sugar and ¼ tsp vanilla extract or paste, or the seeds from ½ vanilla pod, to serveFor the sauce150g dark chocolate200ml double or whipping creamPinch of saltMilk, or water or liqueur of your choice (optional)Prepare the pears some hours before you’re intending to eat. Find a wide, fairly deep pan and cut out a circle of greaseproof paper of the same diameter. Fold this in half then in quarters, then in eighths, and cut a small hole in the centre to let out steam.View image in fullscreenAdd the lemon zest and juice to the pan. Split open the vanilla pod, scrape out the vanilla seeds and add these to the pan with the empty pod, sugar and salt, if using. Pour in a litre of water and bring to a simmer, stirring to dissolve the sugar.Peel the pears, leaving the stalks intact, and cut a small slice off their bottoms so they’ll stand up straight later. Scoop out some of the woody core from the bases, then lay down the pears in the panView image in fullscreenUnfold the paper cartouche, use to cover the fruit, then leave the pears to simmer gently for about 25 minutes, until cooked through but not too soft. Take off the heat, leave to cool in the poaching liquid, then put in the fridge to chill.View image in fullscreenWhen you’re ready to eat, chop up the chocolate. Put the cream in a small pan, heat to a bare simmer, then take off the heat and add the chocolate. Leave to sit for a couple of minutes, then stir until melted and smooth.View image in fullscreenAdd the salt, if using, and if the chocolate mix feels too thick to pour easily, stir in a dash of milk, water or liqueur, too.View image in fullscreenTo assemble, drain the pears and pat them dry with kitchen paper (the poaching liquid makes a lovely drink, or reduce it to make a syrup to drizzle over future desserts). Divide the fruit between shallow bowls, standing them upright.Either pour a spoonful of chocolate sauce down one flank, or serve the sauce separately for everyone to pour their own. Add a spoonful of ice-cream or chantilly cream, scatter with toasted nuts or violets, and serve immediately.Poires belle helene: is this the most beautiful of pear-based desserts or have you fallen for something less operatic – an upside-down cake, perhaps, or a boozy sorbet?Explore more on these topicsFoodHow to cook the perfect ...FruitDessertAutumn food and drinkChocolateFrench food and drinkrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Buvette, London WC2: ‘It’s actually rather lovely’ – restaurant review | Restaurants | The Guardian
description: This offshoot of a New York favourite isn’t reinventing the wheel, but it does bring a touch of Gallic glam to the neighbourhood
Author: Grace Dent
Headline: This offshoot of a New York favourite isn’t reinventing the wheel, but it does bring a touch of Gallic glam to the neighbourhood
Content: Buvette, London WC2: ‘A version of French dining that won’t scare the horses.’Photograph: Beca B Jones/The GuardianView image in fullscreenBuvette, London WC2: ‘A version of French dining that won’t scare the horses.’Photograph: Beca B Jones/The GuardianGrace Dent on restaurantsRestaurantsReviewBuvette, London WC2: ‘It’s actually rather lovely’ – restaurant reviewThis offshoot of a New York favourite isn’t reinventing the wheel, but it does bring a touch of Gallic glam to the neighbourhoodGrace DentSun 18 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 14.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfaux-French, cult-hit New York brasserie has opened in Neal’s Yard, deep in the hairy armpit of Covent Garden among alleyways where holistic therapy rooms, walk-in back rub spaces,Neal’s Yard Remediesand26 Grains cafeare its immediate neighbours. The windchimes and the whiff of patchouli part the air round these parts, and the footfall is yoga pant-clad and hungry for hummus.Buvette, meanwhile, has brought a touch of Gallic glam to the neighbourhood, and is clearly aimed at theEmily in Parisgeneration with itstotalement françaismenu featuring croque monsieur with roast mushrooms and gruyere,rillettes de saumonor salade niçoise withharicots vertsand amolletegg; there’s also a Macvin champagne and muscadet spritz, pastis on the rocks, warm scones with jam, and almond croissants.This is the London arm ofJody Williams’ West Village gastrothèque, and its menu is a pretty card listing 25 dishes to choose from, none of them above £18. It clearly thinks it’s a hot, fresh, new thing, but I’m not sure it’s anything new at all. We used to call places that looked like thisCafé Rouge: that is, recognisably French, and by that I mean recognisable if you have a working GCSE knowledge of La Rochelle cafe life. It’s that version of French dining that won’t scare the horses, or at least the horses that the French haven’t minced coarsely and served in their own gastroduodenal canals with an exemplary homemademoutarde.View image in fullscreenBuvette’s pommes frites come served in a copper pot.Buvette’s cute red frontage gives way to something heartstoppingly pretty inside: marble-topped tables, bentwood chairs, a zinc bar, good-looking, chipper staff – though, let’s be honest, that latter chipper bit wouldneverhappen in a lunchtime Paris tourist spot. It’s all very charming and ought to be packed, but on this midweek lunchtime there are plenty of seats to spare in this 80-cover space. In fact, almost all of them are empty. This is Buvette’s second attempt at cracking London – the first, in Notting Hill in 2020, came and went within four years.As I peruse the gorgeous little cut-card menu, 12 northern ladies with pull-along suitcases sit down at the next table, read it, confer briefly and leave sharpish.Mais pourquoi, Julie? This is a quickcafé au laitand a freshly squeezed orange juice joint (though they’ve missed a trick not servingOrangina), or a longersaumon grilléwithbetteraves(beetroot salad) on the side and a mousse au chocolat for pudding kind of place. Nobody is being asked to sit a GCSE French oral exam, which is a blessing, because the memory of being dragged into a room in Carlisle in 1991 and being expected to discuss Scottish devolution in French still wakes me at night.View image in fullscreenBuvette’s grilled salmon is ‘crisped correctly and has clearly been cooked as if someone truly cares’.And maybe that’s Buvette’s problem. It’s so coy and cool that it scares away the normals, but it’s not cool enough to ensnare foodies who’d rather be chucking money at Fergus Henderson’s wine bar just across the way; the local yoga brigade, meanwhile, would rather be queuing outside a clandestine juice shack to hand over £28 for juiced turnip and echinacea. Even so, and to make a plaintive case for Buvette, it’s actually rather lovely.We order the croque madame, which is a classic construction: thick, white toasted bread, melted cheese, all draped in thin ham, snowed over with more grated cheese, topped with a vivid egg yolk and garnished with a flourish of tiny, crunchy cornichons. It is a noble and considered attempt. That grilled salmon comes dressed insauce ravigote, a sharp, herby, caper-spiked vinaigrette, and with dressed green beans and apetite salade vertealongside. The skin is crisped correctly and the fish moist, and it’s clearly been cooked as if someone downstairs truly cares. We share a copper pan filled with pommes frites and pick at a meaty, sharply dressedsalade de poulet. As for those betteraves, these chunky, sweet, glossy roast beets with horseradish creme fraiche are the kind of thing you don’t get as a side any more, and you find yourself wondering why not.View image in fullscreen‘Chunky, sweet, glossy’: Buvette’sbetteraves, or beetroot salad with horseradish creme fraiche.Photograph: Beca B Jones/The GuardianTheset lunch menu at £23 is ridiculous value: salmon, green beans and green salad, or burger, fries and salad, or a croque and two salads, all with a coffee to finish. And this in Covent Garden, where you usually have to sell a kidney to afford a crepe. Buvette isn’t reinventing the wheel, but it’s somewhere to pop in for lunch and end up lingering over pots of fresh mint tea and a rather incongruous offering of warm scones with raspberry jam and cream, or almond croissants hot from the oven. Cafe Rouge lasted for years because it wasn’t terribly French, or terribly hot, but it was fantastically useful. Perhaps Buvette needs to reposition itself as a pit stop rather than an Instagram backdrop. Then more people might want to mange tout.Buvette2 Neal’s Yard, London WC2, 020-3540 4989. Open all week, lunch 11.30am-4pm, dinner 4-9pm (10pm Thurs-Sat). From about £40 head à la carte;formuleset lunch (main, two sides and coffee) £23, all plus drinks & serviceExplore more on these topicsRestaurantsGrace Dent on restaurantsFoodFrench food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: More peas, please! 17 delicious ways to devour Britain’s most brilliant vegetable | Vegetables | The Guardian
description: They’re healthy, versatile, sustainable and available. Yet pea consumption in the UK is at a 50-year low. Here are the curries, dips, pasta dishes and even cakes that could turn all that around
Author: Tim Dowling
Headline: They’re healthy, versatile, sustainable and available. Yet pea consumption in the UK is at a 50-year low. Here are the curries, dips, pasta dishes and even cakes that could turn all that around
Content: Food to set your pulse racing … Ravinder Bhogal's pea and mint dip.Photograph: Rita Platts/The GuardianView image in fullscreenFood to set your pulse racing … Ravinder Bhogal's pea and mint dip.Photograph: Rita Platts/The GuardianVegetablesMore peas, please! 17 delicious ways to devour Britain’s most brilliant vegetableThey’re healthy, versatile, sustainable and available. Yet pea consumption in the UK is at a 50-year low. Here are the curries, dips, pasta dishes and even cakes that could turn all that aroundTim DowlingSun 18 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s not good news for the pea farmers: pea consumption in the UK has fallen to a 50-year low. According to data from Defra, the average Britonate just 37g of peas per week in 2025, down from 144g per week in 1975.Though a classic British staple, peas are not for everybody. Apparently only 22% of gen Z associate peas with Britain at all (which is patently ridiculous:90% of the peas we consumein the UK are grown here, while we produce about160,000 tonnes for freezing aloneeach year).But if I’m honest, I ate zero grams of peas last week; ditto the week before. I like peas – or at least I’m rarely offended by them – but as a suppertime option, they seem a little mundane. And while all the pak choi and purple sprouting broccoli in the fridge risks going floppy with age, frozen peas can be postponed indefinitely.It shouldn’t be this way. Peas are healthy, versatile, sustainable and insanely available. If you’re like me, you don’t even need to buy peas to eat them: I’ve always already got some. But if you’re still in need of inspiration, here are 17 delicious ways to help keep the UK pea industry afloat.View image in fullscreenIdeal distillation … Felicity Cloake’s perfect pea soup.Photograph: Felicity CloakePea soup is a good place to start – especially if it’s Felicity Cloake’sperfect pea soup, an ideal distillation of this classic dish. As with all these recipes, frozen peas are called for at this time of year – but, as Cloake says, frozen and fresh are pretty indistinguishable in soup. In one sensefrozen peas are fresherthan fresh peas anyway – chilled within 150 minutes of picking, before they develop any starchiness. If you’re after something a bit fancier, Tori Haschka’spea soup with almond and chorizo crumbsalso contains courgette, broccoli, kale and a diced red apple – all blitzed smooth at the end and accessorised with crumbled chorizo on top.Ravinder Bhogal’s easypea and mint dip– which includes feta and a lightly pickled radish salsa – can be served with bread or crudites or both, and is allegedly even good on toast for breakfast. Simpler still is Jamie Oliver’speas with broad beans, chilli and mint: all the ingredients are in the title, apart from a squeeze of lemon and a dash of olive oil.View image in fullscreenIngredients you may well have to hand … Rachel Roddy's pasta with peas and cream.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The GuardianChorizo and pea risottomakes for a quick yet rather elegant midweek supper. Rukmini Iyer’sgreen pea pulaois another rice dish, topped with a fried egg and spiced with cardamom. Hugh Fearnley-Whittingstall mines a similar vein in a different genre with a dish featuringbaby peas, bacon, garlic and risoni– a rice-shaped pasta more commonly known as orzo (although not in Italy, apparently).Rachel Roddy’speas and pastaoffering uses ingredients you may well have on hand right now: peas, cream, onion, butter, lemon, some kind of hard cheese, a single tablespoon of cream cheese and pasta (macaroni, penne, fusilli or similar). Apotato gnocchi with peasfrom Masha Rener is finished with ricotta salata – salted ricotta. If you haven’t got gnocchi, Rener says linguine can step in as understudy.View image in fullscreenPerfect with bread … Rosie Sykes’s peas and potato pav bhaji.Photograph: Yuki Sugiura/The GuardianMany of us normally serve peas as a side dish with meat – as an afterthought, even – but Yotam Ottolenghi’slamb shoulder chops with marinated feta and peasgives them a strong supporting role. You’ll struggle to secure the pea shoots he suggests at this time of year, but rocket makes a perfectly acceptable substitute. For Nigel Slater’shake with pea salsa, the just-cooked peas are whizzed with coriander, parsley, mint, oil and vinegar.Slater also has a recipe forpea, herb and mozzarella pie, which calls for leeks and courgettes too.Rosie Sykes’spea pav bhajiis a spreadable curry made with potatoes and eaten on bread rolls. Thisspiced green pea coconut curryfrom Maunika Gowardhan is yet another pea and potato pairing – this one using kokum petals, if you can find them, and tamarind paste if you can’t.Should there be any peas left in the bag at the end of the night, here are three slightly weird desserts you can try. In the first, apea sorbetfrom James Knappett, frozen peas are blitzed with sugar syrup, citric acid and salt before returning to the freezer, eventually to be served with sliced strawberries and mint oil.Thispea moussecombines a thin custard with gelatine, white chocolate and frozen petit pois. And odd as it sounds, Kate Hackworthy’svegetarian pea cakeis actually everything you would expect from an ordinary Victoria sponge, plus peas. And yes, it is green.Explore more on these topicsVegetablesFoodFood & drink industryFarmingMain courseDessertfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: My longterm boyfriend died last year. Is it too soon to date someone new? | Family | The Guardian
description: Only you can know when you are ready, but a year is not long to process grief, and you seem to have doubts about this man
Author: Annalisa Barbieri
Headline: Only you can know when you are ready, but a year is not long to process grief, and you seem to have doubts about this man
Content: Illustration: Alex Mellon/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Alex Mellon/The GuardianAsk Annalisa BarbieriFamilyMy longterm boyfriend died last year. Is it too soon to date someone new?Only you can know when you are ready, but a year is not long to process grief, and you seem to have doubts about this manAnnalisa BarbieriSun 18 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 02.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy longterm boyfriend diedof cancer last year. We’d been together for16 years, since I was 21 and he was 23.I had given birth to ouronly child three weeksbefore his diagnosis. My son was just shy of 10 months old when his dad died, and he’snow turned two.I loved my late partner deeply and had planned to stay with him for ever. We wereembarking on an 18-year project together, raising our son.NowIthink, how can I ever be happy again?Before he died, my partner told me to find a single dad to go out with. When I returned to work, a colleague Ihad considered a flirt was away – getting chemo.Nowhe’s in remission. He’s also a singleparent.Lately, I’ve realised I have a crush on him. His life has been touched by tragedy and he knows what’s important to him. He’s very kind, like my late partner, and I think we click.What gives me a lot of pause is that I find him toblow hot and cold.Also,because I’m a solo mumI don’t really have time for someone else.But he has recentlyleft the company, so I wouldn’t bedating a co-worker.Is it remarkable to meet a single dadyou genuinely like? Or are there more out there than I think?Please tell me what you think I should do.What a devastating loss you’ve experienced, and at such a tender time of motherhood. I’m so sorry.I spoke to UKCP-registered psychotherapist Stephanie White, who wondered, given that you were with your partner almost your entire adult life, “if you have learned to trust your gut and made ‘good enough’ decisions on your own”. You seem to look outside yourself to validate what you’re doing: your partner “told you” to find a single dad to go out with. You ask me to tell you what you “should do”. Ultimately, we all need our own internal guide, and I’d like you to think about yours.double quotation markGrieving is a long process, and an important part is accepting that the death has occurred and, in your case, the expected narrative arc of your lives has now endedI wouldn’t want to stop you having fun – you deserve it – but you have “a lot of pause” about this new man. This could be because he has a lot going on in his life, but it could also be because something doesn’t feel right for you. Also, are you in a place to potentially take on his issues?White said: “There seems to be something here about an expected narrative thread getting cut: you were ‘embarking on an 18-year project together’, but reality is not panning out as expected. This can lead to feeling stuck.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMy husband never stops working, but he won’t discuss it. Should I leave him?Read moreShe also felt there could be a “trauma bond” between you and this other man – his life has been “touched by tragedy” too – and wondered if there was “something about wanting to skip, perhaps unconsciously, the phases of the grieving process by substituting a ‘facsimile’ for your former partner”.“But grieving is a long process,” White warned, “and one of the most important parts is accepting that the death has occurred and, in your case, that the expected narrative arc of your lives has now ended. At some level, you seem to know this new man is not ideal. You’re not a widow years out of bereavement who finds love; you’re a year in, and that’s no time at all.”You have a young son to care for. We wondered about your support network. Lean into it, maybe look into some therapy or support groups such asWidowed and Young. Take it slowly, and put yourself and your son first. Don’t rush into a new caring role beyond this just yet. But that doesn’t mean you can’t – or shouldn’t – love and have fun again.Every week, Annalisa Barbieri addresses a personal problem sent in by a reader.
