title: This is how we do it: ‘After marriage counselling, she no longer wants the lights off and the covers on’ | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Financial, work and childrearing pressures had killed off their sex life, but therapy gave Henry and Kelly an insight into each other’s perspective
Author: Elena Angelides
Headline: Financial, work and childrearing pressures had killed off their sex life, but therapy gave Henry and Kelly an insight into each other’s perspective
Content: Illustration: Ryan Gillett/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Ryan Gillett/The GuardianThis is how we do itLife and styleThis is how we do it: ‘After marriage counselling, she no longer wants the lights off and the covers on’Financial, work and child-rearing pressures had killed off their sex life, but therapy gave Henry and Kelly an insight into each other’s perspectiveHow do you do it? Share the story of your sex life, anonymouslyAs told toElena AngelidesSun 18 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHenry, 63double quotation markI stopped trying to initiate sex. If it passed the six-month mark, she would initiate. Like she wanted to be a dutiful wifeKelly and I met in our early 20s in a gym-slash-nightclub – she was an aerobics teacher and I was a bartender. I remember spying her incredible figure from afar, through all the chrome decor and disco balls. A year after marrying, we became parents and the sexiness got squeezed by screaming children, bills and responsibilities.During these fraught years, I would frequently initiate sex, but I was often met with “my hair is a mess” or “the dishes are not done” – and eventually, I stopped trying. If it passed the six-month mark Kelly would initiate, but I got the sense she was just playing the dutiful wife. She would want to do it with the lights off and the covers up to her chin.When our kids left the nest, all of our tensions around child-rearing went away, but so many issues remained around how much I was spending and socialising. I suggested we try marriage counselling, and I learned that she wasn’t nagging at me to stop spending money on golf because she was being selfish; and she realised I wasn’t being selfish for wanting to spend time with friends. It helped me to see that Kelly worries about money, and her to see that I’m just desperate for a bit of me time amid the chaos of everyday life.double quotation markSomething changed in Kelly. It was like the flood gates opened. Now she gives me specific directionsIt was on a trip visiting family, three months into therapy, when something changed in Kelly. This time she didn’t care about having the lights off or the covers on. It was like the floodgates opened, and ever since we’ve started having sex weekly. In the past, when I would ask her what she wanted during sex, she would respond: “Nothing. I don’t have anything to tell you.” Now, she gives me specific directions. We are much better at communicating – even if it’s not working. We might say let’s watch TV instead.I think not giving up on our marriage has brought us closer together. We hold hands now when we walk down the street. I feel as if I have my girlfriend back from when we first started dating – although she wears less neon spandex, her body is still as incredible as it was when we first met.Share your experienceIf you’re keen to talk to us about your sex lives you can get in touch by filling in the form below. It is very important that both sexual partners are happy to participate.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. For more information please see ourterms of serviceandprivacy policy.Tell us hereYour responses, which can be anonymous, are secure as the form is encrypted and only the Guardian has access to your contributions. We will only use the data you provide us for the purpose of the feature and we will delete any personal data when we no longer require it for this purpose. For alternative ways to get in touch securely please see ourtips guide.First name of partner oneFirst name of partner twoLength of relationshipContact number or email address of partner onePlease include your country's area code if outside of the UK.Contact number or email address of partner twoPlease include your country's area code if outside of the UK.Do both parties agree to being contacted by a journalist from the Guardian?YesBy submitting your response, you are agreeing to share your details with us for this feature.SubmitShow moreKelly, 62double quotation markI realised our two dogs were the glue holding us together. It shocked meA couple of years ago, I asked Henry: “What would our relationship be like if we hadn’t got dogs?” He replied: “I think we’d be divorced.” I realised in that moment that our two dogs were the glue holding us together since our kids had left home. It shocked me. As we approached retirement age, Henry felt as though we were coexisting roommates, rather than husband and wife. He wanted more of a relationship and more intimacy. I realised I needed to step up and move in that direction.At the time, our sex life was typical of a couple who had been together for ever. It was a big deal for Henry that we’d spend such long stretches of time without having sex, but it wasn’t a big deal for me. From the beginning of our marriage, we had a lot of financial stress. As a nurse, I worked night shifts and at home I was busy attending to three children. I was tired all the time.Sexstarted to feel like a chore. I’ve never had a hard time orgasming, so I would come first and then count down until he finished.double quotation markThe newfound intimacy has reminded me why I started dating Henry in the first placeThis is how we do it: ‘As a sexual abuse survivor, I’ve had to relearn how to have healthy sex’Read moreLast year, we started counselling and became more intentional about our relationship. I realised I could hold off my orgasm and enjoy being together. It shifted my perspective, from thinking of sex as a chore to something fun. Another important shift is feeling more confident in my body. I always thought I needed to be thinner, but seeing this recent craze of women my age getting very thin, it strikes me that they look frail and older. It’s helped me embrace my body.The newfound intimacy has reminded me why I started dating Henry in the first place. When we met, Henry would wine and dine me, even though we were 20 and at university. No other guy had done that for me. He was fun to be around and open to new experiences – and we’ve rekindled that sense of fun together.Names have been changedExplore more on these topicsLife and styleThis is how we do itSexRelationshipsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: £3,500 and no work done: the offer to help that’s really a roofing scam | Scams | The Guardian
description: Citizens Advice warns of its No 1 scam as growing number of people are targeted by criminals posing as roofers
Author: Shane Hickey
Headline: Citizens Advice warns of its No 1 scam as growing number of people are targeted by criminals posing as roofers
Content: The charity says it received more than 2,200 complaints about suspected roofing scams in the year to August in England and Wales.Photograph: lolostock/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenThe charity says it received more than 2,200 complaints about suspected roofing scams in the year to August in England and Wales.Photograph: lolostock/Getty Images/iStockphotoScam watchScams£3,500 and no work done: the offer to help that’s really a roofing scamCitizens Advice warns of its No 1 scam as growing number of people are targeted by criminals posing as roofersShane HickeySun 18 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe builder who calls at your door says they are doing some work in the area and has spotted a loose tile on your roof. They offer to fix it for a good price that you agree to.But when they go up on their ladder to inspect the problem, they see another problem. Rain has been splashing out of the gutters and the wood around them is getting damaged. The only solution, the builder says, is to have rigid PVC trays installed to divert the water.More rain is forecast and you are worried about what damage could be done so you pay the builder via bank transfer to get the job done there and then. They are gone within an hour, having apparently completed the work.But nothing was done because there was no problem with your guttering. Instead you were one of a growing number of people who have been targeted by criminals posing as roofers, only to make off with payment after doing unnecessary or no work.The charity Citizens Advice says suspected roofing frauds were the top scam it heard from consumers about in the last year. It received more than 2,200 complaints of suspected roofing scams in the year to August in England and Wales, about 10% more than the previous year.“The vast majority of cases is … somebody just knocking on your door saying that they’ve noticed that there’s something wrong with your roof and they’re in a position to help you,” says Ruwani Purcell, the director of external affairs at Citizens Advice.“The difficulty is [that] your roof is out of sight and out of reach. You can’t fully see what’s going on.”Purcell says the fraudsters use really persuasive tactics to offer you confidence and reassurance that they know what they’re talking about. “And you might not be familiar with [the] terms,” she says. “In the worst case scenarios, they’ve been quite intimidating to compel people to hand over money there and then.”What it looks likeWhile more than three-quarters of the roofing scams reported to Citizens Advice start with someone knocking at the door, some criminals look online for potential victims.In one case dealt with by Citizens Advice, a 65-year-old woman posted on an online platform that she needed someone to fix a dripping sound in her gutters. A builder phoned her to say that it would cost £250 but when he and another man came and examined her roof they said they had discovered more problems and the price quickly grew. At one point they showed her a bucket of cement and said it was crumbling from under the tiles.The woman said the man and his accomplice said the work needed to be done immediately and once they claimed to have finished they wanted the payment straightaway.“I was afraid, two men in front of me in the dark, demanding money and making it clear they weren’t moving,” the victim told Citizens Advice. “They knew I was alone, I didn’t feel like I could deal with anything that might happen after, so I paid £3,500.”She paid it using bank transfer. “The next day there was no trace that any work was done,” she said. “I felt stupid, and tried to contact them, but couldn’t get through.”What to doBe wary of anyone offering unsolicited work by cold calling and demanding confirmation of a job and payment there and then. No reputable builder will do that, says Purcell.To check the roofer’s authenticity, ask for references and for all proposed work to be confirmed in writing. Treat it as a red flag if they refuse this or if they insist on being paid in cash.To see if a trader is reputable, you can check your local council’s website as it often lists trusted traders. The government runs theTrustMarkscheme which lists approved tradespeople.Citizens Advice says that if a trader has done a poor job without reasonable care and skill, the victim is entitled to ask for the problem to be fixed or get a refund under the Consumer Rights Act 2015. Keep any paperwork and receipts, take photos and document what happened to make your case.Explore more on these topicsScamsScam watchConsumer affairsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Going nowhere fast? Personal trainers on why you aren’t seeing results in the gym | Fitness | The Guardian
description: From doing too much cardio to wasting time – PTs reveal the common fails stunting your progress, and how to avoid them
Author: Joe Stone
Headline: From doing too much cardio to wasting time – PTs reveal the common fails stunting your progress, and how to avoid them
Content: Photograph: Kellie French/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Kellie French/The GuardianFitnessGoing nowhere fast? Personal trainers on why you aren’t seeing results in the gymFrom doing too much cardio to wasting time – PTs reveal the common fails stunting your progress, and how to avoid themJoe StoneSun 18 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou’re in a boomand bust cycleWe’ve all done it. Launched ourselves head first into a new regime – perhaps as the result of a new year resolution, recent breakup or aggressively unflattering photo. “You go all in and train five days a week,” says Elizabeth Davies, personal trainer and author ofTraining for Your Old Lady Body. “Then life happens. You miss a few sessions, then stop completely. You feel deflated that you couldn’t stick to it. Then some time later, motivation strikes again and the cycle repeats itself.”A better approach is to devise a realistic training schedule that actually aligns with your lifestyle. “When getting started, lower the bar,” she suggests. “Aim for two weekly strength sessions done consistently. If you manage that, and have the time, energy and inclination to do more, you can always add in a third. It’s much easier to build on something you’re doing consistently than repeatedly start over with something that’s unsustainable.”You’re changing your programme too often“There’s an outdated belief that you must ‘keep the body guessing’ in order for it to adapt, by continually switching up your workouts,” says Nick Finney, who has trained Robbie Williams and Jennifer Lopez. “I understand that people want to avoid boredom by changing what they do each workout, but it ends up hindering their progress. You need to practise your technique, become more proficient and give your body time to improve and get stronger. If you keep changing things up, then it’s impossible to measure progress by comparing what you achieved in previous workouts.”Instead, he suggests adopting the principle of “progressive overload”. Simply put, this means gradually increasing the reps or weight of your lift, in order to stimulate your body to react by growing stronger. “There is a very simple formula: you might be able to lift 60kg on a bench press for five reps. If over time you are able to increase this to eight reps you can then increase the load to 64kg, which may then put your maximum reps back down to five. So you keep practising until you can get to eight reps at 64kg, before increasing the load again.”You’re too focused on cardio“For decades, people have associated getting fit with running, cycling or other forms of cardiovascular exercise,” says David Vaux, an osteopath and author ofStronger: 10 Exercises for a Longer, Healthier Life. “These activities are excellent for heart health, weight management, joint health and mental wellbeing – but focusing exclusively on cardio means you may be neglecting one of your body’s most valuable ageing assets: your fast-twitch muscle fibres. We lose these at a faster rate as we age, which is one of the major contributors to frailty, falls, reduced mobility and loss of independence later in life. For most people, the healthiest approach is to combine regular movement with resistance training two or three times each week.”You’re adding ‘junk volume’Victorian poet Robert Browning coined the phrase “less is more”. He wasn’t writing about Bulgarian split squats, but he might as well have been. “People often assume more is better: more weekly sessions, more exercises within each session, more sets,” says Davies. “But you don’t need to cram 10 different movements into a session. This can actually just add fatigue without much benefit.”If muscle growth is your goal, you need to be training “close to failure” – the point at which you could not manage another good rep.“If you’re stopping each set when you’re reaching an arbitrary number rather than because the set has become genuinely challenging, you may not be providing your body with enough stimulus to adapt,” she says. “And don’t confuse ‘feeling the burn’ with being close to failure. That burning sensation is largely associated with the buildup of metabolites during exercise, especially very high-rep sets, which are popular in some classes. It can be very uncomfortable, but discomfort isn’t necessarily the same thing as your muscles reaching the point where they could not do another good rep.”You’re trying to out-train a bad diet …Finney warns that bad nutrition is “by far” the most common factor holding gym-goers back from reaching their goals: “Working out hard all week can be completely negated simply by eating whatever you want. People believe workouts burn tons of calories, but most barely even burn off a balanced meal. You must tackle your nutrition if you are serious about any physical change.”View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Kellie French/The GuardianIf your goal is weight loss, you need to be working in a calorie deficit. If you want to build muscle, you need to be eating a surplus of the right kind of calories, including about 2g of protein for every kilo of body weight. And don’t fall into the trap of thinking that a frenzied hour-long workout is the best way to burn off a burger. “Blitzing a bootcamp-style workout that leaves you feeling like you’re dying may only burn about 150 more calories than doing a calmer, focused weights workout. That’s about the same amount of calories as one and a half apples. And yet the difference in effort and fatigue and potential for injury is huge.” If your goal is weight loss, he suggests finding a type of exercise you enjoy, and focusing on training at a sustainable pace while eating a deficit of about 500 calories a day.…and you’re drinking your caloriesAccording to trainer and women’s wellness coach Aimee Victoria Long, “People often focus on what they’re eating and forget about what they’re drinking. Coffees, juices, smoothies, soft drinks and alcohol contain a surprising amount of sugar and calories – they add up incredibly quickly.” Long is a proponent of everything in moderation, but cautions: “If your goal is fat loss and you’re not seeing results, it’s worth looking at what’s in your favourite drinks.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionYou’re training too hardForget “go hard or go home”. In practice, this can mean “go hard and tear a ligament”. “I often see people in my clinic who have thrown themselves into high-intensity workouts six or seven days a week, believing more intensity – longer, faster, heavier – must mean better,” says Vaux. “Unfortunately, our bodies don’t work like that.Fitnessis built through consistency, not punishment. The body needs time to adapt to exercise, especially if you’ve been inactive for a while. In particular, our connective tissues, such as tendons and ligaments, need time to adapt to training and increase their strength.”You also need to allow time between sessions for the body to recover. “If we have not fully recovered before our next training session, the risk of injuries such as tendinitis increases,” says Vaux. “This can leave us weaker and less fit than we were before. Think of exercise as a long-term investment rather than a short-term fix. Start with a programme you can realistically sustain and gradually build from there.”You have unrealistic expectationsNot content with rotting our brains and destroying democracy, it seems social media is also giving us skewed expectations of what we can hope to achieve in the gym. “A big problem, especially for young people, is that they see fitness influencers with visible veins and rippling six-packs, and feel despondent about their own lack of progress by comparison,” says Finney. “The reality is that many influencers have been training for years, edit their pictures and even use performance-enhancing drugs. It’s often not a realistic or healthy goal to emulate.” Progress takes time, and attempting a quick fix is likely to leave you disappointed.“Some people want to lose weight very quickly and restrict calories too severely,” Finney says. “Crash dieting often means losing muscle alongside fat, resulting in a ‘skinny fat’ appearance. Creating a steady calorie deficit allows you to slowly chip away at fat stores, while maintaining strength and energy. A solid and realistic weight loss result is to lose 1lb a week. If your strength in the gym is significantly diminished, that’s a sure sign your calorie deficit is too severe. As a very generalised guide, people can healthily gain 1lb-2lb of muscle a month. This will taper off after the first year of training.”You’re wasting timeIs there anything more annoying than someone hogging a machine while scrolling on TikTok? Take satisfaction from the fact they aren’t just robbing you of precious minutes atop the Booty Builder – they’re also short-changing themselves. “Something I see all the time is people saying they train for an hour, but spending half of that chatting to friends, checking their phone or taking far too much rest between sets,” says Long. “Suddenly that hour-long workout is only 30 minutes of meaningful training.”Instead, she suggests “putting your phone away, having a plan before you start, and being intentional with your rest periods. If you’re training to build muscle, rest for 60-90 seconds between sets, or 90-120 seconds if you’re training to increase strength.” How long should a typical session last? “If you’re being efficient, you can get a solid workout done in 45 minutes, but there is nothing wrong with doing 60-90 minutes, depending on your training plan.”Models: Parsha and Tom Trossero at Street Cast Models.
