title: ‘We hang on to summer a little longer here’: five of the best places for autumn sun in Europe and Turkey | Europe holidays | The Guardian
description: If you’re looking for a last blast of summer, these sunny resorts offer quiet beaches but enough life to stave off the end-of-season blues
Author: Annabelle Thorpe
Headline: If you’re looking for a last blast of summer, these sunny resorts offer quiet beaches but enough life to stave off the end-of-season blues
Content: Kalkan, where October sunsets are particularly lovely.Photograph: Stephen Hughes/AlamyView image in fullscreenKalkan, where October sunsets are particularly lovely.Photograph: Stephen Hughes/AlamyEurope holidays‘We hang on to summer a little longer here’: five of the best places for autumn sun in Europe and TurkeyIf you’re looking for a last blast of summer, these sunny resorts offer quiet beaches but enough life to stave off the end-of-season bluesLiz Boulter, Carolyn Boyd, Daniel James Clarke, Lois Pryce andAnnabelle ThorpeSun 18 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKalkan,TurkeyA Kalkan sunset is always a beautiful thing – the horseshoe-shaped bay deepening to azure blue against an apricot-rose sky – but, in October, when the light is low and the sun drops early, it’s almost transcendentally lovely. In some Turkish resorts, you’d be sitting watching it surrounded by quiet streets, half-empty bars and that melancholic sense that another season is over. In Kalkan, it still feels like summer; the harbourfront restaurants throng with visitors, the day gulets (wooden boats) still putter in and out of the bay and you don’t have to wait an hour to get a taxi back to your villa.For me, the best thing about an autumn break – besides the sunsets – is that I can visit some of my favourite places that just get overrun in summer. The glittering beach at Kaputas, sandwiched into a triangular gap on the mountainous Kalkan-Kas road, has become a victim of Instagram; from May to September, it’s impossible to get near. In October, the waters are still warm and the beach – although still busy – has plenty of space for a dip and a laze.double quotation markBecause the season’s end is in sight, the whole place swings with an end-of-term vibeAbout 20 minutes’ drive inland, the mountain village of Bezirgan, which used to serve as a summer retreat for wealthier Kalkan residents, settles back into complete peace in autumn, save for the woodpeckers battering away at the bark of the almond trees and the squirrels skittering through the leaves. TheLycian Wayweaves through the village, past Ottoman-era grain stores, with the lush gardens of the Pirha Köy Sofrası restaurant a great bet for a plate of traditionalmanti(dumplings in yoghurt) orkofte(meatballs), before setting off for a hike (they do fantastic breakfasts too).Back in Kalkan, it’s always cocktail hour somewhere; often on a roof terrace, with a jazz soundtrack floating out above the streets of the Old Town. This year, theFountain Terrace Cocktail Barhas been popular, but I still love sitting in theMerkez Cafe, a Kalkan institution since the early 1990s, smack-bang in the heart of the village and a prime spot for people-watching when the evening begins.View image in fullscreenThe glittering beach at Kaputas near Kalkan.Photograph: daphnusia/AlamyAnd because the season’s end is in sight, all the restaurant owners and waiters are cheerfully giddy, and the whole place swings with an end-of-term vibe. Sitting at theBlue Marlin(tucked away beneath the Pirat hotel) with a cold Efes beer and a selection of the town’s best meze, the only thing that makes me rueful is that it will be several months before I’ll be back here again.White Househas doubles from£120 B&BAnnabelle ThorpeAgua Amarga, SpainView image in fullscreenThe village of Agua Amarga, where Sexy Beast was filmed.Photograph: Juana Mari Moya/Getty ImagesAlong Spain’s wild Costa de Almería are a handful of exquisite little towns and villages. San José is probably the best known, put on the map by its most famous inhabitant, the late Joe Strummer, but 25 miles east is the real jewel of the Almería coast. Agua Amarga is a typical Andalucían fishing village moonlighting as a stylish low-key holiday destination, perfect for late-season sun-seekers.Its location, on a crescent bay, makes for spectacular sunrises and sunsets over the arid headlands that bookend the 500-metre-long beach. In the narrow, whitewashed streets, a lush palm grove and splashes of pink bougainvillaea remind you that north Africa is just a short hop across the Mediterranean. In the summer, Agua Amarga’s unspoilt sands and turquoise waters attract plenty of visitors, but the vibe remains relaxed. There are a handful of restaurants and bars around the main plaza, and a few eateries on the beach, includingLos Tarahis, a traditionalchiringuito(beach bar) where you can enjoy dishes such asarroz negro con bogavante(black rice with lobster) with your toes in the sand. In winter, the town goes into hibernation, but in autumn the sun and sea are still warm and the bars and restaurants are still open for business.double quotation markAt this time of year, the sun and sea are still warm and the bars and restaurants are openAgua Amarga is not the place to go to party. It’s a world away from the overdeveloped costas to the west and north, but it is the perfect base to immerse yourself in nature. Hiking trails lead from the village over the cliffs to a string of isolated coves and the ruins of 18th-century forts dotted along the headlands. And if you tire of following the shimmering sea, you can strike out inland to explore theCabo de Gata nature reserve, with its windingramblas(dry riverbeds), prickly pears and eerie abandoned goldmines.View image in fullscreenThe sea by Agua Amarga is still warm in autumn.Photograph: Dronie_Spain/ShutterstockThis corner of Spain is famous for its movie locations, notably Sergio Leone’s spaghetti westerns and Hollywood blockbusters including Lawrence of Arabia and Conan the Barbarian. For UK cinephiles, British gangster classic Sexy Beast was filmed in Agua Amarga, and Ray Winstone’s swanky villa is available as a holiday rental (minus the boulder in the swimming pool).The name Agua Amarga translates as “bitter water”, dating back to the 19th century and the contamination caused by mining iron ore. Those days are gone, and now Agua Amarga couldn’t be sweeter.Hotel Las Calashasdoublesfrom £80Lois PryceCascais,PortugalView image in fullscreenCascais was once the summer retreat of Europe’s nobility.Photograph: Chunyip Wong/Getty ImagesAs many of Portugal’s southern resorts prepare to hibernate for winter, Cascais’s green-fingered municipal workers set to work on the town’s well-manicured flower beds, ensuring a seamless seasonal rotation. Violas, primroses and cyclamen furnish pops of purple, magenta and orange below tall palms lining a promenade punctuated with palatial homes and pockets of golden sand. Even in late autumn, the semi-tropical scene banishes the blues.My happy place when the off-season rolls around, Cascais has enough energy and atmosphere to entertain, and is arguably at its finest after summer’s beach throngs and Lisbon day trippers (Cascais lies 20 miles west of the city, a 30- to 40-minute train ride from Cais do Sodré station) have receded.double quotation markCascais’s main off-season pull is for those who like to be active outdoorsOnce the summer retreat of Europe’s nobility, Cascais is now Portugal’s year-round crowd-pleaser – and come autumn, accommodation prices are far less aristocratic. There are stately manors and spa hotels aplenty, but my pick isCasa Vela, a surprisingly spacious sidestreet bolthole. Its sauna, shrouded in tropical gardens imported by the owner and his grandfather, brings joy even on the chilliest days. And if rains do come, there are a clutch of cultural attractions in the town, including the pyramid-shaped, terracotta-huedCasa das Histórias Paula Rego, featuring works by the acclaimed Portuguese-British artist.Still, with about 300 sunny days a year, Cascais’s main off-season pull is for those who like to be active outdoors. Blue-sky mornings see waterfront joggers pass pretty squares carpeted in black-and-whitecalçada portuguesa(the distinctive patterned pavement mosaics), the hulking 15th-centurycitadel, and amustard-hued palaceoverlooking a cove. Swimming is bracing, but kayaking on the calmer waters where the Tagus River meets the Atlantic more than compensates.View image in fullscreenCasa das Histórias Paula Rego in Cascais.Photograph: Witold Skrypczak/AlamyBetter still, hire a bicycle and trace the craggy coastline, which grows wilder as it arches north-west, with sheer cliffs appearing in the distant haze. Praia do Guincho is the star, a glorious dune-backed beach battered by winds that keep surfers of all stripes well sated.A half-hour bus ride from Cascais, Sintra’s iconic palaces andquintasunfurl across the forest-clad mountains. Summer in the town will test your patience. But with fewer crowds in the off-season, the essence of this former elite enclave and trove of European Romantic architecture returns. Hiking the hewn stairs to theMoorish Castlein thick fog is magical, while the vibrant burgundy-and-yellow facade of the fairytaleNational Palace of Penabrightens the greyest of days.As the nights start to draw in, you can chase the dwindling sunlight by heading to windswept Cabo da Roca at Portugal’s far western tip. Not only are the sunsets here spectacular, for much of autumn and winter they are the latest in mainland Europe – a sweetener for the shorter days.Casa Velahasdoubles from €79 room-onlyDaniel James Clarkeskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSenigallia,ItalyView image in fullscreenSenigallia and its Velvet Beach.Photograph: Michal Szymel/AlamyVelvet Beach (Spiaggia di Velluto) is the alluring name for the miles of fine sand that fringe the town of Senigallia, in Italy’s Marche region. But from May to September, that golden loveliness all but disappears under the umbrellas and sunbeds of beach clubs.Italians love the place, some returning every summer for decades, but in high season it is probably best left to them. However, Senigallia has an allure beyond the beach that can be enjoyed year-round – and autumn is particularly rewarding.double quotation markIt’s hard to eat badly here, but fish fans will relish the exquisitely prepared raw stuff at Cuoco di BordoIt’s known in Italy as the “five-star town” for the number of Michelin stars its top two restaurants hold between them. AtUliassi(three stars) andMadonnina del Pescatore(two), ambitious locally born chefs have kept one another on their toes for decades, and their fame has encouraged other restaurateurs to up their game.If Uliassi’s famous €280 tasting menu is beyond your budget, Senigallia has plenty of innovative, quality places that are more affordable. It’s hard to eat badly here, but fish fans will relish the exquisitely prepared raw stuff atCuocodi Bordo(two courses from €34) on the seafront. The more rusticRimante(two courses from €27), in the cobbled centre, offers super-friendly service, great pasta and a roast goose speciality. For pizza nights, nearbyO’sarracinhas superlative margheritas (€8.50) and tasty ragù-filledarancinito start.View image in fullscreenSenigallia is renowned for seafood restaurants such as the Michelin-starred Madonnina del Pescatore.Photograph: Brambilla SerraniPizza al formaggio, by contrast, isn’t pizza at all, but a sort of savoury panettone, flavoured with parmesan and pecorino cheese, maybe with chunks oozing out of a warm slice. It’s usually an Easter treat, but bakeryPandefràmakes it from October until May. Autumn in Senigallia also brings amazing fresh produce (chestnuts, persimmons, grapes and pomegranates; pumpkins, greens and radicchio) to chefs and market stalls.And, of course, it brings the olive harvest, with new oil to taste in local delis and at theFesta dell’Olio Nuovo(6-10 November) in Scapezzano, three miles inland, reached by a pleasant hour’s walk up the quiet Strada di Fontenuovo (there’s a bus back).With so much eating, you do need to work up an appetite. Hiking theHeron Trailalong the Misa River will help, and offers downy oaks in their autumn finery, but the best walk for me starts at the splendidRotonda a Maregallery on its 1930s pier, heads inland on quiet lanes to Gabriella and Montignano villages, then descends to the coast for a sunset stroll back along that – now peaceful – Velvet Beach.Al Foro Annonariohasdoublesfrom €80 B&BLiz BoulterSaint-Jean-de-Luz,FranceView image in fullscreenSaint-Jean-de-Luz holds on to the warmth of summer a little longer than the rest of France’s west coast.Photograph: Mehdi33300/AlamyTucked away in the corner of France just before the Basque coast runs into Spain, Saint-Jean-de-Luz hangs on to the warmth of summer a little longer than the rest of the west coast. Its enticing crescent beach is sheltered by two headlands and so, as the Atlantic crashes against the rest of the coast, you can dig your toes into the golden sand as the sea gently laps the shore and truly feel as if you’ve escaped the world.The town makes for a great introduction to the French Basque Country, with its traditional red or green timber-framed architecture, adorned in many cases with strings of the localespelettechilli pepper – its gentle heat infuses many of the local dishes. Pick up a pot at the local market hall, which is a good place to find other hero products of the local cuisine, such as Ossau-Iraty cheese and black cherry jam.double quotation markAs you cruise past the Flysch cliffs, you might spot a few silver flying fish jumping out of the steely blue AtlanticElsewhere, the patisserieMaison Adamis the place to find the local almond macaron called theparegabea(it means incomparable in Basque), which was first made in 1660 to celebrate the marriage of King Louis XIV and Marie-Thérèse of Spain. Their nuptials took place just round the corner at the Saint-Jean-de-Baptiste church – half-built at the time – which has an extraordinarily detailed gilt altarpiece that was installed in 1669, as well as a three-tiered gallery for the congregation. Meanwhile, a votive ship hanging from the ceiling is a nod to the town’s close relationship to the sea, with small fishing boats departing the neat harbour to fish for hake, a local speciality.You can venture out on to the seas too, with aboat tripon the small cruiser Nivelle V (€20), which goes along the coast towards Spain, first passing the 17th-century cylindrical fort at Socoa and its sea wall that juts across the bay. As you cruise past the Flysch cliffs, which look like layers of diagonally stacked cardboard, you might spot a few silver flying fish jumping out of the steely blue Atlantic.View image in fullscreenThe neighbouring village of Ciboure.Photograph: Andia/AlamyOn arrival back at port, take the short walk across the bridge that spans the River Nivelle to the neighbouring village of Ciboure. It’s a warren of red and green Basque townhouses that overlook narrow streets winding up the hill. Between them sits the restaurantChez Mattin(mains from €28), a local institution, where chef Michel Niquet serves his signature dish, ttorro, a fish stew that was invented by his grandfather.TheMadisonhas doubles from€125. For more information, seesaint-jean-de-luz.comCarolyn BoydAll accommodation prices are for October/November and were correct at the time of publicationExplore more on these topicsEurope holidaysPortugal holidaysItaly holidaysSpain holidaysFrance holidaysBeach holidaysTurkey holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Never put away a damp one!’: 15 expert tips for perfect pans | Food | The Guardian
description: Should you buy cast iron, copper or stainless steel? How do you store them? And what about seasoning? Here is everything you need to know
Author: Ammar Kalia
Headline: Should you buy cast iron, copper or stainless steel? How do you store them? And what about seasoning? Here is everything you need to know
Content: Choose your weapon.Photograph: Maskot/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenChoose your weapon.Photograph: Maskot/Getty ImagesFood‘Never put away a damp one!’: 15 expert tips for perfect pansShould you buy cast iron, copper or stainless steel? How do you store them? And what about seasoning? Here is everything you need to knowAmmar KaliaSun 18 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 00.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChoosing the right pan can be a mind-boggling task. There’s a plethora of options, from stainless-steel skillets to heavy cast-iron pans, non-stick products coated in PTFE chemicals to carbon steel, blue steel, copper, ceramic and enamel, to name just a few. Are some materials and styles better to cook with than others? Do you need to tailor your pan to the type of hob? And once you have selected your cookware, how do you take care of it properly? Here is everything you could possibly want to know about pans.What are pans typically made of?Most pans fall into three categories: stainless steel, non-stick and cast iron. Stainless steel pans tend to be a favourite for restaurant kitchens owing to their durability and even heating capability, while cast-iron skillets, griddle pans and casserole pots also withstand high heating and retain temperatures for searing and frying. Non-stick pans – often known as Teflon – are usually coated in PTFE chemicals to allow for easy cleaning and cooking with less oil. Chemical-free non-stick pans generally have a ceramic coating.Carbon steel pans are a lightweight hybrid of stainless steel and cast iron designed to be more reactive to heating. Other metal alloys include copper (a historical favourite of haute cuisine French kitchens due to its extremely sensitive heat conductivity) and titanium, which is used for its durability. “There isn’t one type of pan that works for everything,” says Nicola Lando, founder of online cookware shopSous Chef. “It’s down to personal preference and the type of cooking you like to do.”View image in fullscreenNo pan is a magic bullet. Pick the one that works best for you.Photograph: Lyndon  Stratford/Getty ImagesWhat is the best all-round pan?“Stainless steel is a fantastic all-rounder,” says Lando. “It can take a bashing, be cleaned in the dishwasher and is very versatile. It gives a deep, even caramelisation to whatever’s being cooked in it.” Lando recommends a “tri-ply” – three layers of stainless steel fused together – for the most consistent durability. A heavy-bottomed copper insert in the base of the pan offers the benefits of copper’s conductivity at a fraction of the cost of a full copper pan.“Home cooks can be preoccupied with food sticking on stainless steel, but if you start with it on a high heat for a few minutes, until when you flick water on to the surface it beads off, it will behave like a non-stick,” she says. “Then you can turn it down if you need – just make sure you’re using enough oil. And if you’re searing meat, leave it for long enough to form a crust before you move it around the pan. Over time and lots of use, the stainless steel will build its own slightly non-stick patina from the emulsions created through cooking.”What about heavy-duty cooking?Cast iron is heavier and denser, making it better for high temperatures or prolonged, low-and-slow cooks. “The thickness and density of the material means heat remains in the pan, rather than being transferred immediately to the ingredients,” says Tom Walker, the head of operations and food education atHackney School of Food. “That means it might take a while to get it hot, but once it’s up to temperature it will stay there, making it great for stews that need simmering for a long time. Its durability also means cast iron can deal well with open flames.”Cast iron also builds even more of a patina than stainless steel over time, lending a smokiness or charred flavour to ingredients.Studies have shownthat cooking in cast iron can even increase your levels of iron consumption, through small amounts of iron leaching into food. It’s important to remember that most cast iron and stainless steel pans don’t have heatproof handles and need to be used with tea towels or mitts once hot – though this also means they’re ovenproof.View image in fullscreenCast iron is heavy, dense and durable, making it great for high temperatures.Photograph: leolintang/Getty ImagesIs there a good pan for beginners?For Walker, a non-stick pan with a PTFE or ceramic coating is an essential for any home cook. “It takes the stress out of cooking, since you might not know what heat levels are right for your pan or how much oil to use, and non-sticks are very forgiving. They’re great for delicate, tricky items like eggs or fish,” he says. “Provided you don’t use metal utensils or harsh scourers on them and scratch off the non-stick coating, they can be very easy to wash up and keep using.”What about the rest?Copper pans are known for their responsive heat conduction, meaning they will get hot faster and cool down quicker than other pans. “They give chefs more control when cooking,” Lando says. “You can’t have the copper come into contact with food so older pans are lined with tin, which has a natural sort of non-stick to it but it will wear off with time, while newer ones are coated with stainless steel.”Carbon steel, blue steel and spun steel are all hybrids of stainless steel and cast iron that are oxidised and prepared using slightly different methods. “They’re nice pans but the challenge is that they oxidise, so you have to dry them thoroughly, otherwise they rust,” says Lando. “They’re good value and they develop a nice patina but you have to take care of them.”View image in fullscreenA home cook might only need two sizes of pans.Photograph: John Keeble/Getty ImagesDoes size matter?Yes! Your pan should correspond with the size of your hob. If you use a small pan on a large cooker plate, for instance, you run the risk of dirtying or damaging the outside edges of the pan. Gabriel Waterhouse, chef-owner of London’sWaterhouse restaurant, recommends only two sizes of pans for home cooks. “You can reduce it to a medium-depth skillet pan with sides that you can saute and fry and move ingredients around in, and a two-handled casserole pot with a lid,” he says. “You should be able to do all of your jobs on all different levels of heat with those.”Should I buy specialist pans for different types of cooking?Although the frying pan and casserole combination is a good catch-all, if you find yourself constantly coming back to one type of dish or preparation, it might be worth investing in a specialist pan. “At our restaurant we do a lot of cooking over open fire, so cast iron is great for that,” says Ben Chamberlain, head chef atMediterranean restaurant Wild. “A lot of people use griddle pans for steaks but I wonder about aesthetic over flavour with those. You have nice bar marks but ultimately you want maximum surface contact for a nice caramelised crust.”View image in fullscreenWoks are great pans for stir-frying and other types of fast cooking.Photograph: simonkr/Getty ImagesWalker also recommends buying a wok if fast cooking and stir-frying are on the menu. “You need to get them very hot so that oil smokes when you add it, but woks are so thin it’s like cooking over an open flame,” he says. “Flat-bottomed woks are really versatile. When I went off to university that’s all I took with me and it was perfect.”For Palestinian chef Fadi Kattan, co-founder ofNotting Hill’s Akub, specialist pans can have a personal connection to culture and heritage. “The fukhara, our traditional Palestinian earthenware pot, heats slowly and gently, encouraging a completely different relationship with cooking. You cannot rush it,” he says. “These vessels connect us to generations of Palestinian cooking, local pottery traditions and the relationship with the land.”Think about what you’re cookingAs important as your choice of pan is the preparation of your ingredients. “You need to make sure that fish is patted dry before you put it into the pan skin-first, otherwise it will stick,” says Roberta Hall-McCarron, chef-owner ofArdfern restaurant. “Allow things to take on a proper sear first and don’t turn your ingredients too fast or they will break apart. Have confidence in getting the pan hot enough, particularly if it’s stainless steel, and don’t overcrowd the pan, otherwise it’ll draw the heat out too quickly.”How does the type of cooker I have affect my pans?Most modern pans should work across the three main types of cooker: gas, electric and induction. Since induction works using magnetism, the metal alloy in the pan needs to be appropriately conductive for it to work, and it is worth checking the details on the box before buying. “Older copper pans with a tin lining won’t work on an induction hob but almost all others do,” says Lando. “You should also be careful if you have a really thin pan on an induction as the magnetic vibration could damage its shape or structure.”View image in fullscreenMost of your pans should work across gas, electric or induction cookers.Photograph: Lighthouse Films/Getty ImagesWhat is seasoning?Seasoning is a way to protect your pan and help it to develop an emulsion and patina after repeated use, which adds flavour to your dishes. On cast iron this might look like a light crust on the base of your pan, while on stainless steel it’s a barely noticeable slick of oil. Most non-stick pans don’t need seasoning, although hybrid brands like HexClad recommend heating with oil before your first use, and some pans will come pre-seasoned.“With cast iron pans, typically you would get them hot and then coat with a small amount of oil before your first use,” says Ryan Vaughan, senior teacher atLeiths culinary school. “Then, after each time you use them and wash them up, get them dry and coat them with a small amount of neutral oil to keep that layer intact. With brand new woks you also need to heat them to oxidise the surface and then add a thin layer of oil.”If you accidentally scrub off the patina on a cast iron pan, you can take it back to the base metal and begin again. “It’s a great benefit of cast iron as it’s so hardy and forgiving,” says Lando. “You can re-season by scrubbing and then coating with layers of oil that you heat up or bake in the oven and it makes it good as new.”How should I clean my pans?Stainless steel pans can be scrubbed and scoured, as well as placed into the dishwasher, while non-stick and cast iron pans should be handled more delicately. “Cast iron builds up a natural seasoning after use that you don’t want to get rid of, so make sure to wash with warm water and a gentle soap and sponge,” says Vaughan. “It’s amazing what a good soak can do if you have something really stubborn stuck on. With non-stick coatings and ceramics you want to make sure not to scratch it and take that coating off. Similarly, use a soft sponge and soak, and don’t use metal utensils.”View image in fullscreenA soft sponge is vital for maintaining your pans.Photograph: Pekic/Getty ImagesAnd how should I store them?“Never put away a damp pan,” says Lando. “Otherwise pans might start to develop rust. If you’ve been using a pan for a while, it might develop a slightly sticky emulsion on the surface that you don’t want to damage, so if you’re stacking them in a drawer you can put a tea towel or bit of kitchen paper between them.”What is Teflon?Discovered in 1938 by 27-year-old chemist Dr Roy J Plunkett, polytetrafluoroethylene or PTFE was a plastic found to have extreme heat and chemical resistance. During the second world war the polymer was used in the Manhattan Project in the construction of the atomic bomb, and NASA has used the material in its insulation and thermal shields for the Apollo moon landing. The trademark Teflon was registered by Plunkett’s employer DuPont, and by the 1950s it had been bonded to stainless steel to create the first non-stick cookware.View image in fullscreenAll non-stick coatings eventually wear off. Replace them once they start to chip or scratch.Photograph: Kathrin Ziegler/Getty ImagesWhat are the risks of PTFE coatings?PTFE is often referred to as a “forever chemical”, since it takes thousands of years to degrade, making it potentially environmentally toxic if disposed of incorrectly. Thankfully, non-stick cookware production renders PTFE inert, although if you manage to scorch your pan at over 260C, the coating begins to break down and can cause what has been nicknamed the “Teflon flu” – a feverish headache developed after breathing in toxic fumes.“People generally don’t cook above 180C or 200C so you shouldn’t be at risk of breaking down that material,” says Lando. “If you buy from a well-regarded UK retailer, they would have done food safety checks and it should be completely fine. But all non-stick coatings will come off eventually, and once they start to chip or scratch you should replace them.Can I make my pans last for ever?“Treat your pans well and they will treat you well,” says Chamberlain. “There’s no reason why stainless steel and cast iron pans can’t last for life if you take care of them properly. It’s often worth investing a bit more in a good quality pan at the beginning – it will pay off as you use it for many years to come. They’re an inheritance.”Explore more on these topicsFoodRestaurantsChefsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘There’s a lot of racism, a lot of hatred’: Far right gains predicted as Israel heads to the polls | Israel | The Guardian
description: Whether or not Netanyahu can hold on to power, Israelis are expected to vote in a more rightwing Knesset
Author: Emma Graham-Harrison
Headline: Whether or not Netanyahu can hold on to power, Israelis are expected to vote in a more rightwing Knesset
Content: Itamar Ben-Gvir, Israel’s national security minister, is head of the far-right Jewish Strength party, forecast to win nine seats on 27 October. Photograph: Ilia Yefimovich/AFP/Getty ImagesWhether or not Netanyahu can hold on to power, Israelis are expected to vote in a more rightwing KnessetByEmma Graham-HarrisonSun 18 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 10.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFour decades ago, when the extremist rabbiMeir Kahanewon a single seat in Israel’s Knesset, other legislators passed a law to prevent him running again, left the chamber when he rose to speak and worked together to block discussion of his ethnonationalist proposals.These ranged from mass expulsions of Palestinians to apartheid provisions such as segregated beaches and the criminalisation of sex between Jews and gentiles.This month, Kahane’s political heirs may claim more Knesset seats in national elections than the remains of the once mighty Labor party, home of Yitzhak Rabin, Shimon Peres and Golda Meir.View image in fullscreenRightwing leader and rabbi Meir Kahane carried by supporters through the streets of Jerusalem after he won a seat in the Israeli parliament in July 1984.Photograph: APAt an election rally this week, Israel’s national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, mixed calls for ethnic cleansing and jokes about starving Palestinian prisoners with a proud anecdote about hisconvictionin 1998 over bumper stickers that read “Rabbi Kahane was right”.A poll for theIsraelHayom newspaper, published on Friday, forecast his Jewish Strength party would win nine seats in the 27 October election. The Democrats, successor to the Labor party led by former general Yair Golan, were predicted to claim eight seats.Ben-Gvir’s rise is one of the more extreme manifestations of a broad shift to the right among Jewish citizens of Israel. It is particularly pronounced among the young and will shape the country’s next government, regardless of who becomes prime minister after closely fought elections.More than 500,000 Israelis have reached voting age since the last election in 2022, and three-quarters of first-time Jewish voters define themselves as right or centre-right, a recent poll for Channel 12 television found (itdid not surveyPalestinian citizens of Israel).View image in fullscreenYoung supporters of Itamar Ben-Gvir shout slogans as he tours a market during a meet and greet in Ramla on 14 October.Photograph: Ilia Yefimovich/AFP/Getty ImagesThe generation voting for the first time came of age after the Oslo process collapsed, when the prospect of negotiating a political resolution to the Israel-Palestine conflict seemed to be fading.They were teenagers during the Hamas attacks on 7 October 2023, which resulted in the deaths of about 1,200 people, the majority of them civilians. Militants took 251 living hostages and dead bodies to Gaza, leading to a two-year hostage crisis.“There’s a lot of people, especially young people, who think that there is no solving the conflict, that we’ll always be at war. There’s a lot of racism, a lot of hatred, but most of all, there’s fear,” said Erez Uzan, vice-chair of the Young Democrats.Bucking global trends, young Israelis are more rightwing than older generations and are likely to vote in a new Knesset with morerightwing membersthan the current chamber, said Dahlia Scheindlin, a political analyst and public opinion researcher.Consistently rightwing ultra-Orthodox and nationalist religious communities make up a growing proportion of Israel’s Jewish population but still account for only around a quarter of the electorate, so demographics alone do not explain the growing age gap on political issues.View image in fullscreenA mural titled RUN by artist Alexsandro Palombo, depicting Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and politician Gadi Eisenkot wearing bulletproof vests and carrying batons as they chase Bart Simpson, portrayed as a young Hamas fighter, in Tel Aviv.Photograph: Jack Guez/AFP/Getty Images“All Israelis, and particularly younger people, have been living in a political environment where not only is the government rightwing but the general terms of debate are really populist and ultra-nationalist. That’s all they know. They’re socialised into it,” Scheindlin said.“There’s been a real downplaying of anything to do with democracy, universal values or human rights. Those are seen as weak, if they’re discussed at all, possibly as bad as betrayal. And very few politicians talk about peace, concessions, negotiations, Palestinian self-determination, or even Palestinian wellbeing.”A consistent majority of Israeli polls show prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s current coalition bloc with the ultra-Orthodox and the far right will fall well below the threshold of 61 seats needed to form a government.View image in fullscreenPeople protest outside the Israeli high court in support of granting Arab parties the right to run in the upcoming general elections.Photograph: Debbie Hill/UPI/ShutterstockThe opposition has a clear path to power through an alliance with parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel, known as Arab parties inside the country. But the political shift right means most of the Jewish-led parties have ruled out such a coalition, although similar promises have been broken after past elections.Particularly when it comes to Palestine, most offer little challenge to Netanyahu’s claim that security can only be pursued through military domination and annexation of territory from Gaza to Syria and Lebanon.The peace deals that secured Israel’s borders with Jordan and Egypt, once seen as no less an existential threat than Iran is today, do not feature in political debate as an alternative path.Their campaigns focus on other issues, from promises to tackle corruption and bring accountability for the 7 October attacks to improving schools and stopping ultra-Orthodox draft dodging.View image in fullscreenGadi Eisenkot, former Israeli army chief of staff and head of the Yashar party, delivers a statement during a press conference at the Black Arrow memorial site near the Mefalsim kibbutz, adjacent to the Gaza Strip, on 15 October.Photograph: Ilia Yefimovich/AFP/Getty ImagesUnpolished, anti-Bibi, but evasive on peace: who is the Israeli opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot?Read moreThe man leading the field to replace Netanyahu,Gadi Eisenkot, is a former head of the Israeli military who formulated thenotorious Dahiya doctrineof using “disproportionate force” to cause damage and destruction.Naftali Bennett is a former prime minister and former chair of the settler council, who supports annexing much of the West Bank. Avigdor Lieberman wants to dismantle the Palestinian Authority and replace it with an Israeli-Jordanian confederation (though apparently he did not consult the Jordanians about thisplan).View image in fullscreenFormer Israeli prime minister Naftali Bennett, leader of the Together (Beyachad) alliance, attends a ‘Democratic festival’ event in Ramat Hasharon on 13 October.Photograph: Amir Cohen/ReutersNo Jewish-led party backed a future Palestinian state and only the Democrats opposed settlement expansion, the Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper reported, after seeking all parties’ positions on the future of the occupied West Bank.Eisenkot’s Yashar party pledged to strengthen and expand settlements, which are legal under Israeli law. All settlements are illegal under international law.The Democrats, the only remaining political home for Israel’s Zionist left, are led by Golan, a former general and deputy head of Israel’s military who personally rushed to border communities under the Hamas attack on the morning of 7 October to rescue civilians.View image in fullscreenYoung Israelis gather to listen to the Democrats party leader and former Knesset member, Yair Golan, at a campaign event in Tel Aviv.Photograph: Ilia Yefimovich/AFP/Getty ImagesAlthough Golan supports a negotiated end to the conflict, he has avoided referencing a two-state solution in this campaign. He has put together a policy platform that would be solidly centrist in much of Europe. Yet even so, Israel’s political shift to the right is so pronounced that the party’s campaigners have been repeatedly attacked – physically and verbally – as a radical fringe.Last week, rightwing thugsassaultedDemocrats volunteers manning a stand at Jerusalem’s historic Mahane Yehuda market, kicking, hitting and spitting at the group and stealing a phone while police stood by and watched.View image in fullscreenDemocrats protest against a visit by the Israeli finance minister and leader of the Religious Zionist party Bezalel Smotrich to the Mahane Yehuda market on 9 October.Photograph: Abir Sultan/EPAThe scale of abuse prompted the party to train campaigners in non-violent direct action, “so they know how to handle themselves in a situation where they can keep safe and de-escalate,” said Uzan of the Young Democrats.The far right is on the rise globally, but Israeli politics that “revolve round constant conflict” heighten the appeal of ethnonationalist messages, Uzan said.“We grow up in fear, seeing war all around us – and that leads to a certain perspective. In the last 20 years, our leadership in the centre-left camp has avoided talking about security issues,” Uzan said, adding they had ceded that ground to the right.Now he and fellow campaigners are trying to tackle that failure at a grassroots level, including speaking to young people about the peace agreements with Egypt and Jordan that were unpopular when signed but have brought lasting stability.The process is slow but effective, he says, pointing to an active young membership several thousand strong, well above parties who attract more young voters.View image in fullscreenA man with a flag wrapped around his shoulders featuring an image of Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, walks through Mahane Yehuda market in Jerusalem on 16 October.Photograph: John Wessels/AFP/Getty ImagesComedian turned activist Lior Schleien has been trying to have similar conversations with groups of young Israelis about the deadly futility of pursuing “total victory” in endless wars. He posts footage of some of the most shocking exchanges, featuring smiling teens advocating on camera for the mass killing or expulsion of Palestinians.“Lots of Arabs live here. They were born here, they are citizens like you and me. What will you do with them?” Schleien asksone group.“Kill them … give me a knife and I’ll murder them,” says one young man.Ben-Gvir is particularly adept on social media, where posts like a recent AI video laying outplansfor ethnic cleansing have helped build moreengagementwith young voters than any Israeli politician except Netanyahu.But he is not an outlier for extremism among allies of the prime minister. Finance minister Bezalel Smotrich is a messianic settler who recentlycalled to“wipe out Gaza”, and has vowed to “bury” a future Palestinian state.View image in fullscreenPeople walk past a bus with an election campaign banner for Moshe Feiglin of the Zehut party in Jerusalem.Photograph: John Wessels/AFP/Getty ImagesFor this election, Smotrich has joined forces with Moshe Feiglin, afundamentalistwho has long called for the mass expulsion of Palestinians and the construction of a biblical Jewish temple where the al-Aqsa mosque compound now stands.The rise of the far right and religious fundamentalism, combined with Netanyahu’s assault on institutions protecting Israel’s partial democracy (Palestinians living under Israeli military rule in the occupied West Bank do not have the rights of citizens), mean many Israelis on the centre and left see this vote as existential.David Harel, the president of the Israel Academy of Sciences and Humanities, says the country’s current path leads towards a bleak future as a corrupt, impoverished pariah state, dominated by messianic fundamentalists maintaining a “violent, cruel occupation”.“We are already in ‘stoppage time’. If we lose this time, there will be no second chance. The country we love so dearly will breathe its last. Plain and simple!” he told a rally in the northern city of Haifa.“That is why I have come here today, to ask and to implore. And if necessary, I will get down on my knees and beg. Please, please, please! Just go out and vote!”Explore more on these topicsIsraelMiddle East and north AfricaThe far rightIsrael-Gaza warBenjamin NetanyahufeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Getaway cars, affairs, Dubai fugitives: Trump’s pick Ken Paxton brings baggage to Senate race in Texas | Ken Paxton | The Guardian
description: The Republican state attorney general appears uniquely ill-chosen as a candidate – but he is a political survivor who could yet frustrate Democratic dreams
Author: J Oliver Conroy
Headline: The Republican state attorney general appears uniquely ill-chosen as a candidate – but he is a political survivor who could yet frustrate Democratic dreams
Content: Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general and Republican US Senate candidate, in San Antonio on 7 October 2026.Photograph: Christopher Lee/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKen Paxton, the Texas attorney general and Republican US Senate candidate, in San Antonio on 7 October 2026.Photograph: Christopher Lee/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesKen PaxtonGetaway cars, affairs, Dubai fugitives: Trump’s pick Ken Paxton brings baggage to Senate race in TexasThe Republican state attorney general appears uniquely ill-chosen as a candidate – but he is a political survivor who could yet frustrate Democratic dreamsJ Oliver ConroySun 18 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 10.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDepending how you look at the situation, it is either predictable thatKen Paxton,Texas’s attorney general and Republican candidate forUS Senate, is struggling in the polls – or impressive that he is not doing worse. Beloved by hardcore Maga voters and regarded with skepticism by the broader voting public, Paxton is also puzzlingly bland. Recently, Donald Trumptolda crowd of supporters that the 63-year-old Paxton “may not dress right, he may not talk exactly perfectly, and he may not be the best-looking guy I’ve ever seen”. The president was endorsing him.Yet it is Paxton’s ability to attract – and somehow scrape through – scandal that makes him a less charismatic, perhaps, but still kindred spirit of “Teflon Don”: nothing sticks. He has survived state prosecution (on securities-related charges that he settled without admitting guilt), impeachment by theRepublican-led Texas legislature (on abuse-of-office charges of which he was later acquitted), and so many controversies that it can be difficult to pin down the most outrageous.There was the time in 2011 that God appeared to a tech entrepreneur in a red-roofed Dairy Queen in McKinney,Texas, and told him to give 100,000 shares of company stock to Paxton, then a state legislator, in what the entrepreneur called a gift and critics called an illegal commission. (Paxton and the entrepreneur denied that allegation.) There was the time in 2013 that Paxton allegedly stole a fellow lawyer’s $1,000 Montblanc pen. (Paxton said that it was a mix-up while going through a security screening at a courthouse.)Then there was the time in 2020 that eight of Paxton’s staffers asked the FBI to investigate whether their boss had, as attorney general, abused his office to help a real estate investor and political donor – in return for a free kitchen renovation and a job for a woman with whom Paxton was having an affair. (Paxton and the real estate investor denied those allegations; the investor was never charged with a crime and Paxton’s impeachment over the matter ended in acquittal.)View image in fullscreenDonald Trump and Ken Paxton at a rally in San Antonio on 7 October 2026.Photograph: Evan Vucci/ReutersAnd there was the time in 2022 that Paxton’s wife, state senator Angela Paxton, allegedly helped him escape, in a Chevrolet truck, from someone trying to serve him with a subpoena for a federal court case. (Paxton said that the man was harassing him.) That screwball romcom ended sadly, however, when Angela Paxton filed for divorce last year on “biblical grounds”. Ken Paxton’s scandal sheet includes two alleged extramarital affairs.Paxton v Talarico: tens of millions of dollars pour into closely watched Texas Senate raceRead moreAll of it may be catching up to Paxton – an ultraconservative Republican, in a diverse but still very right-leaning state, who has somehow found himself in a muddy political trench fight with a babyfaced Democratic state legislator, James Talarico, whom Republicans have likened to a “Coexist”bumper stickerin human form. Talarico, 37, is a former teacher and a seminarian affiliated with an arch-progressive mainline Christian church in Austin. (Trump has dubbed him “Talafreako”.)Texas has not elected a single Democrat to statewide office since 1994 – the worst state losing streak, for either party, in the United States. But Paxton and Talarico are in a dead heat. Some polls evenshowTalarico leading.“This is the closest race that we’ve seen in the state in three decades,” James Henson, a political scientist and pollster who directs the Texas Politics Project, said. Rightwing groups in “red-alert mode”, he added, are pouring millions of dollars into the state to prop up Paxton and otherRepublicansfighting for election next month.Polls have, famously, been wrong before. But the fact that a Republican candidate in a Republican stronghold is struggling would be notable by itself even if this were not also one of the most high-profile of all the midterm elections. The race is critical to either party securing a Senate majority. It is already one of themostexpensiveof its kind in US history.View image in fullscreenDemocratic candidate James Talarico at a rally in San Marcos on 15 October 2026.Photograph: Eric Gay/APThe situation has put Paxton – a hard-right Maga sycophant endorsed by Trump over the misgivings of some other Republicans – under a harsh and unflattering light. Paxton has repeatedly dodged opportunities todebateTalarico, enabling Talarico’s campaign to paint him as cowardly.Less than a month before the election, Paxton’s woes keep growing. This week the Wall Street Journalreportedthat in 2024, he was filmed at a New Year’s Eve party in Dubai in the company of an extramarital girlfriend and two men who were under indictment for federal healthcare fraud and considered fugitives from justice. One of them had donated $190,000 to Paxton.His campaign has shrugged off the new reporting. “Like President Trump, Ken Paxton has been politically persecuted for years,” a spokesman told the Wall Street Journal. “[A]nd every time, voters have seen through it and sent him back to office because they know he has always fought for Texas.”Yet in a series of audio clips leaked to the news media by unnamed sources over the past several weeks, even Paxton could be heard admitting, in closed-room conversations with conservative allies, that he and other Republicans in Texas were struggling.In one clip, he seemed to say that Trump’s recent midterm convention in Texas – where voters, as elsewhere, are furious about high fuel costs worsened by the Iran war – had hurt more than helped. (Trump’s approval numbers, according to recent polling, are at adire low.) In another, he said, “I’ve never been in a race where I felt less control over the campaign … it’s all coming – you know – from DC.”View image in fullscreenGas prices at a Shell station in Houston on 2 October 2026.Photograph: Ronaldo Schemidt/AFP/Getty ImagesWere the tapes leaked by Republicansunhappyat the resources the party is expending to save the flailing Paxton? Or by loyalists of John Cornyn, the longtime Republican senator whom Paxton knifed in a party primary, earlier this year, and displaced as the Republican nominee?Whatever the case, the tapes are embarrassing. “I thought that was a bad look for Ken Paxton,” Brandon Rottinghaus, a political scientist at the University of Houston, said. “It makes it look like he’s not grateful for all of the help that’s come to him. He needed all the attention that Trump can give. It may be that it comes with these caveats, and it’s not an unqualified good. But without Donald Trump, there would be no Ken Paxton.”‘Scandal resilience’As attorney general of Texas, Paxton sued the states of Pennsylvania, Michigan, Wisconsin and Georgia for, he claimed, voting irregularities that had stolen the 2020 presidential election from Trump. The lawsuit lacked evidence and critics on both sides of the aisle accused the lawsuit of being a political stunt and legal farce; some evenspeculatedthat Paxton was vying to win Trump’s favor in case his legal problems necessitated a presidential pardon. (Paxton’s campaign did not reply to an opportunity to provide comment for this story.)Earlier this year Trump repaid Paxton’s loyalty when he endorsed him for Senate over Cornyn – the more bipartisan, respected and generally less scandal-prone politician who had represented Texas in the Senate, as a conservative Republican, since 2002.Journalists, ex-employees, and political opponents have alsoquestionedPaxton’s expensive and jet-setting tenure as attorney general, as well as the perks he has enjoyed and the energy he has often seemed to devote to building a national profile in the Maga movement, according to critics, instead of solving problems in Texas.View image in fullscreenSenator John Cornyn at the US Capitol last month.Photograph: Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty ImagesOf course, many Texans are well aware of Paxton’s alleged trespasses, some of which go back years, and have repeatedly elected him to office anyway. (The pen-theft allegation is less well-known, though the Talarico campaign – which did not respond to a query from the Guardian – recently begansellingballpoint pens marked “Not Ken Paxton’s Pen”.)Jed Silverman, an attorney who prosecuted the state securities case against Paxton, noted that, in the eyes of the law, Paxton has a clean bill of health. “My opinion of him, my subjective belief one way or another, really doesn’t matter,” he said. “He made an agreement with the state, did what he was supposed to do, and got his cases resolved.”For his part, Rottinghaus, whose recent research has studied politicians’ ability to navigate scandal, views Paxton’s career as “a textbook example of ‘scandal resilience’”. Political polarization, he noted, “has raised the standards for what a scandal breaking point is”. Voters in the Republican or Democratic bases are more likely to weigh their candidate’s alleged ethical lapses against a sense that their party “needs to win”.Bill Miller, a Texas political consultant and lobbyist, made a similar point. “Baggage is something that the American public seemingly has learned to accept,” he said. Trump has “been elected twice, and everyone knows who he is and all that comes with that. I mean, people don’t expect squeaky clean. They hope theygetsqueaky clean, but they elect people who aren’t.”Miller noted that he has known Paxton for years and is friendly with him; despite Paxton’s blotted public image and reputation as bumbling and less than charismatic, he described him as a savvy operator with a Bill Clinton-style facility for remembering people’s names and a history of being underestimated by political opponents.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly, plus breaking news alertsSign up toThe Stakes 2026A weekly guide to what really matters in the US midterms, plus breaking news alerts.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSilverman, similarly, called Paxton a “political animal”.The national political climate is overwhelmingly tough right now for Republican candidates, and strategists and pollsters are predicting that the midterm elections could be a bruising referendum on Trump’s second presidency. From that vantage, Paxton is facing uniquely fierce headwinds, or is uniquely ill-chosen for the moment, or both. His unorthodox opponent has benefited.“TheDemocratswere looking for somebody who wasn’t a traditional politician,” Rottinghaus said. “Talarico fit that mold. He kind of looks like a youth minister, he talks like a choirboy and he’s committed to his values, which Democrats like and independents feel like they can trust. He’s a good candidate in that way. There’s baggage, though, that people are ignoring.”View image in fullscreenJames Talarico at a grocery drive in Dallas on 9 September 2026.Photograph: Brandon Bell/Getty ImagesTalarico has never held a statewide elected office. And, though he has tilted toward the center, he has arecordof statements and policy stances that would be eyebrow-raisingly “woke” in Brooklyn, let alone in suburban Texas. Republicans are growing frustrated, Rottinghaus added, because they believe that he has been able to define himself to the public in a “way that isn’t the real James Talarico”.Based on remarks Talarico made in the past about the environmental costs of eating meat, conservatives have even accused him of being a closeted vegetarian, a charge that he denies. In March, his campaignposteda photograph, hostage-style, of Talarico eating barbecue.This month Talarico disappeared from the campaign trail for more than a week, prompting Democratic concerns as well as wild Republican rumors that he was secretly seeking mental health treatment in Ohio; his campaign has said that he had a bad flu, and had never been to Ohio. The campaign went so far as toprovidethe New York Times with time-stamped security camera footage from the days-long stretch that he was convalescing at home.‘The hide of a rhinoceros’Flipping a Texas Senate seat or governorship is a holy grail of the Democratic party: a seismic political victory that many hope could set the party on a path to winning the second-largest state in the union in a presidential election. The last time that happened was 1976.Anatomy of a lie: James Talarico got the flu – sending rightwing midterm misinformation machine into overdriveRead moreFor Republicans, losing to Talarico would be psychologically shattering – though there are those who might argue, perhaps with some credence, that Paxton was a uniquely flawed candidate.Yet the memory of Beto O’Rourke’s 2018 longshot bid to unseat Senator Ted Cruz still haunts Democrats. O’Rourke attracted enormous Democratic enthusiasm and money but ultimately lost by 2.6 percentage points. Democratic donors felt burned. After a short-lived presidential bid, O’Rourke ran again in 2022 – for Texas governor, against incumbent Greg Abbott – and lost by an even larger margin.Despite Paxton’s tainted image and tight poll numbers, there are factors in his favor.One ismoney. Nationally and in Texas – and even as Democrats are reporting impressivefundraisingin key races – Republicans have a considerable advantage in campaign spending. To protect the seat of Governor Abbott, a Republican fighting for re-election against the Democratic state representative Gina Hinojosa, a conservative political action committee has beenspending, by one estimate, nearly $1m a day.“Paxton or any other Republican on the ballot is a beneficiary” of Abbott’s spending, Miller said, “because what that money does is find Republicans under every bush and rock and make sure that they’re motivated and they vote.”And Elon Musk is personally bankrolling a Super Pac to back Paxton’s Senate bid.View image in fullscreenKen Paxton watching Vice-President JD Vance speak at a rally in Tyler, Texas, on 13 October 2026.Photograph: Saul Loeb/Pool AFP/APRepublican get-out-the-vote efforts, meanwhile, seem aimed less at reaching undecided voters, according to Henson, the political scientist and pollster, and more at “shoring up support and enthusiasm among a probably relatively small, but still crucial, band of Republican voters who might be considering either sitting this election out entirely or at least not voting for Paxton”.Even Angela Paxton has nowappearedin a political ad urging Republican voters to support the ticket. “Either we hold every Republican seat, or we hand the future of Texas to the other team,” she argued. She did not mention her ex-husband, but the message was clear.The other advantage Paxton holds is the political composition of Texas. Although the state’s major cities tilt Democratic and the state has become more diverse, urban and “purple” in recent years, a slightly higher percentage of its population isruralcompared with other large states such as Florida and California. “Those small communities”, Miller said, were “not purple, they’re not orange, they’re blood-fucking-red”.So far, according to polling, Democrats in Texas are seeing higher enthusiasm from their base than Republicans are seeing from theirs, Henson said, though Republican enthusiasm has begun to pick up. In a few weeks, Texas will find out the results. Even if Paxton loses, he will no doubt land on his feet somewhere in Maga political world.“They say you need the sensitivity of a violinist and the hide of a rhinoceros to be good in this business,” Miller said. “Well, I don’t know if he has the sensitivity of a violinist, but he’s damn sure got the hide of a rhinoceros.”Explore more on these topicsKen PaxtonUS midterm elections 2026TexasRepublicansDemocratsUS politicsUS SenatefeaturesShareReuse this content
