title: Hilarious quips and ‘100,000-volt’ energy: the hypemen (and women) redefining Afrobeats music | Nigeria | The Guardian
description: Style of emceeing based on high-octane, ad-libbed vocals has flourished thanks to its unique way of captivating crowds
Author: Eromo Egbejule
Headline: Style of emceeing based on high-octane, ad-libbed vocals has flourished thanks to its unique way of captivating crowds
Content: Toby Shang, one of the leading lights of the growing Afrohype genre. Photograph: Sogo Oladele/The GuardianStyle of emceeing based on high-octane, ad-libbed vocals has flourished thanks to its unique way of captivating crowdsByEromo Egbejulein LagosSun 18 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 09.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor the 2015 freshmen cohort of the history degree programme at the University of Lagos, their classmate’s first-semester presentation was so captivating that they began calling him Toby Shang, after the 16th-century Chinese dynasty he had focused on.His crowd engagement that day had been harnessed from his high school days as a ginger-man (energiser) in a three-man band and as a private tutor. By his final year at university, his viral catchphrases and infectious energy had resulted in a hit song, Shedibalabala. Today, he is one of the self-acclaimed “evangelists and pioneers” in the Afrobeats sub-genre some are now calling Afrohype or lamba.View image in fullscreenToby Shang by the waterfront in the Lagos suburb of Akoka.Photograph: Sogo Oladele/The Guardian“Even my mother calls me Shang now,” the 32-year-old, born Tobi Michael Adeyeye, said in an interview near the university’s lagoon waterfront, where he once emceed gatherings.Since then he has hosted his own rave, released two EPs and run four editions of his School of Hype – a one-day masterclass with online mentoring that has launched several rising stars.Allow TikTok content?This article includes content provided byTikTok. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueHypemen neither sing nor rap entirely, but perform high-octane ad-libbed vocals“and onomatopoeic sounds” over fresh beats or popular instrumentals such as Dorime, a made-in-Nigeria version of 1996’s Ameno by the French group Era, a song that has become a continental nightclub classic. In response, nightclub patrons donate or spray money – the Nigerian custom of throwing or placing money on someone to celebrate them.Hype is now omnipresent at wedding after-parties, raves and corporate parties. On Instagram, one teenage sensation is now known for recording 30-second hypes for birthday celebrants at the request of friends or relatives.View image in fullscreenToby Shang made a name for himself while still a student at the University of Lagos.Photograph: Sogo Oladele/The Guardian“Hypemen have the gift of the gab and fine mic control,” said the London-based doctor and cultural critic Dami Ajayi, who encountered one at a party in Tirana last month. “He used the spaces between lyrics for hilarious quips, many of which were frontally risque and misogynistic,” he said.Despite being a male-dominated sub-genre, a few women have made their mark, such as the Yaoundé-based bikutsi artist Lady Ponce, known as the “100,000-volt lady” because of her energy. Other notable female figures in the scene includeDeborah ‘Hype Queen Baddy’ Francis– an alumnus of Shang’s school who died in September – and the radio presenter Melody “M.I.A” Adigo, both from Lagos.The art of hyping as it is known in west and centralAfricahas its roots in praise-singing and call-and-response music styles ingrained for centuries in Black populations on both sides of the Atlantic. In west Africa, this tradition took the form of oral historians known as griots. In the US, it was sustained by negro spirituals, sacred folk songs created by enslaved African Americans.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Long WaveNesrine Malik, Micha Frazer-Carroll and the team guide you through the biggest Black stories from around the worldEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe west has a blinkered view of African music – and it’s hurting the whole continent’s cultureRead moreThese styles laid the foundation for theatalaku(meaning “look here, look at me” in the Kikongo language of the DR Congo) tradition that came alive in 1980s Kinshasa, followed by today’s hype scene.Exponents of this style include the American gospel singer Kirk Franklin as well as the Congolese rumba bandleader Koffi Olomide and the Congolese singer Awilo Longomba.The success of Olomide and Longomba at the turn of the 21st century set off a craze in Côte d’Ivoire, wherecoupé-décalémusic embraced theatalakutrend alongsidefarotement, the act of showing off by throwing cash at performers or guests at parties.View image in fullscreenThe Congolese singer Koffi Olomide performing at a festival in Abidjan in September 2021.Photograph: Sia Kambou/AFP/GettyA line encouraging audiences to gallop like a horse in the Ivorian star DJ Arafat’s 2003viral homageto a late friend – “Tout le mondegalope, kirikata kirikata” – influenced later hits from Nigerian Afrobeats musicians Flavour N’abania and Skales.Côte d’Ivoire’s national television network, RTI, ran anatalakutalent hunt for several years. Lili Djely, an Ivorian woman of Malian origin, won the 2006 edition with a mix of Ivorian nouchi and French, defeating men to take the crown. In recent years, an MC/hypeman of the year category was introduced at the Ghana DJ awards as hype flourished there too.Allow TikTok content?This article includes content provided byTikTok. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueThanks to the success of Afrobeats, Afrohype is now widely recognised as a full-time career. As artists became more expensive to book after Covid-19, promoters turned to hypemen – previously criticised for simply doing voiceovers. Some are now reportedly paid as much as 5-8m naira (£2,844–4,550) for a 30-minute or one-hour performance.Some observers, however, say hype is a nuisance, amping up noise levels at events or encouraging fraudulent lifestyles, and that many performers do not customise language and tempo to fit the event.View image in fullscreenThe Congolese musician Awilo Longomba performing at the All Africa music awards in Lagos in November 2019.Photograph: Pius Utomi Ekpei/AFP/GettyNevertheless, hypemen are now a permanent fixture on the entertainment scene. For Shang, they are helping fun-seekers and club-goers get back on the dancefloor.“People are facing a lot of challenges … they need somebody to tell them money is coming in the new week,” he said. “Also, everybody wants to press their phones or show Birkin bags in clubs. Nobody wants to dance because dancing is seen as for small kids. You need a hypeman to bring out that childlike part in every person. A 60-year-old woman can start dancing like a young girl if the hype is good enough.”Explore more on these topicsNigeriaAfricaClub culturefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: An extraordinary life: descendant welcomes biography of woman ‘gifted’ to Queen Victoria | Colonialism | The Guardian
description: A girl called Àìná was captured by an African king and later taken to England to become Sarah Forbes Bonetta, protege of the imperial monarch
Author: Chris Osuh
Headline: A girl called Àìná was captured by an African king and later taken to England to become Sarah Forbes Bonetta, protege of the imperial monarch
Content: Sarah Forbes Bonetta was brought to England by Frederick Forbes, of the Royal Navy’s West Africa Squadron.Photograph: William Bambridge (1819-79)/Royal Collection TrustView image in fullscreenSarah Forbes Bonetta was brought to England by Frederick Forbes, of the Royal Navy’s West Africa Squadron.Photograph: William Bambridge (1819-79)/Royal Collection TrustColonialismAn extraordinary life: descendant welcomes biography of woman ‘gifted’ to Queen VictoriaA girl called Àìná was captured by an African king and later taken to England to become Sarah Forbes Bonetta, protege of the imperial monarchChris OsuhCommunity affairs correspondentSun 18 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen she was seven years old, Bayo Randle’s great-great-grandmother Sarah Forbes Bonetta was presented toQueen Victoriaat Windsor Castle as a “diplomatic gift” from an African king.Victoria would go on to pay for Bonetta’s education, approve her marriage to one of west Africa’s wealthiest men, and become godmother to her eldest daughter.But while Victoria took a genuine interest in Bonetta’s welfare, making the orphan a royal protege and meeting with her over the years, their relationship was part of a bigger agenda.Now, as a biography is published –Becoming Sarah Forbes Bonetta: A Yorùbá Woman in Queen Victoria’s Court– Randle has spoken of his family history.“I don’t think a human being, who has agency, could be ‘gifted’ from one to another, but had she not been gifted to Queen Victoria, would I be here today?” said Randle, a British-Nigerian barrister from London.View image in fullscreenBayo Randle, Bonetta’s great-great-grandson, is a barrister in London.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianThe new book, by a Canadian academic, Prof Henry Lovejoy, charts how Bonetta was brought to England by Frederick Forbes, of the Royal Navy’s West Africa Squadron, which was set up to enforce the abolition of the transatlantic trade.Born in 1843 in Òkè-Òdàn, south-west Nigeria,Bonettawas originally called Àìná. Her family was killed in 1848 when her town was attacked by King Ghezo of Dahomey’s forces.Bonetta, then five, is believed to have been captured by theagodjié– the all-female regiment depicted in the Hollywood movieThe Woman King– and held at King Ghezo’s court.View image in fullscreenThe book by Henry B Lovejoy.Photograph: suppliedIn 1850, Forbes went to Dahomey – which is nowBenin– to petition Ghezo to sign an anti-slavery treaty. The mission failed but Forbes asked Ghezo if he could take Bonetta to England.Bonetta would go on to live a life of renown, becoming one of the most artistically represented and widely reported African women of her time. But she was never truly free.Lovejoy’s book describes how, before Forbes arrived in England with her – giving her his own name and that of his ship, the Bonetta – he petitioned for her to be “the property of the crown”.This meant Bonetta was “effectively indentured to Queen Victoria until age 19” under the post-abolition legal structures, Lovejoy said. Bonetta was then married off to James Pinson Labulo Davies, a merchant and philanthropist, of whom she would write: “I don’t feel a particle of love for him.”Lovejoy’s research for the websiteliberatedafricans.org, developed with Kartikay Chadha, documents how, after abolition, more than 700,000 Africans “liberated” from enslavers were forced into indentures of up to 14 years “to pay for the cost of their own freedom” by governments including Britain’s.Lovejoy claims Bonetta was at the elite end of this bonded labour system, “educated to be a missionary who would Christianise Africa”. In her lifetime her image was exploited as imperial iconography, promoting the idea that British colonialism of Africa was a “civilising mission”.View image in fullscreenBonetta was a famous figure in 19th-century England.Photograph: AlamyLovejoy, of the University of Colorado Boulder, said: “Sarah’s imagery was used to project the idea of the queen’s benevolence – at a time when ‘liberated’ Africans are being forced into indentures.”Nonetheless, when Bonetta attended the 1858 wedding of Queen Victoria’s daughter, the Princess Royal, American abolitionists saw it as proof that Victoria, then the most powerful woman on Earth, believed in equality.For Randle, a plaster bust of Bonetta sculpted in 1851 by Benedetto Pistrucci, the Royal Mint’s chief engraver, symbolises the story’s “duality”. Randle saw it last year after Lovejoy had tracked it down to a private family collection in his research.“Who gets to see what their great ancestor looked like as a child, the cultural markings on her face? That is amazing. But at the same time it was a bust prepared for phrenological purposes, within a racist framework, where [Bonetta] was shown as an ‘excellent specimen’,” Randle said.Randle first learned his family history from his father, Adekunle Randle, a retired lawyer. The family still has the engraved goblet and plate that Queen Victoria gave to Bonetta’s daughter, Victoria, who, with the queen’s help, was educated at Cheltenham ladies’ college.Lovejoy’s book challenges the myths that Bonetta was a Yoruba princess, that she herself was Queen Victoria’s goddaughter, and that she spent most of her life in England.Randle, 37, who maintains his family’s ancestral ties with Òkè-Òdàn, welcomes research into Bonetta, who was a gifted linguist, musician, travel writer, educator and leading woman in 19th-century Lagos, until her death from tuberculosis in Madeira in 1880, aged 37.“Whether [Lovejoy’s] book is comfortable for me is beside the point,” Randle said. “It’s for the advancement of knowledge and how we learn from the past. Where the real discomfort lies is in what [Bonetta] was the symbol of, what she was used for.“But it would be a mistake to paint her story as entirely tragic,” he added. “My great-great-grandmother was very capable, courageous and dignified through adversity – through the trauma of losing her family, being displaced, and changing like a chameleon to fit into a culture so alien from what she’d known, she thrived. She is an early example of Black Britain.”Explore more on these topicsColonialismQueen VictoriaMonarchyBiography booksBeninAfricaRacenewsShareReuse this content

title: Four people killed in ‘violent, fast-moving’ fire at Canadian military base | Canada | The Guardian
description: Prime minister Mark Carney describes blaze as ‘one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime’
Author: Leyland Cecco
Headline: Prime minister Mark Carney describes blaze as ‘one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime’
Content: 1:46Canadian soldiers killed in fast-moving grass fire at military base – videoCanadaFour people killed in ‘violent, fast-moving’ fire at Canadian military basePrime minister Mark Carney describes blaze as ‘one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime’Leyland Ceccoin Toronto, Guardian staff and agenciesSun 18 Oct 2026 19.53 EDTFirst published on Sat 17 Oct 2026 22.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFour people have been killed and dozens more seriously injured after a “violent, fast-moving” fire tore through one of Canada’s busiest military training bases in Alberta, the country’s prime minister said on Sunday.Mark Carney called the incident “one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime”.Winds up to 96km/h (60mph) fed the blaze, which broke out at 4pm on Saturday during high-intensity combat training at the base. Alberta premier Danielle Smith said at a press conference on Sunday evening that 39 people were in hospital after the fire, with at least 19 of them in a critical condition.Maj Gen Wade Rutland, commander of the 1st Canadian Division, said that a grass fire ignited in a training area of the military base, which spread quickly.The cause of the fire was being investigated, he said.The military identified those killed as Sgt Morgan Wong of the Loyal Edmonton Regiment and Privates Shaun Farrell, Aidan Goulding and Hayden Lykkemark of the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light infantry. All four were serving with the battalion, based in Edmonton.Rutland said military officials knew about the fire for hours but believed it was contained before winds suddenly shifted, sending flames racing toward the soldiers.“The fire was a kilometre away when the wind shifted. That is not normal for a fire to move a kilometre in 36 seconds,” he said at a news conference in Edmonton.“I’ve certainly never seen anything like it,” he added.The fire broke out during high-intensity combat training involving Charlie Company of the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light infantry, sweeping into the area where the simulated attacks were taking place.About 84 soldiers were in the company, which was split between a grenade range and an area where soldiers practised attacks on simulated enemy positions.“The nation is in mourning for those brave members of our armed forces whom we have lost. And I have asked the flags on all federal buildings to be flown at half-mast to honour them,” Carney told the nation in an address from Ottawa. “We are praying for the wounded.”Carney said he had requested a “detailed account” from military officials on the ground about what had happened.View image in fullscreenEmergency crews and military personnel gather at the Wainwright Health Centre on Saturday.Photograph: John Ulan/The Canadian Press/APThe country’s defence minister, David McGuinty,described the event as a “terrible incident” as he travelled to the scene to meet senior officials and first responders.“I cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory,” he said, adding that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) were involved in the investigation.McGuinty did not provide details about what caused the incident and theCanadian armed forces said on Sunday that its“immediate priority” was notifying next of kin and helping those affected by the fire.The armed forces and federal, provincial and local authorities were coordinating the emergency response, they said.Canada’s top soldier, Gen Jennie Carignan, who serves as chief of the defence staff, called the incident “a profoundly difficult moment for the entire Canadian armed forces”.View image in fullscreenThe nearby community of Wainwright was providing hospital and firefighting support.Photograph: Jennifer Gauthier/ReutersThe nearby community of Wainwright provided hospital and firefighting support. Flares were spotted in the sky and military medical paratroopers dropped in on a local school football field.Health staff in ‌Edmonton said a “code orange,” or mass-casualty ​event, was declared to coordinate ​the medical response for patients being transported from Wainwright.A doctor at a hospital in the city of Edmonton, 180km (112 miles) north-west of Wainwright, told Canada’s national broadcaster thatWainwright’s healthcare facilities had been inundated.“This number of patients would overwhelm the city of Edmonton,” Dr Warren Thirsk, an emergency department physician at the Royal Alexandra hospital, told CBC News. “It is more patients than any of us want to count right now. It’s a disaster. It’s a one in every 15- to 25-year disaster.”Officials asked people in Edmonton to avoid the emergency department at the University of Alberta hospital in order to prioritise victims from the military base. Air ambulances were dispatched from Saskatoon and Edmonton.View image in fullscreenCanada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, said the nation was ‘in mourning for those brave members of our armed forces whom we have lost’.Photograph: Patrick Doyle/The Canadian Press/APJust 14% of Albertans want independence from Canada. Can a conference in a Calgary ballroom change that?Read moreThe fire at the military base swept into the area where the simulated attacks were taking place, crossing established firebreaks before being contained with help from municipal firefighters.The Canadian military said there were no indications of terrorism.On Sunday, the Alberta premier described the fire as “heartbreaking” and said it had affected many military personnel.“On behalf of the government of Alberta, I extend my deepest condolences to the families who have lost loved ones and wish those who have been injured a full recovery. Our thoughts are also with the military personnel, families and colleagues facing uncertainty and grief during this incredibly difficult time,” Smith said.The premier said many of the injured would require “weeks and months” of specialised, intensive medical care. She is due to travel to meet senior officials in Edmonton.The Saskatchewan premier, Scott Moe, said his province was sending assistance to Alberta but did not specify what resources were being deployed.View image in fullscreenCFB Wainwright is one of Canada’s busiest military bases.Photograph: Daphne Lemelin/AFP/Getty ImagesCFB Wainwright is one of Canada’s busiest military training bases, where soldiers prepare for combat operations. It is home to the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre, which conducts realistic battlefield exercises, and the 3rd Canadian Division Training Centre, which provides military training.“On behalf of the Nato military committee, we extend our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives in the tragedy at CFB Wainwright, and our wishes for a full recovery to all the injured,” Adm Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, the chair of the Nato military committee, posted on social media. “Those who fell there served our common security, and the military committee will honour their memory.”Canada’s Conservative leader, Pierre Poilievre, said he had spoken with Carney and the defence minister to offer support to those affected by the fire.“Pray for Wainwright, everyone,” Poilievre said in a social media post. He urged people in the area to follow emergency instructions and keep roads clear for first responders.Explore more on these topicsCanadaAmericasMark CarneynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘4,000 people minding our own business’: four decades on, Falklands again face a hostile Argentina | Falkland Islands | The Guardian
description: Facing a slump in the polls, Argentina’s president is making economic attacks on the islands’ oil industry, and suggesting its key fisheries industry could be next
Author: Daniel Boffey
Headline: Facing a slump in the polls, Argentina’s president is making economic attacks on the islands’ oil industry, and suggesting its key fisheries industry could be next
Content: A Falklands flag flies over the road from Mount Pleasant to Stanley.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA Falklands flag flies over the road from Mount Pleasant to Stanley.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianThe Sunday readFalkland Islands‘4,000 people minding our own business’: four decades on, Falklands again face a hostile ArgentinaFacing a slump in the polls, Argentina’s president is making economic attacks on the islands’ oil industry, and suggesting its key fisheries industry could be nextDaniel Boffeyin Port Stanley, Falkland Islands; photographs and video bySean SmithSun 18 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 11.26 EDTShareA dozen local people and a uniformed military police officer (“Do you mind if I sit in?”) took their seats at the back of the handsome wood-panelled courtroom that doubles as the Falkland Islands’ legislative assembly. Outside, it was a typically blowy early evening. It may nominally be spring in the south Atlantic, but Stanley harbour, with its dark grey water speckled with historical shipwrecks, was a cauldron of swells and churn.Six of the assembly’s eight members – five men, one woman – waited patiently at a row of desks and microphones. The heating had been turned up to just short of uncomfortable. Behind them, a portrait of King Charles. From the other walls, dusty photographs of governors peered down on the scene.The Falkland Islands, home to approximately 3,600 residentsProceedings started at the raised hand of a bored-looking young man wearing headphones in the corner. He was transmitting the question and answer session via radio across the dozen or so inhabited islands that make up the 778-strong archipelago.It was not clear how many of the Falklands’ 3,600 residents were listening in from their farm houses out in the diddle-dee shrub that coats much of the islands, or in the front rooms of Port Stanley’s white clapboard cottages with the pretty coloured roofs; likely not on a par with the number who learned 44 years ago from the Falkland Islands broadcasting station that their lands had been invaded.“There’s no turning back, we can expect them by dawn,” the governor, Rex Hunt, had said then.But for those who did tune in on Monday evening, there was much to dwell on. Not so much the answers about the local internet contract or the consultation on the contentious plan for a salmon farm.“I have another one for you,” piped up one enthusiastic quizzer with a heavy local accent, a West Country burr with a slight antipodean lift. That intervention prompted a little shuffling of tired bums. But a rather more significant announcement was to come.View image in fullscreenAssembly members Roger Spink, Stacy Bragger and Lewis Clifton before the monthly meeting.Lewis Clifton, an assembly member who can date his family’s residence on the Falklands to the late 1870s, advised the islanders that an unprecedented economic war was being waged against them – a community no bigger than an English village – by a country of 46 million people.“I am concerned that the level of Argentinian thrust this time has been at a different level,” Clifton said. “Perhaps a more vehement and belligerent tone than [seen since] 1982, because it has the potential to threaten our very economic development.”Facing a downturn in his domestic polling and with an upcoming election, Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, has legislated to criminalise companies and individuals involved in the Falklands’ nascent oil industry, and suggested the fisheries industry on which it currently relies for its prosperity could be next.The British forces capability at Mount Pleasant airbase – 1,800 personnel there and on Ascension island, four typhoon jets, a ground-based air defence system and with HMS Medway patrolling the waters – makes a military threat from Argentina largely hypothetical. But Buenos Aires has launched a full spectrum attack of another sort.View image in fullscreenAerial view of a new port and floating jetty being built in the Falkland Islands.In response this week, Andy Burnham and his foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, restated the UK’s solidarity with the islanders’ desire to remain British, and promised legislation that might offer some protection against the financial damage imposed by Argentina’s economic sanctions. Interpolreceived Foreign Office representationssuggesting they reject an Argentinian request for arrests relating to the dispute.For the islanders, it was a welcome show of muscularity. They have never felt entirely confident in the spine of those in power back on the homeland. It was arguably the indifference of Westminster that led Argentina to launch its invasion in the first place back in 1982.“I have never trusted the Foreign Office and I have been proven right,” said Norma Edwards, 84, whose husband, Roger, 80, a former Royal Marine, was attached to the SAS in the 1982 conflict. “Catching up time,” said Clifton, of what he saw as a belated toughness from London this week. But things remain precarious.View image in fullscreenRicky Evans, who runs a guesthouse and other businesses, carries post and supplies for Pebble Island.The Falkland Islands might be described as a British success story. Four decades ago, there were 1,800 inhabitants, and its tiny wool-centric economy, 300 miles (480km) east of mainland South America, was dependent on UK government handouts.Today the population, growing at 3% year-on-year in recent times, includes about 70 different nationalities, attracted by the 26% top rate of tax, good pay and opportunities in a growing and entirely self-reliant economy.There are Zimbabweans who came to de-mine after the war. Construction workers from South Africa who came to rebuild. Chileans who found something they liked after taking a Latam Airlines flight. The largest minority group is the Filipinos, who came to work in social care and the service industry in the late 1980s and 90s.View image in fullscreenChilean tourists pose for a photograph outside the Stanley post office.Working behind the bar at Groovy’s, a Nepalese waiter said he had come from Dubai. The money was better in the Falklands, he said, and “the people are nicer”. “The locals start at Deano’s bar, then it’s the Victory bar and here – then it is the Globe, for dancing,” he said with a smile. “After that they go to house parties.”Such has been the Falklands’ success in attracting people that a permanent residency scheme, capped at 90 people a year, has been frozen for 12 months. The islands, for all their challenges, are somewhere people want to be.View image in fullscreenJohn Barton, chair of the Falkland Islands fishing companies association and James Bates, the executive secretary.All of this had been made possible because of squid, said John Barton, chair of the fishing companies association. “It has been transformational,” he said.In 1986, the UK allowed the Falklands to establish a 200-nautical-mile exclusive fishing zone in which those wanting to operate had to be licensed by the islands’ government. Licences sold to fleets of Spanish, Korean and Taiwanese “jiggers” have delivered major revenues, but the locals are increasingly running the vessels too.The islands’ gross domestic production per capita soared as a result, from about £2,000 in 1982 to £85,000 in 2025, putting the islands sixth in the world league table, just behind Norway. The tourism industry is also going strong, with 75,000 or more people spilling out of cruise ships every year at Stanley port, but that is at best a nice addition.View image in fullscreenJames Wallace, who runs the Fortuna fishing company, onboard his harbour launch.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA worker packs filleted toothfish into plastic bags at a Falkland Islands processing factory.James Wallace, 41, is chief executive of Fortuna, the largest fishing company on the island. It is a growing operation, which last year acquired Cornwall’s oldest fishing business, the Ocean Fish Group. But he is diversifying his business for a reason.The squid populations in the Falklands waters, on which his company and the islands rely, are hugely variable and it is clear that “catches are declining”, he said. “We have commissioned a bunch of inshore work to see what is happening but the answer is that we don’t yet know,” he said. But there is another natural resource on which the islanders’ hopes are pinned.View image in fullscreenA bust of Margaret Thatcher by the 1982 war memorial.About 136 miles north of the Falkland Islands, work is continuing at pace on the Sea Lion oil project led by Israeli firm Navitas and its British partner, Rockhopper Exploration.Independent estimates suggest the offshore oil field could triple the Falkland Islands’ GDP and deliver a Norway-style sovereign wealth fund. The companies involved remain confident that drilling will commence within months. A new jetty is busy with activity. But the impact of Argentinian pressure cannot be discounted. Two major contractors recently pulled out of the project.View image in fullscreenChief executive of the Falklands government, Andrea Clausen, in the room where Argentinian forces surrendered.Andrea Clausen, as chief executive of the Falklands government, its top civil servant, works from a building on Thatcher Drive. Her office is opposite the room where Brig Gen Mario Menéndez signed Argentina’s letter of surrender on 14 June 1982. The letter remains on the wall.Clausen was 10 at the time of the invasion and remembers the Argentinian solders’ arrival. She also recalls cowering with her family in their home in Goose Green, 60 miles west of Stanley, as the British Harrier jets came in with their cluster bombs. “Even now I struggle to cope with the sound of fast jets,” she said.Clausen sees trauma throughout the islands. “I guess, some extreme behaviour,” she said. “Anger, aggression on certain political subjects.” She is evidently frustrated by the recent Argentinian actions.“The Falklands has since [19]82 ensured that we are financially independent – save for defence,” she said. “We had no money in 82 and we never want to be in that position again.”The oil is their insurance, she suggested. “I like to think that better people will de-escalate this because, honestly, we are 4,000 people minding our own business, we have a history deeper and older than theirs.”View image in fullscreenFalkland Islands reserves (from left): Cpl Chris Stenning; Justin McPhee, director of emergency services; Lt Alastair Baylis; and warrant officer second class Paul Watson.There are cycles to Argentinian bellicosity. The opportunistic but ill-fated invasion ordered by Argentina’s dictator general Leopoldo Galtieri, leading to the death of 649 Argentinians and 255 British military personnel, along with three islanders, has cast a pall over Argentinian-UK relations ever since.But at times, notably in the 1990s, Buenos Aires adopted a hearts-and-minds approach to the islanders, sending videos of the animated series Pingu to their children. Such kindness has tended to evaporate away, though, when an Argentinian government is losing public support at home, as Milei is experiencing now.But if any one attribute sums up the islanders, it is resilience, said Dot Gould, an assembly member who owns Pebble, a 20-mile long island north-west of the Falklands. She and her husband share the island with a couple who run a lodge, 5,000 sheep, 100 cattle, a load of spectacular wildlife, but not much else.View image in fullscreenDot Gould, who owns Pebble island.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianRampaging around the undulating terrain in her 4x4 vehicle, avoiding colonies of Rockhopper and Gentoo penguins, Gould points out the scattered remains of an Argentinian fighter jet and the graves of two of the airmen killed during battle. As a child on Pebble, she used to play with the parachutes left by the Argentinians, using them as sails for a go-kart.“I think, since 1982, this is probably the most serious it’s been for us,” she said. “How effective they will be, we don’t know yet … it’s almost two fingers up: we’ll get on with it, we have to.” But there is much that they want to do.The islands are dependent on a narrow range of freight links from the UK and South America for much of their fresh produce. Any glitch, and peculiar shortages can emerge. There was a period without milk. A time without beer. During one cherry tomato shortage, which saw their price shoot up, the main supermarket opted to cut them in half and sell them like that to spread the joy.A sorry-looking cabbage will set you back £8 at the West Store on the front. The local newspaper is the Penguin News (“This one’s not for Penguin News but …” is the traditional opening when disseminating islands gossip). But Facebook is the key means of communication. “Grown men and women use Snapchat like teenagers, often to arrange their extramarital affairs,” said one local.View image in fullscreenChildren during school lunch break.Other peculiarities include the Falklands government paying for children from the age of 16 to complete their secondary and university education in the UK. The size of the islands’ population makes it impractical to offer such levels of education at home, said Sarah Stannard, the islands’ director of education.But if the oil money comes online, she would rebuild the primary school. Children from the countryside – it is known locally as “camp” – are offered board in Stanley, although there are also peripatetic teachers and lessons done on the telephone.The children grow up quickly here, and tend to be keen to broaden their horizons. Oliver Lee, 15, was keen to join the merchant navy. “I would like to see other places,” he said. “The Mediterranean, hotter places basically.” Layla-May Vatemanu, 14, said: “A lot of the boys especially in my class do a lot of sport. Our [friendship group] doesn’t have a lot to do.”View image in fullscreenSchool students (from left): Oliver Lee, Layla May, Tessa Blake and Paul Green.There are no bus services anywhere, and the more distant parts of the islands are only accessible via boat or the Falkland government’s twin-engine aircraft service. On a landmass half the size of Wales, there is only one cashpoint.Touch rugby – rather than full-contact rugby – is played, in part because the islands’ hospital does not have the capability to deal with complex injuries. Much of the health budget goes on medi-evacs to South America. Yet, for all that, most of the children who leave at 16 do return.All places are shaped by their history and geography, but some have more history and geography than others. “We are British with a twist,” said Stacy Bragger, a former journalist who represents the Stanley constituency in the assembly.“We have our own identity. If you were to ask what are the traits of a Falkland islander – resourcefulness, resilience, making do. Because if something breaks you can’t just go down the road. You have to make do. That’s our version of Britishness.”View image in fullscreenMike Summers (left) and Liam Short, members of the chamber of commerce.The islanders also have long memories. “I used to read the Guardian when I was a good deal younger,” said Mike Summers, 73, who sits on the board of the local chamber of commerce. “But I stopped reading it in 1982 when [the editor] Peter Preston just fucked me off so much. He was: ‘Oh well they are a long way away and there is only a few of them – so why don’t we just sell them?’”On the Argentinian rhetoric, Summers added: “There are a lot of people who still suffer effects from the war – PTSD among the older people. I bumped into someone at the supermarket the other day who I have known for ever. She said: ‘Oh, I’m wondering if I should sell my house and move away. The Argies are going to invade again.’ It seriously affects some people and it is cruel actually.”View image in fullscreenSocial influencer Roxy King-Clark at her home in Stanley.Roxy King-Clarke, 40, describes herself as the Falklands’ biggest influencer, with about 60,000 followers. She picked up a major following when posting in response to the Argentinian men’s football team brandishing a “Las Malvinas son Argentinas” [The Malvinas are Argentinian] banner at the World Cup.She is regularly subjected to abuse for her posts. “The most common insults are to call us pirates, usurpers and colonisers,” she said. “It’s a bizarre thing to be on the receiving end of it all as they speak like we’ve just tipped up here. I can trace my family back to my earliest ancestor arriving here in 1842.”Her generation too, she suggests, have taken lessons from what happened four decades ago. King-Clarke said she would take a “hard line” to avoid any misinterpretation. “We need to learn from history,” she said, “and not make the same mistakes.”

title: Alleged gunman charged after Sydney suburb of Dulwich Hill plunged into lockdown | Sydney | The Guardian
description: Police responding to reports of an alleged stolen car in Dulwich Hill were told a man was armed with a firearm
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Police responding to reports of an alleged stolen car in Dulwich Hill were told a man was armed with a firearm
Content: Dulwich Hill in Sydney’s inner west was locked down after reports a man was allegedly seen with a firearm.Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAPView image in fullscreenDulwich Hill in Sydney’s inner west was locked down after reports a man was allegedly seen with a firearm.Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAPSydneyAlleged gunman charged after Sydney suburb of Dulwich Hill plunged into lockdownPolice responding to reports of an alleged stolen car in Dulwich Hill were told a man was armed with a firearmGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastGuardian staffSun 18 Oct 2026 18.48 EDTFirst published on Sun 18 Oct 2026 17.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn alleged gunman with “shaggy hair” has been arrested following reports of a confrontation about an allegedly stolen car which was set on fire prompting him to flee the scene.The 32-year-old man was arrested late Sunday in Sydney’s inner west, after being on the run since Friday morning, following an appeal by the police.He was arrested in Burwood but initially evaded being caught, sustaining a minor injury.Officers were called to a basement car park of a residential building in Dulwich Hill after they were told the man had allegedly torched a vehicle after stealing it and threatening owners who confronted him.Fire and Rescue NSW attended the scene and extinguished the fire with no injuries recorded.The man then allegedly fled on foot through a nearby park with police releasing an image of the suspect on social media and the suburb going into lockdown for several hours with helicopters roving above.View image in fullscreenPolice were appealing for anyone in the Dulwich Hill area with phone or dashcam vision to come forward.Composite: NSW Police Force via FacebookMark Swan, a resident in the building, heard loud arguments when two men and a woman confronted the alleged offender before hearing a bang.“We heard a bang, which I took to be a shotgun, and a fellow yelling, “I need a fire extinguisher’,” he said on Friday.“So I opened my kitchen window and yelled ‘there’s a hose reel behind the wall there’ but the garage had already filled up with smoke.”skip being of Caucasian appearance and about 160cm tall “with a thin build and shaggy hair”, the man sporting a black hooded jumper and black pants was charged with seven offences including possessing a shortened firearm without authority.He is due to appear in court on Monday.Explore more on these topicsSydneyNew South WalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Electricity costs put UK steelmakers in worst position in three years against EU rivals | Steel industry | The Guardian
description: Premium paid over French counterparts has risen to almost £30 a megawatt hour, analysis by lobby group finds
Author: Jasper Jolly
Headline: Premium paid over French counterparts has risen to almost £30 a megawatt hour, analysis by lobby group finds
Content: British Steel’s Scunthorpe works. Analysts blame the UK’s high electricity prices on its reliance on gas for power generation.Photograph: Ian Forsyth/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBritish Steel’s Scunthorpe works. Analysts blame the UK’s high electricity prices on its reliance on gas for power generation.Photograph: Ian Forsyth/Getty ImagesSteel industryElectricity costs put UK steelmakers in worst position in three years against EU rivalsPremium paid over French counterparts has risen to almost £30 a megawatt hour, analysis by lobby group findsJasper JollySun 18 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritish steelmakers have been pushed further behind European rivals on electricity costs after the US-Israeli war on Iran caused a surge in global gas prices.The premium paid by the British industry over its French counterpart has risen to almost £30 a megawatt hour (MWh), its highest level in three years, according to analysis by the lobby group UK Steel.Energy prices have long been one of the main factors businesses cite when asked what is holding back British industry. For Andy Burnham they represent perhaps the biggest obstacle to hisgoal of “reindustrialising” the UK.Analysts blame the UK’s high electricity prices on its reliance on gas for power generation, which is crucial forcleaner steelmaking with electric arc furnaces.The way the market is set up means that the wholesale gas pricedetermines the price of electricityeven from other sources that cost much less to produce, such as wind or solar power, and Iran’s closure of the strait of Hormuz in response to Donald Trump’s bombing campaign has causedglobal gas prices to soar.Electricity prices inFranceare mainly determined by its nuclear reactors, while in Germany heavily polluting coal still plays a large role in generation.Graph showing electricity costs in UK, Germany, France and Canada.Comparisons with European rivals are particularly important for the UK because the EU is often the main market for British manufactured products, including about 75% of exported steel, worth about £3bn.The gap with France had fallen in the previous three years to reach £18 a MWh last year, although it remains below the £153 reached in 2022 when Russia’s invasion of Ukraine caused a crisis in the global gas market. The gap with Germany this year fell slightly to about £12.Under Keir Starmer most of the costs added by government policy to heavy industrial businesses’ electricity costs were removed last year. The main option to bring the price down further, however, would be to set up more cheap renewables – a challenge in the short term – or to directly subsidise prices.The director general of UK Steel, Peter Brennan, said direct subsidies were the only option to help steelmakers. The lobby group hasproposed a cap on pricesthat it estimates would cost about £51m a year. The government would pay the difference when prices go above that level, while the industry would pay the government if prices go below.“British steelmakers are being asked to compete with one hand tied behind their backs,” Brennan said. “Despite welcome government action, our electricity prices remain vastly higher than those of our European and global competitors, and the gap with France is getting worse.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The government has rightly made reindustrialisation a national priority. But we cannot rebuild British manufacturing while forcing our steelmakers to pay substantially more for electricity than their competitors.”Separately, the government announced measures on Monday to support more than 100,000 workforce opportunities in the eight key growth sectors in its industrial strategy. The “jobs plans” are intended to help young people find work, with a focus on professional and business services, the defence sector and construction.Similar plans for financial services, clean energy and life sciences have already been announced. Plans for advanced manufacturing and the creative industries are expected to follow shortly.A government spokesperson said: “We are tackling industry’s number one concern head-on by reducing electricity bills by up to 25% for over 10,000 manufacturing businesses, and cutting costs for hundreds of our most electricity-intensive businesses by around £1bn per year – delivering on the prime minister’s pledge to reindustrialise Britain.”Explore more on these topicsSteel industryEnergy industryIndustrial policyGasFranceEuropean UnionEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Macron criticises ‘unbridled violence’ after days of unrest and 2,400 arrests across France | France | The Guardian
description: Ministers, officials and police under pressure over response to protests as government holds crisis talks amid ‘colossal failure of the state’
Author: Angelique Chrisafis
Headline: Ministers, officials and police under pressure over response to protests as government holds crisis talks amid ‘colossal failure of the state’
Content: People stormed and torched the town hall in Limoges, central France, destroying the 19th-century building.Photograph: Pascal Lachenaud/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeople stormed and torched the town hall in Limoges, central France, destroying the 19th-century building.Photograph: Pascal Lachenaud/AFP/Getty ImagesFranceMacron criticises ‘unbridled violence’ after days of unrest and 2,400 arrests across FranceMinisters, officials and police under pressure over response to protests as government holds crisis talks amid ‘colossal failure of the state’Angelique Chrisafisin ParisSun 18 Oct 2026 14.57 EDTFirst published on Sun 18 Oct 2026 11.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe French president, Emmanuel Macron, has criticised “unbridled violence” after one of the most violent days of unrest in years left public buildings burned, hundreds of shops destroyed and looted and at least 2,400people arrested in cities across the country.“Watching these images, we have all asked ourselves how could French people do this toFrance?” he said in a televised address.Macron said “nothing justifies” violence and that local state officials would be able to ban certain street gatherings if they deemed it necessary.He said a distinction must be drawn between what he called genuine, peaceful demonstrators making demands over the cost of living and the education system, and others who “destroy, ransack and loot”. He criticised what he called “factious groups from the ultra-left, joined by numerous delinquents”.2:31Emmanuel Macron condemns violence in televised address – videoPoliticians on the left and right called for the resignation of the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, after the government appeared to have been caught by surprise by the scale of violence on Saturday as state buildings were stormed and torched, bus stops smashed, roads barricaded and shops broken into and destroyed. Protests also took place in Spain, Italy and Portugal.Crowds clashed with police at Place de la République in centralParison Sunday afternoon as violence flared for a second day. Electric bikes were piled in some streets and set alight. Bottles and rocks were thrown and thick plumes of smoke rose from burning bins. Police responded with teargas and stun grenades.View image in fullscreenPolice officers stand guard as a fire burns in Paris on Sunday night.Photograph: Abdul Saboor/ReutersView image in fullscreenA car burns in a Paris street near graffiti reading ‘introduction to civil war’.Photograph: Guillaume Saligot/AFP/Getty ImagesPolice and officials faced challenges of different types on Saturday. First, tens of thousands of peaceful protesters attended calm marches through major cities including Paris, supporting schoolchildren’sdemands for more teachers and repairs to decrepit schools. Those marches, which came after four weeks of street marches andbarricades of schools, were attended by parents, teachers and grandparents as well as students and workers protesting over the high cost of living. The demonstrators carried banners saying the government was not listening to them and calling for more money for public services.But separately to those peaceful demonstrations, different groups caught police and officials by surprise with moving gatherings, sporadic burning, the barricading of streets and clashes with police in cities including Paris, Bordeaux, Nice and Marseille.View image in fullscreenA protester throws a smoke flare towards gendarmes in Bordeaux, south-western France.Photograph: Christophe Archambault/AFP/Getty ImagesFinally, masked looters took advantage of what French media called the “chaos” on the streets to smash shopfronts and grab goods. In Paris, groups of looters, some of whom appeared to be children, were seen running through the night with clothes and shoeboxes after masked adult men smashed shopfronts.In Paris, where police said a record 855 people had been arrested, the burnt-out remains of barricades built using bikes, bins and other materials littered streets on Sunday. Several streets had smashed shop windows and the remains of torched cars. The capital had experienced “a level of violence that we have never seen before, I believe”, said the Socialist deputy mayor, Lamia El Aaraje.View image in fullscreenMasked protesters by the graffiti-covered Statue de la République on Sunday evening.Photograph: Matthieu Rondel/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBurnt-out cars, smashed windows and the remains of barricades littered the streets of Paris on Sunday.Photograph: Stéphanie Lecocq/ReutersIn Limoges in central France, where the 19th-century town hall was burned down, the mayor, Guillaume Guérin, said the people who stormed his building “were not demonstrators that defend causes” but “people organised for war”. He said those who stormed and torched the town hall had told a building caretaker he would be killed, and told elected officials they would “burn”. He said there had been a failure of the state to deal with the crisis.“Around 3.30pm our municipal police, although present in number, found themselves no longer able to fight against the violence of rioters because they had run out of ammunition,” Guérin said. He called this “a colossal failure of the state”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA demonstrator in front of burning barricades in Marseille.Photograph: Sener Yilmaz Aslan/Getty ImagesIn Marseille, where masked groups stormed the city hall and a police station, the Socialist mayor, Benoît Payan, told BFMTV: “I have no words … I never thought I’d ever live through something like this. Hordes of rioters and looters attacked our common [state] buildings … with no real demands, but with the sole aim to wreck the demands of those who had demonstrated legitimately.”Payan said questions must be asked about policing tactics, as other town hall buildings, for example in Lille, were also targeted.View image in fullscreenProtesters arrive to force entry into the town hall in Lille, northern France.Photograph: Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP/Getty ImagesGrégory Doucet, the Green mayor of Lyon, said he had never seen such violence in his city, including the torching of the historic tourist office. He told Le Monde: “I’m stunned by the violence against public and state property. I saw and heard fear and anger. Shop owners felt abandoned.”Doucet said the government must find a “sense of nuance” in properly examining what happened and “avoiding stereotypes”. He said the government needed to give a political response to long-running societal demands from peaceful demonstrators on one hand, and also examine the roots of violence.Traders’ unions said more than 1,500 shops and businesses had been ransacked, with the cost running into tens of millions of euros. “This had nothing to do with the peaceful protesters,” said one shoe shop owner in Paris. “These were organised groups who were breaking things and looting. We’d never seen anything like it.”View image in fullscreenA protester wrapped in a French national flag stands in front of Lyon’s burning tourism office.Photograph: Jeff Pachoud/AFP/Getty ImagesOpposition politicians questioned the government’s policing tactics, saying there had been a lack of state intelligence.The interior ministry said there had been nearly 2,400 arrests and almost 1,000 police and gendarmes injured on Saturday, seven seriously. A 17-year-old boy had his right hand blown off by a crowd-control grenade in the east-central city of Saint-Étienne. A 17-year-old girl lost an eye in Mulhouse and a police investigation was opened into the circumstances.Macron’s centrist government and the far-right frontrunner for the presidential election, Marine Le Pen, both blamed what they called “ultra-left” groups for the violence. The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said the government would not be “intimidated” by ⁠violence, and blamed the unrest on the “ultra-left” and criminals.The radical-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who attended the peaceful street demonstration in Paris on Saturday, accused the government of organisational failings that had “opened the door to chaos”.Lecornu replied on social media: “Laying the responsibility for violence on heads of police is a dangerous and cynical reversal of responsibilities.”Explore more on these topicsFranceParisProtestEmmanuel MacronEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Shabana Mahmood to hold talks with EU over law enforcement cooperation | European Union | The Guardian
description: UK home secretary’s meeting comes after PM said he wanted to rejoin European law enforcement databases
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: UK home secretary’s meeting comes after PM said he wanted to rejoin European law enforcement databases
Content: Shabana Mahmood is also expected to discuss counter-terrorism efforts with the senior EU official during their meeting on Monday.Photograph: Marcin Nowak/Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenShabana Mahmood is also expected to discuss counter-terrorism efforts with the senior EU official during their meeting on Monday.Photograph: Marcin Nowak/Anadolu/Getty ImagesEuropean UnionShabana Mahmood to hold talks with EU over law enforcement cooperationUK home secretary’s meeting comes after PM said he wanted to rejoin European law enforcement databasesLisa O’Carrollsenior correspondentSun 18 Oct 2026 14.13 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 14.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK home secretary,Shabana Mahmood, will meet the EU’s home affairs commissioner on Monday for further talks just days after Andy Burnham said he wanted to rejoin European law enforcement databases from which the UK has been locked out of since Brexit.According to theEuropean Commission, they will discuss “migration, border management, law enforcement cooperation and counter-terrorism”, with the latest Frontex data published on Monday showing a 43% decline in small boats crossing the Channel.It will be the second time Mahmood has met Magnus Brunner in two months and comes amid an increase in engagement between London and Brussels since Andy Burnham announced he would use an upcoming EU-UK summit to “lay out to the country” what he believes are the “different options for Britain’s long-term relationship” with the EU.Brexit’s back – but are British voters ready to contemplate a reversal?Read moreBrunner said “the UK’s contribution is indispensable” to continuing efforts to suppress irregular migration after the EU introduced a suite of new laws aimed at speeding up asylum decisions and deportations.On the agenda for Monday’s meeting will be talks on the UK rejoining some of the police and security databases it was locked out from after Brexit and rejoining a new database,Eurodac, centring on migration.Last weekBurnham told MPsthat “one of the most positive aspects of my meeting with [the European Commission] president [Ursula] von der Leyen in New York, was her openness to the conversation about restoring data sharing on immigration across the UK, across Europe”.He said it was “control” that the UK “lost” and should get “more attention” in the debate aboutBrexit. “I will work hard to see if we can get a practical arrangement on that very issue at the summit in November,” Burnham said.View image in fullscreenMagnus Brunner will discuss ‘migration, border management, law enforcement cooperation and counter-terrorism’ with Shabana Mahmood, according to the European Commission.Photograph: Dursun Aydemir/Anadolu/Getty ImagesBrunner will also meet the MI5 director general, Ken McCallum, and visit the National Counter Terrorism Security Office, as well as meet senior officials from the UK’s child sexual abuse centre to discuss joint efforts to tackle such crimes.He has also been chosen to deliver a lecture at King’s College London on migration and asylum, where he will talk about the impact of the EU’s new Pact on Migration and Asylum, a framework of 10 pieces of legislation overhauling how the EU manages its borders, processes asylum applications and shares information among member states.Brunner will tell those he meets that the new laws have already had a significant impact along with a shift in political priorities around migration in key countries such as Germany, Italy and France.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe said the “reforms are paying” off in the UK too, with illegal crossings down 43%.“We must stay on this course, including along all relevant migration routes, and the UK’s contribution is indispensable,” he said. “We have put our European house in order. Illegal crossings at our external borders are down 55% over two years, with a further third this year, and asylum applications are at record lows in the countries that used to be main destinations.”One key database the UK wants access to is Eurodac, a new platform which collects fingerprints and facial images of asylum seekers from the age of six, and security flags for people linked to terrorism or serious crime.Another is the Schengen Information System (SIS), which contains data on missing persons, stolen goods, vehicles and number plates, and fugitives crossing internal EU borders. About 20m searches are made daily on the SIS, according to EU data, mostly on cars.The Home Office has not commented.Explore more on these topicsEuropean UnionShabana MahmoodBrexitUK security and counter-terrorismCounter-terrorism policyImmigration and asylumEuropean CommissionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Zelenskyy thanks Trump for resumed intelligence sharing after US Starlink ‘message’ | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Two people killed and at least 17 injured as Russia and Ukraine continue to trade strikes on power infrastructure
Author: Sam Jones
Headline: Two people killed and at least 17 injured as Russia and Ukraine continue to trade strikes on power infrastructure
Content: Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country’s recent Starlink problems were ‘a message from [the] American government’.Photograph: Omar Havana/APView image in fullscreenVolodymyr Zelenskyy said his country’s recent Starlink problems were ‘a message from [the] American government’.Photograph: Omar Havana/APUkraineZelenskyy thanks Trump for resumed intelligence sharing after US Starlink ‘message’Two people killed and at least 17 injured as Russia and Ukraine continue to trade strikes on power infrastructureAndrew Rothin Kyiv andSam JonesSun 18 Oct 2026 12.37 EDTFirst published on Sun 18 Oct 2026 10.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVolodymyr Zelenskyy on Sunday thanked theTrump administrationfor resuming intelligence sharing between the two countries, but maintained the US had intentionally throttled its Starlink satellite internet access so that Donald Trump could send a “message” in his ongoing feud with the Ukrainian president.In an interview on NBC, Zelenskyy said the US had “unblocked” intelligence on impending Russian ballistic missile strikes, which have pounded the country’s energy infrastructure as winter draws in.“It was blocked for some period of time. And then it was deblocked by the American side. We are very thankful for this. Now it works,” Zelenskyy told NBC’s Meet the Press. “Only [the] United States has this unique intelligence to tell our side when Russia uses ballistic missiles. And we didn’t get it during ballistic attacks during three days.”Zelenskyy also said that Elon Musk’s SpaceX was responsible forsuddenly limiting the speedat which Starlink terminals worked in Ukraine, hampering drone operations on the frontlines as well as some air defence missions.“It was a message from [the] American government to limit the speed,” he said. “And technically, SpaceX did it.”Two people werekilled and at least 17 injured as Russia and Ukraine continued to trade strikes on each other’s power infrastructure, afterthe breakdownof Trump’s short-lived and unilaterally declared “energy ceasefire”.View image in fullscreenA Ukrainian drone strike on the St Petersburg oil terminal.Photograph: EPATrump has increasingly sought a detente with Moscow, inking a deal toimport diesel fuel from Russiaand waiving sanctions voted for overwhelmingly by both houses of Congress. Zelenskyy has become increasingly critical of Trump’s actions as the US has piled pressure on Ukraine to cease striking refineries in Russia and end the war quickly on Putin’s terms.“We want to trust him and I hope that he will change his decisions,” Zelenskyy said of Trump. “Because I think that it’s all mistakes and it will not help us. And it will not help [the] United States.”Zelenskyy on Sunday said that he had spoken with Steve Witkoff andJared Kushner, the two Trump envoys charged with ending the war in Ukraine, as part of Ukraine’s “virtually nonstop communication” with the Trump administration.But the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, in a separate interview on NBC on Sunday said that Zelenskyy had been “reckless” to accuse the Trump administration of standing behind the throttling of Starlink.“President Trump and Secretary Rubio have categorically said that no one in the Trump administration did that,” said Bessent. “And I think it is very reckless for President Zelenskyy to make such a charge.”He added: “President Zelenskyy should be very careful about making statements like this that aren’t true.”On Sunday night Trump said Zelenskyy did not want his nation’s more than four-year war with Russia to end, writing on his Truth Social platform that he was in the process of negotiating a peace between Russia andUkraineand making “great progress” but claimed: “Zelenskyy doesn’t care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him … he doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did.”Ukraine has resumed striking refineries in Russia and on Sunday attacked one of the country’s main oil terminals.One person was killed and 15 wounded overnight after Ukraine used more than 1,000 drones to target Russian oil depots, logistics facilities and datacentres in one of its largest ever aerial bombardments.View image in fullscreenSmoke billows into the sky after Ukrainian drone strikes on an industrial zone in St Petersburg.Photograph: APSt Petersburg’s governor, Alexander Beglov, said on Sunday that fires ⁠had broken out overnight at the city’s oil terminal, ​an oil depot and industrial ‌warehouses. A logistics centre belonging to the Russian retailer Ozon and a datacentre for the local tech company VK were also targeted, both companies confirmed.Alexander Drozdenko, the governor of the Leningrad region that surrounds St Petersburg, said 145 drones had been shot down and about 20,000 people were without electricity after the raid. “A large-scale [unmanned aerial vehicle] attack continues to be repelled,” he wrote on Telegram.Fears that the conflict could be spilling over into Nato’s borders were stoked again on Sunday morning afterLithuaniatold residents in central and ⁠northern parts of the country to seek shelter for about an hour after an unidentified flying object entered its ⁠airspace.During the red alert, Nato fighter jets were ‌scrambled to the area and Kaunas airport, near Lithuania’s second largest city, was temporarily closed, the national crisis management centre said.The Nato aircraft were unable to visually identify the object due to cloudy weather and did not attempt to shoot it down, the centre said.Ukraine’s foreign ministry later said ⁠it regretted the possible diversion of its ⁠drones into ⁠Lithuanian airspace ​on Sunday, which it said may ⁠have been caused by Russian electronic warfare.“We apologise for any ​disruption, risks and concern this may have caused,” a spokesperson, ‌Heorhii Tykhyi, wrote on X. “We are committed to ⁠sharing all relevant information with ​our ​Lithuanian partners to ​establish the full circumstances ​of ‌the incident.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenRescue workers walk in front of a residential building damaged by a Russian airstrike in Zaporizhzhia on Saturday.Photograph: Kateryna Klochko/APMeanwhile, local officials in the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia said Russian strikes had killed a woman and wounded at least two other people, including a six-year-old girl. Two apartment buildings, 18 cars and an educational institution had been damaged by the attack, according to Mykhailo Semikin, the head of the Zaporizhzhia regional military administration.Tensions are deepening between Kyiv and Washington, with the US presidentcriticising Ukraine for its strikeson Russian oil infrastructure, despite continued Russian aggression.Trumpannounced an “energy ceasefire”last week – which neither side said they agreed to beforehand – that quickly collapsed as Moscow continued its strikes on Ukraine’s power grid and Kyiv eventually resumed its hits on Russian oil refineries.The Russian defence ministry said its air defence units had downed 1,015 Ukrainian drones around the country overnight. The Tass news agency quoted the ​Kremlin ​spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, who said Russia was responding with systematic, large-scale ⁠strikes.“The Kyiv ​regime is resisting, but this cannot ​change the course ‌of events,” he ​said, ​answering a question about how Russia might respond to Kyiv’s attack on St Petersburg.On Saturday, Russia said it had carried out a major overnight attack, targeting Ukraine’s largest steelworks in the city of Kryvyi Rih and ⁠vessels using the port of Odesa. In a ‌statement, Russia’s defence ministry said its forces had also hit an electricity substation in the north-western city of Zhytomyr and another steel ‌plant in Zaporizhzhia.View image in fullscreenA house damaged by a Russian airstrike in the frontline city of Sloviansk in eastern Ukraine.Photograph: State Emergency Service Of Ukraine/ReutersIn the Trump administration’s latest effort to reduce tensions with Russia, the US president announced on Friday that he wouldput a hold on a sweeping new sanctions packagetargeting the Russian economy, telling Congress the pause on the legislation passed by both chambers was in the national interest.Trump has yet to give details about what he has decided regarding further sanctions on Russia.“We’ll figure it out, and you’ll figure it out,” he told reporters at a fundraising dinner at his Florida estate on Saturday. “But it’s a very good decision, and it’s going to be a decision that’s good for the country, and I think good for the world.”In a post on X on Sunday, Zelenskyy said in the week since Trump’s announcement of an energy ceasefire Russia had attacked Ukraine’s energy, oil and gas sectors 76 times.He also said that the previous night alone, energy facilities in four Ukrainian regions had been attacked and tens of thousands of families were still without power. He accused Russia of trying to cause a blackout.Trump’s pause on Russia sanctions is ‘reward’ for Putin, Zelenskyy saysRead more“America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements,” he said. “On the contrary, they take every signal of an opportunity to make money as proof that their bet on war is paying off and they can keep fighting.”Zelenskyy also stressed that the war was continuing due to Russia’s invasion – not because Ukraine was defending itself. “It is Russia that must face pressure for peace to have a chance. Thank you to everyone who understands this and helps,” he said.Ukrainian drones have repeatedly entered Nato airspace in the ​Baltic region in ‌recent months. Kyiv ​has said they ​were steered off course by Russian signal jamming. Such incidents have stoked concerns that Russia’s war in Ukraine could spread.Reuters, the Associated Press and Agence France-Presse contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsUkraineRussiaEuropeDonald TrumpTrump administrationVolodymyr ZelenskyyLithuanianewsShareReuse this content

title: Arrests over France protests rise to 1,800, with whole streets in Paris ‘devastated’ – Europe live | France | The Guardian
description: Interior minister says ‘the Republic will not yield’ to France’s worst protests in years
Author: Harry Taylor
Headline: Interior minister says ‘the Republic will not yield’ to France’s worst protests in years
Content: 11h ago10.50 EDTSummaryIt’s approaching 5pm in Paris, as we await French President Emmanuel Macron’s televised response to large-scale protests and unrest acrossFranceon Saturday.Here’s a summary of today’s eventsMacron will address the French public on TV at 8pm (7pm BST) after crisis meetings with ministers on Sunday.France’s interior minister Laurent Nunez said “the Republic will not yield” after 1,800 were arrested across the country on Saturday.Protests which had begun about education and schooling conditions in France have broadened to wider cost of living issues.Buildings were set alight, including Limoges City Hall in central France, as other cities suffered widespread vandalism.More than 500 police officers, gendarmes and firefighters were injured.Nunez blamed thousands of “far left” protesters along with criminals who “looted and ransacked” buildings.The numbers of protesters on Saturday have varied, with authorities saying 550,000 took to the streets nationwide, but organisers said it was about 800,000.Paris police said 110,000 took part in a march. Sunday has not seen similar incidents.The cost of damage to shops will run to hundreds of millions of euros, according to the president of a trade body.US president Donald Trump said “France is burning” and blamed immigration in a post on Truth Social.Other protests took place against the cost of livingin Spain, Italy and Portugal.Share

title: Guardian reporter filmed masked militants seconds before West Bank attack on French mayor | West Bank | The Guardian
description: New video footage of Israeli settler assault on European delegation as Netanyahu attempts to raise doubt
Author: Emma Graham-Harrison
Headline: New video footage of Israeli settler assault on European delegation as Netanyahu attempts to raise doubt
Content: Despite video footage, Netanyahu’s office described reports of the attacks as ‘unproven allegations’.Photograph: UGC/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDespite video footage, Netanyahu’s office described reports of the attacks as ‘unproven allegations’.Photograph: UGC/AFP/Getty ImagesWest BankAnalysisGuardian reporter filmed masked militants seconds before West Bank attack on French mayorEmma Graham-Harrisonin JerusalemNew video footage of Israeli settler assault on European delegation as Netanyahu attempts to raise doubtSun 18 Oct 2026 14.39 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 16.36 EDTShareHours after Israeli militantsattacked a delegationof European diplomats, French clerics and a visiting mayor in the occupied West Bank, Israel’s leader, Benjamin Netanyahu, responded by questioning the delegation’s account of the assault.“Serious accusations require serious evidence” was the all-caps headline of a social mediapostfrom the office of the prime minister. As news of the attack spread globally there was no pledge to find those accountable and bring them to justice.Instead Netanyahu’s team dismissed video of Bernard Baudoux, the mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries in northern France, on the ground grimacing in pain and shock, photos of the smashed window of a diplomatic car, and footage of masked men threatening diplomats and activists with sticks.“These images alone do not establish the complete sequence of events or individual responsibility,” the statement said, warning of “concerns about a coordinated campaign to smear Israel”.The prime minister’s office went on to cast doubt on the integrity of senior French, Belgian and Polish diplomats in Jerusalem and clergy from the Catholic church who witnessed and reported the attack.“We call on the public and responsible journalists to demand verifiable evidence, reject hearsay and refuse to turn unproven allegations into a collective indictment of the Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria [the occupied West Bank],” it said.Guardian footageFootage below filmed by the Guardian (no audio) shows the moments before Israeli settlers attacked the French mayor Bernard Baudoux, who was in the Palestinian town of Taybeh with a delegation of European diplomats. A second clip shows the immediate aftermath of the attack. The final section shows one group of settlers attacking the car carrying Baudoux and others.0:36French mayor attacked by Israeli settlers in occupied West Bank – videoVerifying the details of attacks can be painstaking journalistic work, seeking out eyewitness accounts, photos and videos for confirmation.But this weekend the Guardian was in Taybeh, and witnessed the masked militants speeding up a hill in order to attack diplomats and French visitors who had spent a morning peacefully harvesting olives with Palestinians who own the groves.View image in fullscreenThe smashed window of the car carrying Bernard Baudoux.Photograph: Emma Graham-Harrison/The GuardianShortly after 1pm, they were warned that settlers had attacked Palestinians harvesting olives nearby. Keen to avoid confrontation, the group decided to leave and were approaching their vehicles as the militants closed in, masked, menacing and brandishing sticks.The Guardian filmed the moments before Baudoux was assaulted, showing him approaching an SUV with his wife and Vincent Dollmann, the archbishop of Cambrai, escorted by diplomatic security. Our vehicle pulled away, making room for the two parked by the road to follow.Moments later the settlers attacked, apparently determined not only to force the foreigners to flee but to extract a price for joining Palestinians on their land.It was clear the group contained foreign dignitaries because the cars had diplomatic plates, and Baudoux was apparently targeted for his nationality, because he was wearing his mayor’s sash of office. One of the attackers aggressively shouted “France, France” before pushing him to the ground, eyewitnesses said.Metadata from that video shows there were just 22 seconds between the last shot of Baudoux remonstrating with his attackers and footage of him slumped on the ground taken by activists in the second car.The embassy security team then helped him into the vehicle but the attack continued as they drove off. Footage filmed from the hillside opposite shows the settlers attacking the SUV as pulls away.The force of their blows smashed one of the reinforced windows at the back of the car, which can be seen intact in the first video. A photo of the crumpled pane taken minutes later in the relative safety of Taybeh shows the force of the impact.If the militant settlers had broken one of the windows next to the passengers, it is unlikely those inside would have escaped injuries.View image in fullscreenFormer Israeli ambassadors and employees demonstrated outside the foreign ministry, demanding the prime minister and his government ‘Stop Jewish Terrorism. It’s in your hands’.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianIsraeli authorities have repeatedly attempted toobfuscatedetails of attacks on Palestinians and undermine survivor or witness accounts.For the prime minister to deploy the same tactics on senior diplomats from European allies – however strained their current relationship – marks a new embrace of isolationist extremism.A day earlier the American photojournalist Heidi Levine washospitalised after a brutal attackby Israeli militants blocking the Palestinian olive harvest in another village.
