Netanyahu’s office described it as an “alleged assault” and a “disputed incident” adding “the facts … remain unclear and are under investigation”.The message from the very top of Israel’s government, that the state was reluctant to impose consequences or seek justice for that attack, may have emboldened the attackers on Saturday.View image in fullscreenThe protest outside the foreign ministry in Jerusalem drew a response from conservative passersby.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianThere was one unprecedented response in Jerusalem, however. On Sunday, more than a dozen of Israel’s top former diplomats gathered outside the foreign ministry where they had all worked for decades for an unprecedented protest.Two former directors general, one deputy director general and a host of ambassadors held up signs calling for action on the campaign of terror by Israelis against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.“Bibi [Netanyahu], foreign minister [Gideon] Sa’ar. Stop Jewish Terrorism. It’s in your hands,” read one banner.Explore more on these topicsWest BankIsraelPalestineMiddle East and north AfricaBenjamin NetanyahuanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Flydubai captain describes blocking axe blows as co-pilot attacked him | Flydubai plane incident | The Guardian
description: Capt Smit Machchhar said he screamed for help as he reached to open the cockpit door on flight FZ1073
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Capt Smit Machchhar said he screamed for help as he reached to open the cockpit door on flight FZ1073
Content: Capt Smit Machchhar said the scariest thing he felt was the aircraft nose ‘steeply going down’.Photograph: Israel's Foreign Ministry/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCapt Smit Machchhar said the scariest thing he felt was the aircraft nose ‘steeply going down’.Photograph: Israel's Foreign Ministry/AFP/Getty ImagesFlydubai plane incidentFlydubai captain describes blocking axe blows as co-pilot attacked himCapt Smit Machchhar said he screamed for help as he reached to open the cockpit door on flight FZ1073ReutersSun 18 Oct 2026 13.27 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 15.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe captain of a flydubai flight who was attacked by a co-pilot who intended to crash the plane has described ⁠blocking axe blows to his head and screaming for help as he reached to open the cockpit door.Capt Smit ⁠Machchharhas been hailed ⁠as a ​herofor his role in averting disaster on the flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv last month, helping to thwart what the UAE ⁠attorney general has said was an attempted suicide attack by the co-pilot who hadintended to crash the planeinto Ben Gurion airport.Speaking in an interview with ⁠The National newspaper from a hospital bed in Abu Dhabi, his head and left arm bandaged, Machchhar ​said that when the first blow landed ‌he thought something had gone “horribly ‌wrong with the aircraft structure”, before quickly realising he was being attacked and things had “taken a drastic turn”.“The ‌next thought was I need to get help in here,” he said. “My immediate action was to free myself from the seatbelts and I tried to just block the blows as much as I could.”He pointed to his arm, which had been wounded as he defended himself. “The blows were coming on the head. Immediately my ‌hand went to the knob which opens the door and [I was] screaming for my colleagues, screaming his name. I believe that was the first time when I ​lost my consciousness.”View image in fullscreenDubai’s crown prince, sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, visited Machchhar in hospital in Abu Dhabi.Photograph: Government of Dubai Media Office/APFlight FZ1073 was in Saudi airspace when the co-pilot attacked Machchhar with a crash axe, an item typically kept in the cockpit for emergency use.The incident caused the airliner to plunge 16,000 ft (4,900m) in 30 seconds before the attacker was overwhelmed and two other pilots who were ⁠on board landed the aircraft safely inSaudi Arabia. The suspect, an Omani ​national, was transferred to the ​UAE, flydubai’s home country.The plan was ​inspiredby the 11 September 2001 attacks on the US, UAE public prosecutors ​said as a ‌result of their criminal ​investigation, which was launched on ​1 October.Machchhar said he heard the cockpit door opening and screaming “between my colleague and the guy”. He said the scariest moment was when he felt was the aircraft nose “steeply going down”.“I was not very sure that I’ll make it out alive from this. Did I give up? No.”Explore more on these topicsFlydubai plane incidentIsraelDubaiSaudi ArabiaUnited Arab EmiratesMiddle East and north AfricaAir transportnewsShareReuse this content

title: US ambassador to Israel calls West Bank settler attack on American photojournalist ‘terror’ | West Bank | The Guardian
description: Mike Huckabee calls for arrest and prosecution of those responsible as Heidi Levine, 63, recovers in hospital in Israel
Author: Sam Jones
Headline: Mike Huckabee calls for arrest and prosecution of those responsible as Heidi Levine, 63, recovers in hospital in Israel
Content: Heidi Levine is recovering in hospital in Petah Tikva, near Tel Aviv.Photograph: Ariel Schalit/APView image in fullscreenHeidi Levine is recovering in hospital in Petah Tikva, near Tel Aviv.Photograph: Ariel Schalit/APWest BankUS ambassador to Israel calls West Bank settler attack on American photojournalist ‘terror’Mike Huckabee calls for arrest and prosecution of those responsible as Heidi Levine, 63, recovers in hospital in IsraelSam Jonesand agenciesSun 18 Oct 2026 13.02 EDTFirst published on Sun 18 Oct 2026 11.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, has denounced the settler attack that left theWashington Postphotojournalist Heidi Levine badly beaten and needing surgery as a “despicable act of terror” and called for the arrest and prosecution of those responsible.Levine, 63, an award-winning journalist who lives in Israel, wasset upon last Fridayby masked Israeli settlers who used clubs and other weapons to attack Palestinian people attempting to harvest their olives in occupiedWest Banktowns.The photographer, who is in a hospital in Petah Tikva near Tel Aviv recovering from hand surgery, broken ribs and other injuries she sustained in the attack, said she was beaten for more than 10 minutes by the settlers, who also stole her camera, passport and phone.1:57American photojournalist recounts Israeli settler attack in the occupied West Bank – video“I was attacked, pushed to the ground,” Levine said. “Luckily, I had my flak jacket and helmet, otherwise I probably wouldn’t even be here, because they just kept kicking and kicking me.” She said the attack ended when her Palestinian colleagues intervened to save her.Huckabee, a rightwing ally of PresidentDonald Trumpwith a track record of hardline, pro-Israel rhetoric, was notably blunt in his condemnation of what he called the “vicious and cowardly attack” on Levine. In a post on X on Saturday, he noted that she was a US citizen who had been clearly identifiable as a journalist.“We have called for a full investigation, arrest, and prosecution to the fullest extent of the law to whoever participated in this,” Huckabee added. “Attacking a female photographer is despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards. Dishonorable act of senseless violence.”View image in fullscreenMike Huckabee, the US ambassador to Israel, said it wa a ‘vicious and cowardly attack’.Photograph: Ohad Zwigenberg/APIsrael’s prime minister,Benjamin Netanyahu, has been ambiguous in addressing Levine’s assault, condemning “violence against anyone” but referring to the attack as “alleged” and saying its circumstances remain unclear.In an interview with the Associated Press on Sunday, Levine said she had been “shocked and insulted” to hear that Netanyahu referred to the attack on her and others as “alleged”, adding that the prime minister “had all the evidence on the table”.But she described the sharp condemnation of settler violence expressed to her in a call from Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, and in a letter signed by several of the country’s top former security and intelligence officials, in which they all expressed shame over the attack.Levine blamed “Jewish terrorists” for Thursday’s attack and added: “I’ve been covering this region for over 40 years, and I have never seen this country in such a state as it is today.”The photojournalist also said she was planning to return to work when she had recovered from her injuries. “I’ve invested decades of blood, sweat and tears into this,” she said. “They cracked my bones, they haven’t cracked my spirit.”View image in fullscreenHeidi Levine said she was planning to return to work when she had recovered from her injuries.Photograph: Ahmad Gharabli/AFP/Getty ImagesThe attack on the Palestinian farmers and Levine was followed on Saturday byanother outbreak of settler violencedirected against European diplomats, a French mayor and the archbishop of the French city of Cambrai, who were visiting the occupiedWest Bank.Bernard Baudoux, the mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries, was wearing his red, white and blue sash of office and attempting to enter a vehicle with diplomatic plates when he was assaulted and knocked to the ground. A masked militant shouted “Vive la France!” as he launched the attack, a witness said. Badoux’s wife and Vincent Dollmann, the archbishop of Cambrai, were also threatened by the group of seven men, some armed with clubs.View image in fullscreenBernard Baudoux, wearing his mayoral blue, white and red sash, was assaulted during a visit to the Palestinian town of Taybeh.Photograph: UGC/AFP/Getty ImagesThe group had joined the olive harvest on lands belonging to the Christian town of Taybeh, along with the French consul general in Jerusalem, his wife and other diplomats, and the Belgian and Polish consuls.“I think that if settlers are behaving like this, there is a tolerance on the part of the Israeli government,” Baudoux told Agence France-Presse after he was attacked. “The whole world needs to know what’s happening. For me, I’ll go back to my country and everything will be fine. Those who continue to suffer the most are those who are here.”Violence is surging ahead of bitterly fought elections to be held on 27 October, with Palestinians’ annual olive harvest being repeatedly disrupted by Israeli settlers as Netanyahu seeks to shore up his pro-settlement rightwing base.France’s foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, has called on Israel to “urgently halt criminal violence” and to arrest those responsible for attacking Baudoux. The EU has condemned the attack and urged “full accountability as well as effective measures to prevent continued acts of violence and violent harassment against Palestinians, including during the ongoing olive harvest season, as well as against journalists”.The European Commission executive vice-president, Teresa Ribera, went further, posting an interview with Levine in hospital and adding the caption: “They want no witnesses.”Israel’s foreign ministry has condemned the attack on the diplomats and Israeli police promised to open an investigation.Herzog, who holds a mostly ceremonial role, called Levine in hospital on Saturday, saying the attack was “outrageous and shocking” and was weighing on his conscience.View image in fullscreenIsaac Herzog, Israel’s president, said the attack on Levine was ‘outrageous and shocking’.Photograph: Ilia Yefimovich/AFP/Getty ImagesNetanyahu’s main rival in the elections, the former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, criticised the prime minister over the violence, saying it was “burning away the little legitimacy the state of Israel still possesses”. He described the attacks as “Jewish terrorism, under the auspices of the Israeli government”.Trump endorsed Netanyahu for re-election in a post on his Truth Social network on Sunday, hailing him as “a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran”. He added: “Bibi Netanyahu has been Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself.”The Washington Post has reiterated its call for a full and transparent investigation into the attack on Levine, even though Israel rarely investigates settler violence fully.Yesh Din, an Israeli rights group, says about 94% of investigations into settler violence since 2005 have ended without an indictment, with just 3% leading to full or partial convictions.The Associated Press and Agence France-Presse contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsWest BankMike HuckabeePalestineIsraelJournalist safetyTrump administrationBenjamin NetanyahunewsShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham launches campaign against ‘headphone dodgers’ on public transport | Transport policy | The Guardian
description: Passengers urged to ‘share the carriage, not the noise’ as guidance sets out £100 penalties for nuisance behaviour
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Passengers urged to ‘share the carriage, not the noise’ as guidance sets out £100 penalties for nuisance behaviour
Content: Andy Burnham said: ‘It’s a simple thing, but one that will make journeys that little bit better for all of us.’Photograph: Jeff J Mitchell/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham said: ‘It’s a simple thing, but one that will make journeys that little bit better for all of us.’Photograph: Jeff J Mitchell/AFP/Getty ImagesTransport policyAndy Burnham launches campaign against ‘headphone dodgers’ on public transportPassengers urged to ‘share the carriage, not the noise’ as guidance sets out £100 penalties for nuisance behaviourKiran StaceyPolicy editorSun 18 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has announced a crackdown on “headphone dodgers” who play loud music on public transport, as he extends his promise to give voters “breathing space” in the confines of a train carriage.The prime minister will unveil a campaign against nuisance behaviour on public transport on Monday, alongside guidance allowing local transport authorities to levy fines of up to £100 for non-compliance.The move makes him the latest senior politician to promise action against people who play videos or music out loud in public spaces, something that about 60% of voters back.Burnham said in a statement: “We’ve all been on the train when someone starts blasting music or videos from their phone. It gets on your nerves and can quickly spoil the journey.“So, we’re launching a nationwide campaign reminding passengers to use headphones on trains. On top of that, we’re giving local leaders new powers to tackle loud music, vaping and littering on buses.“It’s a simple thing, but one that will make journeys that little bit better for all of us.”Under the plan, ministers will issue guidance to local transport authorities advising them on how they should use new powers granted under the Bus Services Act, which allows them to set and enforce their own rules on board.The guidance will say authorities should issue fines of up to £100 if bus passengers refuse to comply with a request to stop certain nuisance behaviour.Officials said drivers would not be expected to enforce such rules. That job would be left to transport safety officers or police officers. Train operating companies already have the power to issue fines of up to £1,000 for similar behaviour.Alongside the new powers, the government is launching a poster campaign to discourage people from playing videos or music on their phones out loud on public transport.Under the slogan “share the carriage, not the noise”, passengers will be encouraged to use headphones, avoid making calls on speakerphone and watch videos quietly.The campaign makes Burnham the latest in a series of politicians to promise to tackle headphone dodgers.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe London mayor, Sadiq Khan,unveiled a campaignin the summer urging passengers to “travel kind”, including by wearing headphones. The Liberal Democratshave called forbus travellers to face £1,000 fines as well as those on trains.The scramble for politicians to react comes as polls show noise on public transport is a major annoyance for British people.Arecent pollby YouGov found voters would back £1,000 fines for people playing music out loud on buses and trains. Aseparate surveyby the same company found that voters listed people talking on speakerphones as one of their top three irritants.Unions, however, said the new enforcement regime would do little to protect transport workers.The general secretary of Unite, Sharon Graham, said: “The government’s proposals are well-meaning but wholly inadequate to tackle the challenges and violence bus workers are facing on a daily basis. The proposed penalties are not going to deal with the issues facing workers.”Explore more on these topicsTransport policyRail transportRoad transportPublic transportLabourTransportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Warning signs could predict inflammatory bowel disease a decade before diagnosis | Medical research | The Guardian
description: Antibody patterns in the blood may help doctors identify people at risk so they can be treated earlier, research shows
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Antibody patterns in the blood may help doctors identify people at risk so they can be treated earlier, research shows
Content: IBD has only been able to be treated at a later stage, but scientists found that the immune system leaves warning signs long before diagnosis.Photograph: Teodor Lazarev/AlamyView image in fullscreenIBD has only been able to be treated at a later stage, but scientists found that the immune system leaves warning signs long before diagnosis.Photograph: Teodor Lazarev/AlamyMedical researchWarning signs could predict inflammatory bowel disease a decade before diagnosisAntibody patterns in the blood may help doctors identify people at risk so they can be treated earlier, research showsHanad AhmedSun 18 Oct 2026 18.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePatterns of antibodies in people’s blood could predict the onset of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) a decade before diagnosis, according to research that raises hopes for catching the condition early.Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis, the two main forms of IBD, are typically treated only after symptoms appear, when the gut has already been damaged. But scientists found that the immune system sends warning signals up to a decade before diagnosis, paving the way for potentially earlier detection and even prevention.“For too long we have only been able to treat inflammatory bowel disease once the damage is done, and for many people that is too late,” said Dr Arno Bourgonje at the University Medical Centre Groningen in the Netherlands and the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York.“What we have shown is that the disease begins years before symptoms appear, and the immune system leaves warning signs long before diagnosis,” Bourgonje added. “This is not yet a test that can tell someone they will become ill, but it is an important step towards catching the disease earlier and, one day, preventing it.”At least 3.8 million people worldwide live with IBD, an immune condition that drives chronic inflammation of the digestive tract, causing pain, diarrhoea and fatigue. The exact cause is unknown, but a misfiring immune system, genetics and microbes living in the gut can all contribute.Treatment relies on anti-inflammatory and immune-suppressing drugs, but many patients do not respond, and a significant number go on to have surgery to remove damaged sections of bowel. Longstanding inflammation also raises the risk of bowel cancer. This has prompted scientists to look for the earlier signs of disease, in the hope of identifying people at risk before damage begins.Bourgonje and colleagues at Mount Sinai and the Medical University of Vienna ran tests on blood samples taken from US military personnel. They examined 2,000 samples from 500 people, 200 of whom later developed Crohn’s disease, and 200 who went on to develop ulcerative colitis. The remaining 100 developed neither condition.The blood samples were screened for antibodies that the immune system might have churned out in response to hundreds of thousands of fragments of proteins from bacteria, viruses, food and even the body’s own tissues.In people who went on to develop Crohn’s disease, antibodies against Epstein-Barr virus, which causes glandular fever, were more common, and the differences were already visible a decade before diagnosis. The signal was strongest in those who later developed more severe, complicated disease, which can narrow the bowel or create abnormal channels.People who developed ulcerative colitis showed a different pattern, including antibodies against one of the body’s own proteins.The findings, published in the journalGutand presented at the United European Gastroenterology meeting in Barcelona, need to be confirmed in other groups of people, and the results show a link rather than proving the infections cause IBD. But the hope is that IBD could eventually follow the path of type 1 diabetes, where a blood test can identify people whose immune systems have begun attacking the pancreas before any symptoms appear, allowing treatment that delays the onset of disease.James Lindsay, a professor of gastroenterology at BartsHealth, who was not involved in the research, said the study provided “important insights into the causes of Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis, potentially adding new tools to help identify those at risk of IBD”. But he cautioned that the techniques were “very much a research tool” and not yet ready for the clinic.Marianne Radcliffe, the chief executive of Crohn’s & Colitis UK, a national patient charity, said: “For people affected by Crohn’s and colitis, research like this is an important step forward. Every new insight helps build a clearer understanding of how these conditions develop, including the changes that may occur years before symptoms appear.”Explore more on these topicsMedical researchHealthDigestive disordersnewsShareReuse this content

title: Cut benefits to fund work support for young people, says Neet review author Alan Milburn | Youth unemployment | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Former health secretary says upfront investment in support is needed ‘if we are going to end the Neet crisis’
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Exclusive: Former health secretary says upfront investment in support is needed ‘if we are going to end the Neet crisis’
Content: Milburn said the welfare system ‘just isn’t working for young people’.Photograph: Jeff Moore/PAView image in fullscreenMilburn said the welfare system ‘just isn’t working for young people’.Photograph: Jeff Moore/PAYouth unemploymentCut benefits to fund work support for young people, says Neet review author Alan MilburnExclusive: Former health secretary says upfront investment in support is needed ‘if we are going to end the Neet crisis’Anna BawdenandKiran StaceySun 18 Oct 2026 14.30 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 14.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMinisters should cut welfare spending to fund more employment support if it wants to end the youth Neet crisis, the author of a government-led review has said.Alan Milburn, the Tony Blair-era health secretary, told the Guardian he believed ministers should reduce benefits payments to help pay for more employment support, opening a potentially contentious debate within theLabourparty over welfare cuts.His intervention comes in the run-up to John Healey’s first budget, at which the chancellor is under pressure to explain how he will reduce a multibillion-pound black hole in the country’s finances and pay for more cost of living support without increasing borrowing.“We’ve got to have a different conversation about the welfare system, it just isn’t working for young people,” Milburn told the Guardian. “We need to redistribute money from the welfare system to more employment support if we are going to end the Neet crisis.”Milburn’s review of why so many 18- to 24-year-olds are not in education, employment or training calculated that a record1 million young people are now classed as Neet. The former cabinet minister said this was far more than a cyclical youth unemployment problem – it was a “youth detachment” problem, pointing to the fact that 60% of these Neets have never had a job.Ministers have pushed back Milburn’s final report until after the budget, at which Healey is expected to use a tax raid on banks to help pay for cost of living schemes such as a new energy support package.The chancellor has signalled his willingness to spend more money on youth unemployment programmes in the short term, however, even if the welfare savings take longer to be realised. He announced a £100m “local apprenticeship service” at last month’s Labour conference, calling it “a downpayment on Alan Milburn’s work”.In a joint interview with Peter Fonagy, the chair of the government’s landmarkindependent review of mental health, ADHD and autism, Milburn said his final recommendations were not just about tackling youth unemployment but also improving wellbeing.“The Neet crisis is a health crisis,” he said. “We’re in this vicious cycle where ill health is driving higher Neet rates. Non-participation is a disaster for young people’s mental health.”Milburn’s review is likely to recommend that employment, health and benefits support become more integrated. “We have got to change how the wealth, health and welfare systems work and how they interact with each other, because right now they’re plunging far too many young people into a life on benefits, which is ruinous to their life chances, rather than the opportunity to work,”he said.“No one [in government] is responsible for ensuring that young people both avoid the trap door of becoming Neet and get support to get them out of being Neet.”View image in fullscreenPeter Fonagy said a system was needed ‘that actually addresses [young people’s] potential and what it is that they can do’, rather than just identifying disability.Photograph: Maya Balanya Archdc/Album/AlamyFonagy’s review found that the number of people suffering mental distress has risen significantly across all age groups in England since the 1990s, especially the under-18s. It recommended providing help at the point of need, not after a diagnosis.“The current system isbased on identifying disability, why a person can’t do something,” Fonagy said. “We need a system that actually addresses their potential and what it is that they can do.“If nothing is done, and the trends go on as up till now, then there will be not one in five young people with diagnosable mental disorders, but one in four,” which, he added, increased the chances of them becoming Neet.While there will always be a group of young people whose physical or mental health mean work is not an option, “forthe vast majority of young people with autism, ADHD, anxiety or depression, the starting point has to be what could you do, what would you like to do, and how can the state help them do it,”Milburn said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘Work is good for you’: how UK scheme could help tackle youth mental health crisisRead moreYoung people with health needs should get prompt needs assessment, a personalised health plan and a wider “participation plan”, the review is likely to recommend.The kind of transformation Milburn and Fonagy describe would cost hundreds of millions of pounds in investment, sources believe. While they would not comment on the level of funding required, both were clear that upfront money would be crucial. “I think everybody in government is very, very well aware of the need to invest behind this priority,” Milburn said.“Over the medium term, it is entirely possible that you can reduce the benefits bill, but in order to do that, you’ve got to provide the support for young people. You’ve got to increase the opportunities that are available for young people and then provide the support for them to enable them to grab those opportunities.”“This is not a workshy, snowflake generation, you know, who are making mental distress up,” Milburn added. “If we provide more opportunities and we provide more support, the overwhelming majority of young people will take that, because that’s what they want. The system isn’t delivering what young people want, which is a job.”But Milburn also hinted at possible consequences for those who don’t engage. “Equally, there has got to be an obligation on young people to take up those opportunities, of course,” he said.The problem with the system was that it was “over-indexed to cash” and didn’t provide enough support, he added. “The consequence is calamitous for young people who could be working and are not being helped to do so, who then end up on a trajectory to a lifetime on benefits.”But intervening earlier and providing better support would in turn help relieve the pressure on the mental health waiting list. “I would hope that, for the first time, we could also introduce a maximum waiting time for mental health services, particularly for young people,” said Milburn.Explore more on these topicsYouth unemploymentWelfareBenefitsUnemploymentYoung peopleLabourMental healthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Zack Polanski says application of Zionism is racist and no state has right to exist | Green party | The Guardian
description: Green leader in England and Wales calls ‘debates about words’ unhelpful and denies recent motion was controversial
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Green leader in England and Wales calls ‘debates about words’ unhelpful and denies recent motion was controversial
Content: The Green Party leader in England and Wales, Zack Polanski, spoke to the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg on Sunday.Photograph: Jeff Overs/PAView image in fullscreenThe Green Party leader in England and Wales, Zack Polanski, spoke to the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg on Sunday.Photograph: Jeff Overs/PAGreen partyZack Polanski says application of Zionism is racist and no state has right to existGreen leader in England and Wales calls ‘debates about words’ unhelpful and denies recent motion was controversialKiran StaceyPolicy editorSun 18 Oct 2026 13.38 EDTFirst published on Sun 18 Oct 2026 06.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleZack Polanski has said Zionism in its current form is racist, that no country has a right to exist, and that theGreen party motionon the issue was not controversial.The leader of theGreen partyin England and Wales gave an unapologetic interview to the BBC on Sunday two weeks after his party approved a motion equating Zionism with racism.Polanski did not attend the vote, prompting accusations of a lack of leadership, but he made clear he agreed with the broad thrust of it even if he felt it was unhelpful to have what he called a “debate about semantics”.Asked by the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg whether he thought Zionism was racist, Polanski said: “I don’t think this is actually controversial.“What’s controversial is that 75,000 Palestinians have been murdered in the last few years, including more child amputees than ever in modern history. So when you take that to account, the fact that they’re being murdered because they’re Palestinian – that’s very obviously a racist ideology.”He added: “I think Zionism is racism in the practical application of it. Now the conference had a debate about the motion, about the word. I said I think debates about words are unhelpful, and I still think that.”Asked whether he believedIsraelhad a right to exist, Polanski, who is Jewish, said: “I don’t think any state has a right to exist under international law,” adding that the idea of a two-state solution was “for the birds” given Israel’s opposition to it.He also insisted he had no regrets about the way he had handled the recent controversy, despite criticism from some prominent Jewish Green members,including Vivien Lichtenstein, the chair of the Jewish Greens.Polanski said: “I’m not sorry at all. Vivien is someone I’ve had respect for and do have respect for, and partly co-founded the Jewish Greens together … Actually, when the Jewish Greens were surveyed about this motion, a majority supported it.”In response,Lichtenstein later said: “Zack should have joined conference online, listened to the speeches for and against and, crucially, spoken for those amendments he supported, then voted.“None of that took an inordinate amount of time. There was no excuse for his not participating.”She also said polling of Jewish greens on the Zionism motion showed they were evenly split, contrary to Polanski’s claims.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLabour councils told to end agreements with Greens who do not condemn ‘Zionism is racism’ policyRead morePolanski’s defiant interview comes after the most difficult two weeks of his leadership of the party since he took over last September, during which he has endured the fallout from the conference vote andlost the Holborn and St Pancras byelection.His strategy of shifting his party to the left, focusing on economically populist ideas and leaning into debates onPalestineand Gaza initially paid dividends, with the party jumping from about 10% in the polls to 18% earlier this year.In recent months, however, the party has tumbled, beset byquestions over his tax affairs, apublic spat with the policeafter the Golders Green attack and the recent row over Zionism.He said on Sunday that he was confident voters would return to his party once they had seen more of Andy Burnham’s leadership of the country. “People more and more will see from Andy Burnham a change in rhetoric, but not a change in action, and know the Green party have been right all along,” he said.Explore more on these topicsGreen partyZack PolanskiIsraelPalestineAntisemitismGazanewsShareReuse this content

title: Police investigate Reform mayor for allegedly sharing ‘naked and sexualised’ images of himself | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Female colleague says she was forced out shortly after incident with Luke Campbell, Hull and East Yorkshire mayor
Author: Josh Halliday
Headline: Female colleague says she was forced out shortly after incident with Luke Campbell, Hull and East Yorkshire mayor
Content: Luke Campbell, right, with the Reform UK party leader, Nigel Farage, in 2025.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersView image in fullscreenLuke Campbell, right, with the Reform UK party leader, Nigel Farage, in 2025.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersReform UKPolice investigate Reform mayor for allegedly sharing ‘naked and sexualised’ images of himselfFemale colleague says she was forced out shortly after incident with Luke Campbell, Hull and East Yorkshire mayorJosh HallidayNorth of England editorSun 18 Oct 2026 11.18 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 11.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAReform UKmayor is under police investigation for allegedly showing “naked and sexualised” images of himself to a female member of staff.Luke Campbell, a former Olympic boxing champion and the mayor of Hull and EastYorkshire, is understood to have been questioned under caution by Humberside police earlier this month.In an incident first reported bythe Observeron Sunday, Campbell allegedly showed a senior female colleague four fully naked and sexualised images of himself in May.The woman said she had felt “shocked, embarrassed and humiliated” and claimed she had been forced out of her job soon after, according to documents submitted as part of an internal grievance procedure atHulland East Yorkshire combined authority (Heyca).Campbell, who was elected last May, has not responded to requests to comment. It is understood that he has not been arrested in relation to the allegations, which Reform UK has said he “firmly denies”.View image in fullscreenLuke Campbell, pictured in 2012, won gold at the London Olympics.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianA Reform UK spokesperson said: “Luke firmly denies the allegations. They come from a disgruntled employee attempting to leverage a settlement in a meritless workplace dispute.”The allegations against Campbell came to light after a year-long ITV investigation uncovered racist commentsfrom a number of Reform UK councillorsand a prospective MP.An aspiring Reform UK MPwas suspendedafter telling an undercover reporter that Muslims could not be British and asylum seekers crossing the English channel should be put in “concentration camps”, in footage due to be broadcast on Sunday night.Nigel Farage’s party said it had opened investigations where activists or members had “clearly behaved inappropriately”, adding that there was “no room for racism” in the party.Nadine Dorries, a former Conservative minister and now a Reform UK member, came to Campbell’s defence on Sunday by claiming that the “sexualised” image was in fact a 2013 magazine cover showing the former boxer posing naked from the waist up after hewon gold at the 2012 London Olympics.However, that appears to be at odds with witness testimony submitted as part of an internal grievance procedure at Heyca, where Campbell is mayor.In one document, corroborated by the Guardian, a senior female colleague said Campbell had called her over to a computer screen, where she was shown “several naked and sexualised images” of the mayor.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUK ‘an outlier in Europe’ for letting Farage and other politicians present TV showsRead moreA separate witness said they saw a naked man with a tattoo in one of the images, whereas no tattoo is visible on the magazine front cover.The main complainant said in a witness statement: “I was deliberately exposed to naked and sexualised images involving the mayor in the workplace, without my consent, and was laughed at when I was visibly embarrassed.“In my view, this was unwanted conduct of a sexual nature which violated my dignity and created a humiliating, degrading and offensive working environment.”About three weeks after the alleged incident, the female officer, who was working as a contractor but had accepted the offer of a permanent role, was allegedly told on a Teams call that the offer had been withdrawn.In a separate document, a second colleague said they had felt “uneasy” after allegedly seeing Campbell and two male colleagues ushering over a female officer to look at his laptop, which showed an image of a naked man with a tattoo.The Guardian understands that this second employee recalled comments then being made about Campbell’s tattoo and that they saw the mayor lift his shirt to show the tattoo.A spokesperson for Heyca confirmed to the Observer that a police investigation was under way. He said: “As with all public authorities, the combined authority has a standards process that can be engaged to deal with complaints about members and a complaints procedure that can be used to deal with complaints about officers.“The standards process and the complaints procedure must be carried out in a fair and independent manner.”Humberside police has been contacted for comment.Explore more on these topicsReform UKYorkshireMayoral electionsHullLocal governmentLocal politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Outrage after Meta suspends No Kings Instagram account during protests | US midterm elections 2026 | The Guardian
description: ‘Meta owes us an explanation,’ group says as organizers fear censorship after account goes dark for several hours
Author: Sanya Mansoor
Headline: ‘Meta owes us an explanation,’ group says as organizers fear censorship after account goes dark for several hours
Content: Protesters gather for a No Kings rally on Saturday in New York.Photograph: Madison Swart/APView image in fullscreenProtesters gather for a No Kings rally on Saturday in New York.Photograph: Madison Swart/APUS midterm elections 2026Outrage after Meta suspends No Kings Instagram account during protests‘Meta owes us an explanation,’ group says as organizers fear censorship after account goes dark for several hoursSanya MansoorSun 18 Oct 2026 19.53 EDTFirst published on Sun 18 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe coalition leaders behind nationwide pro-democracy protests that have drawn millions of Americans to the streets in recent years were frustrated when its Instagram account was temporarily shut down during itslatest demonstration on Saturday.The No Kings movement’s account went dark for several hours while protests focused on increasing early voter turnout were underway, sparking censorship fears.Meta apologized on Saturday and blamed the account’s temporary suspension on an automated action that’s triggered “when accounts post, share or comment at very high frequencies”.“Unfortunately, that automated action was clearly taken in error,”Meta spokesperson Andy Stone, wrote on X. “Everything is now working as it should and we sincerely apologize.”“We have regained access to our accounts, but Meta still owes us an explanation,” the No Kings Coalitionposted on their Instagram page, on Sunday. “Restricting communications about voting in the middle of an election is unacceptable.”In a longer statement, Stone cited the “high volume” of reading profiles, posts and hashtags in “intense bursts” on Saturday caused their AI tool to detect the activity as automated bot traffic.“This activity caused our automated protections to incorrectly take the No Kings Instagram account offline. An automated re-review of the removal action an hour later recognized that shouldn’t have happened and restored the account,” Stone said. “It unfortunately took additional time for us to straighten out the situation with admin access to the IG account. We want to reiterate our sincere apology for the error.”Organizers remained skeptical about Meta’s explanation that high-frequency posting triggered an automated response, and said members “posted only a handful of times and livestreamed to thousands”.Senator Bernie Sanders alsoexpressed concerns on Sunday, on X, saying that “billionaire ownership of the media” had resulted in the suspension of the No Kings account.Connecticut senator Chris Murphy called for an investigation into the incident in his ownsocial media post, saying it was an indictment of Meta’s “outsized influence” on US culture and politics. “How were they not ready for the biggest day of anti-Trump protest of the campaign?” Murphy said. “An investigation is warranted, at the very least, to understand why Meta (which effectively functions these days as a private government) was unable to protect protest against Trump, while it spends so much time trying to get close to Trump.”Despite the technical blip,hundreds of planned events continued. At theLincoln Memorial in Washington, a band played for a few hundred people in caps and coats, many of whom were dancing and held signs saying “VOTE EARLY” and “HANDS OFF MY VOTE!”InAtlanta, city councilman Michael Julian Bond told the crowd: “The constitution gives you one power, right? That is the power to vote. Are you gonna use that power?”On the streets of downtown Los Angeles, protesters carried umbrellas to protect them from the sweltering heat and a band trailed behind them on a rolling stage, theNew York Times reported; the crowds cheered calls for abolishing ICE and passing California’s billionaire tax.The No Kings movement began last summer, in response to a broad set of concerns about federal layoffs, immigration enforcement and foreign wars. The demonstrations have continued to tackle a wide range of issues, and typically lean into anti-Trump fervor.This year’s focus on voting ahead of the midterm elections is in part due to the supreme court’sgutting of the Voting Rights Act,as well as fears about Trump once again sowing chaos bybaselessly calling election results into question.No Kings organizers said they planned to recruit volunteers at Saturday’s events to mobilize in case of “election sabotage”, Leah Greenberg, a co-executive director of Indivisible, a progressive group that helps organize No Kings events,previously told the Guardian.Explore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026Protest (US)Trump administrationDonald TrumpUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Obama condemns comments by ‘border czar’ that Ilhan Omar could ‘of course’ be denaturalized | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: Former president urges Americans to defend congresswoman, saying ‘there’s no reason to believe it will stop with her’
Author: José Olivares
Headline: Former president urges Americans to defend congresswoman, saying ‘there’s no reason to believe it will stop with her’
Content: Homeland security officers carry boxes from the Washington DC residence of Ilhan Omar, on 12 October.Photograph: J Scott Applewhite/APView image in fullscreenHomeland security officers carry boxes from the Washington DC residence of Ilhan Omar, on 12 October.Photograph: J Scott Applewhite/APTrump administrationObama condemns comments by ‘border czar’ that Ilhan Omar could ‘of course’ be denaturalizedEx-president urges Americans to defend congresswoman, saying ‘there’s no reason to believe it will stop with her’José OlivaresandSanya Mansoorin New YorkSun 18 Oct 2026 19.51 EDTFirst published on Sun 18 Oct 2026 13.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFormer US president Barack Obama condemned comments by Donald Trump’s “border czar” that the Republican presidential administration could “of course” strip Democratic congresswomanIlhan Omarof her citizenship and deport her.Obamawrote Sunday morning, on X, that “the full weight of the federal government is being brought down on a law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticize the president.”He urged all Americans to defend Omar, regardless of their political beliefs, adding: “if this becomes the new normal, there’s no reason to believe it will stop with her – or that future presidents, in either party, won’t do the same.” Obama, too, has had his citizenship scrutinized by Trump, who more than a decade agofueled false conspiracy theoriesthat Obama was born in Kenya and therefore not eligible to be president.Ilhan Omar’s attorneys say federal search of her home was ‘neither justified nor lawful’Read moreTom Homan, Trump’s “border czar”, was asked on Saturday by a Fox News host whether the investigation into Omar could involve “denaturalizing and then deporting her”, Homan answered: “Of course”.“If you lie during the naturalization process, there is a process to denaturalize somebody,” Homan said. “We’ve done it before. It’s a long, tedious process, but it’s been done before.“And certainly, if the evidence points that way, that could happen.”Homan’s comments were the first remarks explicitly mentioning denaturalization and deportation in connection with Omar that were attributed by name to a topTrump administrationofficial since federal agents raided the Minnesota US House representative’s home on 12 October.The search of Omar’s home sparked majorbacklashand accusations that the Trump administration was weaponizing the federal government to target a political rival whom the president and his supporters have openly fantasized aboutdenaturalizinganddeporting.The federal government’s investigation into the most prominent Somali American in the US is to see whether Omar or her family violated any laws when obtaining her citizenship. The investigation was launched only weeks before the Novembermidterm elections, in which Omar is on the ballot.Homan also seemed to imply during his Fox News appearance that the federal government is investigating Omar for other allegations – but refused to give details.“I’m not going to go there,” Homan said. “I know things, but that’s a question for the FBI.”Omar – a naturalized US citizen fromSomalia– was a child when her father filled out the immigration paperwork which the federal government is evidently scrutinizing. Her father, Nur Omar Mohamed, died in June 2020.View image in fullscreenTom Homan applauds as Donald Trump speaks at a rally in Syracuse, New York, on 9 October.Photograph: Mandel Ngan/AFP/Getty ImagesObama stated in his post on X that Omar arrived in the US with her father when she was 12, and five years later, when her father became a naturalized citizen, she became one, too, because she was 17. (An 18-year-old would have had to apply for citizenship separately, he noted.)“Now the Administration is actively trying to deport Congresswoman Omar, seemingly based solely on the unsubstantiated theory that she was actually 18 when her father was naturalized, and therefore is not a citizen,” he wrote. “Federal agents have raided her home, confiscated personal records, and seized her phone – all to try and uncover a nonexistent smoking gun from 20 years ago that will somehow make their case.”In a letter after her home was searched, Omar’s attorneysaccused the US justice departmentof potentially influencing an election in violation of longstanding internal policy.The move to investigate Omar came amid a heightened offensive by the administration in pursuit of its aggressive anti-immigrant crackdown. In addition to funneling resources and deploying droves of officials to arrest, detain and deport undocumented immigrants throughout the country, the administration has also escalated its onoffensive on legal migration.The administration has been pursuing dozens of cases nationwide in which they are attempting to denaturalize Americans born outside of the US, who they claim fraudulently obtained their citizenship.As Homan alluded to on Sunday, the lengthy denaturalization process requires a federal investigation and drawn-out court proceedings.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNonetheless, as of April, the US justice department hadreportedly identifiednearly 400 foreign-born citizens that it sought to investigate.The investigation into Omar follows unsubstantiated accusations by rightwing figures who support Trump that she obtained her citizenship fraudulently. Omar denies the accusations, which also includeallegationsthather ex-husband is her brother, whom she only married so he could obtain immigration status in the US.Ilhan Omar’s phone seized and relatives subpoenaed in criminal inquiry, source saysRead moreThe federal government reportedlyseized Omar’s phoneduring the raid on her home and has issued more than a dozen subpoenas, including of Omar’s relatives.Omar’s attorneys have demanded that the federal government return her property and preserve any audio or video taken during the search.Omar has said she and her family fled Somalia’s civil war when she was eight and spent years in a refugee camp in Kenya. She and her family came to the US in the 1990s, and she became a naturalized US citizen in 2000, according to her lawyers.There is “no legitimate basis for any suggestion that she has violated any law concerning her citizenship status”, said her attorneys’ letter, which was first reported by theWall Street Journal.Even veterans at the Department of Justice expressed shock over the targeting of Omar, according toreporting by NBC News. “I was astounded to see a search of a sitting congressperson this close to an election,” said Peter Carr, a former career justice department spokesperson, NBC News reported.“Historically, the department has been very adamant that politics plays no role in investigative decisions they make and they try very hard to avoid taking overt actions that might even have the perception of influencing an election.”After the raid on her home, Omarposted on Xthat she was “ok”.“Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” Omar also wrote. She said: “Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns” for years – and “this is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation.”“I will not be silenced,” Omar added.Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationUS immigrationUS politicsIlhan OmarUS CongressHouse of RepresentativesSomalianewsShareReuse this content

title: Times’s investigation adds more intrigue to infamous OJ Simpson case | OJ Simpson | The Guardian
description: Report reveals that a shady mobster-turned-informant may have been involved in helping cover up murder
Author: José Olivares
Headline: Report reveals that a shady mobster-turned-informant may have been involved in helping cover up murder
Content: OJ Simpson reacts with lawyers after court clerk announces not guilty verdict in his murder trial on 3 October 1995.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenOJ Simpson reacts with lawyers after court clerk announces not guilty verdict in his murder trial on 3 October 1995.Photograph: ReutersOJ SimpsonTimes’s investigation adds more intrigue to infamous OJ Simpson caseReport reveals that a shady mobster-turned-informant may have been involved in helping cover up murderJosé OlivaresSun 18 Oct 2026 19.35 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 19.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn in-depth investigation by theNew York Timesis raising further questions about the high-profile OJ Simpson case, in which the former football player was accused in the 1990s of killing his ex-wife – and whether a shady mobster-turned-informant may have been involved in helping cover up the murder.The Times’s investigation revealed thatCaliforniaprosecutors were unable to fully investigate whether Simpson, who was accused but not convicted of his ex-wife’s murder, may have had an accomplice at the scene of the crime.The extensive journalistic investigation, based on previously sealed court records and interviews, adds further intrigue to the infamous Simpson case. No one was ever criminally convicted for the 1994 murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman.That year, Nicole Brown Simpson and Goldman were found stabbed to death outside her home inLos Angeles. The American professional football player and actor, OJ Simpson, was suspected in the murder. Simpson’s prosecution gained international attention and became a media spectacle, being deemed the “trial of the century”.Simpson was acquitted by a jury in 1995 after a lengthy trial. The Los Angeles police department, which investigated the case, had a long history of racism. Simpson’s attorneys pointed to the racist policing practices and the department’s handling of key evidence, helping them secure the acquittal. Simpson was later held liable for the deaths by a jury in a civil case.But the New York Times has now revealed that a shady informant began revealing information about Simpson’s case towards the end of the prosecution. The informant, a wealthy mobster named Joseph Ippolito, had become a snitch after spending years on the run from the federal government.The information Ippolito had may have been key to the trial, but it was far too late for the prosecution to include his testimony.Ippolito, a longtime drug runner throughout the US known as Joey, came from the New Jersey underworld, where his father was a player within the DeCavalcante crime family, a major Italian American criminal organization. After a stint in prison for trafficking drugs in the east coast, he moved to California in the late 1980s and managed an Italian restaurant.There, he was able to embed himself in the inner circles of the Los Angeles elite. Ippolito befriended Al Cowlings, a former football star and close friend ofOJ Simpson. But while he spent time with Los Angeles celebrities, Ippolito continued selling and trafficking drugs.In 1992, he was arrested by authorities again in a sting operation. But in May 1994, eight months after his sentencing, Ippolito escaped from his Florida prison. His brother helped him arrive back in Los Angeles, where he remained in hiding as a wanted fugitive.That year, the murder of Nicole Brown Simpson and Goldman took place in Los Angeles. When authorities attempted to arrest OJ Simpson, he fled. His friend Cowlings, the former football player, led the police on a widely-publicized chase through Los Angeles with Simpson in the car.After Simpson’s arrest, officials found Ippolito’s information in Cowlings’ wallet, leading them to urgently search for the mobster-at-large. Eventually they found Ippolito and arrested him. But he decided to flip and become an informant for the US government.As an informant, Ippolito revealed information about various drug deals throughout the country and helped federal agencies set up sting operations. But Ippolito also reportedly shared information with the government about the Los Angeles murders.The New York Times raises three separate theories for Ippolito’s involvement in the Simpson case, which he was seemingly willing to share with authorities:1) In one version, Ippolito told federal prosecutors he had information he learned from Cowlings about the murders, including the supposed location of the missing weapon.2) In another version, Ippolito’s brother told a reporter with the Times that Ippolito may have been at the scene of the killings. The brother said Ippolito literally had blood on his hands.3) And in a third version, Ippolito was prepared to help Simpson escape during the wild police chase throughout Los Angeles.“Taken together, the material points in different directions but veers significantly from the official account that has been proffered by the police and prosecutors,” the New York Times reports. “With many of the key players now dead, it’s possible the full truth will never be known.”Ippolito’s brother, who told the Times he had seen his brother’s hands with blood on them, later asked the publication for money and then recanted his statement to the publication. According to the report, the brother said he had been “offered a ton of money” to share his story elsewhere, likely a television program.The extent of Ippolito’s involvement is not fully known. Authorities interviewed by the Times expressed doubts on how involved Ippolito was and the value of his information in the case.Explore more on these topicsOJ SimpsonCaliforniaUS crimeWest CoastLos AngelesnewsShareReuse this content

title: EPA quietly backtracks on claims US has phased out toxic Pfas compounds | Pfas | The Guardian
description: Agency changes wording on website as Texas-based firm continues manufacture of plastic container barriers
Author: Tom Perkins
Headline: Agency changes wording on website as Texas-based firm continues manufacture of plastic container barriers
Content: Though the agency stopped short of a ban, the ‘phase- out’ was viewed as major progress on reining in Pfas pollution.Photograph: Rohane Hamilton/AlamyView image in fullscreenThough the agency stopped short of a ban, the ‘phase- out’ was viewed as major progress on reining in Pfas pollution.Photograph: Rohane Hamilton/AlamyPfasEPA quietly backtracks on claims US has phased out toxic Pfas compoundsAgency changes wording on website as Texas-based firm continues manufacture of plastic container barriersTom PerkinsSun 18 Oct 2026 18.53 EDTFirst published on Sun 18 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Environmental Protection Agency has quietly backtracked on a claim that the US has phased out two of the most dangerousPfascompounds – Pfoa and Pfos.The EPA has found thatvirtually no level of exposureto either in drinking water is safe, and the International Agency for Research on Cancerclassifies Pfoaas “carcinogenic to humans” and Pfos as “possibly carcinogenic”. Still, the EPA is allowing Houston-based Inhance to produce containers from which Pfoahas been foundto leach at high levels into the containers’ contents. The company makes up to 200m barriers annually for plastic containers used across the US economy.The containers present an “ongoing serious and ongoing threat to public health,” said Kyla Bennett, a former EPA scientist who is now science policy director with the Public Employees for Environmental Responsibility (Peer) non-profit.Inhancehas deniedthat the chemical leaches out in measurable levels, and told the Guardian in a statement that any Pfoa from its products are an “impurity”.The EPA has written that the company is “manufacturing“ PFAS.The “phase-out” was put in place after documents made public duringlandmark early 2000s litigationon DuPont’s Pfas pollution in West Virginia laid bare the ubiquitous chemicals’ dangers and serious health risks. In 2015, facing intense pressure to act, the EPA reached an agreement with eight Pfas producers to “phase out” production of Pfoa and Pfos, a similar chemical produced by 3M.Though the agency stopped short of a ban, the “phase out” was viewed as major progress on reining in Pfas pollution. Officialsoften repeatedthe claim that the chemicals had been phased out, giving the impression that they were no longer produced or used in the US.Last month, the EPA quietly changed wording on its website that claimed Pfoa and Pfos had been phased out.. In fact, both have been produced in the US this whole time, and at levels that independent science suggest are quite high.The EPA sitepreviously stated: “The manufacture and import of Pfoa has also been phased out in the United States.”It now reads: “Quantities of Pfoa may be produced, imported, and used by companies … ”The change was made in response toa complaint filed by Peer, which pointed out that the EPA was allowing Pfoa to be produced in the US. Under the Information Quality Act, data and information made public by federal agencies be complete and accurate.“They were giving the false impression and saying, ‘Nothing to see here because Pfoa is not being produced in the US,’” Bennett told the Guardian. “But that was demonstrably false, and now they have admitted it.”Anepidemiological panel convenedduring the West Virginia DuPont case found Pfoa and Pfos likely causes cancer, heart disease, liver disease, kidney disease. The panel’s findings were the scientific basis for the phase-out.The EPA did not immediately provide a comment to the Guardian. Inhance in its statement to The Guardian stressed that there was never a ban in place and it was not one of the eight companies that agreed to stop producing Pfoa.The reversal underscores why phase-outs are inadequate, and the EPA needs to put in place bans, Bennett said.“If you have a chemical and there’s no safe level of it, then why on earth would you allow it to be manufactured?” she said. “This all makes perfect sense if you understand the reality that the EPA is an arm of industry, especially under the Trump administration.”The EPA’s reversal marks the latest twist in a six-year legal battle over Inhance’s Pfoa-infused containers.The EPA seemed unaware that Pfas were being “manufactured” during plastic container barrier production until late 2020 testing by Peer found high levels of Pfas in pesticides stored in Inhance bins. The subsequent EPA investigation unearthedwide-scale contamination of plastic containers, prompting the agency to subpoena Inhance for information.It publiclyremindedthe plastics industry that companies must submit for a safety review if they manufacture Pfoa. Inhancedismissed the agency’s evidenceand claimed its containers did not leech Pfoa, but the EPA disagreed, again ordering Inhance in March 2022 to “immediately cease” production.Two weeks later, Inhanceput outa press release stating that its products did not “impart” Pfoa, and it did not cease production.Subsequent EPA testing found the containers still contained Pfoa. Facing legal pressure from Peer, the EPA by December 2023 again ordered Inhance to stop making the containers. That banwas overturnedby a federal appeals court. Peer later sued, but the case was dismissed because a federal judge ruled that the group lacked standing.In its statement, Inhance said that it made adjustments to reduce by 90% the level of Pfoa “impurities”.“Published peer-reviewed third-party risk assessments conclude that estimated exposure does not present an unreasonable risk to human health or the environment,” Inhance chief commercial officer Patricia van Ee wrote. “We have shared our process data with EPA throughout its review.”The EPA appears to have given up on enforcing the phase out and legally pressuring Inhance. Still, the EPA maintained on its website that Pfoa had been phased out of production, drawing the formal complaint from Peer.In a response dated 18 September, EPA assistant administrator for chemical safety and pollution prevention, Douglas Troutman, wrote: “In response to Peer’s request, the EPA is updating its websites.”The update also notes that Pfos is in US production in some “limited, ongoing uses”.“This rare touch of candor by EPA is welcome, but it does not address the free flow of toxic Pfas saturating our food, water, and soil,” Bennett said. “Now that EPA has admitted that these two legacy Pfas are still manufactured in the US, it is past time to take effective enforcement action.”This article was amended on 18 October 2026 to correct Patricia van Ee’s title, and the story previously stated that Inhance manufactures plastic containers. They make the containers’ barriers.Explore more on these topicsPfasPlasticsUS Environmental Protection AgencynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We are beyond heartbroken’: Cindy Crawford, Rande and Kaia Gerber share tributes to Presley | Celebrity | The Guardian
description: Family post emotional statements to Instagram a month after their son and brother died at a rehab facility
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Family post emotional statements to Instagram a month after their son and brother died at a rehab facility
Content: Rande Gerber and Cindy Crawford with their son Presley Gerber, who died on 20 September.Photograph: Rodin Eckenroth/WireImageView image in fullscreenRande Gerber and Cindy Crawford with their son Presley Gerber, who died on 20 September.Photograph: Rodin Eckenroth/WireImageCelebrity‘We are beyond heartbroken’: Cindy Crawford, Rande and Kaia Gerber share tributes to PresleyFamily post emotional statements to Instagram a month after their son and brother died at a rehab facilityPress AssociationSun 18 Oct 2026 18.52 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 20.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCindy Crawford and Rande Gerber have said they are “beyond heartbroken” in a tribute to their “sweet beautiful” son, Presley.Their eldest childdied aged 27at a rehab facility on 20 September, according to Los Angeles county medical examiner records. The cause of his death has not been disclosed.Crawford and Gerber posted an emotional statement on Instagram on Sunday.“We are beyond heartbroken to lose our beloved son and brother,” it said. “We feel so blessed to have had Presley in our lives for 27 years.“He is a sweet, beautiful soul who loved and is loved, now and forever. We are so proud of how he showed up in the world, with kindness and vulnerability.Death of 27-year-old Presley Gerber being investigated as suspected overdoseRead more“We are grateful for the outpouring of love and support from so many who know and love our family and even strangers who feel our pain.“Til we meet again our sweet boy.”The message was signed “with love forever” from Crawford and Gerber and their daughter, Kaia Gerber.Kaia, who like her mother is a model, also expressed her support in the comments, shared a message on her own page alongside a carousel of images and videos of herself with Presley.In a letter addressed to her brother, she wrote: “Prez, I don’t have the words. Maybe the tiny mercy is that we didn’t need them all along.”She wrote that she had “none of the answers” and could not articulate the “magnitude” of losing her brother.“You know how much I loved being your sister. It has always been, and will forever be, my favourite thing about myself.”The letter described her older brother as “inherently good” and her “ultimate teacher”, recounting childhood memories as she reflected on her grief.“I am learning how to love you when I cannot see you,” Kaia she. “How to tell you something without picking up my phone to call you. How to be your sister in a world that I can’t reach for you in. I don’t know how to do that yet.”She concluded: “My best buddy, my great protector, the hardest I’ve ever laughed and the one true love of my life. You lit all of my candles and took all of my monsters away, and I love you.”The post was set to the song First I Was by Jake Minch, which Kaia described as “the last thing we talked about”.The actors Taylor Lautner and Patrick Schwarzenegger, the singer Suki Waterhouse and the socialite Paris Hilton commented on the post.“My heart breaks for you and your family,” Hilton wrote. “Presley was truly one of a kind, and I feel so lucky to have known him. I’ll always remember him with so much love.”Presley was signed by IMGModelswhen he was 15 and modelled for brands including Burberry, Dolce & Gabbana and Bottega Veneta.He spoke frequently about his struggles with depression and substance abuse.Explore more on these topicsCelebrityBereavementSocial mediaModelsnewsShareReuse this content

title: NFL roundup: Panthers pile pain on slumping Eagles; Cardinals shock Rams | NFL | The Guardian
description: Caleb Williams completed his first 12 passes in his return from a hamstring injury, while the Eagles’ tough start to the season continued
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Caleb Williams completed his first 12 passes in his return from a hamstring injury, while the Eagles’ tough start to the season continued
Content: Nick Sirianni contemplates another loss for the Eagles.Photograph: Ricky Fitchett/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenNick Sirianni contemplates another loss for the Eagles.Photograph: Ricky Fitchett/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockNFLNFL roundup: Panthers pile pain on slumping Eagles; Cardinals shock RamsInjury-riddled Philadelphia fall to defeatChicago hold off Atlanta comeback in QB’s returnCardinals beat Rams with final play of gameAgenciesSun 18 Oct 2026 16.57 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 19.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCarolina Panthers 25–14 Philadelphia EaglesBryce Young threw for 281 yards and two touchdowns to Tommy Tremble, and Chuba Hubbard ran for 120 yards and a score to lead the Carolina Panthers (3-2) past the injury-riddled Philadelphia Eagles (2-4). The Panthers had little trouble in the second half picking apart the Eagles, who were missing quarterback Jalen Hurts and running back Saquon Barkley. Hurts is on injured reserve and will miss at least four gameswith a blood clot in his calf. Tanner McKee started for Philadelphia and finished 26 of 45 for 215 yards and a touchdown.Chicago Bears 31–23 Atlanta FalconsCaleb Williams completed his first 12 passes in his return from a hamstring injury, D’Andre Swift ran for two touchdowns and the Chicago Bears (4-2) beat the Atlanta Falcons (2-4). The Bears led 31-7 before holding off Atlanta’s comeback attempt in the final quarter. Bears cornerback Kyler Gordon, who returned from a calf injury, had three sacks and two forced fumbles. Gordon’s big day was capped by a sack of Michael Penix Jr and forced fumble with 2:54 remaining and the Bears protecting a 31-23 lead.Arizona Cardinals 18-16 Los Angeles RamsChad Ryland kicked his sixth field goal, a 43-yarder as time expired, and the Arizona Cardinals rallied for a stunning victory over the Los Angeles Rams. Punter Ethan Evans kicked the go-ahead extra point after Colby Parkinson caught a touchdown pass from Matthew Stafford with 47 seconds to play for the vaunted Rams, who struggled all day before mounting a desperate final scoring drive. But the Cardinals immediately moved 36 yards into field goal range on Jalen Brooks’ long reception and an unnecessary roughness penalty on Josh Wallace. Three snaps later, Ryland buried his final kick to seal a shocking upset for Arizona. Evans came through with his first career placekick after new Rams kicker Blake Grupe injured his knee making a tackle in the first quarter. Both teams are 2-4 on the season.Buffalo Bills 33–30 Las Vegas RaidersJosh Allen passed for 255 yards and two touchdowns, and the Buffalo Bills (5-1) held off the Las Vegas Raiders (3-3). Allen’s second TD pass moved him into a tie with Hall of Famer Jim Kelly for the most in Bills franchise history. He showed his improvisational brilliance on that throw, when he avoided a sack andshot-putted the ball to Keon Colemanfor a 12-yard TD. James Cook rushed for a three-yard touchdown with 4:43 left to put the Bills ahead for good, and Tyler Bass made it a two-score game with a late field goal.Los Angeles Chargers 6–22 Kansas City ChiefsKenneth Walker III rushed for 128 yards and two touchdowns and Patrick Mahomes passed for 272 yards to boost the host Kansas City Chiefs ⁠to victory. Kansas City improved to 5-0 to remain the lone unbeaten team in the AFC. The skidding Chargers (0-6) are ⁠off to the franchise’s ⁠worst start since ​the 2000 San Diego Chargers lost their first 11 games during a 1-15 season. Los Angeles coach Jim Harbaugh started five games at quarterback for that team.Baltimore Ravens 10–13 Cleveland BrownsDeshaun Watson connected with Jerry Jeudy for 33 yards to set up Andre Szmyt’s 37-yard field goal on the final snap, and the Cleveland Browns rallied past the Baltimore Ravens. Cleveland’s first-year coach, Todd Monken, picked up an improbable victory over the Ravens, for whom he spent the previous three seasons as offensive coordinator. Cleveland relied on their defense for long stretches and got just enough playmaking from Watson in the end. The Ravens had Tyler Huntley at quarterback for the second straight week because Lamar Jackson has an ankle injury. Baltimore scored on their first two possessions but did nothing from there. Both teams have 4-2 records.New York Jets 19–26 New England PatriotsDrake Maye tossed three touchdown passes and the New England Patriots extended their winning streak to three games. Maye completed 18 of 32 passes for ⁠235 yards. Romeo Doubs, ⁠DeMario Douglas and ​Hunter Henry had New England’s touchdown receptions, while Douglas caught seven passes for 86 yards. New York’s Geno Smith completed ⁠20 of 30 passes for 252 yards and a touchdown but was intercepted for the first time this season. The Jets (2-4) got four ⁠field goals from Jason Sanders and a game-high 11 tackles (six solo) from Jamien Sherwood. Sanders ​pulled the Jets within 26-19 by ‌kicking a 36-yard field ‌goal with 32 seconds to play, but New England (4-2) recovered the onside kick.Pittsburgh Steelers 26–19 Tampa Bay Buccaneers (OT)Aaron Rodgers threw touchdown passes in the fourth quarter and overtime and Chris Boswell made four field goals to lead ⁠the Pittsburgh Steelers to a comeback overtime win. The Steelers (4-2) erased a 16-3 ⁠fourth quarter deficit with ⁠16 unanswered points ​in the period. The Bucs (1-5) tied the game at 19 with three seconds left on a 53-yard field goal by Chase McLaughlin. Rodgers led a 12-play, 70-yard drive, capped by a six-yard touchdown pass to Germie Bernard with 3:15 left in overtime. Jalon Daniels, who ​made his third consecutive start for the injured ‌Baker Mayfield, scrambled 10 ‌yards to Tampa Bay’s own 37 for a first down on fourth- and-nine on the ‌Bucs’ ensuing drive. Five plays later, Daniels was sacked on fourth down by Jalen Ramsey on a corner blitz to end the game.Houston Texans 34–31 Jacksonville JaguarsKa’imi Fairbairn kicked a 49-yard field goal as time expired, CJ Stroud threw three touchdown passes and the Houston Texans beat the Jacksonville Jaguars on the slick grass of Wembley Stadium. Cam Little’s 60-yard field goal had tied the game at 31-31 with just under two minutes left after Travis Hunter intercepted Stroud’s pass in the end zone. Hunter also hauled in a seven-yard touchdown pass at the other end – becoming just the fifth player in the Super Bowl era, including the playoffs, to score a touchdown and intercept a pass in the same game. Marvin Harrison Jr made his debut for the 2-4 Texans as Houston earned back-to-back wins to gain ground on the AFC South-leading Jaguars (4-2).New Orleans Saints 34–27 New York GiantsTyler Shough threw three touchdown passes and ran for a score, and the New Orleans Saints (2-4) scored 34 consecutive points, holding on to defeat the New York Giants (3-2-1) and end their three game-losing streak. Isaiah Stalbird forced a fumble on a kick return late in the first half that flipped the momentum in favor of the Saints. Giants fans streamed to the exits after Jameis Winston threw his second interception of the afternoon early in the fourth quarter, and the stands were half-empty by the time JJ McCarthy led multiple scoring drives and fell just short of an improbable comeback.Tennessee Titans 26–20 Indianapolis ColtsJoey Slye connected on a tie-breaking 49-yard field goal with 2:03 left on Sunday as the visiting Tennessee Titans upset ⁠the Indianapolis Colts for their first win of the season. It was the third field goal of the game for Slye, ⁠who added a ⁠44-yarder with 43 seconds ​remaining after Tennessee (1-5) got a fourth-down stop. The comeback from a 13-point halftime deficit gave head coach Robert Saleh his first win ⁠with the team. Cam Ward completed 11 of 22 passes for 102 yards with a touchdown and an interception for the Titans. Tennessee notched six sacks, ​including two apiece by Jeffery Simmons and ‌Jermaine Johnson II. Daniel Jones ‌hit 22 of 42 passes for 269 yards with one touchdown and two interceptions for ‌Indianapolis (2-4) while Jonathan Taylor ran for 94 yards on 21 carries.Explore more on these topicsNFLUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Elite-level incompetence is Manchester United’s problem – not Michael Carrick | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: Getting rid of Michael Carrick is not going to solve the problems that led to his appointment. Perhaps it’s worth, for once, doing something different
Author: Barney Ronay
Headline: Getting rid of Michael Carrick is not going to solve the problems that led to his appointment. Perhaps it’s worth, for once, doing something different
Content: Michael Carrick’s Manchester United are a lowly 13th in the Premier League after the 1-1 draw at Leeds.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAView image in fullscreenMichael Carrick’s Manchester United are a lowly 13th in the Premier League after the 1-1 draw at Leeds.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAManchester UnitedAnalysisElite-level incompetence is Manchester United’s problem – not Michael CarrickBarney RonayGetting rid of head coach is not going to solve the problems that led to his appointment.
