Content: Lucia Di Guglielmo celebrates scoring her first NWSL goal as the Washington Spirit beat Gotham FC 1-0 to clinch a playoff berth on Saturday at Audi Field in Washington, DC.Photograph: Brad Smith/ISI Photos/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLucia Di Guglielmo celebrates scoring her first NWSL goal as the Washington Spirit beat Gotham FC 1-0 to clinch a playoff berth on Saturday at Audi Field in Washington, DC.Photograph: Brad Smith/ISI Photos/Getty ImagesNWSLWashington Spirit clinch NWSL playoff berth as Gotham miss chance to seal ShieldDi Guglielmo scores first NWSL goal in 1-0 victoryGotham denied chance to clinch NWSL ShieldSan Diego secure top-four seed as Angel City rallyAgenciesSun 18 Oct 2026 02.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLucia Di Guglielmo scored her first National Women’s Soccer League goal and the Washington Spirit clinched a playoff spot with a 1-0 victory over Gotham FC on Saturday.In otherNWSLaction, the San Diego Wave beat the North Carolina Courage 2-1, Angel City FC defeated the Denver Summit 3-2 and the Kansas City Current shut out the Utah Royals 2-0.It was the first win for the Spirit (16-8-4) over Gotham since 23 June 2024.Saloons, school and specialty coffee: NWSL players enjoy new era of side hustlesRead moreThe road loss at Audi Field denied Gotham (16-5-7) a chance to clinch the NWSL Shield and snapped their four-match unbeaten streak.Spirit midfielder Mélissa Bethi delivered a pinpoint lobbed pass to Di Guglielmo in the 70th minute. She slipped her shot past Gotham goalkeeper Ann-Katrin Berger.Spirit goalkeeper Sandy MacIver made two saves for her 10th clean sheet of the season.Leicy Santos returned from injury and started for the Spirit in her first appearance since 8 August.After her contract was terminated by the Chicago Stars, Gotham defender Leila Ouahabi started on her debut for her new club.Wave secure top-four playoff seedGoals from Melanie Barcenas and Trinity Byars lifted the Wave (17-8-3) to a road victory over the Courage, clinching a top-four playoff seed for San Diego.Barcenas struck a long-range shot to give the visitors a 1-0 lead in the fourth minute. The 18-year-old forward scored her seventh goal of the season, breaking the NWSL single-season record for goals by a teenager.Midfielder Gia Corley’s through-ball found Byars in stride, allowing her to chip goalkeeper Kailen Sheridan to make it 2-0 in the 52nd minute.North Carolina forward Ashley Sanchez found Vilde Bøe Risa in the 83rd minute for her first NWSL goal.The Courage (13-12-3) have now lost four of their last five matches.View image in fullscreenMelanie Barcenas celebrates with teammates after scoring her seventh goal of the season as San Diego Wave beat North Carolina Courage 2-1 to secure a top-four NWSL playoff seed.Photograph: Matt Kelley/NWSL/Getty ImagesAngel City erase two-goal deficit in comebackEvelyn Shores and Gisele Thompson combined for three assists as Angel City (13-8-7) scored three unanswered goals in a 3-2 comeback victory at the Summit (10-10-8).Denver forward Melissa Kössler’s tap-in from a corner gave the hosts the lead in the second minute. Midfielder Lindsey Heaps’ volley doubled the advantage in the 18th. It was her fourth goal in three games.Angel City responded when defender Shores provided her eighth assist of the season for Sveindís Jónsdóttir in the 32nd minute. Seven minutes later, Thompson slipped a through-ball to Taylor Suarez to make it 2-2. Ally Sentnor scored the winner in the 43rd minute.Angel City are unbeaten in their last eight games.Hopkins double gives Current third straight winHaley Hopkins scored twice to lead the Current (14-9-5) to a road victory over the Royals.Hopkins headed home the opener from a corner by midfielder Vanessa DiBernardo in the 21st minute. A counterattack in second-half stoppage time saw forward Temwa Chawinga draw the defense toward her before laying the ball off to Hopkins for her second goal.Lorena made four saves to earn her fourth clean sheet of the season.The Utah Royals (14-10-4) have been shut out twice in their last four games.Explore more on these topicsNWSLWomen's footballUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: Fundora brutally knocks out Hadribeaj with one second left to retain 154lb title | Boxing | The Guardian
description: Sebastian Fundora stopped Ermal Hadribeaj in the final second of their 12-round fight in Las Vegas to retain his WBC super welterweight title
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Sebastian Fundora stopped Ermal Hadribeaj in the final second of their 12-round fight in Las Vegas to retain his WBC super welterweight title
Content: Sebastian Fundora throws a punch at Ermal Hadribeaj during their WBC super-welterweight title fight on Saturday night in Las Vegas.Photograph: Cris Esqueda/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSebastian Fundora throws a punch at Ermal Hadribeaj during their WBC super-welterweight title fight on Saturday night in Las Vegas.Photograph: Cris Esqueda/Getty ImagesBoxingFundora brutally knocks out Hadribeaj with one second left to retain 154lb titleFundora lands decisive blow at 2:59 of final roundChampion makes fourth successful title defense6ft 5in fighter targets undisputed crown at 154lbAgenciesSun 18 Oct 2026 01.06 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 02.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSebastian Fundora kept his pursuit of an undisputed championship on track with a second to spare.Fundora stopped Ermal Hadribeaj with a left hand at 2:59 of the 12th round on Saturday night at the Chelsea at the Cosmopolitan of Las Vegas to retain his WBC super welterweight title.Daniel Dubois delivers devastating second-round stoppage of Fabio Wardley to retain WBO titleRead moreFundora (25-1-1, 17 KOs) made his fourth successful title defense and handed Hadribeaj (23-1-1) his first professional loss.“It was an interesting fight,” Fundora said. “I had to go back and fight on the inside and show everyone again that I can still do that. It was dramatic to knock him out at the last second. But we’ll go back to the gym and fix some things.”Fundora entered the bout looking toward a chance to unify the 154lb division, but first had to get past a stubborn mandatory challenger.Hadribeaj attacked the body early, crouching beneath Fundora’s punches and landing looping shots over the top. Fundora caught him in the second round, and Hadribeaj increasingly resorted to holding to disrupt the champion’s offense.Hadribeaj was deducted points for holding in the third and 11th rounds. Fundora found room for uppercuts inside and applied pressure through the middle rounds before delivering the decisive left hand in the final second.“I told the ref in the fourth round that I was hurting him,” Fundora said. “I kept landing body shots and was looking for that special shot to get him out of there.View image in fullscreenSebastian Fundora knocks down Ermal Hadribeaj in the final second of their WBC super welterweight title fight on Saturday night in Las VegasPhotograph: Cris Esqueda/Getty Images“I was hitting him in the rib cage the whole time with the left hand and when I went up the middle, I heard the noise that he made. So I just kept touching that and knew it would break him.”Fundora, 28, has won five straight fights since Brian Mendoza knocked him out in April 2023. The 6ft 5in southpaw from Coachella, California, nicknamed the Towering Inferno, captured the WBC and WBO titlesagainst Tim Tszyu in March 2024, then stopped Chordale Booker, Tszyu and Keith Thurman in successive defenses.“I want to go for undisputed in this division,” Fundora said. “We’ll break eitherJaron Ennisor Josh Kelly down. Just like the last guy and the guy before that. We’ll keep breaking them down.”Hadribeaj, an Albanian fighter based in Miami, earned his title opportunity with a victory over the previously unbeaten Bakary Samake earlier this year.In the co-main event, Armando Resendiz (17-3) outlasted Australia’s Koen Mazoudier (16-5-1) by unanimous decision in a 10-round super middleweight bout. The judges scored it 98-92, 97-93 and 97-93.View image in fullscreenSebastian Fundora has set his sights on becoming the undisputed super-welterweight champion after successfully defending his WBC title against Ermal Hadribeaj in Las Vegas.Photograph: Cris Esqueda/Getty ImagesResendiz landed punishing left hands through the middle rounds, but Mazoudier kept trading inside and rallied late. Resendiz finished strongly, sending Mazoudier stumbling backward in the final minute.“We pulled this off because we had great preparation,” Resendiz said. “This was the kind of fight that I expected. I had to change my game plan and box and move a little bit because this was a very tough fight.”Marco Romero (16-0, 14 KOs) stopped Matias Ferreira (8-4) with a crushing right hand at 1:54 of the first round in their scheduled eight-round super middleweight bout.“He was too slow,” Romero said. “His speed and experience didn’t matter.”Jaime Osuna (12-0) remained unbeaten with a majority decision over Cristian Cangelosi (13-1-1) in an eight-round middleweight bout.“It was a fight that took everything I had from beginning to end,” Osuna said.Explore more on these topicsBoxingUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: World Bank says ‘small AI’ could transform developing countries | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Bank’s chief knowledge officer says the tech could speed up economic development from centuries to decades
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Bank’s chief knowledge officer says the tech could speed up economic development from centuries to decades
Content: ‘Small AI’ models can run on a mobile phone with low connectivity, and could help accelerate development for emerging economies.Photograph: Zuma Press/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Small AI’ models can run on a mobile phone with low connectivity, and could help accelerate development for emerging economies.Photograph: Zuma Press/AlamyAI (artificial intelligence)World Bank says ‘small AI’ could transform developing countriesBank’s chief knowledge officer says the tech could speed up economic development from centuries to decadesHeather Stewartin BangkokSun 18 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheWorld Bankis urging developing countries to kickstart the creation of “small AI” models, which can run on a mobile phone with low connectivity, to reap the full benefits of artificial intelligence.While Silicon Valley big tech firms are focused on ever more sophisticated consumer products, Paschal Donohoe, the World Bank’s chief knowledge officer, said AI could also accelerate development for emerging economies – but only if it was adapted to local needs.Small AI uses specialised models that are trained using narrower datasets for a specific purpose.“We argue that economic development in the countries that we serve and partner with that could have taken centuries to make happen, the potential is there for that economic development now to happen within decades,” Donohoe said.“Small AI would be available in a local setting, with low connectivity, and in the local language of the community – and tends to be available on your mobile phone.”Donohoe, a former finance minister for Ireland, cited the example of Indian farmers engaged in the World Bank’s agricultural scheme, AgriConnect, who needed to access soil analysis in their own language.“There’s not going to be enough scientists and agricultural experts to do that for every small farm in India. And this is where what we describe as ‘small AI’ comes in. Because small AI is AI that would be available on your phone, that can help deliver against those information needs.”He suggested such products could emerge from collaboration between the World Bank, governments and the private sector.The impact of AI on jobs and growth is a central theme of the annual meetings of the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF), which are being held this week in Bangkok, Thailand.Speaking on a panel about the impact of the technology on Monday, Kristalina Georgieva, the IMF’s managing director, called on governments to provide the preconditions for AI to succeed.She said: “You need access to electricity. You need access to digital infrastructure. People have to be geared to adoption. And the government should be able to give some safety, protect against bad actors so that adoption can work.“If we work hard to have the basics for it, [adoption] can be very democratic. As democratic as the cellphone.”The World Bank’s annual world development report, published in August, hailed the potential benefits of AI. But it pointed out that, for example, almost a third of rural schools in sub-Saharan Africa lacked electricity and more than two-thirds did not have a consistent internet connection.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGeorgieva warned that over time 40% of jobs worldwide were likely to be either augmented or eliminated by AI, with the impact particularly acute for young people at the start of their careers.“When we look at this, what we recognise is that the people to worry about, first and foremost, are young people that are coming into the labour market,” she said. “Normally they would get into these routine, repetitive jobs and then go up the ranks. But if they’re gone, I don’t think any young person wants to be a barista in a coffee shop as a professional future.”Under its president, Ajay Banga, the World Bank has made attracting private-sector funding into emerging economies a focus of its work.Donohoe said the World Bank had mobilised $120bn (£90bn) of private capital in the past year using guarantees and other financial instruments, at a time when many countries, including the US and the UK, were cutting their aid budgets.“We want to highlight the link between private capital mobilisation and jobs and economic development,” he said.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)World BankInternational Monetary Fund (IMF)Emerging marketsGlobal economyEconomicsTechnology sectornewsShareReuse this content

title: What are self-replicating ‘AI worms’, and why is Anthropic worried about them?  | Technology | The Guardian
description: The tech company says successful AI worms need more capability on less powerful devices, but current trends make that feasible by the end of the year
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The tech company says successful AI worms need more capability on less powerful devices, but current trends make that feasible by the end of the year
Content: ‘Whatever claims the labs are making, they are not warning us enough. We need to understand that nobody can stop the AI storm.’Photograph: Kim Kyung-Hoon/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Whatever claims the labs are making, they are not warning us enough. We need to understand that nobody can stop the AI storm.’Photograph: Kim Kyung-Hoon/ReutersTechnologyExplainerWhat are self-replicating ‘AI worms’, and why is Anthropic worried about them?The tech company says successful AI worms need more capability on less powerful devices, but current trends make that feasible by the end of the yearJoseph Menn in San FranciscoSun 18 Oct 2026 09.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWarnings about what artificial intelligence might do in the future – together with alarming reports of what it has gotten up to already – are being issued so quickly that even security experts have difficulty triaging what to worry about.Yet areportthis week from Anthropic’s offensive research team grabbed attention by describing a new, practical threat, one devoid of human characteristics or apocalyptic musings. The red team, as such internal testers are called, said it created a malicious AI program that spread autonomously through internet-connected “smart” televisions and could do the same inside other ordinary devices. While machines running AI usually need a fair amount of computing power, the researchers said that their programsplit parts of itselfamong 15 televisions and was still able to function by using a bit of power from each.AI in your oven? Anthropic warns models ‘months away’ from self-replication on smart devicesRead moreIn addition to evoking the horcruxes that kept pieces of Lord Voldemort’s soul alive within objects in the Harry Potter series, the report alarmed some professionals because the generally weak security of smart televisions and many other “internet of things” devices would be very hard to correct, even with a concerted effort.“It’s something to worry about just like every other wave of cyber-attacks. We need to mitigate the possible effects,” said Joshua Saxe, who led development of Meta’s AI security effort. “I’m concerned right now that folks in the cybersecurity community are not taking these kinds of real risks as seriously as they should be.”The damage of such “AI worms” could be astonishingly large. Self-replicating computer viruses, which need not trick a human to propagate, are known as worms, and earlier worms have wreaked some of the worst havoc in the history of the internet.That legacy includes the Morris worm of 1988, which arrived before the mainstream consumer internet, when a graduate student released a program that took advantage of various software flaws and weak passwords, copying itself so rapidly that many infected machines slowed to a stop. The US and Israel brought worms into international espionage with the stealthy Stuxnet in the lat 2000s, which sabotaged Iranian nuclear centrifuges. Other worms like the RussianNotPetyaand North Korean-attributed WannaCry have caused tens of billions of dollars’ worth of damage worldwide.Many of the world’s most destructive worms have depended on known vulnerabilities that device owners have not patched, sometimes months after patches became available. TheAnthropicteam predicted that a worm like theirs could function in the same way and be harder to stop, because smart devices receive patches less often than phones or laptops. Worse, they theorized that an AI worm could keep adapting to other types of hardware by researching newly disclosed vulnerabilities.What differentiates AI worms from typical reproducing viruses is that AI models can learn as they go, said Ariel Herbert-Voss, an early security expert at OpenAI who now runs AI security startup RunSybil. Existing cybersecurity infrastructure is not ready for the proliferation of such threats, Herbert-Voss said. “We need to better enable our security teams. We need to be giving them more resources to fix problems.”Worms could also be used for benevolent purposes, suggested Chris Inglis, a former deputy director of the National Security Agency who served as National Cyber Director in the Biden White House.“The question of whether AI worms are plausible has been settled by several breakout events over the past six months,” Inglis said by digital message. “The better question is how we will employ them, counter them, and/or combine them with other emerging technologies.”Anthropic researchers said a successful AI worm would need to have more capability on less powerful devices than is possible right now – but they added that current trends will make that feasible by year’s end. Their research follows apaperpublished by experts at the University of Toronto a few months ago, which infected a full-size computer and could spread to similar machines more rapidly than the television worm.“The capabilities have been developing very rapidly,” said co-author and Toronto PhD student Jonas Guan.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGuan and other experts said that, as a practical matter, an AI worm should not top anyone’s list of AI fears. The Anthropic version moves very slowly, Guan said, and worms have predictable and detectable actions that can be blocked at multiple layers. Basic security hygiene, including requiring strong passwords and two-factor authentication, would stop most worms and other hacking, experts said.“Nothing about this is truly feasible or impactful,” said Juan Andres Guerrero-Saade, vice-president of research at security firm SentinelOne. “It’s nifty stunt hacking that’s getting way more amplification in service of the ridiculous doomer narratives that suggest models have a mind and will of their own.”Anthropic did not respond to an interview request.Outside Washington, many in the AI and security worlds believe greater government oversight of AI is now essential. But members of Congress have introduced mutually conflicting bills, while the White House has so far created only asmall review board.Security researchers and laypeople alike find themselves weighing the motivations behind fearful prognostications from AI companies, which range from espousing quasi-religious beliefs, to seeking legislation to exclude rivals or save money, to hyping the anticipated multi-trillion-dollar public valuations of the San Francisco AI giants.“The claim that a lot of this is marketing is correct, but the reality dwarfs any PR,” said Gadi Evron, who is running a conference on AI security in San Francisco this month called Unprompted. “Whatever claims the labs are making, they are not warning us enough. We need to understand that nobody can stop the AI storm.”Explore more on these topicsTechnologyAI (artificial intelligence)AnthropicWormsVirusesComputingHackingexplainersShareReuse this content

title: Wikipedia often gets taken for granted – but its history is fascinating, and its future is fragile | Richard Cooke | The Guardian
description: Wikipedia’s 68m articles have been consulted trillions of times. Not bad for a website that has barely changed since it was founded 20 years ago
Author: Richard Cooke
Headline: Wikipedia’s 68m articles have been consulted trillions of times. Not bad for a website that has barely changed since it was founded 20 years ago
Content: Wikipedia’s ‘amateurish, homegrown ethos’ was off-putting to a lot of writers and journalists, Richard Cooke writes. ‘Most of the people seriously interested in Wikipedia were a handful of academics.’Photograph: Boris Roessler/EPAView image in fullscreenWikipedia’s ‘amateurish, homegrown ethos’ was off-putting to a lot of writers and journalists, Richard Cooke writes. ‘Most of the people seriously interested in Wikipedia were a handful of academics.’Photograph: Boris Roessler/EPAWikipediaWikipedia often gets taken for granted – but its history is fascinating, and its future is fragileRichard CookeWikipedia’s 68m articles have been consulted trillions of times. Not bad for a website that has barely changed since it was founded 20 years agoSun 18 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 19.07 EDTShareAfew years ago, I was struck by the tension between howWikipediawas used, and how it was talked about. Everyone was on it all the time, and yet its reputation had stalled at “don’t trust it”, because it was the “free encyclopedia that anyone can edit”.Clearly peopleweretrusting it, so much so it had become part of the fabric of everyday life since it was founded by Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger in 2001. But despite the fact it now has been consulted trillions of times by billions of people (English Wikipedia alone is 5.2bn words long), it inspires an odd lack of curiosity. Even people donating to Wikipedia might say the money was “for the factcheckers”, though there aren’t any – not paid ones, anyway. Meanwhile, the internet in the social media era had begun to feel like a much uglier place, and some digital nostalgia was setting in: here was this holdover that had somehow survived; a website that functions – and even looks – much the same as it did 20 years ago.‘People thought I was a communist doing this as a non-profit’: is Wikipedia’s Jimmy Wales the last decent tech baron?Read moreYou could say that I fell down a Wiki rabbit hole, especially when it came to the website’s early years. Almost everything important about the project came together quite quickly. Its amateurish, homegrown ethos was off-putting to a lot of writers and journalists, and that meant many questions about why it had worked had no answers. Most of the people seriously interested in Wikipedia were a handful of academics – so I decided to write a book about it.I’m not a tech journalist. Instead, I have a background in the humanities. Wikipedia actually does, too: philosophy, and even off-piste disciplines like town planning and poetry, played a much bigger role in its inception than pure technology. Ward Cunningham, who invented the wiki in the 1990s – that’s a webpage anyone can edit, and the foundational tool of Wikipedia – thought very carefully about how the power of computers might be democratised. He drew on all sorts of oblique concepts for it, such as constructivism and the Zen concept of wabi-sabi – beauty in imperfection – and it’s remarkable how well the culture he created has persisted. Especially wabi-sabi – Wikipedia is, after all, always in a state of incompleteness.View image in fullscreenWikipedia co-founder Jimmy Wales. ‘Lots of people in the dotcom boom started online encyclopedias, but Wales was the only one to hire a philosopher.’Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesPhilosophy drew Wikipedia’s co-founders together as well. Though Wales worked in tech and finance, he corresponded with philosophers for years. And though Sanger was an academic philosopher, he spent lots of time arguing online – only “amateurs” seemed to share his sense that philosophy had life-and-death stakes. Lots of people in the dotcom boom started online encyclopedias, but Wales was the only one to hire a philosopher. In fact, theonlyperson he hired was a philosopher. It was such an unpredictable choice, and an important clue to what made Wikipedia work: it sprang out of this digital “republic of letters”, where all sorts of people were thinking about facts and why they were important.Because Wikipedia is so massive, writing an “exhaustive” book on it is impossible, like trying to represent a mountain with a grain of sand. Instead, I concentrated on the human history – the small, sometimes very small, number of people who really influenced what Wikipedia became. Wikipedians can be difficult, and the most ornery get a bad wrap – even the Wikimedia Foundation’s leadership has made comments about their “Dorito-stained fingers”, or tendency to stay home on a Saturday night. But by the end of the process, I was in awe of them, and I still am.double quotation markThe first woman to edit Wikipedia, Gaytha Langlois, wrote about two things dear to her: Rhode Island and standard poodlesWales and Sanger are prominent, but many other important early Wikipedians are unknown. The first woman to edit Wikipedia, Gaytha Langlois, hasn’t had much attention. She wrote about two things dear to her: Rhode Island and standard poodles – small states and big dogs. Wikipedia has always had a gender imbalance, which has proved stubborn –Sandi Toksvig is only the latest in a long line of critics trying to address it. She is part of an effort to create a more balanced alternative to Wikipedia called Mappa Mundi, which has the potential to feed back into Wikipedia as well.I became fascinated too with a little-known contributorwho had the first biographical page for a woman on Wikipedia (today, it would be called a user page). Her name was Ruth Ifcher, and she was a very intelligent grammar pedant, with a PhD, who had been forced out of the workforce with severe agoraphobia. Wikipedia came along later in her life and opened a whole new avenue for creative and meaningful work.Proust said that neurotics alone “composed our masterpieces”, and that’s true here.Neurodiversity is so central to Wikipedia that one former head of the Wikimedia Foundation told me the encyclopedia is a “city built by Asperger’s”. You can sense that energy in familiar topics – planes, trains and automobiles, comic books, weather, and all the rest. Often, Wikipedians are so prolific that they write too much, a phenomenon called “fancruft”. “Road geeks” (like trainspotters for roads) kept having their work about minor roads deleted, so a whole lot of them left in a huff, and started a separateonline wiki encyclopedia for roads. That’s almost a microcosm of the inclusionists v deletionists debate, which is the biggest philosophical rift on Wikipedia – a rolling argument about what should be included, and what shouldn’t.View image in fullscreenThe co-founders had once believed that 100,000 articles would be “a reasonable size” for an encyclopedia, because that’s how big Britannica was. Today, Wikipedia has 68m, and Pew Research estimates that it served 1.9tn page views between 2015 and 2025. Because it is so monumental, I never expected Wikipedia to feel fragile or vulnerable – but as I was finishing the book, AI had begun to encroach on Wikipedia in an existential way by diminishing the web traffic it relies on, for instance, or by editors contributing huge volumes of poorly written AI-generated text. People ask me “is Wikipedia under threat?”, and it is, but so is everything from Hollywood to pure mathematics. I do think it will survive, but the quaking foundations made it feel urgent to say “we saw this made, and we won’t see anything like it again”.The Last Best Place on the Internet: A Human History of Wikipedia by Richard Cooke is out now through Black Inc in Australia, and WW Norton in the US. It will be released in the UK on 5 November, via GrantaExplore more on these topicsWikipediaInternetTechnology booksAustralian booksAI (artificial intelligence)commentShareReuse this content

title: ‘I felt disgusted’: MEP speaks out over nude deepfakes and urges EU action | Online abuse | The Guardian
description: Lena Schilling of Austrian Greens says images are ‘digital violence against women’ and a threat to democracy
Author: Ashifa Kassam
Headline: Lena Schilling of Austrian Greens says images are ‘digital violence against women’ and a threat to democracy
Content: Lena Schilling is one of 50 MEPs, 46 of them women, who have been targeted by sexualised deepfakes.Photograph: APA-Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenLena Schilling is one of 50 MEPs, 46 of them women, who have been targeted by sexualised deepfakes.Photograph: APA-Images/AlamyOnline abuse‘I felt disgusted’: MEP speaks out over nude deepfakes and urges EU actionLena Schilling of Austrian Greens says images are ‘digital violence against women’ and a threat to democracyAshifa KassamEuropean community affairs correspondentSun 18 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 00.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn Austrian MEP has spoken out about her experience of being “stripped naked” online without her consent and has urged the EU to take action, as a report found that one in six female MEPs had been targeted by sexualised AI-generated content.Lena Schilling of the Green party said she had learned last month about nude deepfakes of herself circulating online. When she opened the links, she found herself staring at images from one of her first ever press conferences – but the images had been digitally altered to remove her clothing.It was a shocking twist on a defining moment of her career. “I felt disgusted,” she said. “I remember how nervous I was and how much I had prepared for the press conference. And then to see someone using this image in a way aimed at harming and humiliating me was really hard to grasp.”Schilling is one of 50 MEPs – 46 of them women – who have been targeted by sexualised deepfakes, accordingto a reportby Agora Digitale Transformation (ADT).View image in fullscreenSchilling said some of the other female MEPs who were also targeted had expressed fears about speaking out.Photograph: Martin Bertrand/Hans Lucas/AFP/GettyThe Berlin-based thinktank, which alerted Schilling to the presence of the images online, said the finding laid bare how deepfake pornography had become a “systemic threat to women in European politics”.An earlier ADT reportfound that 138 female parliamentarians from 22 EU countries had been affected, and that women were 33 times more likely than their male colleagues to be depicted in or associated with deepfake pornography.Schilling described the images as a form of “digital violence against women” piled on top ofthe already disproportionateamount of sexist abuse, harassment and violence that women in politics faced.The result was a potent threat to democracy, she said: “These things make going into politics even harder than it is already. Just imagine what would happen to our society if more and more women disappear from public life.”Schilling said she had spoken to some of the other female MEPs targeted, but they had expressed fears about coming forward. “But there’s nothing to be ashamed of. People misused your photos, you did nothing wrong,” she said. “And I think that’s the moment when you say: ‘OK, this has to stop.’”The sentiment was captured in a recent letter to the EU initiated by Schilling and the German Green MEP Terry Reintke. Signed by 119 MEPs, it called on officials to ensure that aforthcoming banon apps and websites that use AI to undress women, scheduled to take effect across the EU on 2 December, would be paired with mechanisms capable of enforcing the prohibition.“A ban on paper protects no one until it is enforced,” the letter said, pointing to the widespread use of “nudifier” apps in which photos of women can be undressed with just one click.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionElon Musk’s xAI sues Minnesota over law banning ‘nudification’ technologyRead more“Its purpose is humiliation and control over women’s bodies, and its effect is to make public life more hostile for female politicians,” the letter said. “Every young woman considering a political career now must factor in that this could happen to her.”Schilling said the aim was to push national authorities to close any loopholes or workarounds that would allow the apps to continue to function in the EU. “We were stripped naked without our consent,” she said. “This cannot become the new normal.”The call for action was why she had decided to speak up, she said, in the hope that sharing her story would convince member states to crack down on tech companies for which this sort of digital violence could be a viable business model.“It’s quite simple,” she said. “Every woman who wants to run for office should be able to do so without being afraid of being undressed against her will.”Explore more on these topicsOnline abuseDeepfakeEuropean UnionEuropeViolence against women and girlsSexual harassmentGendernewsShareReuse this content

title: The best toys and gifts for eight-year-olds, tested by eight-year-olds | Toys | The Guardian
description: From science kits to karaoke machines, shower sets to brain-boosting games, here are the presents our mini testers loved the most
Author: Zoë Phillimore
Headline: From science kits to karaoke machines, shower sets to brain-boosting games, here are the presents our mini testers loved the most
Content: Composite: Sandra Navarro/Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenComposite: Sandra Navarro/Guardian DesignGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterToysThe best toys and gifts for eight-year-olds, tested by eight-year-oldsFrom science kits to karaoke machines, shower sets to brain-boosting games, here are the presents our mini testers loved the mostThe best gifts for seven-year-oldsZoë PhillimoreSun 18 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEight is such a wonderful age. Kids are old enough to have their own interests and hobbies, but still young enough to get swept up in play and be absorbed for hours if you find the right toy for them.By eight, children’s interests and skills are taking shape. They’re more confident readers, more strategic thinkers and curious about how things work. And while they think they’re extremely grown up, eight-year-olds still need plenty of time to play for their overall wellbeing.Here’s a rundown of toys and gifts that will keep eight-year-olds occupied for months to come: a roster of creative kits, clever games, outdoor adventures and timeless toys that will keep them happy and busy (while sneakily learning).How I selectedAs an experienced toy tester, I am living an eight-year-old’s dream. I have written about toys and parenting for almost 10 years and have also worked in schools and children’s publishing. As well as professionally observing children’s play, I also have three children, and in these guides I aim to balance what kids love to play with and what parents want in their house.I also asked children’s play specialists and development experts about the best toys to support the developmental stage most eight-year-olds are at – from school skills to wellbeing – for a holistic approach.A gang of lively eight-year-olds were enlisted to test toys and gifts on my behalf, and they weren’t shy in telling me what they thought of them. Their own gift picks can be found throughout this guide.The toys and gifts that made the cut here balanced all these needs. Sustainability was always on my mind when compiling this list, with the guiding principle of buying well, not more. I selected toys and gifts that my testers came back to over and over and should last them well into the tween stage.The best toys and gifts for eight-year-oldsView image in fullscreenPlay away: our testers recommended a wide range of gifts (for themselves and others).Photograph: Zoë Phillimore/The GuardianLife in 3DThose of a certain age may remember the TV show Penny Crayon; everything Penny drew came to life, getting her and her mates out of all kinds of strife. Well, this pen can (sort of) make the Penny Crayon dream come true for your child. The 3Doodler pen delivers a stream of BPA-free plastic, which cools as it hits the air, allowing children to create what they draw – “I made a pair of sunglasses and a very creepy-looking robot,” my tester reported with glee. The use of plastic made me hesitate to include it in this guide, but it kept my tester absorbed for hours. The filaments are made from a biodegradable material but can’t be put in household recycling.View image in fullscreen3Doodler Start+ 3D essential pen set£40 at John Lewis£39.99 at AmazonMaterials:plasticSuitable for:6+Game knight“An eight-year-old’s interests include more complex games,” saysLaura Moore-Williams, an early years consultant. Around this age, many children are taught to play chess at school, and the benefits are huge. It builds focus and critical thinking, while teaching patterns, spatial awareness and sequencing. All this will build important neural pathways in the developing brains of eight-year-olds. This board is a gift for life – it’s made from walnut and sycamore, and the pieces are handcarved. It folds in the middle with the pieces stored inside. My eight-year-old tester plays chess at school (many primary schools teach it at this age to develop problem-solving skills and mathematical and numerical reasoning), so their eyes lit up when they saw this board. They loved playing with a “proper” set rather than the tiny board they had been using.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Zoë Phillimore/The GuardianJaques of London complete folding chess board£40.99 at Jaques of London£34.99 at AmazonMaterials:wood, baize base for piecesSuitable for:6+The plot thickensEight is a great age for getting kids into a book series they can independently read and enjoy. Tom Gates was a huge hit with the eight-year-olds I spoke to. The books follow the slightly hapless but likable schoolboy Tom as he tries to wind up his annoying older sister, get his band going and eat as many caramel wafers as possible – while avoiding doing any homework. The books are filled with illustrations and aren’t too text heavy. My eight-year-old tester is a slightly reluctant reader, but they were racing through the books and begging for the next one.View image in fullscreenTom Gates Series 1 byLiz Pichon£25.13 at Rackhams£24 at AmazonMaterials:paperSuitable for:8+Build them up“For eight-year-olds I rate advancedLegosets,” says Moore-Williams. My eight-year-old tester loved this Mario Kart Lego set, whooping “awesome” with gusto as they clapped eyes on the box. Beyond the unboxing, it’s fun to build, with nothing that’s too repetitive, and they’re left with an amusing toy they can either display or play with (my tester definitely opted for the latter).View image in fullscreenLego Mario KartPiranha Plant Power-Up Pursuit£44.99 at Lego£35.34 at AmazonMaterials:plasticSuitable for:8+P-P-Pick up a pigeon“We started to have a Saturday afternoon games session with friends, and they brought this over to play,” said one eight-year-old tester. “It was fun for the adults and the kids, and it was easy to get the hang of.” When I tested this game with eight-year-olds and their younger siblings, it had them all giggling. It’s easy to get playing quickly (eight-year-olds don’t want to read dissertation-length instructions) and it’s pretty rapid fire – a game is won or lost within minutes – so it’ll hold even the shortest of attention spans. It’s also small enough to slip into a bag and whip out at a restaurant or pub on a rainy afternoon to keep kids from getting fidgety.View image in fullscreenOh My Pigeons! party game£12.99 at Smyths Toys£12.99 at AmazonMaterials:plastic, paperSuitable for:8+The fast and the curiousWe all know getting kids outside is vital for their physical and mental wellbeing, but it’s often easier said than done. For this guide, I looked for gifts that would get them to break cover, and this scooter fared well.Built for bigger kids (and adults), it’s got plenty to keep eight-year-olds excited. It has large, speedy wheels to cover longer distances – particularly handy if your kids are scooting to school. The chopper-style handlebars look cool and offer a good degree of control. Our eight-year-old tester was keen to take it to the skate park to test and had plenty of fun showing it off as well as racing it around. It is more expensive than other scooter models, but it’s also built to be easy to service and repair. Micro Scooters sells almost all the spare parts for its scooters – it even has aspares findersection on its site and avideo librarywith how-to guides for most adjustments. Despite having a warranty of only two years, this scooter will probably last the recipient way into their teenage years and survive being handed down plenty of times.View image in fullscreenMicroScooters Micro Speed deluxe scooter£165 at Selfridges£164.95 at AmazonMaterials:aluminium, metal, polyurethaneSuitable for:8+Open goal“Outdoor toys are a worthwhile investment if you have space for them,” says Daisy Upton, play specialist and author of theFive Minute Mumbook series. This football kit requires some space – but if you’re looking for an outdoor toy for eight-year-olds and have a decent-size garden, it’s a winner.My eight-year-old testers flocked to this kit, playing together and crucially not thinking about screens or schoolwork. “Developmentally, an eight-year-old needs to build strong peer relationships through play,” says Moore-Williams. While kids may have a football goal already before they’re eight, I picked this set because it feels like a step up that’s right for around this age. The goal is big enough (8ft x 6ft) for a proper-ish game, plus there’s a rebound net and target-practice sheet. The resistance parachute was wildly entertaining on its own. The goal is built to be up in all weathers, but it comes with a storage bag if you want to pack it away.View image in fullscreenRebo portable PVC football goal with training kit£99.99 at Outdoor ToysMaterials:PVC goalposts, net, anchors, fabric bag, football, pump, plastic cones, training ladder, fabric parachute, fabric target-practice sheet, elastic togglesSuitable for:3+skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionComic timingMy eight-year-old testers loved this idea: a weekly comic that comes in the post. Inside is a range of strips, which the reader becomes familiar with over time. Most issues we received included the wildly popular and zany Bunny vs Monkey by Jamie Smart, and serialised strips that depicted exciting adventures. There are also activities inside showing readers how to make their own comics, which my trio of testers loved. And, as a journalist, it is heartening to see that print is not dead for gen Alpha. You can subscribe for an initial six issues for just a quid, after which it auto-renews every 13 weeks for £36.99.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Zoë Phillimore/The GuardianThe Phoenix comic subscriptionFrom £1 at the Phoenix ComicFrom £1 at the MagazineMaterials:paperSuitable for:7+Pulling stringsWhether you have space outside or are just heading to the park or woods for an hour, this kit is brilliant. My eight-year-old testers were obsessed with the idea of making their own “booby traps” – thanks in no small part to Home Alone’s Kevin McCallister – and it was a joy to watch them use it.“I’ve got so many plans for how I’m going to use this, I can’t wait to tell my friends about it – they’re going to want one for themselves,” my eight-year-old tester said after one session of play. Inside the drawstring bag are a wooden plank, wooden box, rope, string, two pulleys, carabiners and some cards that suggest challenges to attempt.View image in fullscreenThe Den Kit Co pulleys kit£34.50 at the Den Kit CoMaterials:jute, wood, string, metalSuitable for:6+, adult supervision requiredSing loud enough to scare the demons off“Everyoneis obsessed with KPop Demon Hunters,” one eight-year-old told me, as if I was 1,000 years old and had been living under a rock. I generally sought to avoid potentially fleeting trends when compiling this list, but this one has real staying power beyond the Demon Hunters craze. While there are loads of karaoke machines on the market, this one feels robust – it survived being thrown about by many of my testers – and comes with two mics, a light and eight built-in games. A button on the mic adds vocal effects, and you can connect a Bluetooth device to use it as a speaker. Unfortunately for my headache, my testers went back again and again to this karaoke machine, which is why it made the cut.View image in fullscreenVTech electronic karaoke light party£59.99 at John Lewis£38.99 at AmazonMaterials:plastic, electronics, metalSuitable for:14+ (manufacturer’s age suggestion)Model behaviourEvery adult I’ve mentioned Fimo to during testing has the same wistful reaction about playing with it as a child. It’s just as good as you remember it, folks. My eight-year-old testers loved making animals out of the multicoloured pack and baking them in the oven. This is relatively mess-free crafting, without any rigid rules to follow (although there’s plenty of inspiration online if you’re stuck for ideas). Fimo is single use, but the idea is you make something to play with once it’s cured – my testers loved creating their own characters.View image in fullscreenStaedtler Fimo soft oven-hardening polymer modelling clay£14.50 at Cass Art£8 at AmazonMaterials:polymer claySuitable for:8+Switched onMoore-Williams also recommended Stem (science, technology, engineering and mathematics) kits. This particular set has 100 projects to keep eight-year-olds’ minds and fingers busy.“As soon as I saw this set, I wanted to make a security alarm!” one eight-year-old tester said. Personally, it gave me flashbacks to school physics, but my testers loved it: “We can pick what we do from loads of options, which is sooo fun,” said one. There are plenty of projects in this Stem set to keep kids busy on rainy days.View image in fullscreenOn Bots 100electronics kit£29.53 at CPC£29.95 at AmazonMaterials:plastic, metalSuitable for:8+Bath goals“I really need some beauty products,” an eight-year-old tester said to me. I glanced at their parents and could see that perhaps their hopes didn’t align.This Lush gift set is a perfect compromise for those not-quite-tweenagers. Yes, it’s a beauty product, but still playful. Inside is a zingy Happy Hippy shower gel that’s more citrus-leaning than candy store, and Lush’s Outback Mate. This is a solid soap bar with a minty scent – a nice change from some of the cloyingly sweet scents that make up lots of products for children this age. This gender-neutral set is great for even the most determined mini soap-dodgers.View image in fullscreenLush Fresh As gift set£14.50 at LushMaterials:soap, shower gel; packaging: recycled board, recycled paper, recycled plastic bottlesSuitable for:3+What to buy for an eight-year-oldView image in fullscreenGet creative: choose gifts that encourage children to explore their interests.Photograph: Zoë Phillimore/The GuardianEvery play expert I spoke to championed a “less is more” approach for children of all ages when it comes to toys. “Common mistakes adults make when choosing toys are being swayed by fads that hold children’s attention for only a few weeks,” says Moore-Williams. They’re “overloading children with too much choice instead of curating a smaller, versatile collection”.Winning toys tend to be a bit more complex for kids this age – there’s a longer attention span for strategy games, puzzles and creative projects. At eight years old, children are more likely to be developing specific hobbies and interests that last longer than a common cold. For any gift, it’s always a good idea to tap into the recipient’s interests.“As children get older, we should be asking, ‘What specific play does this child enjoy the most?’ ‘What are their special interests?’ ‘Can we get something to encourage this further?’” says Upton. “Really lean into what they love to do most, what lights them up, and you can’t go wrong.”Do they love to sit and draw? Get them some open-ended craft supplies – some decent felt-tip pens, stacks of paper and notebooks never miss in my experience. If they love sport, look at what might help them enjoy playing more – kit for keen footballers, goggles for swimmers and warm-up gear for dancers would be useful and show that you know the child and support their interests.What to get for eight-year-olds who don’t play with toys?At this age, experiential gifts are a great idea if space is tight or your recipient isn’t hugely into toys.You can buy vouchers fora trip to Legolandfor £39, and this theme park is specifically aimed at this age – there are plenty of rides suitable for many eight-year-olds. If you want something more sedate, theatre vouchers were a gift lots of eight-year-olds told me were on their wishlists. Buying vouchers from services such asTheatre Tokenswill let your child have some agency and pick tickets at more than 300 theatres throughout the country.For more, read our guides to thebest toys and gifts for seven-year-oldsand thebest sustainable toys for kidsZoë Phillimore is a journalist with 20 years of experience. She’s tested many things, from mattresses to makeup, and she’s slightly obsessed with finding small new businesses to spotlight. Aside from this, Zoë loves travel, being outside – especially on the beach – and finding screen-free things to keep her threeactive children busy. She shares her discoveries onInstagramExplore more on these topicsToysThe FilterFamilyGadgetsLegoComics and graphic novelsBoard gamesChildren's books: 8-12 yearsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Small business owners are doing OK – but will that help Trump overcome his low approval ratings? | Gene Marks | The Guardian
description: Overall, economic sentiment for Trump is poor, but small businesses seem fairly confident, according to several surveys
Author: Gene Marks
Headline: Overall, economic sentiment for Trump is poor, but small businesses seem fairly confident, according to several surveys
Content: A barista makes coffee in a cafe. Small business in the United States are an important voting block.Photograph: JohnnyGreig/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA barista makes coffee in a cafe. Small business in the United States are an important voting block.Photograph: JohnnyGreig/Getty ImagesUS small businessSmall business owners are doing OK – but will that help Trump overcome his low approval ratings?Gene MarksOverall, economic sentiment for Trump is poor, but small businesses seem fairly confident, according to several surveysSun 18 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 08.14 EDTShareThere are 34m small businesses in the United States. They employ approximately half of the country’s workers and generate about half of the country’s GDP. They’re an important voting block. So how are they feeling about the economy as we head into November’s midterm elections? Overall, economic sentiment forDonald Trump is poorbut small business – admittedly a diverse demographic that’s hard to poll – seems fairly confident. A number of recently published surveys and reports can help understand their mood.Confidence is generally stable.This week, the National Federation of Independent Businesses said that itsSmall Business Optimism Indexfell to just below its long-term average, while uncertainty rose slightly. Labor quality was the top concern for 26% of owners and inflation for 20%. Expansion plans weakened, though 17% still plan to add jobs during the next three months.However, small-business confidence improved significantly in the third quarter, according to the recently publishedJustworks/US Chamber Small Business Index. Some 72% of the 750 small businesses surveyed say they are comfortable with their current cash flow, but only 27% believe the US economy is in good health. Inflation remains the biggest problem, cited by 54% of owners.Hiring is not strong, but not weak either.HR platformGustoestimated that small businesses added 28,000 jobs in September, making it the eighth consecutive month of employment gains following a decline in January. According to the company’s data, hiring accelerated from August’s revised gain of 18,500 jobs and growth was broad across industries, regions and company sizes, with healthcare and social assistance among the strongest sectors. Particularly notable is that some of the smallest employers continue to participate in the expansion, rather than job growth being concentrated solely among larger companies.In its latestSmall Business Employment Watchreport, Paychex, another large HR and payroll processing service (and a client of my company), said that hiring in September essentially matched its 2026 year-to-date average with overall employment among companies with fewer than 50 employees appearing “stable”.ADP, the country’s largest HR and payroll processing service, reported that US private employers added 90,000 jobs in September, with hiring accelerating for the first time since May following three months of slowing growth. Education and healthcare and leisure and hospitality led the gains, while financial activities and professional and business services were weaker. Importantly for small businesses, establishments employing one to 19 workers added 18,000 jobs. According to ADP, private-sector employers have not shifted into recession mode and although hiring has cooled from earlier periods, businesses are still adding employees.Intuit painted a slightly different jobs picture. Its IntuitQuickBooks Small Business Index, which is based on data it gathers from its millions of QuickBooks customers, found that employment at US businesses with one to nine employees fell by 7,000 jobs in September and that jobs declined across most sectors and regions.Revenues remain solid.Intuit’s QuickBooks data shows that revenues moved sharply up this past month as inflation-adjusted average monthly revenue increased 1.68% and growth occurring in 11 of 12 industries, every region and 19 of 20 states.Fiserv, a payment-processing service, said that its September data showed improving sales among US small businesses. However, the company reports that consumer behavior remains selective and that traffic has been weaker even as customers spend more when they do shop.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly, plus breaking news alertsSign up toThe Stakes 2026A weekly guide to what really matters in the US midterms, plus breaking news alerts.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRetailers are making returns harder. A carpet seller taught me why that’s a mistake | Gene MarksRead moreEconomic growth continued in the third quarter.Overall, US manufacturing remained firmly in expansion territory in September. The Institute for Supply Management’sManufacturing Purchasing Manager’s Indexmarked its ninth consecutive month of growth after years of contraction. Despite rising prices, new orders, production and employment all remained expansionary and order backlogs increased. As usual, the ISM reported yet another month of expansion in theservice sector(it’s been 27 consecutive months) with new orders remaining “particularly strong”.The Wall Street Journal and other media sources reported recently that first-quarter annualized growth was revised to 2.5% from 2.1%, and second-quarter growth was increased to 2.2% from 1.5%, which,its editors argued, shows that the “US economy is performing considerably better than pessimistic headlines imply”.Philadelphia lags in business creation.My business is based in Philadelphia, a heavily Democratic area in a swing state. My clients appear to mostly be doing well so far this year but, like most small businesses around the country, continue to struggle navigating higher costs and a tight labor market.This anecdotal evidence is somewhat supported by a May survey byWSFS Bankthat found “surprisingly strong confidence among Philadelphia-area businesses” despite inflation and economic uncertainty. In that study, 92% of owners and business decision-makers say their companies are meeting or exceeding expectations, while 66% anticipate growth during the next year.Philadelphia, however, has its own unique problems, particularly adding fewer small businesses per capita than other large cities. A recent study fromPew Researchfound that the number of Black-, Hispanic- and female-owned small businesses increased 39% between 2012 and 2022, showing meaningful entrepreneurial growth, but barriers including access to capital, regulatory requirements, taxes, commercial space and the difficulty of scaling companies continued to restrain business formation in the city.The Democratic strategist James Carville once said that when it comes to electing candidates, “it’s the economy, stupid”. The good news for the Republicans is that the economy is resilient and the overall mood of the country’s small businesses is generally optimistic, despite the many challenges they face. But will that overcome the president’s low approval ratings?Explore more on these topicsUS small businessUS midterm elections 2026Donald TrumpUS economyEconomicsUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: If Trump fells 430 trees in the middle of a golf course, do they make a sound? | Dave Schilling | The Guardian
description: In attempting to turn a public space in DC into an enclave for elites, Trump is moving the US capital closer to Graceland
Author: Dave Schilling
Headline: In attempting to turn a public space in DC into an enclave for elites, Trump is moving the US capital closer to Graceland
Content: Donald Trump’s crusade to clear more than 400 trees to redevelop East Potomac Golf Links into a championship-level course isn’t happening. For now.Photograph: Giorgio Viera/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump’s crusade to clear more than 400 trees to redevelop East Potomac Golf Links into a championship-level course isn’t happening. For now.Photograph: Giorgio Viera/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionDonald TrumpIf Trump fells 430 trees in the middle of a golf course, do they make a sound?Dave SchillingIn attempting to turn a public space in DC into an enclave for elites, Trump is moving the US capital closer to GracelandSun 18 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 07.16 EDTShareWhen is a tree not a tree? When it’s an obstacle to a par-3. If a tree falls in the middle of a golf course, does it make a sound? Yeah, probably. I wasn’t there, but I have to assume, based on my limited knowledge of the laws of physics.What I do know is that Donald Trump’s crusade to clear more than 400 trees for the purposes of redeveloping East Potomac Golf Links into a championship-level course isn’t happening. For now.The US district judgeAna Reyes shut down the project this week, though the administration claimed it had already cleared 430 of the planned 529 trees. This was after aMay order from Reyesto require the White House to request approval for cutting down more than 10 trees. Reyes ordered a full stop to the tree clearing until 26 October, and threatened contempt of court if the administration doesn’t abide.As is always the case with this president, he is attempting to assert some manner of control over a public asset. In this case, said asset is a golf course, which means he’sreallyinvested. You might not be able to get him tostop staring at Jon Husted’s assto sort out inflation, gas prices or the conflict in Iran, but you better believe he can put aside the senator from Ohio’s manly posterior long enough to sort out dramatic changes to a public golf course.By seizing control of East PotomacGolfLinks without any oversight or approval, the administration is essentially seizing that asset from the American people. By turning East Potomac into a championship-level course with an 18-hole layout, strategic hazards and expensive maintenance, Trump is inching the course away from being a public good and toward a private enclave for the elites.Yes, I’m talking about golf here. I understand the irony of trying to separate this sport from elitism. This isn’t exactly soccer, which you could play in a backyard, the street or inside your parents’ house until you knock a ball through the flatscreen TV.East Potomac is a popular course with the residents of DC. It has two nine-hole courses, an 18-hole course and a miniature golf area. The mini golf area has, as you’d hope,hazards shaped like national landmarks. Unfortunately, it doesn’t seem like there’s a way to putt a golf ball into Teddy Roosevelt’s mouth. At least not yet.This is yet another instance of the priorities of one person taking precedent over the needs of literally anyone else. Trump clearly wants to play on a fancy, private golf course in DC. All three DC golf courses are publicly owned and operated by the National Park Service (though the park service has a partnership with the non-profit National Links Trust to renovate and operate the courses, which Trump tried toterminate in December of 2025). East Potomac, being the largest, has the most opportunity to be the shrine to our commander-in-chief’s favorite leisure obsession.I can’t stop myself from picturing what the new East Potomac Golf Links would look like under Trump’s control. The first thing is, it would surely become Trump-East Potomac Golf Links, since a facility without his name on it is a facility wasted.Would the mini golf course survive? Doubtful, as mini golf is strictly for poor people, and the PGA and the United States Golf Association would be too busy laughing at the windmill hazards to schedule the US Open there.But if it stayed, I’d guess there’d be at least a few changes to the layout of the course. Perhaps you’d have to knock your ball past recreations of Trump Tower, a gold-plated toilet and the outstretched fist of the president himself.As much as I care about the beautiful old trees being torn out for no reason, I’m equally flabbergasted by what’s at the core of this project – the lust to turnWashington DCinto Graceland, or a worse, Donald Trump-themed version of that. Graceland is the final home of Elvis Presley, and has become a popular tourist attraction since his passing.It’s a shrine to all things Elvis, full of merchandise and memorabilia. The area of Memphis around the home is designed to facilitate tourism and commerce.I love commerce as much as the next red-blooded American, and DC has long been dependent on tourism to prop up its economy. But the lure of DC was American history, not one man’s vanity project.Without oversight or lawful procedure, DC will become Graceland – a place for fans of a famous person to get their picture taken with his old shoes. As Trump’s tenure at the center of American life comes to an end in the next two years, he’s only going to accelerate his attempts to turn the nation’s capital into an extension of his own, very lucrative brand ventures.There are alreadynumerous golf courses with Trump’s name on them, so the novelty isn’t even that potent. It’s that this course is ours, and by that, I mean it belongs to the taxpayers of this country. Taking it and its history and molding it to his will is the fun of it for Donald Trump. That it isn’t his, but it can be, makes it a conquest worthy of his time. Like the Kennedy Center, he can put his name on it, he can try to change it, but it will never truly be his.Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humoristExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionWashington DCGolfUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Blunder in, abandon allies and court a dictator: it’s the Trump doctrine, now playing out in Myanmar | Steve Bloomfield | The Guardian
description: The US condemned the genocide and military rule there, but now that Trump craves its rare earths, that’s all changed. For democracy activists, that’s a disaster, says former Observer international editor Steve Bloomfield
Author: Steve Bloomfield
Headline: The US condemned the genocide and military rule there, but now that Trump craves its rare earths, that’s all changed. For democracy activists, that’s a disaster, says former Observer international editor Steve Bloomfield
Content: Protesters opposed to the military junta in Myanmar at a rally in Quezon City, Philippines, 11 April 2025.Photograph: Rolex dela Peña/EPAView image in fullscreenProtesters opposed to the military junta in Myanmar at a rally in Quezon City, Philippines, 11 April 2025.Photograph: Rolex dela Peña/EPAOpinionMyanmarBlunder in, abandon allies and court a dictator: it’s the Trump doctrine, now playing out in MyanmarSteve BloomfieldThe US condemned the genocide and military rule there, but now that Trump craves its rare earths, that’s all changed. For democracy activists, that’s a disasterSun 18 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 12.37 EDTShareMarco Rubio was once adamant that the US had to do everything in its power to end what he described as the “ethnic cleansing” of the Rohingya in Myanmar. In a 2017letter he signed along with 20 other US senators, Rubio called for “strong multilateral sanctions against specific senior Burmese military officials associated with the gross human rights abuses”. Those responsible for the atrocities should be prosecuted, he argued.In the years since, the Myanmar military’s crimes have only increased. What was then deemed ethnic cleansing of the Rohingya is now widely viewed, including by the US, as genocide. What little democracy existed in Myanmar was eradicated in 2021 whenAung San Suu Kyi was arrested and imprisonedand her party’s election victory overturned, and the military took full control.This sparked a civil war that has now turned into a brutal series of overlapping conflicts between the military, resistance forces and a medley of ethnic militias. Around100,000 people have been killedin the conflict, which has forced 5 million people to flee their homes. The UN estimates that 16 million are now in need of urgent assistance. It is one of the world’s biggest humanitarian disasters – and entirely human-made.Earlier this year, Myanmar held sham elections, and Min Aung Hlaing – the general most responsible for Myanmar’s genocide and one of the targets of Rubio’s letter –became president.But Rubio, now the US secretary of state, no longer believes that Min Aung Hlaing should be prosecuted. Instead he’d rather like him to become an ally. This month the Trump administration decided to upend nearly a decade of united western policy and open direct talks with theMyanmarregime. The possibility of lifting sanctions is now being discussed. The move has shocked other western nations – none of which, it appears, was warned.Inevitably, a Maga figure lingers in the background. This time it’s Roger Stone, the Donald Trump ally who wasfound guilty in 2019 of lying to Congress, witness tampering and obstructing the investigation into whether the Trump campaign conspired with Russia in the 2016 presidential election.Stone, who was spared jail after Trump commuted his sentence, recently startedworking as a lobbyist for the Myanmar regime, helping to “rebuild relations between the Republic of the Union of Myanmar and the United States”.It seems to be working. Earlier this month Michael Vance, the assistant secretary of ​state for intelligence and research,travelled to Myanmar’s capital Naypyidaw. The trip was supposedly to secure the release of a US citizen, but Vance also held talks with the generals. The purpose of the talks was not to persuade the military regime to reintroduce democracy or stop its brutal war. Instead it appeared to be about securing American access to Myanmar’s rare earth minerals.In recent years, the race to control a steady supply of rare-earth minerals – elements used in a host of military technology and hi-tech manufacturing applications – has become increasingly fraught. China controls most of the world’s rare-earth mines andalmost all of the processing capacity. The Trump administration’s desire to turn the tables has led it to strike one-sided deals with Ukraine and theDemocratic Republic of Congothat have placed US business interests over practically everything else.There are more than 600 rare earth mines in Myanmar, most of which currently supply China. Since the 2021 coup, rare-earth shipments from Myanmar to China have totalled $3.6bn, making up the majority of China’s rare-earth imports. This is the prize the US appears to have its eyes on.Vance’s trip has handed Myanmar’s generals a propaganda victory at a moment when they are doing everything they can to legitimise the regime. The US, unfortunately, is not the only country welcoming Myanmar’s generals back into the fold. Min Aung Hlaing this month flew to Malaysia, once a strong opponent of the junta, where the prime minister Anwar Imbrahim floated the idea ofMyanmar being welcomed back into the Association of Southeast Asian Nations(Asean). Trips to Indonesia and Brunei are also on the cards, while the Philippines has indicated that it too would like to see relations normalised.The junta’s diplomatic victories follow growing military success. Over the last two and a half years, with the help of more sophisticated drones supplied by Russia and China, and the conscription of another 100,000 young men, the junta has regained control over several towns and pushed the resistance back into the countryside.For Myanmar’s civilians, the long nightmare continues. Last monthmore than 50 people were killedwhen the military bombed a busy market in a rebel-held area. Every week brings fresh atrocities, while the hope of a peaceful, democratic Myanmar slips further into the distance.View image in fullscreenThe aftermath of a military airstrike on a market and the Kisapanadi bridge in Rakhine, western Myanmar, 28 September 2026.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesThe one silver lining that those fighting for Myanmar’s freedom can cling to is that the rest of the west hasn’t given up on it yet. British diplomats are adamant that there will be no change in the UK’s position, while Canada, Australia and the EU are all likely to hold the line too. But even here there are concerns.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCampaigners point to the UK’s recent reduction in aid to Myanmar from £66m a year to £55m. Justhalf of the $889.6mthe UN has requested for Myanmar this year has been provided by international donors. They would also like to see Britain and others engage more directly with Myanmar’s pro-democracy camp, including the resistance.Trump is not the first president to prioritise resources over democracy, as a cursory glance at US relations with Saudi Arabia since it discovered oil in 1938 shows. But Trump’s rapacious attitude to oil and minerals, his willingness to enrich his friends and family, and his brazen support for dictators makes this a very different America. Myanmar is simply another example of the corrosive nature that Trump’s foreign policy is having in every corner of the globe.The question is whether Trump will get what he wants. US policy on Myanmar has been driven by Congress, and there remains bipartisan support for keeping it in place. The House of Representatives recently passed a bill that would extend the sanctions regime for another six years. Particularly at a time when his support is waning, Trump is unlikely to have much joy in persuading senators and members of Congress who have long supported Myanmar’s pro-democracy movement to turn a blind eye to genocide and war crimes.Malaysia begins Myanmar repatriations despite warnings from UN and rights groupsRead moreEven if he did, the bigger question is whether Myanmar’s generals can give Trump what he wants. The vast majority of Myanmar’s rare earth mines are near the border with China and many are controlled by militia groups, not the junta. “There is no way China is going to let the US get anywhere near the rare earths,” Joshua Kurlantzick at the Council on Foreign Relations told me.And yet even if none of this leads to any real change, the Trump administration’s decision to open talks with a genocidal regime responsible for one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises is a disaster for those in Myanmar fighting for their freedom. Many Myanmar resistance figures, including Aung San Suu Kyi, have placed their hope in US help. Like other democrats fighting demagogues, such as Volodymyr Zelenskyy, they have been deserted.Here is yet another example of the Trump administration blundering into a part of the world where it knows little, offering a prize to an authoritarian and leaving with not much to show for it.Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the ObserverExplore more on these topicsMyanmarOpinionMyanmar coupCritical mineralsRohingyaMalaysiaSouth and central AsiaHuman rightscommentShareReuse this content

title: Violence against children in Australia is at a crisis point. We must start listening to kids before our most vulnerable slip through the cracks | Satara Uthayakumaran | The Guardian
description: Our systems are fragmented and siloed, while those who are ‘different’ struggle to be understood. We cannot wait for more children to die to decide their suffering matters
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Our systems are fragmented and siloed, while those who are ‘different’ struggle to be understood. We cannot wait for more children to die to decide their suffering matters
Content: ‘Children fundamentally need love. They need an infrastructure of care, people and services that wrap their arms around them as they grow, recognise when something is wrong and stay beside them before their lives reach crisis point,’ writes Satara Uthayakumaran.Photograph: Sol de Zuasnabar Brebbia/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Children fundamentally need love. They need an infrastructure of care, people and services that wrap their arms around them as they grow, recognise when something is wrong and stay beside them before their lives reach crisis point,’ writes Satara Uthayakumaran.Photograph: Sol de Zuasnabar Brebbia/Getty ImagesOpinionViolence against women and girlsViolence against children in Australia is at a crisis point. We must start listening to kids before our most vulnerable slip through the cracksSatara UthayakumaranOur systems are fragmented and siloed, while those who are ‘different’ struggle to be understood. We cannot wait for more children to die to decide their suffering mattersSun 18 Oct 2026 18.51 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 18.52 EDTShareThe day I turned 14, two of my sister’s friends were found dead.They were 10 and 11 years old. Both had significant disabilities and attended the special-needs school my sister with severe disabilities also attends. Slowly, details emerged: their father had planned a murder-suicide,killing both children, his wife and himself.It’s impossible to imagine what it must be like to lose a child to violence.Childrenwho grow up inside places of abuse are forced to sacrifice themselves in unimaginable ways. Instead of learning to read, they learn how to anticipate anger; instead of playing with their friends, they isolate to keep away, out of fear. And when they cannot escape or do not have the words to explain what is happening to them, our system – and the adults around them – do not see their suffering.‘Manosphere’ warnings as rates of family and sexual violence against Australian children rise sharplyRead moreA new landmark decade-longstudy by University of Sydneyresearchers shows that sexual and family violence against children is at a crisis point. Analysing Australian data from 2014 to 2024, researchers found that recorded sexual assaults against children had increased by 32% among girls under 10, 51% among girls 10 to 17 and 60% among boys 10 to 17. Family and domestic violence-related assaults against children also increased sharply in recent years.This is a national emergency.This study cannot explain exactly why violence is increasing. We know greater reporting, economic pressures and changing online cultures are all contributing factors. But the fact that assault-related hospitalisations and substantiated child maltreatment cases did not rise in step exposes a disturbing gap between what police are recording and what systems around them are capturing.And the picture is so much worse than what these numbers can show.In my work as the former Australian Youth Representative to the United Nations,I travelled across the countryand sat with children who could no longer live with their families. I have also sat with children in prison, for whom abuse, violence and neglect is part of their everyday routine.I remember one 14-year-old girl I met from the Northern Territory, Kate*. Her home was a waking nightmare of abuse. Faced with the imminent violence waiting for her in her own bedroom, she fled to the streets.The alternative was frightening and uncertain, but staying meant confronting a terror she could no longer bear.She was hungry.
