She needed to survive. She stole to feed herself. And because she stole, she was arrested.The system looked at a terrified 14-year-old girl and saw an enemy. It looked past her bruises and failed to see a young child who needed safety, protection and someone to listen.According to theAustralian Institute of Health and Welfare, 65% of children in youth justice systems 2022–23 had interacted with the child protection system. Half of those in detention experienced abuse or neglect during that period.And that percentage is only the ones who reported it.Children fundamentally need love. They need an infrastructure of care, people and services that wrap their arms around them as they grow, recognise when something is wrong and stay beside them before their lives reach crisis point.But frontline services are strained. Families face delays in accessing support, while social workers are forced to turn away clients based on limited time and resources. Government departments continue to operate in silos. But children do not experience their lives in silos.Disability, homelessness, violence and neglect collide, very often in a single child’s life. But our systems are fragmented. Police see a direct confrontation; a teacher notices a slight change in behaviour; a nurse treats physical bruise; and a child-protection worker reads a single report – but because those agencies rarely talk to one another, none of them see the full picture, or the entire child.And for children who are “different”, those gaps are fatal.Australians want a royal commission into femicide. What haunts me is wondering if it’ll be enough to make leaders act | Jess HillRead moreMy sister is non-verbal, and I know that an absence of “words” does not mean having nothing to say. I have seen first-hand how hard her and her peers, who are also non-verbal, have to fight just to be listened to and understood.For any child who struggles with speech, disclosing violence is incredibly hard – and maybe this is why reporting has not kept up with the sheer magnitude of this crisis. These children cannot verbally tell a teacher what happened at home, or their parents what happened at school. They cannot answer rapid-fire questions in a sterile room by police in the “expected” way. Their distress might be seen as a “behavioural problem”, or their silence misunderstood as an absence of pain.Children from refugee or migrant backgrounds who do not speak English as their first language also face barriers to seeking assistance if they lack culturally safe language support.We need accessible and culturally competent services for children to communicate their experiences of violence, easily and without fear. More frontline workers and professionals should be trained to recognise and respond to the different forms of communication and distress that a child exhibits.We need all levels of government to step up, take shared responsibility for child safety and facilitate coordination between agencies. Otherwise our most vulnerable children will slip through the cracks of jurisdictional and departmental boundaries. There must also be long-term investment in prevention and early intervention.But most of all, we must listen to what our kids are saying. Because when a 14-year-old tells you that a cold prison cell feels safer than their own bedroom – that’s how we know we’ve failed our children.We cannot wait until another child is dead before governments decide their suffering matters. A child should never have to find the “right words” for their abuse in order for an adult to finally pay attention. There is no vocabulary for trauma.*Not her real nameIn Australia, children, young adults, parents and teachers can contact the Kids Helpline on 1800 55 1800; adult survivors can seek help at Blue Knot Foundation on 1300 657 380. In the UK, the NSPCC offers support to children on 0800 1111, and adults concerned about a child on 0808 800 5000. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. In the US, call or text the Childhelp abuse hotline on 800-422-4453. Other sources of help can be found at Child Helpline InternationalSatara Uthayakumaran is a writer and Australia’s youth representative to the United Nations for 2025. Satara served on the board of the Domestic Violence Crisis Service and has worked with Anti-Slavery AustraliaExplore more on these topicsViolence against women and girlsOpinionChildrenCrime - AustraliacommentShareReuse this content

title: I saw rioting, looting, above all, anger. If French leaders think more violence will solve this, they’re mistaken  | Oliver Haynes | The Guardian
description: It’s a perfect storm of protesters with heartfelt grievances and others set on conflict. The key here is the sense of betrayal that united them on the streets, says journalist Oliver Haynes
Author: Oliver Haynes
Headline: It’s a perfect storm of protesters with heartfelt grievances and others set on conflict. The key here is the sense of betrayal that united them on the streets, says journalist Oliver Haynes
Content: Clashes between protesters and the French police at Place de la République in Paris, 17 October 2026.Photograph: Abitbol Shana/ABACA/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenClashes between protesters and the French police at Place de la République in Paris, 17 October 2026.Photograph: Abitbol Shana/ABACA/ShutterstockOpinionFranceI saw rioting, looting, above all, anger. If French leaders think more violence will solve this, they’re mistakenOliver HaynesIt’s a perfect storm of protesters with heartfelt grievances and others set on conflict. The key here is the sense of betrayal that united them on the streetsSun 18 Oct 2026 11.06 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 11.58 EDTShareThe first thing I learned on the streets ofParisthis weekend is that there is no arguing with teargas. I arrived at Place de la République just after 1pm yesterday. The mood was festive until police started firing volleys of teargas into the square from Rue du Faubourg-du-Temple.I didn’t see the inciting incident – if there even was one – and tried walking into the cloud of CS gas hanging in the air. It was impossible. The gas clings to your nose and burns your eyes, and you quickly start struggling to breathe. I retreated towards the Boulevard de Magenta, blinking furiously to stop the stinging.This approach to the crowd had been adopted by the authorities early in the day, causing chaos across the city and setting the tone for what would follow. A friend had to return to her home with her elderly parents because police had fired teargas “at random” at a crowd of young people in Strasbourg-Saint-Denis in the 10th arrondissement.I headed back up the Boulevard de Magenta. There I met protesters including a student at the Sorbonne, who had come to “support the highschoolers first and foremost, and to demand more money in public schools, from primary schools to universities”. Another major factor that he said had motivated him to come out on to the street “was the repression faced by highschoolers, who are under 18”, such asan incident in Lens, where a police grenade blew a 15-year-old’s hand to bits.Other protesters I spoke to came from various sections of society: young, old, white and from ethnic minority backgrounds. People were there in their capacity as workers in a union, students in a lycée or individual citizens who had come out in anger at the rising cost of living. The price of petrol, the original motivating factor behind the 2018gilets jaunes(yellow vest) movement, had prompted several people to come out after it hit a record €2.4 per litre at the end of last month.This section of the protest was completely peaceful, marching away from République, making lots of noise and climbing on scaffolding to fly flags, but otherwise doing nothing beyond articulating political demands. Between 550,000 and 800,000 peopletook to the streets across Franceas part of protests like these.When I returned to République around 4pm, I saw that the situation had descended into chaos. Stun grenades were exploding everywhere, and protesters were throwing bottles at the police. Smoke from a blazing car filled the air. A branch of Nicolas, a chain wine shop, had its window smashed in and black-clad protesters looted it – not for the wine but for missiles to throw at police in retaliation for the stun grenades.I was unable to stop and talk to people amid this fury, but my sense was that this was a combination of black bloc – anarchists who come out to many protests to cause trouble –gilets jaunes, young and middle-aged people who were furious at the government and the police, and, of course, opportunistic young men looking for a scrap. As ever with street protests, many people, many motivations.There were cries of the oldgilets jaunessloganMacron Démission(“Resign Macron”). Beyond the organised group of hobbyist rioters, the dominant emotions seemed to be fear and rage. With each stun grenade the non-violent parts of the crowd were thrown into panic, but would then regroup and stand their ground while the rioters continued throwing missiles. Perhaps the feeling could be summed up by a poster I saw the day before the protest: “Lost hope, 17/10 to find it again. Fuck just about everything 17/10. We are already in hell meet on 17/10”.So what next? Withmore than 1,800 arrests, what will become of these people, this movement, these riots?There is a sense among certain parts of the French population that making enough noise, including acts of vandalism, sends a signal to power. And indeed, there is some evidence to suggest this is the case. Neoliberal reforms have been rebuffed successfully on several occasions inFrance, primarily through strike waves or roundabout blockades – though these too had the presence of a radical fringe, willing to set fire to things.As the dust settles, what will be the political repercussions? Marine Le Pen, attempting to profit from the situation, has positioned herself on the side of those angry at the cost of living, while condemning the looters.In a statementshe described the French people as caught between the “austerity and fiscal hammering of those in power and the insurrectionary activists”. She promised to “free” the French “from Macronist toxic policies and protect them from the violence of the far left”. Carefully omitted was the fact that her party is proposing deeper austerity than even the Macronists, but the images of fire and looting that will be broadcast on every news channel reinforce her narrative of restoration of order to the streets.Meanwhile, the French left, chiefly represented by Jean-Luc Mélenchon, is defending the protesters and seeking to channel their anger into the presidential campaign, focusing on the violence of the police over that of the rioters. The left may also be able to make gains from this tense situation.While the government seems determined to continue with its budget unimpeded, it may only be a matter of time before another such explosion occurs. You can’t argue with teargas, but it will only hold the inevitable at bay for so long.Oliver Haynes is a journalist and co-host of Sacré Bleu: the French presidential election podcastDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The upside of anger: can fury be one of the deepest forms of human compassion? | Jackie Bailey | The Guardian
description: Imagine anger as a sign not of moral failure or justified outrage but the desire to care for another
Author: Jackie Bailey
Headline: Imagine anger as a sign not of moral failure or justified outrage but the desire to care for another
Content: Anger can motivate us to act – but it takes skill and wisdom to turn it to a virtue.Composite: Getty Images/Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenAnger can motivate us to act – but it takes skill and wisdom to turn it to a virtue.Composite: Getty Images/Guardian DesignMaking sense of itReligionThe upside of anger: can fury be one of the deepest forms of human compassion?Jackie BaileyImagine anger as a sign not of moral failure or justified outrage but the desire to care for anotherMaking sense of itis a column about spirituality and how it can be used to navigate everyday lifeSun 18 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 19.05 EDTShareAnger is an emotion we are taught to manage, control and suppress. But what if anger is, as poet David Whyte says, one of the deepest possible forms of compassion available to humankind?Philosophers and theologians have long distinguished between virtuous and non-virtuous anger. Aristotle defined anger as “a desire, accompanied by pain, for apparent retribution, aroused by an apparent, undeserved slighting against oneself or those connected to oneself”.Anger appears to combine a physical sensation of torment with a desire to act. The English word “anger” has its etymological roots in the Old Norseangr, meaning grief and sorrow, and the Latinangere,tostrangle, referring to the sensation of chest tightening, fists clenching, blood boiling.It’s never been so easy to find answers. But sitting with uncertainty can ultimately bring wisdom | Muhammad AbdulsaterRead moreHow do we make sure our angry actions are just? Aristotle taught his students that anyone can get angry, but it takes skill and wisdom to turn anger into a virtue. For anger to have a moral quality, you have to get angry at the right person, at the right time, to the right degree, for the right purpose and with the right motive.A complete lack of anger could itself be a vice, according to Christian theologian Thomas Aquinas, in situations where it is reasonable to act to restore justice. Similarly, Persian Muslim theologian Al-Ghazali advocated for a middle ground, identifying forbearance,Ḥilm,as the ideal state, in which anger is subject to reason and divine law.How do we know when our anger is justified? PhilosopherMartha C Nussbaumobserves that anger might be well grounded, as there are many cases of wrongdoing in the world. In these instances, anger is valuable if it quickly transitions into productive action for people’s wellbeing and a better future. However, Nussbaum notes that even justifiable anger, if left to fester, can become narrowly focused on a desire for payback, which in no way supports a better world.The Stoics thought of anger as a type of momentary madness, a response to the unfounded belief that the world is fair. Once we accept that most things are beyond our control, apart from our reactions to them, we can develop equanimity. Buddhists espouse a similar view, identifying anger as one of the “Three Poisons”. Anger signals a distorted understanding of reality involving the belief in a singular ego, leading to a wholesale engagement in the push-pull cycle of desire and aversion at the root of human suffering.Whyte offers a more hopeful view of this much-debated emotion. According to him, we feel anger when we are unable to enact our deep-seated care for others. “What we name as anger is only the incoherent physical incapacity to sustain this deep form of care in our outer daily life.” Perhaps, Whyte observes, anger is our “unwillingness to be large enough and generous enough to hold what we love helplessly in our bodies or our mind with the clarity and breadth of our whole being”.Writer and artistMimi Zhu imagines every emotion, including anger, as a protective spirit, an ancestor “embodied as a feeling, telling me … what I have been taught to overlook”. Zhu notes that the Chinese characters for anger can translate literally to the phrase“to give life to a vital breath”.Hungry for connection? This is what we lose when we stop eating together | Shadi Khan SaifRead moreImagine anger as a sign not of moral failure or justified outrage but the desire to care for another. I might get angry with my daughter for failing to tidy her room. Part of my anger might be about my ego, a fight for dominance; but perhaps it is also about my desire for her to be healthy, and well, and able to find her socks for school in the morning.If I focus on the other’s wellbeing, as Nussbaum writes, then anger inspires a future-oriented project rather than an ego-driven quest for payback. The thought is no longer, “My daughter is disrespecting my rules, and I am worried that she will never be able to look after herself,” but “My daughter is her own person, how can I support her to be well, within her own parameters of flourishing selfhood?”I might have already shouted about the socks. Next time, before I start slamming doors, I can pause and ask myself, what is it that this anger is inviting me to understand about myself and the other?At its worst, anger is a motivation for unspeakable crimes and violence. At its best, it can be a reminder that humans have a default setting to challenge what seems unjust. Maybe that is anger’s greatest gift: the reminder that, even if we feel helpless, we are hardwired for hope, to try to change things for the better.Jackie Baileyis an award-winning author whose latest book isThe Outrageous Good Fortune of Living(HarperCollins/ABC Books). Jackie works as a funeral celebrant and pastoral care practitioner, supporting people to navigate death and dyingExplore more on these topicsReligionMaking sense of itEthicsPhilosophycommentShareReuse this content

title: When you watch the acclaimed TV drama Time, remember this: I’ve seen inside our prisons and they are just as bleak | Alex South | The Guardian
description: The show depicts prisons as places characterised by violence and isolation, with no focus on rehabilitation. It’s depressingly accurate, says former prison officer Alex South
Author: Alex South
Headline: The show depicts prisons as places characterised by violence and isolation, with no focus on rehabilitation. It’s depressingly accurate, says former prison officer Alex South
Content: ‘Beautiful and ugly and exact, all at once.’ The cast of the latest series of Time.Photograph: BBC/BBC Studios/Peter MarleyView image in fullscreen‘Beautiful and ugly and exact, all at once.’ The cast of the latest series of Time.Photograph: BBC/BBC Studios/Peter MarleyOpinionPrisons and probationWhen you watch the acclaimed TV drama Time, remember this: I’ve seen inside our prisons and they are just as bleakAlex SouthThe show depicts prisons as places characterised by violence and isolation, with no focus on rehabilitation. It’s depressingly accurateAlex South is a former prison officer and the author of the memoirBehind These DoorsSun 18 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 12.37 EDTShareThenew series of Timeis not an easy watch. The opening seconds of Jimmy McGovern’s prison drama show a normal woman on a normal bus, as it drives up a normal road. But to the right of that road is a huge concrete wall, topped with barbed wire and CCTV cameras.The wall is only partly visible, just as prisons themselves tend to occupy a space towards the very edges of our thoughts. They exist, but not as part of normal life. But McGovern’s drama shows just how permeable that wall is.The show’s fictional young offender institution, HMYOI Alderwick, is a place that boils with anger. As new arrivals enter the prison, an officer tells them: “Keep going, ignore the noise.” As if you ever could. The sound of prisoners shouting and kicking their cell doors is an assault on the ears. Those scenes are louder than any headline, of which there are plenty these days; overcrowding, escapes from custody, thelatest early-release scheme. What McGovern does is crank the volume so loud it’s impossible to block out.The reality is that prisons are closer to us than they might seem. The Sentencing Act 2026 allows prisoners serving standard determinate sentences to be released after serving only a third of their sentence in custody. The early-release scheme is intended to help relieve the prison capacity crisis, but as therecent recall ratedemonstrates, this solution is temporary.Many of the boys in Time would not be eligible for early release. Murder, manslaughter and rape are among the stated exemptions. But the value of time in prison is not only determined by its length, but by how it is spent. Just as David Tennant’s character bemoans the lack of training or education for young men in custody, so do prison staff across the country. They know what is blindingly obvious: angry people don’t come out of prison less angry if they’ve been banged up for 23 hours a day.Life inside Alderwick demonstrates the futility of keeping people locked up for hours on end, isolated from one another and with nothing to do. The culture of “keep-aparts” is firmly entrenched in many English prisons, particularly those housing young adults. “Keep aparts” are as they sound; groups of prisoners who are quite literally kept apart, often due to gang issues or postcode wars. Prisoners known to have conflict with others end up with a long list of “keep-aparts” on their file. They must associate separately from their “keep aparts” – they cannot attend the gym, education or visits with anyone on that list. This results in staggered regimes that are increasingly complex to manage. Rather than everyone having three or four hours out a day, each group only has one hour.Short-term, this works. But in the long-term, this stifling conflict-management tactic only exacerbates division and violence.View image in fullscreenDavid Tennant and Louis McCartney in Time.Photograph: BBC/BBC Studios/Peter MarleyIn Time, an officer suggests a solution to this issue – perhaps all new entrants could be told that, from now on, they would have to associate with everyone living in their unit. No more “keep aparts”. The governor’s response is: “We’ll park that one for now.” But that’s the problem. We are parking it and never coming back. We are releasing people from prison but not addressing the issues that put them there in the first place. Letting people out early was inevitable; prisons are full. But when80% of all offending in England and Wales is reoffending, it suggests only a small minority come out changed for the better.Most institutions are depressingly similar to Alderwick: no education, no libraries, with prisoners barely allowed any time out of their cells at all. A report this year onchildren in custodyfound that, at almost every establishment in the youth custody estate, prisoners were locked behind their doors for as long as 19 hours a day. The overstretched,understaffed systemdoes not allow for integration, socialisation, healthy forms of argument and discussion, or opportunities for conflict resolution. If it did, perhaps early release might not feel like such a bad thing.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBeing banished to a place characterised by violence and being locked up may seem an appropriate punishment for criminals. But on release day, the only ones being punished are us. Because those angry boys who fight and kick and slash, the ones with the baby faces and sprinkling of acne, are the same boys who grow into men behind that imposing wall. They are the same boys who board that normal bus on that normal road, right next to you and I.This series of Time is beautiful and ugly and exact, all at once. The least realistic bit is the surplus of toilet roll in one boy’s cell. There’s never enough toilet roll inside. But the major flaw of the show is that it only lasts three episodes. Because the boys represented in those fictionalised prisons are still banged up in the real ones, while the rest of us ignore the noise.Alex South is a former prison officer and the author of the memoirBehind These DoorsExplore more on these topicsPrisons and probationOpinionUK criminal justiceTelevisionDavid TennantDramacommentShareReuse this content

title: Ali G answers his critics: ‘Me ain’t the first intellectual to get haterz’ | Sacha Baron Cohen | The Guardian
description: Staines’s finest nailed the zeitgeist of the late 90s and early 00s, and now he’s back – but how does he fit into 2026? He discusses the backlash against his return, his worst ever interviewee and how he’s going to prevent world war two
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: Staines’s finest nailed the zeitgeist of the late 90s and early 00s, and now he’s back – but how does he fit into 2026? He discusses the backlash against his return, his worst ever interviewee and how he’s going to prevent world war two
Content: ‘Most reporters can’t even spell the world “jourmalist” … Ali G.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Most reporters can’t even spell the world “jourmalist” … Ali G.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianSacha Baron CohenInterviewAli G answers his critics: ‘Me ain’t the first intellectual to get haterz’Rich PelleyStaines’s finest nailed the zeitgeist of the late 90s and early 00s, and now he’s back – but how does he fit into 2026? He discusses the backlash against his return, his worst ever interviewee and how he’s going to prevent world war twoSun 18 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 08.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Can you tell people that you’re from Hustler?” Ali G asks me. “Or The Source. Or Guns & Ammo. Speaking to a Guardian journalist ain’t a good look for me in the hood.”At Ali’s request, we are meeting in an independent chicken shop in Staines because – due to some sort of mix-up – he thought the one interview he had agreed to for his new film wasChicken Shop Date, which was “90% likely to lead to boning”. He follows this with an entirely unprintable reminiscence about the first time he and “me Julie” had sex in the disabled toilets of Egham KFC.Now that we have established I am not in fact Amelia Dimoldenberg – and that any boning today will be strictly chicken-related – Ali changes tack. Whenever anyone comes near our table, he loudly explains, to my embarrassment, that we are actually conducting a major drug deal. Having seemingly worked his way through the entire menu, he starts asking what else he would need to buy to get the bill up to £500, after discovering that the Guardian is footing it.It is, in other words, reassuringly easy to tell that not everything about Ali G has changed, even though a lot has happened in the “20 decades” (he means 24 years) since he was last on the big screen in Ali G Indahouse. In that time, the UK has had nine prime ministers, survived a global pandemic and seen the rise of #MeToo and Black Lives Matter. Or, as Ali puts it rather more succinctly in the trailer: “The world went to crap: there was Covid, wars and Ed Sheeran”.View image in fullscreenBack in da house … Ali G.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianNow he’s back in Ali G: Who Iz I? – and, inevitably, not everybody is delighted. The trailer alone has prompted accusations that the fake dreadlocks, Rastafarian imagery and faux-Jamaican persona now look less like satire and more like an outdated racial caricature. Which is how, 24 years after Ali G first took his home town of Staines global, I find myself sitting opposite him in his old manor, trying to work out whether the UK is ready to show him some respect again.Parked outside is the same yellow Renault 5 I remember from Indahouse, now with a homemade Uber sign stuck in the windscreen. Around his neck hangs a diamond teddy bear clutching two sacks of money. It “used to be part of the crown jewels and was worn by the queen, RIP. A bloke who worked as a dog washer at Windsor palace nicked it and then came into the Crooked Billet pub in Iver Heath, where me bought it off him for 20K when me was rich,” he claims.More bafflingly, he is wearing four watches. “Dem are for different time zones – dis one is Staines, dis one is Egham, dis one iz Langley Village and dis one iz Scrotland.” There is plenty more to take in, but I should probably attempt to conduct the interview I actually came here for.double quotation markThere’s always gonna be haterz. it happened to Jesus, to Gandhi and to Brooklyn BeckhamSo how should I address you – Ali, Ali G or Mr G?Me iz known by me mates as “De G”, “G-Dog” and “De Ali-torney G-eneral” … and by Staines Benefits Office as Richard Watkins, Kelvin Matthews and Priyanka Patel.And what happened to the dreads?Me ain’t never had dreads. Me wears the Rasta bonnet because – and me iz trusting you to keep dis secret – dat’s where me keeps me stash, the ganja. Perfect place because the cops ain’t allowed to look under it for religious reasons, innit.We find out in the trailer that you’re about to become a dad. How are you preparing? Are you and your Julie going to NCT classes?Me has actually already become a daddy, something dat for the last 40 years me has prepared for five times every day. Me usually just prepared with me Julie, although one time we also prepared with Cheryl from Abrakebabra in dis marble Jacuzzi me bought off eBay, which tragically didn’t end well. Me put it upstairs at Nan’s house, when me filled it with water and the three of us got in, it was too heavy and broke through the floor and landed on me Nan, who was sitting in the room downstairs. Luckily it killed her instantly, completely squashed her. She died happy because just one week before, me had bought her a new pair of double-F swingaz for her 88th birthday. The weight of the Jacuzzi caused them to literally explode; one of her nipples was found three streets away. Anyway, when one life ends, another one starts, and me iz loving being a dad.View image in fullscreenWho’s the daddy? … Ali G in a still from his new film, with Morgana Robinson as his Julie.Photograph: Amazon MGM StudiosWhat sort of dad are you?There have been some discipline issues. No matter how many times me tells the baby, “Hands off, dem iz mine!”, him keeps trying to grab me Julie’s swingaz. But there you go – like his dad, he iz a boobs man, innit. Me loves him and he iz well brainy, at six months old him can already read audiobooks.Staines officially became Staines-upon-Thames in2012, partly to improve the town’s image after years of association with you – but now there’s a petition calling for a statue of you in the town. Do you feel vindicated? And if they build it, would you pose for it – perhaps naked, like Michelangelo’s David?Firstly, it ain’t because of me they changed the name of Staines. It’s because in 2012 the River Thames started flowing through the town, so they added it to the name, innit. Thirdly, me iz well proud dat they want to put a statute of me in the middle of Staines. Me Julie says the only difference between dat and the real thing iz dat the statute won’t be selling ganja – they’ll both be hanging around the town centre doing nothing, ha ha ha! Unfortunately, as well as loads of people wanting the statute, there are also loads of people who don’t, because of racialism. Me ain’t gonna let them win and iz willing to pay out of me Julie’s pocket for an Ali G erection in the middle of Staines.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI’m with stupid … Ali G meets Donald Trump.Photograph: Channel 4This is your first film in 24 years. Why come back now? Did the world need Ali G, or did Ali G need the world?Dis ain’t actually me first film in 24 years. Me has also made about 300 others with me Julie and iz hoping Amazon will buy them off me and put them in the “members only” part of their site. But to answer your question, the world needed me. Dis movie will be the most important release since the Jeffrey Einstein files, and me made it to increase the peace, bring both sides together and hopefully prevent world war two from ever happening. It has also got more boning in it than the Einstein files – all of it legal – and because me iz now woke, me also included a nude man’s battyhole to keep the LGBLT community happy.The Guardian has already been arguing about whether you should have come back at all.Arwa Mahdawiwrote “Ali G is back. I really wish he wasn’t”, whileJason Okundayeargued that Britain – and the joke – have changed.Jacob Rees-Mogg, meanwhile, has defended you on his Instagram, describing you as “clever, satiric humour that makes the country look faintly foolish. And that’s no bad thing.” So who understands Ali G better in 2026: the Guardian or Jacob Rees-Mogg?Me ain’t never heard of any of those people, but from their names it seems to me dat Jacob Rees-Mogg iz the only person of colour, so him supporting me iz all dat matters. There are always gonna be haterz, innit. Me ain’t the first intellectual to get dat – it happened to Jesus, it happened to Gandhi, it even happened to Brooklyn Beckham. For the good of humanoidkind, me has just got to keep speaking out. People shutting me down ain’t nothing new. In fact, me was cancelled just two years ago by Staines Benefits Office for pretending to be a disabled Albanian woman with seven children. Me just bounced right back with a new name. Don’t never let the authorities oppress you, innit.double quotation markMe’d have a puff with God and ask him: why does him allow terrible things to happen: like wars, diseases and Coldplay?You’ve come back to a world full of influencers, pranksters, podcasters and people asking strangers stupid questions on TikTok. Do you feel like everyone’s basically nicked your act?For real, loads of people have been copying me, especially the way me looks and talks – which makes them cultural appropriators and dat iz well out of order. It makes me well sad how fick the world has become since me was on telly doing interviews 20 decades ago – most reporters now can’t even correctly spell the word “jourmalist”, let alone ask brainy questions like you and me does do, innit.Prince William? David Cameron? JD Vance? Celebrities brace – and Staines celebrates – ahead of new Ali G filmRead moreYou’ve spent your career interviewing politicians, experts and other important people. Who would you most like to interview now?Me has always dreamed big, both in me personal life – for example, last night me imagined doing it with Sydney Sweeney; dat iz a woman, by the way, in case you ain’t heard of her. Me ain’t got nothing against homosapiens, me just ain’t one of them – and also in me professional life. Check dis: me wants to do the biggest interview ever – to go up to heaven and have a chat with none other than God himself. Me’d have a look around heaven – iz it any good, or iz it well boring, just a load of old blokes sitting around playing harps? Then me’d have a puff with God and ask him the tough questions: why does him allow terrible things to happen to the Earth, like wars, diseases and Coldplay? Also, while me was up there, me’d check in on me Nan, see if she’s doing all right and if she can still remember the Netflix password for our house.Who is the stupidest person you’ve ever interviewed?The most fickest person me ever spoke to was Domald Trump. How him ever became America’s prime minister me will never know. Also, how did him get to marry all them really fit women – first Ivanka, then Stormy Daniels and now dat one who looks like a Transformer, Melania?By now Ali has eaten an alarming amount of chicken. I’ve laughed far more than I expected to – including a few times when I probably shouldn’t. He is still crude, badly informed and completely inappropriate. But that was always the trick: every so often, the stupidest person in the room accidentally asks the smartest question. Before we go our separate ways, there’s just one question I need to ask. Does he think I’ve got what it takes to join the West Staines Massiv? Is there some kind of initiation process?“Me’ll have to check with the rest of me posse first – his name iz Dangerous Dave,” says Ali. “Me’ll ask him when he finishes work at HSBC at 5pm.”Ali G: Who Iz I? is in cinemas from23 October.Explore more on these topicsSacha Baron CoheninterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I drunkenly sing Wonderwall off-key and awfully’: Rebecca Ferguson’s honest playlist | Music | The Guardian
description: The singer-songwriter gets a lift from U2 and likes to reminisce to Bette Midler, but which cheesy Euro banger does she secretly like?
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: The singer-songwriter gets a lift from U2 and likes to reminisce to Bette Midler, but which cheesy Euro banger does she secretly like?
Content: Rebecca Ferguson … ‘Hearing I Will Always Love You made me think: This is what I’m going to do’Photograph: -View image in fullscreenRebecca Ferguson … ‘Hearing I Will Always Love You made me think: This is what I’m going to do’Photograph: -Honest playlistMusic‘I drunkenly sing Wonderwall off-key and awfully’: Rebecca Ferguson’s honest playlistThe singer-songwriter gets a lift from U2 and likes to reminisce to Bette Midler, but which cheesy Euro banger does she secretly like?Rich PelleySun 18 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first song I fell in love withWhen I was five or six, my mum wouldn’t let me listen to anything other than Christian gospel. Her friend Jane felt sorry for me and brought me a cassette with Whitney Houston on one side and Cher on the other. My ears couldn’t believe what they were hearing. I Will Always Love You made me think: This is what I’m going to do.The first single I boughtSo Young by the Corrs, from Sainsbury’s in Walton Village in Liverpool. I couldn’t really afford music as a kid, so buying a record was a big deal. I’d heard the Corrs on the radio, liked their voices and thought: I’m buying this.The song that is my karaoke go-toI have a habit of singing Wonderwall by Oasis really badly. It’s like a party trick: I drunkenly sing it completely off-key and awful, but impassioned. I have no idea why.The song I inexplicably know every lyric toI was obsessed with the film Beaches as a kid. Me and my best friend would watch it over and over and I’d pretend I was CC Bloom. The Glory of Love by Bette Midler, Wind Beneath My Wings – I know the lyrics to all of them. I’m getting nostalgic just thinking about it.The best song to play at a partyI like to do a bit of DJing after a few drinks, and Mundian to Bach Ke by Panjabi MC always goes down well, but you’ve got to drop it late in the party. If you play it too early, people aren’t ready.The song I can no longer listen toWhen I was a teenager, I was feeling particularly low, and I feel like that Everybody Hurts by REM saved me that day. It was this gentle reminder: this is life, everybody hurts, get up and get on with it.The song I secretly like, but tell everyone I hateI wouldn’t put Blue (Da Ba Dee) by Eiffel 65 on at one of my parties, but I might play it while I’m doing the dishes.The best song to have sex toI imagine Drunk in Love by Beyoncé would probably work!The song that changed my lifeA Change Is Gonna Come by Sam Cooke, which I sang at my first X Factor audition. I’d prepared three songs and Simon Cowell stopped me from singing the first two. A Change Is Gonna Come made more sense for me emotionally anyway. I thought about myself and members of my family I’d seen struggling and almost went into myself while I sang it.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe song that gets me up in the morningBlasting a bit of Beautiful Day by U2 always helps when you’re feeling a bit crappy or tired after a late night with the kids.The song that makes me cryHope There’s Someone by Antony and the Johnsons. It’s just so sad. The way it’s delivered, you can really hear the pain. It gets me every time.The song I want played at my funeralI’d want something fun that reminded friends and family of good times. I’ve been listening to Movin’ to the Sun by Hugel, Imael Angel and Ultra Naté lately. I’d have that, except – God, it’s morbid thinking about your funeral, isn’t it?Rebecca Ferguson tours The Hits at Christmas, 2 to 12 December.Explore more on these topicsMusicHonest playlistThe X FactorPop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Dance Is Not for Us review – desire and defiance as one revolutionary mover sweats it all out | Dance | The Guardian
description: Omar Rajeh performs out of frustration, resistance and a need to connect in this stream-of-consciousness solo at Dance Umbrella festival
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: Omar Rajeh performs out of frustration, resistance and a need to connect in this stream-of-consciousness solo at Dance Umbrella festival
Content: ‘He dances like it’s a necessary thing to do’ … Omar Rajeh in Dance Is Not for Us at the Barbican.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianView image in fullscreen‘He dances like it’s a necessary thing to do’ … Omar Rajeh in Dance Is Not for Us at the Barbican.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianDanceReviewDance Is Not for Us review – desire and defiance as one revolutionary mover sweats it all outBarbican, LondonOmar Rajeh performs out of frustration, resistance and a need to connect in this stream-of-consciousness solo at Dance Umbrella festivalLyndsey WinshipSun 18 Oct 2026 13.45 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 13.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn August 2019, Omar Rajeh sat in his bedroom, listening to the sound of pounding percussion with his world in crisis. In the midst of political instability, Citerne Beirut, a theatre and cultural centre Rajeh had founded in his nativeLebanon, was forced to close, dismantled by order of the local government, who planned to build an incinerator on the site.View image in fullscreenHeartfelt … Omar Rajeh in Dance Is Not for Us.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianRajeh tells us that as a teenager, coming of age at the end of the Lebanese civil war, dance had always seemed like the most revolutionary thing he could do. Now here he is, more than three decades later, still dancing – out of frustration, defiance, resistance and a desire to connect. As the percussive score gains momentum, Rajeh’s busy body builds up a sweat. In this danced stream of consciousness, Rajeh is not always an especially elegant mover, but he dances like it’s a necessary thing to do.Part of this year’sDance Umbrella festival, Dance Is Not for Us is a solo that appears at times like an explosion of physical instinct, but it is mostly calm, considered musings on the nature of choreography, with all its workings exposed. Rajeh sits and taps at a keyboard as his thoughts appear on screen, all the inspirations, decisions, vacillations and U-turns that go into creating a performance.He tells us of the first “choreographies” he ever saw: a fight between two men, people gathering in the streets to protest, bodies making choices and organising themselves in space – which is what choreography is, after all. The creative and the political are one to Rajeh, who is now based in Lyon, a major loss to Lebanon’s creative life. This piece is an insight into a choreographer’s mind, and it’s a heartfelt appeal to gather, to witness, to share our pain and loss – to look and to listen.Dance Umbrella festivalis at venues across London and online until 27 OctoberExplore more on these topicsDanceBarbicanLebanonTheatreFestivalsProtestreviewsShareReuse this content

title: 4.48 Psychosis review – a dazzling, harrowing opera worthy of Sarah Kane’s furious writing  | Opera | The Guardian
description: Six fearless singers and the Chroma Ensemble, conducted with arresting immediacy by Naomi Woo, rise to the challenge of the brutal musical onslaughts and anarchic orchestrations of Philip Venables’ raw, imaginative score
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: Six fearless singers and the Chroma Ensemble, conducted with arresting immediacy by Naomi Woo, rise to the challenge of the brutal musical onslaughts and anarchic orchestrations of Philip Venables’ raw, imaginative score
Content: In-yer-face … Lauren Young, Sophia Burgos, Jacquelyn Stucker and Hannah Edmunds in 4.48 Psychosis at Linbury theatre.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianView image in fullscreenIn-yer-face … Lauren Young, Sophia Burgos, Jacquelyn Stucker and Hannah Edmunds in 4.48 Psychosis at Linbury theatre.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianOperaReview4.48 Psychosis review – a dazzling, harrowing opera worthy of Sarah Kane’s furious writingLinbury theatre, LondonSix fearless singers and the Chroma Ensemble, conducted with arresting immediacy by Naomi Woo, rise to the challenge of the brutal musical onslaughts and anarchic orchestrations of Philip Venables’ raw, imaginative scoreClive PagetSun 18 Oct 2026 11.03 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 11.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSarah Kanerevolutionised British theatre with five provocative plays written between 1995 and 1999. Her final work, 4.48 Psychosis, was her most personal, confronting the clinical depression she struggled with for years. The play was first performed posthumously in 2000, after she died by suicide in 1999.The Royal Opera and Guildhall School of Music and Drama commissioned Philip Venables to adapt the play as an opera, whichdebuted in 2016. The composer, also known for a certain “in-yer-face” approach, set Kane’s original text almost entirely, realising its 24 disjointed sections in a raw, imaginative score teeming with minimalist licks, prickly synth-pop and consoling nods to the baroque. The libretto shifts between poetic abstraction and scathing exchanges between a patient and a psychologist. An ensemble of six female singers navigates themes of depression, isolation and the agonising choices surrounding medication.View image in fullscreenOne fractured personality … Sophia Burgos, Veena Akama-Makia, Hannah Edmunds and Jacquelyn Stucker in 4.48 Psychosis.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianVenables’ adaptation successfully leverages the unique capabilities of music, tapping into Kane’s non-linear prosody and use of verbal repetition. His dazzling score overlaps vocal lines, introducing a structural complexity that traditional theatre cannot easily replicate. The sprawling narrative is anchored by a single spoken voice over a loudspeaker, evoking Kane’s authorial presence.‘It put me in a fever dream’: Philip Venables on turning Sarah Kane’s 4.48 Psychosis into a shocking operaRead moreWhere matters occasionally falter is in the music’s tendency to prescribe the emotional temperature by tying it to the six-part polyphonic chorus. Tightly controlled, it tethers the freedom of interpretation inherent in Kane’s furious text. Although Venables retains the spoken voice in places, and the opera is an extremely harrowing experience, it tempers the play’s potential to shock.Ted Huffman’s 10-year-old production is successfully revived here with a subtly revised ending. Astute and economical direction ensures the action remains fluid yet focused within Hannah Clark’s institutional white box set. DM Wood’s stark lighting is laser-focused while the amplified sound design lends a kick up the backside to Venable’s most brutal musical onslaughts.London-based collectiveChromaforms the 14-piece chamber orchestra perched above the action. The anarchic orchestrations, which feature a trio of saxophones, piano synthesiser and accordion, hiss with a fierce violence contrasting with moments of hushed beauty and the unsettling sounds of distant waiting-room muzak. Projected text is paired with duelling percussion instruments (including bass drums, carpenter’s saw and shop-counter bell) to punctuate the patient-doctor dialogues bringing brief moments of levity. Catherine Ring and Delia Stevens attack their instruments with sticks and hands, dramatic intent writ large on their faces.View image in fullscreenFluid yet focused … 4.48 Psychosis.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianConductor Naomi Woo brings an arresting immediacy to Venables’ complex score while the six fearless singers – Jacquelyn Stucker, Hannah Edmunds, Sophia Burgos, Veena Akama-Makia, Lauren Young and Marta Fontanals-Simmons – perform with preternatural accuracy. Costumed identically, Huffman suggests – as Kane does – that they may all be fragments of the one fractured personality. Nevertheless, Stucker stands out as the deeply troubled protagonist in a searingly honest and frequently heart-rending performance.AtLinbury theatre, London, until 25 OctoberIn the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsOperaClassical musicSarah KaneRoyal Opera HouseTheatrePhilip VenablesMental healthreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Medieval romance overflowed with sexually active fairies’: the surprisingly long roots of romantasy | Fiction | The Guardian
description: Critics mock romantasy as raunchy trash – but this enchanting genre has its roots in medieval literature, and is much older, and wilder, than you might imagine
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Critics mock romantasy as raunchy trash – but this enchanting genre has its roots in medieval literature, and is much older, and wilder, than you might imagine
Content: La Belle Dame sans Merci by Frank Dicksee.Photograph: Artepics/AlamyView image in fullscreenLa Belle Dame sans Merci by Frank Dicksee.Photograph: Artepics/AlamyFiction‘Medieval romance overflowed with sexually active fairies’: the surprisingly long roots of romantasyCritics mock it as raunchy trash – but this enchanting genre is much older, and wilder, than you might imagineSarah CleggSun 18 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 07.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s a popular genre, filled with beautiful, human-sized fairies having sex with humans (often quite violent sex, but the people reading it seem to enjoy it). Word is that it’s badly written and unashamedly escapist – all golden, glittering palaces, wild adventure and, of course, gorgeous fairies. It’s certainly popular – plenty of the stories have been translated into numerous languages, spreading across continents. Serious commentators are sure it spells bad news: at best, it’s just a load of trash; at worst, it’s actively leading people astray. Most damningly of all, women produce and consume it. Welcome to the 12th century, where fairy romance is all the rage. Sound familiar?The romantasy that fills our shelves and bestseller lists – from Sarah J Maas’s A Court of Thorns and Roses to Callie Hart’s Quicksilver – is not a new genre, but part of a centuries-old heritage. You only need to look at the medieval predecessors of the modern romantasy novel to understand why it’s enjoyed by millions and why, even after hundreds of years, fairy romance has such power over us – and why there are still those who want to diminish and dismiss it.double quotation markThese stories were a place for women to explore their  desires, free from the idea that they should be chasteMedieval romances originated in the French courts of the late 1100s and were wildly popular, quickly spreading throughout Europe, not only from country to country, but also down the social scale, so that even farm workers and impoverished nuns knew the stories. They drew on tales of fairies in earlier myths, especially within Arthurian legends, and were adapted and expanded to be as thrilling as possible, providing people with the same escapism that romantasy does today. Read either the medieval or the modern tales and you’ll find glitter and blood and adventure, not to mention crystal palaces, glorious and perilous enchanted realms, terrifyingly handsome fairy knights, and queens who live in unearthly splendour. As one author of a 13th-century romance pointed out, speaking about the real world brings “grief and torment” – so why not turn to fairies?The wild sexual freedom of modern romantasy was there in medieval romance too, which overflowed with sexually active fairies, both male and female. There are detailed descriptions of fairy bodies, legs and breasts, and while the veil tends to be drawn over the act itself, both fairies and mortals are always “taking what they desire”, “making merry together”, “holding each other in their arms” and getting each other pregnant – even when either the mortal or fairy is married to someone else, or has only just met. And while there are fairy lovers who are kind, gentle and courteous, medieval audiences also thrilled to the idea of a brooding fairy shadow-daddy: the fairies often simmer with threat, never losing their darker edges even when the story ends with the lovers paired off happily. As with romantasy today, the medieval stories, by dint of being fictional, were a safe place to experiment with sex in a repressed society.This was even more important as medieval romance, like modern romantasy, was often written by women (such as the 12th-century poet Marie de France), and had a large female audience (something even Chaucer commented on) – so these stories were often a place for women to explore their desires, free from the idea that they should be chaste and subservient. (For reasons too complex to get into it right now, it was generally accepted that fairy sex didn’t quite count, so women who slept with fairies were still thought of as virgins.)Romantasy still provides this space now: although women may be more sexually liberated than they were in the middle ages, we’re often still uncomfortable with female desires. It’s certainly not a coincidence that many romantasy books today are targeted at teenage girls, who may not be able to talk openly about sex, and arepopular with women from more conservative backgrounds. And while the darker, more coercive side of fairy relationships (in both modernity and the middle ages) likely reflects the common fantasy of being overwhelmed, it also helps to alleviate any lingering guilt – after all, the less consensual the encounter, the less the mortal party can be blamed for it.These stories include a freedom from gender roles as well: in modern romantasy, women are the heroes, the drivers of the plots (the heroine of Saara El-Arifi’s Faebound is an elf military leader; in A Court of Thorns and Roses, a female hunter takes centre stage), while the male love interests, while apparently threatening, are normally intensely loving and vulnerable underneath. Medieval romances also flipped gender roles: you might think it’s a genre of knights rescuing damsels in distress, but more often than not it’s about powerful fairy queens rescuing distressed knights. Take the 12th-century narrative poem Lanval, for example, the story of a penniless and overlooked knight saved multiple times by his beloved fairy queen, that ends with her riding away to fairyland with him behind her on her horse.View image in fullscreenFans of A Court of Thorns and Roses characters at New York Comic Con 2023.Photograph: Roy Rochlin/Getty Images for ReedPopWhile the appeal of all this to the female writers and readers is clear, men happily indulged in these fantasies, too. Lanval was written by a woman but later translated by a man. Even in recent years, it’s been reported that 18% ofromantasy readers in the US are men, who enjoy the tales of male characters who love openly and unashamedly, and the strong, powerful women who love them back.Of course, medieval courts were as familiar with the criticisms of fairy romance as we are. Chaucer even wrote a romance parody – Sir Thopas – about a knight seeking an elf queen. Today, romantasy authors are accused ofcheapening popular cultureby journalists who often compose articles byflipping through the books looking for the naughty bits, just as Chaucer’s parody featured dirty jokes about elf sex. As a genre, it’s easy to mock, easy to dismiss the stories as “smut” and nothing more.But this alone can’t explain the ridicule – after all, there are plenty of modern fantasy books crammed with sex that get praised (take George RR Martin’s A Game of Thrones, for example). Instead, the vitriol seems to stem from the fact that it’s a genre enjoyed by women. In the 14th century we had Chaucer mockingly claiming that women held romances “in full great reverence” and clergymen complaining vociferously about the fact that women listen to romances “joyously and willingly”; today the genre is accused ofmaking women stupid, with critics arguing that sexy queensshouldn’t be discussed at literary festivals.The irony is that fairy romance gave us plenty of great literature, some still well known today (Shakespeare’s Titania and Oberon in A Midsummer Night’s Dream are straight out of romances, while Don Quixote is a romance parody, though heart­breakingly fairy-free); others have been largely forgotten (like one of my absolute favourites, the story of Guingamor). Fairy romance also gave us a huge number of long-forgotten fun romps (my secret heart belongs to the 13th-century Claris and Laris – more than 30,000 lines of pure fairy nonsense).Medieval romance faded from fashion in the late 1500s, after four glorious, fairy-filled centuries, in part because fairies themselves were changing – becoming miniature, flittering things that were less appealing as lovers (unless you had some fairly niche tastes). But while it is depressing that criticism has not moved on since the middle ages, it’s an utter joy to see female-centred fairy fantasies returning, hundreds of years after the first medieval romances were composed. So why not read some of the medieval romances, along with modern romantasy? You’d be participating in a centuries-old genre of freedom, imagination and joy, and I’m not sure you can ask for more than that.Perilous Enchantment: The True History of Faeries by Sarah Clegg is published by Granta. title: Twelfth Night review – Mathew Horne oozes arrogance as a brilliantly buttoned-up Malvolio | Stage | The Guardian
description: The yellow stockings are as funny as ever – yet a haunting, folky live score casts a dream-like uncertainty over Shakespeare’s tangled romance
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: The yellow stockings are as funny as ever – yet a haunting, folky live score casts a dream-like uncertainty over Shakespeare’s tangled romance
Content: Egg on his face … Mathew Horne as Malvolio in Twelfth Night.Photograph: Manuel HarlanView image in fullscreenEgg on his face … Mathew Horne as Malvolio in Twelfth Night.Photograph: Manuel HarlanStageReviewTwelfth Night review – Mathew Horne oozes arrogance as a brilliantly buttoned-up MalvolioCrucible, SheffieldThe yellow stockings are as funny as ever – yet a haunting, folky live score casts a dream-like uncertainty over Shakespeare’s tangled romanceMark FisherSun 18 Oct 2026 06.55 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 09.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou can pictureMathew Horne’s Malvolio as a guest on an early 1970s BBC Two arts show. With his buttoned-up collar, tight black suit and supercilious delivery, he oozes self-satisfaction. Trusting in his superior taste, he has the pose to prove it: stiff, studied and haughty.His fall from grace, tricked into dressing up as a yellow-stockinged morris dancer, is as funny as it ever is in Shakespeare’s comedy. It is the comeuppance of the arriviste. Brought down to size, he is no less indignant for it. In a smart, unyielding performance, he goes from pompous to bruised – and ever unrepentant.Where Malvolio is urbane, Genevieve Dawson’s live score has a folk-club earthiness. Played on clarinet, guitar and violin, it is haunting and whimsical, with a similarly 1970s vibe, like something fromThe Wicker Man.View image in fullscreenIrresistible … Justina Kehinde and Bebe Sanders in Twelfth Night.Photograph: Manuel HarlanCalling the musicians to order, David Birrell plays Feste less as the fool than the troubadour, one blessed with expensive dress and surprising wisdom, as well as a voice correctly identified by Sir Andrew Aguecheek (James Chetwood) as “mellifluous”. His plangent songs cast a note of uncertainty over the comic romance of Jamie Glover’s swift, concise and controlled production.Fielding much the same ensemble that appeared in last month’sKing Lear, with a blood-orange sun presiding over Amanda Stoodley’s stony circular set, Glover brings energy and clarity to the language. Going at a fair clip, the actors wind up the narrative coil in the first half, playing it straight and focused, in order to release the comedic spring in the second.In a play about status, appearance and falsity, the shipwrecked Viola (Bebe Sanders), going undercover as Cesario, is winningly plain-speaking as she inadvertently arouses the passions of Olivia (Justina Kehinde). She is too poetically lovely to resist. Switching from the magisterial to the lusty, Olivia has a tough time reconciling courtly expectations with her desires. For his part, Orsino (Fode Simbo) is plain deluded until Viola’s brother Sebastian (Harry Redding) shows up and he can see the beauty of what is right in front of him.There is merriment in the confusion and its untangling, but also a dream-like instability in a punchy, satisfying show.AtCrucible, Sheffield, until 31 OctoberExplore more on these topicsStageTheatreWilliam ShakespeareSheffield TheatresMathew HorneTwelfth NightreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It was like your worst nightmare’ – Ellie and Natasia on mums, music … and failing to make Bob Mortimer smile | Television | The Guardian
description: They spoofed mothers … and now they are mothers. The comedians talk about moving with the times for the return of their scalpel-sharp BBC sketch show
Author: Rachel Aroesti
Headline: They spoofed mothers … and now they are mothers. The comedians talk about moving with the times for the return of their scalpel-sharp BBC sketch show
Content: Shooting while heavily pregnant posed a few challenges … Natasia Demetriou and Ellie White in the new series of Ellie and Natasia.Photograph: BBC/Nit TV/Jack BarnesView image in fullscreenShooting while heavily pregnant posed a few challenges … Natasia Demetriou and Ellie White in the new series of Ellie and Natasia.Photograph: BBC/Nit TV/Jack BarnesTelevisionInterview‘It was like your worst nightmare’ – Ellie and Natasia on mums, music … and failing to make Bob Mortimer smileRachel AroestiThey spoofed mothers … and now they are mothers. The comedians talk about moving with the times for the return of their scalpel-sharp BBC sketch showSun 18 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBefore Ellie White and Natasia Demetriou were mothers, they were mums. In a skit from their 2019 sketch show pilot, the comedy duo play two straight-talking, hygiene-obsessed matriarchs in gilets and camel-toe-accentuating leggings who record lifestyle vlogs from a pristine kitchen while melodramatically referencing the pressures of motherhood. Ever since, the characters have become a core component of the pair’s comic universe, appearing repeatedly in the first proper series ofEllie & Natasia in 2022.Now the mums are back and moving with the times: reviewing various supermarket white breads – all reassuringly “sterile” options – as car-based food influencers for the show’s second outing. But behind the scenes there has been a bigger shift. The last time they wrote these sketches, White and Demetriou were childless; now they each have two kids.Coming up with material this time around was a different experience, says Demetriou. “I now feel quite a lot of empathy for these women,” says White. “Well, I always felt empathy – I do with all our characters – but I especially am now like: itisactually quite hard.” Even the housework obsession has become relatable. Nowadays, when Demetriou sees the brand of cleaning product she uses “on offer in Waitrose or Tesco, it is a good day for me. Get three just in case – put them in the cupboard.”Today, the pair are in their homes, squeezing in interview time while their youngest babies nap. “I may at some point be handed my child and then flap my breasts out for all and sundry to see,” warns White. They both found out they were pregnant again last September, a couple of weeks into the writing process. Three years had elapsed since series one – a gap they attribute to scheduling issues (both are successful actors; Demetriou is best known for 35-time Emmy-nominated vampire comedy What We Do in the Shadows, while White’s recent credits include Black Mirror, Wonka and Bridget Jones: Mad About the Boy) – but this new biological deadline meant “it was now or never,” says White. “We had to write it very quickly and film it very quickly so that we wouldn’t give birth when we were filming.” (White ended up going into labour halfway through the edit.)View image in fullscreen‘It was now or never” … Natasia Demetriou and Ellie White in their new series.Photograph: BBC/CPL ProductionsShooting while heavily pregnant did pose a few challenges. In some sketches, their stomachs are disguised with voluminous clothes or behind furniture (a pro for Demetriou: “I love acting sitting down, so if you can sit me behind a table I’m the happiest I’ve ever been”). In others, they are incorporated into the premise: the pregnant-again mums do a maternity fashion segment, while the duo’s other long-running sketch, Internet Nails, sees the titular shonky North Circular beauty salon diversify into pregnancy treatments as the owners prepare for motherhood themselves.Still, says White: “We didn’t want it to be ‘the pregnant show’.” Demetriou agrees: “We just wanted it to not be a distraction.” In fact, series two mostly feels like business as usual for the duo, who tend to combine offbeat yet scalpel-sharp observational humour (see: their “special moments with special people” strand, a kaleidoscopic showcase of modern smugness) with an overfamiliar rapport and penchant for dressing up as off-putting men and eccentric old women that is very French and Saunders, a programme Demetriou grew up “absolutely living for”.White, who is 37 and grew up in Oxford, and Demetriou, 42 from north London, met through the latter’s younger brother, Jamie, who had been in a comedy troupe with White at Bristol university. The women quickly bonded, but it wasn’t until a producer friend urged them to combine forces that they formed a double act. Demetriou had been doing a “Greek character who was trying to sell pizza to nightclubs” on London’s alternative comedy circuit, while White was performing as an extremely nervous beauty pageant contestant. When they merged the two on stage, it was “one of the most electric nights of my life”, says Demetriou.Those two characters became the Sexy American Girls, two vaguely eastern European women trying and failing – captivatingly – to embody turn-of-the-millennium celebrity glitz, who in turn evolved into the Internet Nails duo. In the latter, Demetriou plays the imperious Donna, who reels off hypnotic word salad about their services – they offer to style your baby with a “rocker chic lifestyle mixed with denim highlights and zip attachments, cowboy essentials mixed with international rap monger” aesthetic – in grainy VHS footage while her cousin Nikki (White) vibrates with shyness beside her.View image in fullscreenNikki (Ellie White) and Donna (Natasia Demetriou) in the new series.Photograph: Jack Barnes/BBC/Nit TVThis misguided pursuit of glamour is an extraordinarily rich seam for the pair, who bring a similar energy to Sophie and Katia, the pop stardom-chasing pals they play in Jamie Demetriou’s superb Channel 4 comedy Stath Lets Flats. Demetriou puts this through-line down to the fact that “me and Jamie and Ellie all have a very similar sense of humour and similar reference points. We grew up in the 1990s, when the coolest things were all American: Coca-Cola, Mickey Mouse.” That this kind of Americana now seems so lame and dated adds another layer of comedy. But there is also a nostalgia: it’s an opportunity for Demetriou to channel the “stupid teenage girl” she once was; “constantly doing an American accent, practising conversations in the mirror with boyfriends you don’t have”. White agrees. “It reminds me of being a 14-year-old and taking yourself” – and your creative enterprises – “really seriously. And just being like: well, wearereally good.”That said, the pair are no longer living out any pop star fantasies. Highlights of series one included riffs on morose Adele-style ballads, jet-setting rappers and – most pointedly – musicians who infantilise themselves to a disturbing degree (see: the song about being a dummy-sucking “sexy baby”). This time around, however, there aren’t any musical parodies. “For some reason, we just couldn’t come up with an idea,” says Demetriou. The demise of the monoculture was partly to blame. Sketch shows of yore, such as French and Saunders, were able to pastiche things “the whole country’s watched”, but nowadays there are far fewer shared references. As such, White feels culturally “trapped in 2011. Can we do a Little Mix parody? It’s like, well, they broke up years ago.”Instead of specific spoofs, White and Demetriou often make fun of broader movements in the zeitgeist, especially forms of social media content, from “day in the life” videos to visual podcasts to OnlyFans-esque livestreams. That these sketches could slip undetected into someone’s Instagram feed also means a higher chance of viral success. “You do sort of want these things to look like something you’d come across online,” says White. “We want it to almost be like, is that real?”Yet parodying social media tropes comes with its own drawbacks. “I know everyone says this at every time in history, but it does feel like everything’s been done because the internet is so vast,” says Demetriou. The pair were planning a sketch about two fashion content creators from the deep south until White discovered the “real” version online. “There’s a woman who stands there with these absolutely baffling outfits, being like: ‘You gotta wear a long scarf! It falls to the floor and it makes you feel incredible about yourself.’ And I was like, what is this sketch actually adding?”When it comes to added comic value, however, White and Demetriou tend to deliver the goods. A case in point: their appearance on the last season of Last One Laughing UK, the reality gameshow in which comedians compete to see who can remain straight-faced the longest. The duo did a cameo as intimacy coordinators (sporting, incidentally, mum-coded Essex accents and short layered hairdos), who were sent on set to attempt to crack the remaining contestants.‘We were ahead of our time!’: Charly Clive and Ellen Robertson AKA sketch duo Britney on their new TV fame and word-of-mouth hitsRead moreDespite an incredible five minutes of half-improvised comedy, which included discreetly asking Romesh Ranganathan if he knew what “s-e-x” was, they didn’t make anyone laugh. “I’m not kidding when I say it was the most nervous I’ve ever been in my entire life,” admits White. “It was sort of like your worst nightmare.” Not only were they in a room of comedy legends (Bob Mortimer, David Mitchell), but the silence they encountered felt like it was going against “all normal forms of British society”, says Demetriou. Usually we “nod politely and go ‘Brilliant!’” in response to even lacklustre attempts at humour. Here, “Not even a smile!”Speaking of politeness, we have now reached the end of the interview and those babies haven’t made a peep. “I’m slightly worried. He’s been sleeping for a really long time,” says White, bemusedly. At least we’ve been able to talk freely about their return to TV sketch comedy. It is, after all, a real treat to have White and Demetriou – and all the many mums they play – back on our screens again at last.Ellie & Natasia starts on 21 October on BBC Two and BBC iPlayerExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV comedyComedyinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: a very moreish drama about a hellish birthday party  | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Luke Evans and Sarah Solemani star in ITV’s top autumn thriller. Plus, an epic trip through Mongolia with Simon Reeve. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: Luke Evans and Sarah Solemani star in ITV’s top autumn thriller. Plus, an epic trip through Mongolia with Simon Reeve. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Murder on the dance floor? … The Party on ITV1.Photograph: ITV/World ProductionsView image in fullscreenMurder on the dance floor? … The Party on ITV1.Photograph: ITV/World ProductionsTV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: a very moreish drama about a hellish birthday partyLuke Evans and Sarah Solemani star in ITV’s top autumn thriller. Plus, an epic trip through Mongolia with Simon Reeve. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Hannah J Davies,Priya ElanandGraeme VirtueSun 18 Oct 2026 01.15 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 01.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Party9pm, ITV1So far, this Luke Evans and Sarah Solemani-starring drama has been ticking all the right boxes for an entertaining autumn thriller. Now that we know the true messed-up history behind journalist Martin (Evans) and Tory politician Ben’s (Tom Cullen) friendship, the nasty, destructive repercussions are about to unravel at the party – which is terrible for the guests, but very enjoyable for us. Concludes on Monday.Hollie RichardsonThe Reluctant Vampire6.40pm, BBC OneThis macabre comedy – adapted by the Gibbons brothers from Eric Morecambe’s books – can’t quite figure out whether it’s a Ghosts-a-like series for adults, or something better suited to CBBC. Still, it’s rather fun: this week, Val (Lenny Rush) hatches a plan to sneak out to a school prom.Hannah J DaviesKevin McCloud’s Classic Car Road Trips8pm, Channel 4Plummy-voiced smoothie McCloud parachutes out of Grand Designs to careen around Europe in a rotating circus wheel of classic cars. There’s something comfortingly old-fashioned about this genre of telly: posh boys playing at being petrolheads. This week’s old banger is a Citroen DS from the 60s which he takes to Cannes and Monaco.Priya ElanWilderness With Simon Reeve9pm, BBC TwoView image in fullscreenEagle-eyed … Wilderness With Simon Reeve on BBC Two.Photograph: BBC/The Garden/Rocio Lira SalasMongolia is the last leg on the adventurer’s tough tour, which he says is six times bigger than the UK but the world’s least populated country. He starts in the Gobi desert before searching for the snow leopard in the Margaz mountains and meeting an ancient community that hunts with eagles.HRApocalypse9pm, Channel 4The reality series where two tribes tussle to survive in a deserted US town reaches its penultimate instalment. With the factions at peace, posh influencer Freddie and psychologist Kiera find flirty common ground. But drama-loving chef Dean is keen to stir things up with something he calls “Operation Badger”.Graeme VirtueLater … With Jools Holland10pm, BBC TwoTwo greats are remembered at Ally Pally this week: Black Sabbath guitarist Tony Iommi chats about Ozzy Osbourne, as well as his first solo LP in 21 years; and Jools celebrates Amy Winehouse on the 20th anniversary of Back to Black. Music comes from rock duo Royal Blood, contemporary cellist Ayanna Witter-Johnson, drummer Moses Boyd and experimental popper Shygirl.HRLive sportPremier League Football: Leeds v Man United, 12.30pm, Sky Sports Main EventNottingham Forest play Arsenal at 4pm. On Mon, Tottenham play Coventry at 6.30pm.Women’s Super League Football: Man City v Brighton, 1.15pm, BBC TwoAt Joie Stadium.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘How do we welcome the stranger, with humanity or anger?’ The forgotten Germans who found refuge in Ireland | Theatre | The Guardian
description: A new play revisits the story of Ireland’s 18th-century German refugees, whose experience of prejudice and exclusion resonates with today’s debates over immigration
Author: John Kampfner
Headline: A new play revisits the story of Ireland’s 18th-century German refugees, whose experience of prejudice and exclusion resonates with today’s debates over immigration
Content: Sticking together … the cast of Refuge at Staatstheater Mainz, Germany.Photograph: Andreas EtterView image in fullscreenSticking together … the cast of Refuge at Staatstheater Mainz, Germany.Photograph: Andreas EtterTheatre‘How do we welcome the stranger, with humanity or anger?’ The forgotten Germans who found refuge in IrelandA new play revisits the story of Ireland’s 18th-century German refugees, whose experience of prejudice and exclusion resonates with today’s debates over immigrationJohn KampfnerSun 18 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the early 18th century, a few thousand Germans fled religious persecution and near starvation in their homeland and ended up in remote rural Irish villages. The Irish Palatines, as they were known, were poor, conservative homesteaders who couldn’t speak the language and were the object of suspicion and violence – precursors to the displaced Syrians or Afghans of the past decade.Their story is told in Refuge, a co-production between Staatstheater Mainz and the Irish company Fishamble. Part love story, part social commentary, it is performed by a mixed cast, mainly in English but with some German interludes.It focuses on a German couple, Hannah and Peter, who have lost one of their two sons through illness and are trying to make a go of it on farmland on the edge of a small town in Limerick. Their Protestantism and their reluctance to mix with the Irish add to a sense of peril.Peter is driven by another motive. He owes his plot of land to the manor’s (invisible) English squire, Thomas Southwell. The 1st Baron Southwell of Castle Matrix is keen to dilute the locals’ Catholicism and so provides the Germans with cheap rent in return for their obedience. Feudal landlord and dependent tenant find common cause.View image in fullscreenTrouble ensues … (from left) Mary Murray, Sabah Qalo, Hannah von Peinen and Holger Kraft.Photograph: Andreas EtterMore than 100 German families settled on Southwell’s lands, marrying almost exclusively among their own. Over a 40-year period, only seven marriages are recorded as taking place with someone outside the community. The “pure” German population was enlarged by 500 children.Hannah doesn’t think like the rest of them. She begs her husband to extend an olive branch to the locals, but he refuses. She defiantly does so, seeking friendship, and possibly romance, with a local farmer she haltingly calls MrIreland. Trouble ensues.The playwright, Deirdre Kinahan, says she seized the topic with alacrity: “Immigration – and our response to it – is one of the most crucial, yet divisive, issues of our age. How do we welcome the stranger, with humanity or anger?” She adds she knew instinctively that the forgotten story of the Palatines would speak to Ireland and Europe’s present predicament. This led her to include the tale of a contemporary young Afghan boy in the narrative.The production has played at the DublinTheatrefestival and concludes in Mainz, capital of the present-day Land of Rhineland-Palatinate, and the territory from which most of the original settlers came.
