Between the two destinations, it made a diversion to Berlin, at the behest of the Irish ambassador, Maeve Collins. “This story of a relatively unknown episode in Ireland’s history with Germany resonates with the experiences of contemporary audiences,” she says.It all began with an English queen. Early in 1709, hopes for a better life were raised when a “Golden Book” began circulating among the Palatinate’s population, bearing a picture of Queen Anne on the cover, promising a prosperous and easy life in America. The idea was to encourage hearty white Protestants to settle in the American territories without unduly depleting the population of England.This was hugely attractive to the Palatines, who had seen their land ravaged by a series of wars conducted by the expansionist zeal of France’s King Louis XIV.View image in fullscreen‘Our response to immigration is one of the most crucial issues of our age’ … (from left) Mary Murray, Sabah Qalo and Hannah von Peinen in Refuge.Photograph: Andreas EtterA group of these Germans petitioned the English queen, accepting her plan. But instead of an anticipated 500, more than 13,000 refugees set sail along the River Rhine to Rotterdam, before making the crossing on overcrowded small boats. One in five died on the precarious journey. The rest arrived destitute, and were housed in tents in and around London.Such were their numbers that the initially warm reception soon cooled. Wherever they went these Germans were subjected to suspicion, harassment and violence. By the end of November 1709, the first moves were made to deport them.The English government settled on other solutions. A certain number were allowed to go on to America. A smaller contingent of about 3,600 was relocated to underpopulated Ireland, to boost the Protestant stock.It would take several generations before the Palatines began to integrate. Some converted to Catholicism through intermarriage and assimilation, though the majority remained Protestant (either Methodists or members of the Church of Ireland).One of the best-known families was the Switzers, whose chain of department stores in Dublin, Cork, Limerick and Galway supplied luxury goods for a century and a half before the high-street institution was taken over and renamed.Like the Huguenots – who had fled to England, Holland and Germany two decades earlier, after Louis’s revocation of the Edict of Nantes – the Palatines are now hard to differentiate from the original population.For the play’s cast and crew, the “re-discovery” has been a moving experience. Holger Kraft, who plays gruff Peter, says he came to regard the piece less as Irish-German, more as pan-European, and with a universal message that “we all have to stick together”.Refuge is on atStaatstheater Mainz20 and 21 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreEuropeMigrationRefugeesSocial historyIrelandfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Ariadne/Dido and Aeneas review – English Touring Opera conjures two strikingly different mythological worlds | Opera | The Guardian
description: Jessica Cale’s soprano is diamond-bright in Elena Langer and Glyn Maxwell’s captivating monologue, while Rebecca Meltzer creates a compelling schoolyard staging of Purcell
Author: Erica Jeal
Headline: Jessica Cale’s soprano is diamond-bright in Elena Langer and Glyn Maxwell’s captivating monologue, while Rebecca Meltzer creates a compelling schoolyard staging of Purcell
Content: Powerful … Jessica Cale in Ariadne.Photograph: Richard Hubert SmithView image in fullscreenPowerful … Jessica Cale in Ariadne.Photograph: Richard Hubert SmithOperaReviewAriadne/Dido and Aeneas review – English Touring Opera conjures two strikingly different mythological worldsHackney Empire, LondonJessica Cale’s soprano is diamond-bright in Elena Langer and Glyn Maxwell’s captivating monologue, while Rebecca Meltzer creates a compelling schoolyard staging of PurcellErica JealSun 18 Oct 2026 08.43 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 10.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEnglish Touring Opera’s autumn season has a mythological theme – which, in practice, means operas about women getting left behind. Touring alongsideGluck’s Orpheus and Eurydiceis this compact double bill, pairing Dido and Aeneas withElena Langer’s Ariadne, a 20-minute scene for soprano setting words by Glyn Maxwell, which waspremiered by Almeida Operain 2002.Langer’s mini-opera is essentially a monologue, sung persuasively here by Jessica Cale, her powerful soprano diamond-bright. Anna Morrissey’s production, though, has six people on stage: abandonment feels like something active as well as passive. It begins with Theseus leaving, disentangling himself from both the sleeping Ariadne and the red thread that links them, spooling from a heap on the floor – it’s as if he got back from the labyrinth the night before. When Ariadne wakes he’s still there, pacing in the shadows or turning her bed on its rotating platform.View image in fullscreenCatwalk Coraline … Lydia Shariff and Isabelle Atkinson with members of the ensemble in Dido and Aeneas.Photograph: Richard Hubert SmithLanger writes, captivatingly, for four instruments: oboe, violin, viola and cello, playing without a conductor. They combine in high sonorities to reinforce the voice in a way that suggests the play of light on waves. As for Ariadne, she stands on that bed gazing out to sea as Joseph Hornsby’s lighting emulates the sun reflecting off water. The ending, in which Ariadne appears to sew the red thread through her skin, looked fiddly and took a bit too much of Cale’s concentration, even if the concept was good.We’re in a strikingly different world for Rebecca Meltzer’s staging of Dido and Aeneas. While Alex Berry’s set of black rocks and huge frosted glass panels could work for any operatic myth, Meltzer gives the action a playground dynamic (Purcell’s opera was performed early on by the pupils of a girls’ school). Everyone but Dido is in a stylised mishmash of charcoal blazers and pleated skirts, including the men; the look is somewhere between form room and a Thom Browne catwalk show. Lydia Shariff’s Sorceress has the body language of a year eight queen bee, while Isabelle Atkinson’s Belinda, Dido’s frenemy, puts on tiny sunglasses, reminiscent of Coraline’s black-button eyes, to become one of the witches. Dido is gaslit and bullied into her downfall, with the whole chorus, perhaps even Michael Lafferty’s velvet-voiced Aeneas, being complicit.In the pit, Alex Robinson directs the orchestra from the harpsichord with some imaginative touches that are slightly outweighed by steady tempos. Meltzer provides strong movement and it’s a compelling staging – but, despite Samantha Price’s expressive singing in the title role, something is missing. With Dido a victim from the start, there is little sense of a queen – and, by extension, her realm – being brought low by the collision between human passion and the whim of the gods. And that, surely, is the stuff myth is made of.AtBuxton Opera Houseon 24 October, thentouringuntil 21 NovemberExplore more on these topicsOperaClassical musicEnglish Touring OperareviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Shakespeare was a Black woman’: the playwright’s under-recognized connection to Black culture | Exhibitions | The Guardian
description: A new Washington DC exhibition examines how Toni Morrison, Maya Angelou and more used the Bard’s work to help tell their own stories
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A new Washington DC exhibition examines how Toni Morrison, Maya Angelou and more used the Bard’s work to help tell their own stories
Content: Kennedi Carter, Meech, 2020. Archival pigment print. On display as part of To Hear Her Speak: Black Women and Shakespeare.Photograph: Kennedi Carter/Courtesy of ROSEGALLERYView image in fullscreenKennedi Carter, Meech, 2020. Archival pigment print. On display as part of To Hear Her Speak: Black Women and Shakespeare.Photograph: Kennedi Carter/Courtesy of ROSEGALLERYExhibitions‘Shakespeare was a Black woman’: the playwright’s under-recognized connection to Black cultureA new Washington DC exhibition examines how Toni Morrison, Maya Angelou and more used the Bard’s work to help tell their own storiesKaitlyn McNabSun 18 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“William Shakespeare was a black woman.” In 1985,Maya Angelouspoke these words as part of a keynotespeechat a convention in Cedar Rapids, Iowa.There, she spoke of the role poetry played in her transition from muteness as a child and how she fantasized herself triumphantly delivering Portia’s speech fromWilliam Shakespeare’s The Merchant of Venice in front of her entire community at church. Though she never got the chance to perform that rendition, Angelou acknowledged her desire to deliver that rendition as part of a lifelong kinship with Shakespeare, a connection she continued to seek out throughout her life whenever she needed heartening or solace. In her eyes, Shakespeare wrote his emotionally desolateSonnet 29“for” her; how else could he have so aptly described the harsh realities of the Black feminine condition?“Of course he wrote it for me,” Angelou declared. “Of course, he was a Black woman. I understand that. Nobody else understands it, but I know thatWilliam Shakespearewas a Black woman.”Angelou would likely be proud to know thatmanyother Black women – including Dr Patricia Akhimie, the director of the Folger Institute at the Folger Shakespeare Library inWashington DC– do understand. The Bard may not have been a Black woman in the literal sense, but his resonance and centuries-long rapport with Black culture is one area of study that Akhimie has spent her career examining.View image in fullscreenInstallation view of To Hear Her Speak: Black Women and Shakespeare.Photograph: Tim Tiebout. Courtesy of Folger Shakespeare LibraryIn the Folger’s newest exhibitionTo Hear Her Speak: Black Women and Shakespeare, curated by Akhimie, more than 400 years of Black women’s engagement with Shakespeare is collectively explored for the first time, illuminating the ways in which Black women have claimed and reimagined the works of Shakespeare through scholarship and craft. “It’s a performance [and theater] history but it’s also an intellectual history about Black women as writers and artists pulling from Shakespeare to do new and amazing things,” said Akhimie, speaking in a warm conversation in early October.The history of Black women’s connection to Shakespeare is long, but not necessarily storied – To Hear Her Speak reveals just how far back that history goes and under how many layers it’s hidden. There’s likely no better place to begin such an investigation than at the Folger, home of the world’s largest Shakespeare collection.The exhibit, which is the product of more than two years of research, is both immersive and interactive. It contains nearly 100 items including photographs, playbills, books, diaries, illustrations and costumes; there are video displays of notable Black actresses throughout history performing Shakespeare; and within a set replica of playwright Lorraine Hansberry’s living room (based on a 1959Voguephoto spread of the writer in her New York City apartment), visitors can sit on the couch and watch a television set screening clips of Hansberry and other Black women discussing Shakespeare, or browse through the “library” of that same living room set, where there are shelves of books that serve as a mini-archive of writing related to Shakespeare and Black women’s artistic and intellectual endeavors.View image in fullscreenDr Patricia Akhimie.Photograph: Brittany Diliberto/Shoot AuthenticTo Hear Her Speakalso invites visitors to become participants through other immersive aspects such as writing activities throughout, itsexhibit-themed playlist(hitting shuffle will play tracks from Aretha Franklin, Lauryn Hill, Billie Holliday, SZA and more), and its audioguide narrated by Bridgerton star, Shakespearean actor and exhibition chairAdjoa Andoh. The exhibition was designed to be a three-dimensional, multi-sensory experience that can appeal to all ages and its full-color exhibit catalog, created by the To Hear Her Speak research team, was intentionally made for both print and digital consumption for wide accessibility.“It’s not about standing back and looking at something behind glass, but rather about what happens when inspiration strikes, and thenyoubecome the maker and the thinker and the dreamer,” said Akhimie.To Hear Her Speak also builds on new research showing that Black women were very much a presence in Shakespeare’s world while also illustrating how they were represented (and misrepresented) by storytellers of the era, across different mediums. Part of Akhimie’s aim was to challenge that erasure. “[The exhibition’s story] starts with debunking a longstanding myth, which is that the London where [Shakespeare] lived and wrote his plays and where they were first performed was not a diverse place, when it really was,” Akhimie said.View image in fullscreenLeontyne Price as Cleopatra in a 1966 publicity photograph for Antony and Cleopatra composed by Samuel Barber with libretto by Franco Zeffirelli.Photograph: Louis Melançon/Courtesy of Metropolitan Opera ArchiveAlong with her research team, Akhimie quickly discovered that artefacts and records of Black women’s engagement with Shakespeare disappeared around the 18th and 19th centuries. “The obvious reason for that is because that is the time period that coincides with the height of the transatlantic slave trade, when Black women’s experiences are not being documented and preserved, and their humanity is being obscured,” said Akhimie. This time period is arguably one of the most crucial for the exhibition’s narrative, as the 18th and 19th centuries are when the transatlantic slave trade is concurrent with Shakespeare’s rise as an international figure representative of British culture and culture at large.Through objects sourced from within the Folger’s collection and beyond, Akhimie and her research team managed to “tell a story about Shakespeare, sugar, and slavery”, filling the silences of history with materials such as a copy of Shakespeare’s First Folio purchased by a slave-owning British family, a record of the enslaved people forced to work on that family’s sugar plantation, a pair of sugar tongs and a tea caddy both emblazoned with Shakespeare’s bust, and a copybook created by Phillis Wheatley, the formerly enslaved first Black American poet.View image in fullscreenEngraving of Phillis Wheatley from frontispiece of Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral, 1773.Photograph: Scipio Moorhead/Library of CongressTo Hear Her Speak rallies the works of some of the most influential Black female luminaries in history in addition to Wheatley, Hansberry and Angelou, likeToni Morrison’s handwritten notes on her Shakespearean play Desdemona. The exhibition, which is named after Shakespeare’s Sonnet 130 (long speculated to be written about a Black woman by historians and literary scholars), amplifies the voices of prominent Black women who have wielded and wrought the words of Shakespeare in their careers to assert their own humanity, creativity and individual power.Akhimie considers Black women’s consistent return to Shakespeare strategic, describing him as “a reliable partner” for Black female artists of any era to turn to for “inspiration and allyship”; as Angelou noted in her 1985 speech, Shakespeare is one of the most effective conduits for Black female self-expression.“Shakespeare has cultural currency. Shakespeare is a voice that people listen to,” said Akhimie. “Time and again, over centuries, Black women who are themselves artists, thinkers, or educators know that linking yourself to Shakespeare, pulling Shakespeare in, referencing Shakespeare is a way to grab a hold of listeners in a world in which, often, your voice is not heard and is systematically marginalized. Shakespeare has power, and that has been true for all of [the] 400-year period that the exhibition covers.”“[To Hear Her Speak] is not just a chance to share Black women’s voices,” she continues. “It’s also a chance to call people in and say: what can Shakespeare do for you? What will you do with this material to make new work, new ideas, tell new stories, and tell your story?”To Hear Her Speak: Black Women and Shakespeareis on view at Folger Shakespeare Library in Washington DC, until 2 May 2027Explore more on these topicsExhibitionsArtTheatreUS theaterWilliam ShakespeareMaya AngelouToni MorrisonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘A key artist in her own right’: wallpaper and fabrics designer emerges from William Morris’s shadow | Design | The Guardian
description: Creativity and influence of Morris & Co designer Kate Faulkner to be detailed in Cambridge exhibition
Author: Donna Ferguson
Headline: Creativity and influence of Morris & Co designer Kate Faulkner to be detailed in Cambridge exhibition
Content: A drawing of Artemis for a design embroidered by Faulkner for William Morris’s home, Red House.Photograph: Bridgeman ImagesView image in fullscreenA drawing of Artemis for a design embroidered by Faulkner for William Morris’s home, Red House.Photograph: Bridgeman ImagesDesign‘A key artist in her own right’: wallpaper and fabrics designer emerges from William Morris’s shadowCreativity and influence of Morris & Co designer Kate Faulkner to be detailed in Cambridge exhibitionDonna FergusonSun 18 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 08.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor more than a century, she has been little more than a footnote in William Morris’s story, her work mistaken for his, her contribution to British decorative art largely overlooked.Yet, in her lifetime, Kate Faulkner was a pioneer: the first person after Morris to design wallpapers and fabrics for Morris & Co, and one of only four designers he ever trusted to do so. Several of the patterns she designed under her name for the company in the 1870s and 1880s are still sold today.Now,an exhibitionat the Fitzwilliam Museum in Cambridge is seeking to restore Faulkner to her rightful place in art history.A Call to Art: William Morris and the pre-Raphaelites is the first exhibition to celebrate Faulkner and her work as a designer, maker and workshop supervisor at Morris & Co.It will put on public display, for the first time, a monumental 6.3 metre-wide oak and silvered-gesso altarpiece she was commissioned to make for Morris & Co in 1886, alongside her textile designs and wallpaper patterns which helped to make William Morris a household name.View image in fullscreenHighlights include Faulkner’s tile depicting Penelope, made around 1865.Photograph: Michael Jones/The Fitzwilliam Museum, Image LibraryHighlights include her tile depicting Penelope, the heroine of Greek mythology, which is based on a design by Edward Burne-Jones, and some of her painted ceramics, including decorative plates that were sold in the Morris & Co shop.“Kate Faulkner was not simply working in William Morris’s shadow – she was a key artist in her own right,” said Karen Livingstone, senior curatorial adviser to the exhibition, which opens on 23 October. “Her skill and creative contribution were fundamental to Morris & Co, and this exhibition and its new research reveal just how central her artistic voice was to the commercial success of William Morris.”Her1879 Mallow wallpaper designisstill sold by Morris & Co.Other wallpaper manufacturers bought her designs and she earned an international reputation for her work, but her legacy has been overshadowed by Morris’s since she died in 1898.Livingstone is appealing for help from the public to trace the descendants of Faulkner’s sister, Lucy Orrinsmith, whose granddaughter, Lesley Janet Hitch (nee Simmons), died in 1995. She hopes this will uncover a photograph or portrait of Faulkner, as none is known to exist. “I’ve tried really hard to trace her family and to find an image of her, and I have drawn a blank at every turn,” said Livingstone, the author of Women Pioneers of the Arts and Crafts Movement. “I would love to know where her family are so her legacy could be more expanded and revealed.”View image in fullscreenFaulkner would have been part of Morris’s inner circle at Red House, his Arts and Crafts villa in Bexleyheath.Photograph: Bildarchiv Monheim GmbH/AlamyThe overall aim of the exhibition, which runs until 3 May 2027, is to re-examine Morris and his inner circle – including the artists and designers Edward Burne-Jones, Dante Gabriel Rossetti, Elizabeth Siddal and May Morris, the daughter of William and his wife, Jane.One of Morris & Co’s most successful areas of production was embroidery, which wasmanaged by Jane Morrisand her sister, Elizabeth Burden, before May took over in 1885.Faulkner embroidered figurative panels to William Morris’s designs and helped with the design and production of carpets, as well as cutting woodblocks for engravings and painting tiles and designing patterns for textiles and wallpapers.New research by Livingstone has revealed that a design by Morris depicting the Greek goddess Artemis was embroidered by Faulkner for Red House, Morris’s Arts and Crafts villa in Bexleyheath, south-eastLondon, where the idea for Morris & Co was born in 1861.View image in fullscreenCarnation, Faulkner’s first pattern for Morris & Co to be registered under her name.Photograph: Paul Tucker/Pauul TuckerThe Artemis embroidery places Faulkner at Red House at the very moment when Morris and his circle were inspired to create their own interiors company and start making products for sale. “It’s reinstating her in a story which is usually told about the men in that circle … It was during the process of making these embroideries and furnishing Red House that they decided to set up Morris & Co,” Livingstone said.Faulkner, who was a socialist like Morris, would visit the house regularly and spend weekends there. “They [the women in Morris’s circle] used to sit around and embroider together,” Livingstone added.She thinks it is highly likely that Faulkner, whose brother Charles was one of Morris’s co-founders, participated in the discussions about Morris & Co that were happening in Red House at that time. “She was there – the women were all there. They can’t possibly not have been part of the conversation.”Faulkner’s role in making the Artemis embroidery – one of a series of 12 panels planned for the Red House dining room – was previously unknown. While the embroidery itself is now lost, a drawing of the embroidery design will be on display within the exhibition, along with three surviving panels embroidered by Burden.By 1862, Faulkner and her sister were producing embroideries for the firm to sell. But it would take another 13 years for one of her patterns for Morris & Co, Carnation, to be registered under her name in 1875.“I suspect there’s lots more out there that just hasn’t been found or identified,” Livingstone said. “For sure, there’s work she created that is still being attributed to Morris.”Explore more on these topicsDesignWilliam MorrisLondonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘We hang on to summer a little longer here’: five of the best places for autumn sun in Europe and Turkey | Europe holidays | The Guardian
description: If you’re looking for a last blast of summer, these sunny resorts offer quiet beaches but enough life to stave off the end-of-season blues
Author: Annabelle Thorpe
Headline: If you’re looking for a last blast of summer, these sunny resorts offer quiet beaches but enough life to stave off the end-of-season blues
Content: Kalkan, where October sunsets are particularly lovely.Photograph: Stephen Hughes/AlamyView image in fullscreenKalkan, where October sunsets are particularly lovely.Photograph: Stephen Hughes/AlamyEurope holidays‘We hang on to summer a little longer here’: five of the best places for autumn sun in Europe and TurkeyIf you’re looking for a last blast of summer, these sunny resorts offer quiet beaches but enough life to stave off the end-of-season bluesLiz Boulter, Carolyn Boyd, Daniel James Clarke, Lois Pryce andAnnabelle ThorpeSun 18 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKalkan,TurkeyA Kalkan sunset is always a beautiful thing – the horseshoe-shaped bay deepening to azure blue against an apricot-rose sky – but, in October, when the light is low and the sun drops early, it’s almost transcendentally lovely. In some Turkish resorts, you’d be sitting watching it surrounded by quiet streets, half-empty bars and that melancholic sense that another season is over. In Kalkan, it still feels like summer; the harbourfront restaurants throng with visitors, the day gulets (wooden boats) still putter in and out of the bay and you don’t have to wait an hour to get a taxi back to your villa.For me, the best thing about an autumn break – besides the sunsets – is that I can visit some of my favourite places that just get overrun in summer. The glittering beach at Kaputas, sandwiched into a triangular gap on the mountainous Kalkan-Kas road, has become a victim of Instagram; from May to September, it’s impossible to get near. In October, the waters are still warm and the beach – although still busy – has plenty of space for a dip and a laze.double quotation markBecause the season’s end is in sight, the whole place swings with an end-of-term vibeAbout 20 minutes’ drive inland, the mountain village of Bezirgan, which used to serve as a summer retreat for wealthier Kalkan residents, settles back into complete peace in autumn, save for the woodpeckers battering away at the bark of the almond trees and the squirrels skittering through the leaves. TheLycian Wayweaves through the village, past Ottoman-era grain stores, with the lush gardens of the Pirha Köy Sofrası restaurant a great bet for a plate of traditionalmanti(dumplings in yoghurt) orkofte(meatballs), before setting off for a hike (they do fantastic breakfasts too).Back in Kalkan, it’s always cocktail hour somewhere; often on a roof terrace, with a jazz soundtrack floating out above the streets of the Old Town. This year, theFountain Terrace Cocktail Barhas been popular, but I still love sitting in theMerkez Cafe, a Kalkan institution since the early 1990s, smack-bang in the heart of the village and a prime spot for people-watching when the evening begins.View image in fullscreenThe glittering beach at Kaputas near Kalkan.Photograph: daphnusia/AlamyAnd because the season’s end is in sight, all the restaurant owners and waiters are cheerfully giddy, and the whole place swings with an end-of-term vibe. Sitting at theBlue Marlin(tucked away beneath the Pirat hotel) with a cold Efes beer and a selection of the town’s best meze, the only thing that makes me rueful is that it will be several months before I’ll be back here again.White Househas doubles from£120 B&BAnnabelle ThorpeAgua Amarga, SpainView image in fullscreenThe village of Agua Amarga, where Sexy Beast was filmed.Photograph: Juana Mari Moya/Getty ImagesAlong Spain’s wild Costa de Almería are a handful of exquisite little towns and villages. San José is probably the best known, put on the map by its most famous inhabitant, the late Joe Strummer, but 25 miles east is the real jewel of the Almería coast. Agua Amarga is a typical Andalucían fishing village moonlighting as a stylish low-key holiday destination, perfect for late-season sun-seekers.Its location, on a crescent bay, makes for spectacular sunrises and sunsets over the arid headlands that bookend the 500-metre-long beach. In the narrow, whitewashed streets, a lush palm grove and splashes of pink bougainvillaea remind you that north Africa is just a short hop across the Mediterranean. In the summer, Agua Amarga’s unspoilt sands and turquoise waters attract plenty of visitors, but the vibe remains relaxed. There are a handful of restaurants and bars around the main plaza, and a few eateries on the beach, includingLos Tarahis, a traditionalchiringuito(beach bar) where you can enjoy dishes such asarroz negro con bogavante(black rice with lobster) with your toes in the sand. In winter, the town goes into hibernation, but in autumn the sun and sea are still warm and the bars and restaurants are still open for business.double quotation markAt this time of year, the sun and sea are still warm and the bars and restaurants are openAgua Amarga is not the place to go to party. It’s a world away from the overdeveloped costas to the west and north, but it is the perfect base to immerse yourself in nature. Hiking trails lead from the village over the cliffs to a string of isolated coves and the ruins of 18th-century forts dotted along the headlands. And if you tire of following the shimmering sea, you can strike out inland to explore theCabo de Gata nature reserve, with its windingramblas(dry riverbeds), prickly pears and eerie abandoned goldmines.View image in fullscreenThe sea by Agua Amarga is still warm in autumn.Photograph: Dronie_Spain/ShutterstockThis corner of Spain is famous for its movie locations, notably Sergio Leone’s spaghetti westerns and Hollywood blockbusters including Lawrence of Arabia and Conan the Barbarian. For UK cinephiles, British gangster classic Sexy Beast was filmed in Agua Amarga, and Ray Winstone’s swanky villa is available as a holiday rental (minus the boulder in the swimming pool).The name Agua Amarga translates as “bitter water”, dating back to the 19th century and the contamination caused by mining iron ore. Those days are gone, and now Agua Amarga couldn’t be sweeter.Hotel Las Calashasdoublesfrom £80Lois PryceCascais,PortugalView image in fullscreenCascais was once the summer retreat of Europe’s nobility.Photograph: Chunyip Wong/Getty ImagesAs many of Portugal’s southern resorts prepare to hibernate for winter, Cascais’s green-fingered municipal workers set to work on the town’s well-manicured flower beds, ensuring a seamless seasonal rotation. Violas, primroses and cyclamen furnish pops of purple, magenta and orange below tall palms lining a promenade punctuated with palatial homes and pockets of golden sand. Even in late autumn, the semi-tropical scene banishes the blues.My happy place when the off-season rolls around, Cascais has enough energy and atmosphere to entertain, and is arguably at its finest after summer’s beach throngs and Lisbon day trippers (Cascais lies 20 miles west of the city, a 30- to 40-minute train ride from Cais do Sodré station) have receded.double quotation markCascais’s main off-season pull is for those who like to be active outdoorsOnce the summer retreat of Europe’s nobility, Cascais is now Portugal’s year-round crowd-pleaser – and come autumn, accommodation prices are far less aristocratic. There are stately manors and spa hotels aplenty, but my pick isCasa Vela, a surprisingly spacious sidestreet bolthole. Its sauna, shrouded in tropical gardens imported by the owner and his grandfather, brings joy even on the chilliest days. And if rains do come, there are a clutch of cultural attractions in the town, including the pyramid-shaped, terracotta-huedCasa das Histórias Paula Rego, featuring works by the acclaimed Portuguese-British artist.Still, with about 300 sunny days a year, Cascais’s main off-season pull is for those who like to be active outdoors. Blue-sky mornings see waterfront joggers pass pretty squares carpeted in black-and-whitecalçada portuguesa(the distinctive patterned pavement mosaics), the hulking 15th-centurycitadel, and amustard-hued palaceoverlooking a cove. Swimming is bracing, but kayaking on the calmer waters where the Tagus River meets the Atlantic more than compensates.View image in fullscreenCasa das Histórias Paula Rego in Cascais.Photograph: Witold Skrypczak/AlamyBetter still, hire a bicycle and trace the craggy coastline, which grows wilder as it arches north-west, with sheer cliffs appearing in the distant haze. Praia do Guincho is the star, a glorious dune-backed beach battered by winds that keep surfers of all stripes well sated.A half-hour bus ride from Cascais, Sintra’s iconic palaces andquintasunfurl across the forest-clad mountains. Summer in the town will test your patience. But with fewer crowds in the off-season, the essence of this former elite enclave and trove of European Romantic architecture returns. Hiking the hewn stairs to theMoorish Castlein thick fog is magical, while the vibrant burgundy-and-yellow facade of the fairytaleNational Palace of Penabrightens the greyest of days.As the nights start to draw in, you can chase the dwindling sunlight by heading to windswept Cabo da Roca at Portugal’s far western tip. Not only are the sunsets here spectacular, for much of autumn and winter they are the latest in mainland Europe – a sweetener for the shorter days.Casa Velahasdoubles from €79 room-onlyDaniel James Clarkeskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSenigallia,ItalyView image in fullscreenSenigallia and its Velvet Beach.Photograph: Michal Szymel/AlamyVelvet Beach (Spiaggia di Velluto) is the alluring name for the miles of fine sand that fringe the town of Senigallia, in Italy’s Marche region. But from May to September, that golden loveliness all but disappears under the umbrellas and sunbeds of beach clubs.Italians love the place, some returning every summer for decades, but in high season it is probably best left to them. However, Senigallia has an allure beyond the beach that can be enjoyed year-round – and autumn is particularly rewarding.double quotation markIt’s hard to eat badly here, but fish fans will relish the exquisitely prepared raw stuff at Cuoco di BordoIt’s known in Italy as the “five-star town” for the number of Michelin stars its top two restaurants hold between them. AtUliassi(three stars) andMadonnina del Pescatore(two), ambitious locally born chefs have kept one another on their toes for decades, and their fame has encouraged other restaurateurs to up their game.If Uliassi’s famous €280 tasting menu is beyond your budget, Senigallia has plenty of innovative, quality places that are more affordable. It’s hard to eat badly here, but fish fans will relish the exquisitely prepared raw stuff atCuocodi Bordo(two courses from €34) on the seafront. The more rusticRimante(two courses from €27), in the cobbled centre, offers super-friendly service, great pasta and a roast goose speciality. For pizza nights, nearbyO’sarracinhas superlative margheritas (€8.50) and tasty ragù-filledarancinito start.View image in fullscreenSenigallia is renowned for seafood restaurants such as the Michelin-starred Madonnina del Pescatore.Photograph: Brambilla SerraniPizza al formaggio, by contrast, isn’t pizza at all, but a sort of savoury panettone, flavoured with parmesan and pecorino cheese, maybe with chunks oozing out of a warm slice. It’s usually an Easter treat, but bakeryPandefràmakes it from October until May. Autumn in Senigallia also brings amazing fresh produce (chestnuts, persimmons, grapes and pomegranates; pumpkins, greens and radicchio) to chefs and market stalls.And, of course, it brings the olive harvest, with new oil to taste in local delis and at theFesta dell’Olio Nuovo(6-10 November) in Scapezzano, three miles inland, reached by a pleasant hour’s walk up the quiet Strada di Fontenuovo (there’s a bus back).With so much eating, you do need to work up an appetite. Hiking theHeron Trailalong the Misa River will help, and offers downy oaks in their autumn finery, but the best walk for me starts at the splendidRotonda a Maregallery on its 1930s pier, heads inland on quiet lanes to Gabriella and Montignano villages, then descends to the coast for a sunset stroll back along that – now peaceful – Velvet Beach.Al Foro Annonariohasdoublesfrom €80 B&BLiz BoulterSaint-Jean-de-Luz,FranceView image in fullscreenSaint-Jean-de-Luz holds on to the warmth of summer a little longer than the rest of France’s west coast.Photograph: Mehdi33300/AlamyTucked away in the corner of France just before the Basque coast runs into Spain, Saint-Jean-de-Luz hangs on to the warmth of summer a little longer than the rest of the west coast. Its enticing crescent beach is sheltered by two headlands and so, as the Atlantic crashes against the rest of the coast, you can dig your toes into the golden sand as the sea gently laps the shore and truly feel as if you’ve escaped the world.The town makes for a great introduction to the French Basque Country, with its traditional red or green timber-framed architecture, adorned in many cases with strings of the localespelettechilli pepper – its gentle heat infuses many of the local dishes. Pick up a pot at the local market hall, which is a good place to find other hero products of the local cuisine, such as Ossau-Iraty cheese and black cherry jam.double quotation markAs you cruise past the Flysch cliffs, you might spot a few silver flying fish jumping out of the steely blue AtlanticElsewhere, the patisserieMaison Adamis the place to find the local almond macaron called theparegabea(it means incomparable in Basque), which was first made in 1660 to celebrate the marriage of King Louis XIV and Marie-Thérèse of Spain. Their nuptials took place just round the corner at the Saint-Jean-de-Baptiste church – half-built at the time – which has an extraordinarily detailed gilt altarpiece that was installed in 1669, as well as a three-tiered gallery for the congregation. Meanwhile, a votive ship hanging from the ceiling is a nod to the town’s close relationship to the sea, with small fishing boats departing the neat harbour to fish for hake, a local speciality.You can venture out on to the seas too, with aboat tripon the small cruiser Nivelle V (€20), which goes along the coast towards Spain, first passing the 17th-century cylindrical fort at Socoa and its sea wall that juts across the bay. As you cruise past the Flysch cliffs, which look like layers of diagonally stacked cardboard, you might spot a few silver flying fish jumping out of the steely blue Atlantic.View image in fullscreenThe neighbouring village of Ciboure.Photograph: Andia/AlamyOn arrival back at port, take the short walk across the bridge that spans the River Nivelle to the neighbouring village of Ciboure. It’s a warren of red and green Basque townhouses that overlook narrow streets winding up the hill. Between them sits the restaurantChez Mattin(mains from €28), a local institution, where chef Michel Niquet serves his signature dish, ttorro, a fish stew that was invented by his grandfather.TheMadisonhas doubles from€125. For more information, seesaint-jean-de-luz.comCarolyn BoydAll accommodation prices are for October/November and were correct at the time of publicationExplore more on these topicsEurope holidaysPortugal holidaysItaly holidaysSpain holidaysFrance holidaysBeach holidaysTurkey holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to make the perfect poires belle Hélène – recipe | Food | The Guardian
description: Cool, juicy pears, cold ice-cream, hot chocolate sauce and a crunchy garnish – the perfect pudding
Author: Felicity Cloake
Headline: Cool, juicy pears, cold ice-cream, hot chocolate sauce and a crunchy garnish – the perfect pudding
Content: Felicity Cloake’s perfect poires belle Hélène.Photograph: Robert Billington/ood Styling: Flossy McAslan.View image in fullscreenFelicity Cloake’s perfect poires belle Hélène.Photograph: Robert Billington/ood Styling: Flossy McAslan.How to cook the perfect ...FoodHow to make the perfect poires belle Hélène – recipeCool, juicy pears, cold ice-cream, hot chocolate sauce and a crunchy garnish – the perfect puddingFelicity CloakeSun 18 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 08.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s always slightly embarrassing to realise that you’ve missed a pop culture reference, even if it’s 162 years old, so I won’t dwell on the fact that until last week I was unaware of the existence of Offenbach’s 1864 operetta about Helen of Troy,La Belle Hélène, after which today’s dish is named. In any case,the great French chef Escoffierwas so moved by it, or perhaps by its popularity among Parisian diners, to name this simple dessert of vanilla-scented poached pears topped with hot chocolate sauce after the work’s heroine, played by the comely Hortense Schneider.Though other homages (he includes no fewer than five dishes with that name in his1907 Guide Culinaire, none of which involve pears) may, like the music, have faded from public consciousness, this particular pairing, if you’ll forgive the pun, has stood the test of time. As Nigel Slater observes in Tender: Volume 2, “The marriage of pears and chocolate is extraordinary. It is as if they were made for each other.” This, I think, is the duo at its “most sumptuous”.The pearsView image in fullscreenMax Rocha poire belle helene: an ’intensely flavoured but thin sauce’. Thumbnail pics by Felicity.Everyone is agreed that, for best results when poaching pears, you need them to be firm. As Nigella Lawson writes in How to Eat, “In fact, it is a positive advantage to use what would in other circumstances seem rebarbatively firm fruit” (extra points if, unlike my spellcheck, you were already familiar with the word “rebarbative”). Squidgy fruit of the kind that runs down your chin will fall apart during cooking;turn those into cake instead.As far as I can tell from the recipe included inFrançois-Régis Gaudry’s magisterial Let’s Eat France, which claims to have respected “the proportions of the era”, Escoffier poached the fruit in a vanilla syrup, a tradition most versions honour. However,Max Rocha of Cafe Ceciliain London eschews the pod in favour of citrus zest (lemon and orange), rosemary and a stick of cinnamon. (Also, to be fair, Rocha, likeSlater, does not claim to be making poires belle helene, but simply poached pears with chocolate sauce). Very nice it is, too, and I would encourage you to experiment, but, out of deference to the dessert’s creator, I’ve stuck with vanilla.Under-ripe pears tend to be willing recipients of help in the flavour department, so for once I’m in favour of dialling up the sugar, because the pears need to be robust enough to stand up to the intense chocolate sauce. I’ll also be adding the juice of a whole lemon, as Jane Grigson and chefAlain Benech, whose recipe is featured on Delia Smith’s website, suggests. I’ll include the finely grated zest, too; the acidity not only helps the fruit retain its colour, but brings out its perfume as well.View image in fullscreenFlaked almonds: Alain Benech’s poire belle helene.Though everyone uses a slightly different cooking method, from a brief boil (Grigson’s Fruit Book) to keeping the liquid at a very gentle heat throughout (Slater), none proves disastrous; what is key is to keep the pears submerged so they cook evenly (Benech recommends topping them with a cartouche of baking paper, which sounds a faff but really isn’t, especially compared with constantly turning the fruit in the pan once they bob up to the top) and to leave them ever so slightly harder than you’d like them, because they will continue to cook as they cool in the syrup.Grigson and Slater both halve their pears, which, while it does speed up the cooking time, looks less fun on the plate, which feels a shame – this is definitely a show-off sort of dessert. Do, as Benech suggests, remove a little of the stringy core from the base, however – it’ll make them a lot easier to eat with a modicum of decorum.The sauceWithout sauce, the dish would just be fruit, which, as I never tire of reminding my mum, is not a proper pudding. That said, Grigson notes that this is a dish that “has had much criticism from some food writers, for the combination of delicate pears with chocolate sauce … the secret lies in taking very little sauce”. She has a point: chocolate, like tomato ketchup, is a flavour bully – let it in, and it tends to take over – so I would suggest moderating things to an artful drip, or allowing your guests to serve themselves at the table. After all, if they overdo it, they only have themselves to blame.View image in fullscreen‘Box of tricks’: Jane Grigson poire belle helene.Rocha is the only one to use cocoa powder and water rather than melted chocolate and dairy, which results in an intensely flavoured but thin sauce. Initially, I’m quite taken by the idea; it feels a nice counterpoint to any creamy things you might be serving with your pears, but it does mean serving the pear in a puddle of chocolate sauce, rather than allowing it to drip glossily down from its stem (a sentence I have rewritten more than once), so, in the end, I’ve stuck with the traditional melted chocolate. Grigson and Slater both add black coffee, which feels like overcomplicating things (even though it goes well with chocolate), as does Benech’s dash of poire william and the kirschwasser that’s in Grigson’s box of tricks. By all means pop them in, if you like, especially if your sauce needs thinning down a little, but a dash of vanilla extract and a pinch of salt should be quite sufficient.Gaudry makes the sauce with milk, Grigson and Slater whipping cream, and Lawson and Benech double cream. The fattier the dairy, of course, the richer and thicker the result – and double cream tends to be easier to get hold of than whipping, which is another point in its favour – but some double cream is so lusciously dense that it forms an unattractive brown lump, rather than the silky stream I’m after. Give it a good stir first, and loosen the finished sauce with a little milk or water, or even liqueur, if necessary. For extra shine, stir in a knob of butter or a spoonful of golden syrup at the end, but with this proportion of chocolate to dairy, you probably won’t need any help in that department. Do serve the sauce warm and the pears cold, though, because much of this dish’s charm lies in contrast.The dairyView image in fullscreen‘Au naturel’: Nigel Slater’s poire belle helene.Rocha and Slater, classy chaps that they are, serve the pear and chocolate sauceau naturel, but it’s hard to argue that this isn’t improved by an elegant scoop of vanilla ice-cream (what isn’t?) or a billowing spoonful of Benech’s creme chantilly (cream whipped with sugar and vanilla seeds). Whichever you go for, however, don’t overlook one final contrast. A sprinkling of flaked almonds (Benech) or crystallised violets (Grigson) leaves you with cold ice-cream or cream, cool, juicy pears, hot chocolate sauce and a crunchy garnish. Perfection in a dish.Perfect poires belle helenePrep20 minCook30 minServes44 firm, not-too-ripe pears1 unwaxed lemon1 vanilla pod200g white sugar, or golden sugar¼ tsp salt(optional)1 tbsp flaked almonds, toasted, or crystallised violets, to serve4 scoopsvanilla ice-cream, or 150ml double or whipping cream, whipped with 1 tbsp caster or icing sugar and ¼ tsp vanilla extract or paste, or the seeds from ½ vanilla pod, to serveFor the sauce150g dark chocolate200ml double or whipping creamPinch of saltMilk, or water or liqueur of your choice (optional)Prepare the pears some hours before you’re intending to eat. Find a wide, fairly deep pan and cut out a circle of greaseproof paper of the same diameter. Fold this in half then in quarters, then in eighths, and cut a small hole in the centre to let out steam.View image in fullscreenAdd the lemon zest and juice to the pan. Split open the vanilla pod, scrape out the vanilla seeds and add these to the pan with the empty pod, sugar and salt, if using. Pour in a litre of water and bring to a simmer, stirring to dissolve the sugar.Peel the pears, leaving the stalks intact, and cut a small slice off their bottoms so they’ll stand up straight later. Scoop out some of the woody core from the bases, then lay down the pears in the panView image in fullscreenUnfold the paper cartouche, use to cover the fruit, then leave the pears to simmer gently for about 25 minutes, until cooked through but not too soft. Take off the heat, leave to cool in the poaching liquid, then put in the fridge to chill.View image in fullscreenWhen you’re ready to eat, chop up the chocolate. Put the cream in a small pan, heat to a bare simmer, then take off the heat and add the chocolate. Leave to sit for a couple of minutes, then stir until melted and smooth.View image in fullscreenAdd the salt, if using, and if the chocolate mix feels too thick to pour easily, stir in a dash of milk, water or liqueur, too.View image in fullscreenTo assemble, drain the pears and pat them dry with kitchen paper (the poaching liquid makes a lovely drink, or reduce it to make a syrup to drizzle over future desserts). Divide the fruit between shallow bowls, standing them upright.Either pour a spoonful of chocolate sauce down one flank, or serve the sauce separately for everyone to pour their own. Add a spoonful of ice-cream or chantilly cream, scatter with toasted nuts or violets, and serve immediately.Poires belle helene: is this the most beautiful of pear-based desserts or have you fallen for something less operatic – an upside-down cake, perhaps, or a boozy sorbet?Explore more on these topicsFoodHow to cook the perfect ...FruitDessertAutumn food and drinkChocolateFrench food and drinkrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Buvette, London WC2: ‘It’s actually rather lovely’ – restaurant review | Restaurants | The Guardian
description: This offshoot of a New York favourite isn’t reinventing the wheel, but it does bring a touch of Gallic glam to the neighbourhood
Author: Grace Dent
Headline: This offshoot of a New York favourite isn’t reinventing the wheel, but it does bring a touch of Gallic glam to the neighbourhood
Content: Buvette, London WC2: ‘A version of French dining that won’t scare the horses.’Photograph: Beca B Jones/The GuardianView image in fullscreenBuvette, London WC2: ‘A version of French dining that won’t scare the horses.’Photograph: Beca B Jones/The GuardianGrace Dent on restaurantsRestaurantsReviewBuvette, London WC2: ‘It’s actually rather lovely’ – restaurant reviewThis offshoot of a New York favourite isn’t reinventing the wheel, but it does bring a touch of Gallic glam to the neighbourhoodGrace DentSun 18 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 14.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfaux-French, cult-hit New York brasserie has opened in Neal’s Yard, deep in the hairy armpit of Covent Garden among alleyways where holistic therapy rooms, walk-in back rub spaces,Neal’s Yard Remediesand26 Grains cafeare its immediate neighbours. The windchimes and the whiff of patchouli part the air round these parts, and the footfall is yoga pant-clad and hungry for hummus.Buvette, meanwhile, has brought a touch of Gallic glam to the neighbourhood, and is clearly aimed at theEmily in Parisgeneration with itstotalement françaismenu featuring croque monsieur with roast mushrooms and gruyere,rillettes de saumonor salade niçoise withharicots vertsand amolletegg; there’s also a Macvin champagne and muscadet spritz, pastis on the rocks, warm scones with jam, and almond croissants.This is the London arm ofJody Williams’ West Village gastrothèque, and its menu is a pretty card listing 25 dishes to choose from, none of them above £18. It clearly thinks it’s a hot, fresh, new thing, but I’m not sure it’s anything new at all. We used to call places that looked like thisCafé Rouge: that is, recognisably French, and by that I mean recognisable if you have a working GCSE knowledge of La Rochelle cafe life. It’s that version of French dining that won’t scare the horses, or at least the horses that the French haven’t minced coarsely and served in their own gastroduodenal canals with an exemplary homemademoutarde.View image in fullscreenBuvette’s pommes frites come served in a copper pot.Buvette’s cute red frontage gives way to something heartstoppingly pretty inside: marble-topped tables, bentwood chairs, a zinc bar, good-looking, chipper staff – though, let’s be honest, that latter chipper bit wouldneverhappen in a lunchtime Paris tourist spot. It’s all very charming and ought to be packed, but on this midweek lunchtime there are plenty of seats to spare in this 80-cover space. In fact, almost all of them are empty. This is Buvette’s second attempt at cracking London – the first, in Notting Hill in 2020, came and went within four years.As I peruse the gorgeous little cut-card menu, 12 northern ladies with pull-along suitcases sit down at the next table, read it, confer briefly and leave sharpish.Mais pourquoi, Julie? This is a quickcafé au laitand a freshly squeezed orange juice joint (though they’ve missed a trick not servingOrangina), or a longersaumon grilléwithbetteraves(beetroot salad) on the side and a mousse au chocolat for pudding kind of place. Nobody is being asked to sit a GCSE French oral exam, which is a blessing, because the memory of being dragged into a room in Carlisle in 1991 and being expected to discuss Scottish devolution in French still wakes me at night.View image in fullscreenBuvette’s grilled salmon is ‘crisped correctly and has clearly been cooked as if someone truly cares’.And maybe that’s Buvette’s problem. It’s so coy and cool that it scares away the normals, but it’s not cool enough to ensnare foodies who’d rather be chucking money at Fergus Henderson’s wine bar just across the way; the local yoga brigade, meanwhile, would rather be queuing outside a clandestine juice shack to hand over £28 for juiced turnip and echinacea. Even so, and to make a plaintive case for Buvette, it’s actually rather lovely.We order the croque madame, which is a classic construction: thick, white toasted bread, melted cheese, all draped in thin ham, snowed over with more grated cheese, topped with a vivid egg yolk and garnished with a flourish of tiny, crunchy cornichons. It is a noble and considered attempt. That grilled salmon comes dressed insauce ravigote, a sharp, herby, caper-spiked vinaigrette, and with dressed green beans and apetite salade vertealongside. The skin is crisped correctly and the fish moist, and it’s clearly been cooked as if someone downstairs truly cares. We share a copper pan filled with pommes frites and pick at a meaty, sharply dressedsalade de poulet. As for those betteraves, these chunky, sweet, glossy roast beets with horseradish creme fraiche are the kind of thing you don’t get as a side any more, and you find yourself wondering why not.View image in fullscreen‘Chunky, sweet, glossy’: Buvette’sbetteraves, or beetroot salad with horseradish creme fraiche.Photograph: Beca B Jones/The GuardianTheset lunch menu at £23 is ridiculous value: salmon, green beans and green salad, or burger, fries and salad, or a croque and two salads, all with a coffee to finish. And this in Covent Garden, where you usually have to sell a kidney to afford a crepe. Buvette isn’t reinventing the wheel, but it’s somewhere to pop in for lunch and end up lingering over pots of fresh mint tea and a rather incongruous offering of warm scones with raspberry jam and cream, or almond croissants hot from the oven. Cafe Rouge lasted for years because it wasn’t terribly French, or terribly hot, but it was fantastically useful. Perhaps Buvette needs to reposition itself as a pit stop rather than an Instagram backdrop. Then more people might want to mange tout.Buvette2 Neal’s Yard, London WC2, 020-3540 4989. Open all week, lunch 11.30am-4pm, dinner 4-9pm (10pm Thurs-Sat). From about £40 head à la carte;formuleset lunch (main, two sides and coffee) £23, all plus drinks & serviceExplore more on these topicsRestaurantsGrace Dent on restaurantsFoodFrench food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: More peas, please! 17 delicious ways to devour Britain’s most brilliant vegetable | Vegetables | The Guardian
description: They’re healthy, versatile, sustainable and available. Yet pea consumption in the UK is at a 50-year low. Here are the curries, dips, pasta dishes and even cakes that could turn all that around
Author: Tim Dowling
Headline: They’re healthy, versatile, sustainable and available. Yet pea consumption in the UK is at a 50-year low. Here are the curries, dips, pasta dishes and even cakes that could turn all that around
Content: Food to set your pulse racing … Ravinder Bhogal's pea and mint dip.Photograph: Rita Platts/The GuardianView image in fullscreenFood to set your pulse racing … Ravinder Bhogal's pea and mint dip.Photograph: Rita Platts/The GuardianVegetablesMore peas, please! 17 delicious ways to devour Britain’s most brilliant vegetableThey’re healthy, versatile, sustainable and available. Yet pea consumption in the UK is at a 50-year low. Here are the curries, dips, pasta dishes and even cakes that could turn all that aroundTim DowlingSun 18 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s not good news for the pea farmers: pea consumption in the UK has fallen to a 50-year low. According to data from Defra, the average Britonate just 37g of peas per week in 2025, down from 144g per week in 1975.Though a classic British staple, peas are not for everybody. Apparently only 22% of gen Z associate peas with Britain at all (which is patently ridiculous:90% of the peas we consumein the UK are grown here, while we produce about160,000 tonnes for freezing aloneeach year).But if I’m honest, I ate zero grams of peas last week; ditto the week before. I like peas – or at least I’m rarely offended by them – but as a suppertime option, they seem a little mundane. And while all the pak choi and purple sprouting broccoli in the fridge risks going floppy with age, frozen peas can be postponed indefinitely.It shouldn’t be this way. Peas are healthy, versatile, sustainable and insanely available. If you’re like me, you don’t even need to buy peas to eat them: I’ve always already got some. But if you’re still in need of inspiration, here are 17 delicious ways to help keep the UK pea industry afloat.View image in fullscreenIdeal distillation … Felicity Cloake’s perfect pea soup.Photograph: Felicity CloakePea soup is a good place to start – especially if it’s Felicity Cloake’sperfect pea soup, an ideal distillation of this classic dish. As with all these recipes, frozen peas are called for at this time of year – but, as Cloake says, frozen and fresh are pretty indistinguishable in soup. In one sensefrozen peas are fresherthan fresh peas anyway – chilled within 150 minutes of picking, before they develop any starchiness. If you’re after something a bit fancier, Tori Haschka’spea soup with almond and chorizo crumbsalso contains courgette, broccoli, kale and a diced red apple – all blitzed smooth at the end and accessorised with crumbled chorizo on top.Ravinder Bhogal’s easypea and mint dip– which includes feta and a lightly pickled radish salsa – can be served with bread or crudites or both, and is allegedly even good on toast for breakfast. Simpler still is Jamie Oliver’speas with broad beans, chilli and mint: all the ingredients are in the title, apart from a squeeze of lemon and a dash of olive oil.View image in fullscreenIngredients you may well have to hand … Rachel Roddy's pasta with peas and cream.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The GuardianChorizo and pea risottomakes for a quick yet rather elegant midweek supper. Rukmini Iyer’sgreen pea pulaois another rice dish, topped with a fried egg and spiced with cardamom. Hugh Fearnley-Whittingstall mines a similar vein in a different genre with a dish featuringbaby peas, bacon, garlic and risoni– a rice-shaped pasta more commonly known as orzo (although not in Italy, apparently).Rachel Roddy’speas and pastaoffering uses ingredients you may well have on hand right now: peas, cream, onion, butter, lemon, some kind of hard cheese, a single tablespoon of cream cheese and pasta (macaroni, penne, fusilli or similar). Apotato gnocchi with peasfrom Masha Rener is finished with ricotta salata – salted ricotta. If you haven’t got gnocchi, Rener says linguine can step in as understudy.View image in fullscreenPerfect with bread … Rosie Sykes’s peas and potato pav bhaji.Photograph: Yuki Sugiura/The GuardianMany of us normally serve peas as a side dish with meat – as an afterthought, even – but Yotam Ottolenghi’slamb shoulder chops with marinated feta and peasgives them a strong supporting role. You’ll struggle to secure the pea shoots he suggests at this time of year, but rocket makes a perfectly acceptable substitute. For Nigel Slater’shake with pea salsa, the just-cooked peas are whizzed with coriander, parsley, mint, oil and vinegar.Slater also has a recipe forpea, herb and mozzarella pie, which calls for leeks and courgettes too.Rosie Sykes’spea pav bhajiis a spreadable curry made with potatoes and eaten on bread rolls. Thisspiced green pea coconut curryfrom Maunika Gowardhan is yet another pea and potato pairing – this one using kokum petals, if you can find them, and tamarind paste if you can’t.Should there be any peas left in the bag at the end of the night, here are three slightly weird desserts you can try. In the first, apea sorbetfrom James Knappett, frozen peas are blitzed with sugar syrup, citric acid and salt before returning to the freezer, eventually to be served with sliced strawberries and mint oil.Thispea moussecombines a thin custard with gelatine, white chocolate and frozen petit pois. And odd as it sounds, Kate Hackworthy’svegetarian pea cakeis actually everything you would expect from an ordinary Victoria sponge, plus peas.
